Journalist named successor as Uganda buries world's youngest king

12 September 2026•Update: 12 September 2026
The royal council chief of Uganda's Tooro Kingdom, Omujwera Musuuga Charles Kayondo Kamurasi, announced Saturday that journalist Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma is the next monarch, following the death of his cousin, King Oyo Rukidi IV.
Musuuga, the head of the Babiito royal clan from which the Tooro kings trace their lineage, made the announcement before mourners gathered to pay their final respects to the late king, who died at 34 on Aug. 27 in the US, where he was receiving cancer treatment.
King Oyo was crowned at the age of 3 in 1995 after the death of his father. He earned a Guinness World Record as the world’s youngest reigning monarch. He led his people via regents appointed by the kingdom until he came of age at 18.
He died last month in the United States, where he was receiving treatment for cancer.
“I wish to inform Tooro and Uganda at large that Tooro has a new king. The council of the Babiito sat and elected Edward Rukidi. Whatever we’ve done is in accordance with Ugandan law, and we have put our Tooro culture and norms into consideration, let’s all maintain unity and always remember our culture,” Musuuga remarked.
Mixed reactions were heard from the congregation as Musuuga announced the successor, signaling a bitter royal succession dispute in the Tooro Kingdom.
Earlier, King Oyo’s immediate family, notably his mother, Queen Best Kemigisa, and sister, Princess Ruth Komuntale, publicly rejected the clan council's choice, insisting that King Oyo had left a will dictating that his hitherto unknown son should succeed him to the throne. Clan leaders said that a royal child must be officially introduced to elders in order to be considered for leadership.
Still unmarried at his death, he had no children known to the clan members or the public, plunging the kingdom into a rapid succession crisis.
King Oyo was the 13th monarch of the Tooro Kingdom, which was founded more than 200 years ago and ruled over more than two million people. He was laid to rest at the Karambi Royal Tombs in the western Ugandan city of Fort Portal on Saturday.
Traditional monarchs in Uganda
Uganda is a republic ruled by an elected president, but the country retains several traditional monarchies that still preside over their kingdoms. Their power is largely symbolic, but they wield considerable cultural and social influence. They are legally not allowed to engage in partisan politics and have no political authority.
Oyo Nyimba was arguably one of the most recognizable among them because of his unusual story, taking the throne at the age of 3.
His unusual status as a modern “boy king” led to considerable interest early in his reign, including from world leaders like former Libyan strongman Moammar Gadhafi, who repeatedly visited Tooro and supported Oyo and the queen mother for years before Gadhafi’s death in October 2011.
He spent time in the UK at Winchester University to complete his education. This time away from Uganda prompted a failed challenge to his position in 2015, when his cousin Prince David Kijanangoma declared himself the rightful king of Tooro, accusing Oyo of neglecting the region.

Watch first naval battle in history fought entirely by drones: Ukrainian uncrewed boat spots, fires on, and sinks Russian one in Black Sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
19:04:57 UTC
04:04:57 KST

For the first time, two unmanned boats have fought a battle at sea, and the Ukrainian one sank its Russian rival. The Ukrainian Defense Intelligence has spotted a Russian drone in the Black Sea, and a Sargan-3000 naval drone armed with a remote-controlled machine-gun turret opened fire and destroyed it, the Ukrainian Navy said on Telegram, calling it "the first-ever naval battle between unmanned boats."
Drone-versus-drone combat has moved from the sky to the sea. Ukraine has already rewritten naval warfare with uncrewed boats, sinking warships and pushing much of Russia's Black Sea Fleet back to port without a navy of its own to speak of.
Now it has fought and won the first duel between two robot vessels, a glimpse of automated sea combat. The claim is the Navy's. It released a video of the encounter but did not provide a date, an exact location, or the type of Russian craft, and it has not been independently verified.
A gun turret decides the duel
The Russian vessel was detected by units of the Ukrainian Defense Intelligence, the Navy said, before the Sargan-3000 closed in.
The Ukrainian drone carried an automated 12.7mm Protector remote weapon station, a turret of the same type mounted on some NATO warships, and used it to sink the Russian boat.
The published footage shows the two drones engaging and the Russian craft going under.
The Sargan-3000 reaches far
The Sargan-3000 is a Ukrainian multi-purpose strike drone that passed combat testing in April. It has a combat radius of up to 1,600 kilometers, runs at 40 to 55 knots, and carries up to 450 kilograms of payload, according to Militarnyi.
It is the same class of boat that sank the Russian border patrol ship Izumrud near Novorossiysk in July.
Ukraine keeps rewriting naval war
The battle fits a campaign that has reshaped the Black Sea. Ukrainian sea drones have sunk the corvette Ivanovets (link) and the landing ship Caesar Kunikov (link), in 2025, even shot down a Russian Su-30 fighter jet (link), and in the last ten weeks alone struck 285 vessels of Russia's shadow fleet (link).
Russia is now racing to build its own uncrewed fleet, and satellite imagery suggests it is constructing a dedicated naval-drone port in occupied Crimea, a sign that the sea, like the sky, is filling with machines that fight each other (link).

Right-wing US think tank tracked thousands of Muslim Americans for 2 decades: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
19:04:54 UTC
04:04:54 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
12 September 2026•Update: 12 September 2026
A US right-wing think tank has maintained a database of thousands of Muslim Americans and Muslim organizations for about two decades, according to a report by the HuffPost news site on Friday.
The Middle East Forum (MEF), a controversial organization founded in 1994, compiled more than 4 million data points, including individuals' names, social media accounts and tax information, as well as details on mosques, schools, businesses and other organizations, the report said.
The database also includes people and groups considered allies of the Muslim community.
MEF disclosed the existence of the archive after HuffPost questioned the organization about the database and indicated that it planned to publish a report. The group said it would allow scholars, journalists and other researchers to apply for access to the material.
Gregg Roman, MEF's executive director, said the organization had planned to announce the initiative later this year, but welcomed the earlier disclosure.
MEF says its mission is to defend Western values and highlight what it describes as the dangers of "lawful Islamism." Civil rights organizations, however, accuse the group of contributing to Islamophobia and spreading misinformation about Muslims.
The database consists of information obtained from public records, but its scale has raised concerns among civil rights advocates.
Caleb Kieffer of the Southern Poverty Law Center described the archive as "very concerning," pointing to what he called growing anti-Muslim rhetoric in the US.
Mobashra Tazamal of Georgetown University's Bridge Initiative characterized the database as a potential "target list," warning that such information could be used to monitor or intimidate Muslim individuals and organizations.
The revelations come amid heightened concerns among Muslim Americans over Islamophobia, as well as political tensions surrounding President Donald Trump's policies, the crackdown on pro-Palestinian protesters and rhetoric from some Republican lawmakers.
MEF defended its practices, saying that mapping ideological networks is common among US civil society organizations and arguing that other groups maintain similar databases.

El-Toukhy's drama depicts the life of a young nanny and housekeeper who marries her wealthy and older widower employer, but harbours a shameful secret that threatens to unravel her new life and status in the post-World War II anarchy.
“Woman Unknown,” a drama about Denmark in the aftermath of the Nazi occupation directed by May el-Toukhy, won the prestigious Golden Lion at the 83rd Venice Film Festival on Saturday.
El-Toukhy was the only woman to have solely directed a film in the main competition this year.
Her film centres on a young Marie, played by Mathilde Arcel, whose Best Actress win makes it a rare double victory. Marie is a nanny and housemaid who is about to marry her wealthy employer in the immediate aftermath of the war. But she harbours a secret past intimate relationship with a German soldier that threatens to upend her reputation.
South Korean auteur Lee Chang-dong’s poetic portrait of class and labour, “Possible Love,” won the Silver Lion grand jury prize, the runner-up award. “Possible Love” is Lee’s first film in eight years, following his acclaimed 2018 title “Burning.”
“NAZA,” a harrowing documentary about military strategies employed in the war in Gaza from Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, was awarded a special jury prize.
“It is really, really especially important to us that Israelis watch this film,” Abraham said.
The was added to the main competition late — at the request of the filmmakers — and debuted late in the schedule as well, but its impact was felt: It received a record-breaking standing ovation, lasting some 25 minutes, after its premiere.
Shot on the rooftops of Tel Aviv at night in extreme secrecy over three years, “NAZA” features testimony from 24 Israeli military insiders including intelligence officers and soldiers give who insight into the war in Gaza and what they say is the systemic killing of Palestinian civilians.
The jury gave the Silver Lion for directing to Ilya Krzhanovsky for his film “Dau,” a project about the Soviet physicists who built the atomic bomb that has taken over 20 years to make.
Krzhanovsky, who renounced his Russian citizenship in protest of the war in Ukraine, dedicated the prize to Ukrainians, including his mother who was born there.
The Maggie Gyllenhaal-led jury announced the winners in a ceremony on Saturday night, which included a best actor prize for John Malkovich for his performance in the dark CIA comedy “Wild Horse Nine”.
Malkovich was not in attendance at the ceremony, but he sent a video message, explaining that he is shooting in Montreal.
“I am humbled to be chosen for this award which has been given to so many wonderful actors,” Malkovich said.
Martin McDonagh's Wild Horse Nine was also met with a standing ovation, lasting well past 10 minutes. The dark comedy follows two CIA agents travelling to Easter Island shortly before Chile's 1973 military coup.
The film's stars John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell's performances were among the elements that drew attention at the premiere.
McDonagh has previously premiered two films at the festival, Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri and The Banshees of Inisherin.
He has previously won screenplay prizes for both films, while Colin Farrell received an acting award for the latter.
“Unknown Woman” star Mathilde Arcel was visibly emotional accepting the best actress award, which she said was very heavy and decided to place on the floor while she spoke.
“This is my first lead role in a movie and my first time at a film festival,” she said. “I’m extremely honoured.”
French director Stéphane Brizé’s won the screenplay prize for his corporate drama “A Good Little Soldier.”
Malou Khebizi was given the Marcello Mastroianni award for emerging actor for her role in Cédric Kahn’s “15/18 (A Place to Heal)” which is set in an adolescent psychiatric ward in a public hospital.

Afghan woman deported in first use of US Alien Terrorist Removal Court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
19:02:39 UTC
04:02:39 KST

Afghan woman deported in first use of US Alien Terrorist Removal Court
The Alien Terrorist Removal Court was created in 1996, but had never been used before Nazira Haji Zada’s case.
An Afghan woman accused of supporting the ISIL (ISIS) armed group has been deported from the United States in the first case brought before an obscure and long-dormant court created 30 years ago to remove people classified by the government as “alien terrorists”.
The US Department of Justice (DOJ) announced on Friday that Nazira Haji Zada was deported to Afghanistan after being brought before the Alien Terrorist Removal Court.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3US immigration agents arrested more than 49,500 people in July
- list 2 of 3Cuban and Afghan immigrants deported from US under Trump arrive in Guyana
- list 3 of 3‘Handcuffed and blindfolded’: Is the US targeting Ecuadorian fishermen?
The 47-year-old lawful permanent resident, who had been living in Fort Worth, Texas, was arrested in 2024. US Attorney General Todd Blanche filed the papers for her removal on July 15 this year. She waived her rights to challenge her detention and was subsequently deported to Afghanistan.
The DOJ accused Haji Zada of helping conceal an ISIL-inspired plot for a mass shooting in the US state of Oklahoma on election day in 2024. She was never charged with a crime, but her son, Abdullah Haji Zada, and son-in-law, Nasir Ahmad Tawhedi, pleaded guilty to related charges.
The Alien Terrorist Removal Court was created by Congress in 1996 as part of a broader effort to combat international terrorism. It is a specialised US federal court made up of five judges serving staggered five-year terms. It allows the US government to submit classified information in cases where disclosure could threaten national security, while requiring an unclassified summary that the court determines is sufficient for the accused to prepare a defence. The government must prove with strong evidence that the person is an “alien terrorist”.
The defence said that bringing lawful permanent residents before a court while withholding the evidence against them violated due process and predicted the court would eventually be found unconstitutional.
DOJ officials described the deportation as a national security victory.
“Those who support and condone terrorism should not be living in the United States,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said, adding that the case showed the department would use “every tool at its disposal” to protect the country.
Haji Zada’s attorneys said her decision to consent to removal “should not be seen as an endorsement of this court’s legitimacy.”
“Dragging lawful permanent residents into court but refusing to show them or their attorneys the evidence that will be used against them is a plain violation of due process,” the defence lawyers said in a statement. “We are confident that the Alien Terrorist Removal Court will be struck down as unconstitutional as soon as a judge is asked to address the issue.”
It is unclear whether the DOJ would pursue additional cases through the previously unused court.

The Coalition finds voice in One Nation battle and starts new free speech fight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

analysis
Labor will drag Coalition's free speech fight onto harder ground
The dividing line in Australia's next big fight over the internet is not whether online harm exists, but who gets to define it.
As fresh battle lines were drawn up over Labor's proposed digital duty of care this week, another ongoing war entered a new phase.
The escalating stoush between Andrew Hastie and Pauline Hanson got personal after a One Nation video branded the Liberal frontbencher and former SAS officer a traitor.
Hastie viewed it as a slight on all veterans and challenged the One Nation leader to take responsibility for material her party endorsed and authorised.
Angus Taylor has agreed the video should come down.
But the opposition leader has been eager to stress it was a question of "morality" more than "legality".
That distinction was central to Taylor's reasoning for why he could call for the video to be removed in the same breath as criticising Labor's duty of care proposal as a "blank cheque for political censorship".
Wells takes aim at Taylor
Many inside Labor believe the opposition's outcry is instead driven by a desire to "out One Nation, One Nation" and woo conservative voters.
Communications Minister Anika Wells has been at pains to stress the laws are about shifting more responsibility onto tech companies to anticipate and reduce foreseeable harms created by their services.
The Coalition has agreed children need protection but, scarred by the mis- and disinformation laws killed off last term, are convinced the duty of care will become a "backdoor" to censorship.
Their main concern is the ministerial discretion embedded in the proposed laws to add more categories of harm to the duty of care.
Labor may ultimately have to clarify these powers, but senior figures believe the Coalition would simply find some other reason to remain opposed.
The government was disgusted on Thursday when word got around that Taylor had told his partyroom colleagues to be careful with their criticism lest Wells hold a press conference with parents who blame social media for the deaths of their children.
Wells herself took aim at Taylor later that day, accusing the opposition leader of heckling her in Question Time about "hiding behind grieving parents".
"He's wrong on that, this government proudly stands with grieving parents," she thundered back.
It is unedifying for anyone to diminish the agency of those families in order to score a political point.
Tech companies already choose what we see
These parents who have lost children to suicide after bouts of eating disorders, bullying or other harmful content are clear-eyed about the role tech played in their grief.
The problem is that leaving governments out of decisions about what constitutes harm does not leave an internet where nobody is making choices about what Australians see.
Tech companies already do.
Their algorithms decide which posts and videos are recommended, amplified and repeatedly pushed to millions of people.
This opaque system also chooses what content to deprioritise and largely disappear from view.
Even the Coalition acknowledges that problem, with Shadow Communications Minister Sarah Henderson agreeing algorithms are "driving harm".
The Coalition may want a fight about who decides what Australians are allowed to see, but the average parent is far more concerned with what responsibility a tech company has for the harms its systems actively deliver or amplify.
PM heads to the US
That will be front of mind for Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at the end of this week when he travels to the US where he will tour the Apple headquarters in San Francisco before attending the UN General Assembly in New York.
Albanese's Apple adventure was instigated by chief executive Tim Cook, who invited the prime minister to come and learn about the company's new child safety features "inspired" by Australia.
Apple claims it is making it easier for parents to control what their kids see and do online, including setting screen time allowance and limiting the range of apps they can access.
They're precisely the type of changes Australia had hoped would indirectly flow from the social media age ban.
Piecemeal improvements are no replacement for the effective enforcement of that law, but in the David and Goliath battle of regulator versus big tech the small wins still count for something.
But getting a demonstration of the new folding iPhone is far from the main agenda item on Albanese's US itinerary.
Once at the UN, he will be meeting with a raft of world leaders eager to learn more about Australia's tech regulation efforts.
Albanese understands for things like AI data centres or digital safety laws to succeed, the laws must work beyond borders.
Loading
Coalition and Labor try to fight on different grounds
Back home, the Coalition has at best a few months to secure concessions from Labor and orchestrate a climb down from their current position on duty of care.
After years of consultation, the government is not interested in dragging out the issue and would work with the Greens to pass the laws if necessary.
One Nation will remain opposed on free speech grounds.
Even as critics lined up to condemn the "traitor" video, Hanson continued to bait Hastie with a post on Friday thanking him for drawing attention to her cartoons.
Hastie for his part has not blinked.
With each return serve he appears to have galvanised his fellow Liberals into a rare position of strength against the conservative insurgents. It's almost as if that was his plan all along.
Standing up to One Nation over its treatment of Hastie has allowed Liberals to defend the boundaries of political debate, without retreating from free speech.
The duty of care is harder terrain.
One Liberal MP this week privately complained about Albanese "always" going for the "wedge" on free speech issues.
"They want to trap us," the MP said.
The Coalition has chosen censorship as the ground on which it wants to fight it, but Labor will keep dragging the argument back to children and systemic failures.
Taylor can argue against giving politicians broad discretion to define harm, but outright opposition would mean defending a status quo where all that power remains in the hands of big tech.

‘It’s time to go home’: After 57 years in America, a Holocaust survivor comes home to Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
18:54:10 UTC
03:54:10 KST

Morton Pancer, 86, and his wife, Carole, 82, spent 57 years of marriage building a life together in Maryland. This week, after decades in the United States, they decided it was finally time to move home to Israel.
On August 25, the couple arrived on an El Al flight and officially made aliyah with Nefesh B’Nefesh, moving to Israel to be closer to their family and begin a new chapter of their lives.
One of their daughters, Jessica Gertel, made aliyah with her family in the early 2000s, while another, Shoshana Lerner, made aliyah this year with her family, giving them even more incentive to join them in the Jewish state.
For Morton, a Holocaust survivor born in Poland in 1939, whose immediate family survived the war after fleeing to Siberia, the decision to come to Israel is deeply rooted in Judaism.
“We’re Jewish,” he told The Jerusalem Post. “Aliyah – this is the place for the Jews, our own country that we didn’t have for many centuries. It seems like a good thing to do is to come home.”
The Pancers’ move comes as North American immigration reached record levels in August. The Post reported that more than 1,100 North Americans made aliyah through Nefesh B’Nefesh last month, marking a new monthly record for the organization.
The idea of making aliyah had been on their minds for years. Looking back, Morton wonders why they waited so long.
“I don’t understand why we didn’t come right away,” he said.
Carole said she believes Israel is the natural home of the Jewish people – and that Jews who have the opportunity to come should do so.
“I think every Jew should be here. It’s our own homeland,” she said.
Just one week into their new life, Carole said she already knows they made the right choice.
“We’d like to help Israel and contribute in any way we can to the country,” she said. “I think we made the right decision. I can say that even after a week.”
The move also brings the Pancers closer to most of their family. Eight of their 12 grandchildren and seven of their great-grandchildren already live in Israel, while four grandchildren remain in the United States; Carole believes the other four will eventually join them here in Israel.
A life built in America
Carole grew up in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, in a family with several generations of roots in the United States. Her parents were born in the US, while her grandparents came from Lithuania and Russia in the early 20th century.
After graduating from the Art Institute of Pittsburgh, she moved to Baltimore after being offered a job as a fashion illustrator.
She worked for a department store, drawing clothing that was featured in newspaper advertisements, and later as a freelance artist producing illustrations for ads.
In Baltimore, she met Morton on a blind date arranged by a mutual friend. The two married and spent the next 57 years together in Maryland, including 29 years in Silver Spring.
Now Carole hopes to bring her artistic talents to her new home. “I’m an artist, so I’d like to capture Israel on my canvas,” she said.
Carole enjoys painting portraits and nature. She also wants to attend an ulpan to learn Hebrew, volunteer, spend time with her family, make new friends, and have fun in her new surroundings.
Morton spent most of his professional life working for the US government, including at the IRS. Then spent about 25 years working on financial management systems for various branches of the US armed forces. He retired in 1998.
America became the country where the couple built their life. But Morton said that Israel remained the homeland of the Jewish people.
“It’s the land that we all belong to,” he said.
A Holocaust survivor’s journey
Morton was born in Tomaszów Lubelski, Poland, in 1939, shortly before the outbreak of World War II. He was only seven months old when his family fled the town. His parents and older brother escaped toward the Russian side of Poland, while Morton was initially left with his grandmother.
An uncle eventually reunited the family and helped smuggle the infant through the woods along the German-Soviet border.
Soon afterward, the family was transported to Ukraine and then deep into Siberia, where they remained for about five years.
“The Russians saved us,” Morton said.
During their grueling time in Siberia, his father was sent to a slave-labor camp, while his mother struggled to keep the family alive under terrible conditions. Food was scarce, and Morton remembers that at times only one loaf of bread fed the entire family.
His mother sold items on the black market to obtain food.
“If it weren’t for my mother, we would have never survived,” Morton said. “She was one tough lady.”
The decision to flee Tomaszów Lubelski would ultimately save Morton’s life, he and his family believe.
German forces heavily bombed the town in September 1939. Records indicate its Jewish population numbered more than 5,600 at the beginning of the war. The Nazis later established a ghetto there before deporting the town’s Jews to the Belzec extermination camp, where they were murdered.
Had Morton remained in the town, his family believes he would have been killed either in the bombing or during the subsequent destruction of the Jewish community.
When the war ended, Morton was about six years old. The Russians allowed the family to return to Poland, where they hoped to discover who had survived.
Instead, they encountered devastation and found no survivors.
Morton remembers the journey back on wooden cattle cars. Jewish partisans would greet the trains and tell the Jews they would protect them, but the journey remained dangerous, with attacks against Jews returning to Poland. Amid the fear and uncertainty, he distinctly remembers huddling around a stove inside the cattle car for warmth.
“It took several months to get back to Poland,” he said. “I don’t know how we survived. I was scared.”
After the war, Zionist groups sought to send Morton and his older brother to what was then British-mandated Palestine. However, his mother refused to send the children away on their own.
The family remained in Poland for about a year before moving to Austria and then Germany, where they lived in a displaced persons camp under the care of the US Army.
Eventually, a relative in the United States, Rabbi Moshe Boehm, sponsored the family’s immigration.
In 1951, they boarded the USS Hershey for the journey to America.
For Morton, America represented safety and opportunity.
“Everyone wanted to go to the US,” he recalled. “They claimed the streets were paved out of gold.”
The US ultimately became the country where Morton built his career, and where he and Carole raised their family.
From protecting Germany to protecting Israel
After graduating from high school in Baltimore, Morton joined the US Army at age 18. He was sent to Germany for two years with the 3rd Armored Division’s 15th Infantry Battalion.
The assignment struck him as deeply ironic.
“They sent me to Germany for two years, protecting the Germans against the Russians who saved us,” he said. “If that’s not irony, I don’t know what is.”
Morton said he wasn’t happy about the assignment but had no choice.
Decades later, after building a life in Maryland, Morton and Carole made another journey.
This time, they were not fleeing. They were coming home.
Morton said he had always wanted to live in Israel and had returned over the years to support Sar-El, an organization that enables volunteers to support the IDF. During his visits, he worked on army tanks.
The couple currently lives with one of their daughters in Gush Etzion while they search for a more permanent place to live, potentially in an apartment or an independent-living community.
For Morton, his new life in Israel comes with a sense of responsibility.
He said he has always tried to help Israel from the United States, but now wants to contribute from within the country. “It’s the land that we all belong to,” he said. “We have to make sure it grows and prospers.”
He also believes Jews have a responsibility to ensure that Israel remains strong and secure.
“We’ve gone through a lot,” he said. “The Jewish people, for thousands of years, we didn’t have a country. Now that we have a country, we have to make sure we do the right thing and make sure it’s strong and secure.”
His own history gives that belief a deeply personal meaning.
“What happened in the past should never happen again,” Morton said. “We have to make sure this never happens again – the Holocaust.”
Carole, meanwhile, is looking forward to her new life as an artist, wife, mother, grandmother, and great-grandmother in Israel.
For now, she is taking in the experience of finally being here.
And she has a message for other American Jews who may be considering the same journey.
“Now is the chance to come home to Israel before things get worse,” she said. “Every Jew should be here.”

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Democratic Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez were filmed smiling and laughing during a ceremony marking the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks at Ground Zero on Friday, sparking widespread criticism across the United States.
The two were seen speaking and laughing while the names of victims of the attacks were being read aloud. Images from the live broadcast showed Mamdani and Ocasio-Cortez smiling next to each other, while other moments of the ceremony showed victims’ relatives crying as they read the names of their loved ones from the stage.
Footage from Ground Zero draws political backlash
The Ground Zero ceremony was held this year on the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001, attacks, in which nearly 3,000 people were killed. Families of victims continued the annual tradition of reading the names of those killed, alongside moments of silence commemorating the planes striking the Twin Towers, the Pentagon, and the crash in Pennsylvania.
The criticism came amid a dispute that preceded the ceremony over Mamdani’s participation. Families of September 11 victims launched a petition calling on him not to attend, arguing that his presence was inappropriate due to his positions and political affiliations. CBS New York reported in August on the initiative, and the number of signatories increased significantly in the days leading up to the ceremony.
Mamdani, New York’s first Muslim mayor, rejected the calls and said he would attend the ceremony to honor the victims and rescue personnel. Ahead of the anniversary, he also signed an order designating September 11 as a day of remembrance.
Mamdani’s attendance had already sparked controversy
Shortly before the moment that sparked the backlash, another tense encounter took place at the ceremony: Mamdani shook hands with former New York Mayor Rudy Giuliani, who led the city during the 2001 attacks and had called on Mamdani in recent days not to attend the ceremony. The two exchanged a brief and cold handshake at Ground Zero.
The previous evening, a memorial procession was held in Manhattan that passed through Christian, Jewish, and Muslim houses of worship. According to the report, Mamdani joined only at the final stop, at an Islamic center.
Mamdani has previously sparked controversy over the way he has discussed the aftermath of September 11. During his election campaign, he spoke about a relative who, he said, stopped using the subway after the attacks because she did not feel safe while wearing a hijab.
His critics argued that he shifted the focus of remembrance away from the victims and toward the experiences of Muslims following the attacks. His supporters said he was seeking to highlight the wave of hostility toward Muslims that followed the attacks.

Iraq has closed some border crossings with Iran while investigating drone attacks on Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline that it confirms were launched from its territory.
The Iraqi government temporarily closed three of its crossings into Iran after drone launch sites were discovered in the country, an Iraqi security source told Al Jazeera on Saturday.

Reporting from Baghdad, Al Jazeera’s Jack Hewson listed the closed crossings as: Shalamcheh in Basra province, al-Shib in Maysan province, and Mandali in the province of Diyala. He said that Iraq had primarily ordered the closure of the crossings over fears that the perpetrators of attacks could flee to Iran.
Hewson also said the al-Tayyib border area of the southeastern province of Maysan had been shut after drone launchers were discovered there, and a search operation was under way.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi meanwhile approved a request by Iran to conduct a joint investigation into the discovery of drone launch platforms near the border, according to a statement on Saturday by Sabah al-Numan, spokesman for the commander-in-chief of the Iraqi armed forces.
The statement did not provide further details regarding where the drones were found or how many there were.
However, earlier, the prime minister’s office said the attack was launched from Maysan province, and al-Zaidi dismissed the military commander there.
No group claimed responsibility
The attack on the East-West oil pipeline took place on Thursday, with Saudi Arabia announcing it was temporarily suspending the route as a “precautionary measure” the following day.
On Friday, Riyadh said the drones were launched from Iraq, where Iran commands significant influence, including over armed groups.
No group has claimed responsibility for the attack. The Islamic Resistance in Iraq (IRI), an umbrella group of Iran-backed armed fighters, said in a statement that the attack was “an honour that we do not claim”.
However, Riyadh has previously accused Iran-linked groups in Iraq of targeting its oil infrastructure.
United States President Donald Trump, who is currently in Ireland on an unofficial visit, said Tehran was “probably” behind the attacks on the pipeline. Trump did not provide any evidence to support those allegations.
The temporary suspension of the pipeline is a significant blow to Saudi Arabia. The route was Riyadh’s only major alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, which remains partially closed as the US and Iran wrestle for control of the strategic waterway. Without the pipeline, Riyadh has no feasible way to export its oil on a significant scale until the suspension is lifted or Hormuz is officially reopened.
A further decrease in oil exports from the Gulf could push wholesale prices higher, while potentially increasing Iran’s leverage as the US-Israeli war on the country nears the seven-month mark.
The attacks on the pipeline came amid a lightning offensive by the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen, who have seized the country’s entire Red Sea coastline after defeating the armed forces of the internationally recognised government. Riyadh is the government’s main supporter, and the Houthis have since declared that ships belonging to Saudi Arabia will not be allowed to pass through the Red Sea.

“There is real hunger there”: Oleshky, occupied town in Ukraine’s Kherson Oblast, turned 942 this week. Behind Russian blockade, its people eat roadside grass
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
18:47:15 UTC
03:47:15 KST

In the occupied town of Oleshky in Kherson Oblast, people are foraging for grass and picking through bombed-out basements for anything to eat, Natalia Soboleva, an Odesa volunteer who tracks the town, says, Espreso reports. The city turned 942 years old this week and marked the day, as it has more than two hundred before it, under a Russian blockade that lets no food in and no one out.
The starvation is engineered. Oleshky, on the Russian-held left bank of the Dnipro, was flooded when Russia blew the Kakhovka dam in 2023 and has been sealed off since late 2025, its roads mined and its aid convoys fired on. In July, OSCE monitors confirmed the blockade, describing a place where the living starve and the dead go unburied.
According to Kherson Regional Administration Head Oleksandr Prokudin, in Oleshky, hundreds of people remain, elderly, children, while food deliveries have all but stopped for months, and Russian forces prohibit the evacuation.
Residents forage through the ruins
Soboleva describes a population reduced to scavenging.
"People walk around gathering grass and cooking whatever they can, going through wrecked basements looking for scraps of food. There is hunger there, real hunger," she said.
Hundreds of abandoned animals are starving, too, and the residents who remain share what little they scavenge with them.
Russia shells the aid convoys
The blockade is enforced with fire. Russian forces attack the humanitarian vehicles that try to bring in food and water, Soboleva said.
The last attempt, on 1 September, ended with Russian troops shelling four volunteer cars. The turn for the worse came around January and February, she said, after a food run from Kopani was hit last summer, killing people and halting deliveries for good.
No corridor lets anyone leave
The one thing that could save the town, its officials and volunteers agree, is a guaranteed humanitarian corridor, and Russia will not grant one.
Volunteers, working with Ukraine's human rights ombudsperson, have twice collected lists of residents who want to leave, and the lists were reportedly cleared with the Russian side, but the occupiers still refused to open a route.
"We have not forgotten Oleshky, or the unspeakable pain the city's residents are living through," Prokudin said, adding that Ukraine keeps pressing to get people out.

Ireland will be reunified – Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
18:46:49 UTC
03:46:49 KST

Ireland will be reunified – Trump
The Republic of Ireland and the UK’s Northern Ireland will eventually be reunified, US President Donald Trump has predicted.
The Republic of Ireland gained independence from Britain in 1922, while six northeastern counties remained part of the UK as Northern Ireland.
Speaking to reporters after a meeting with Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin in Dublin on Saturday, Trump said that he would “love to see [Ireland] unified.”
“I think it would be a great feather… in everybody’s cap if that happened. It’s going to happen eventually. Might as well happen now,” the US president added, suggesting that Martin is the “right man… to get it moving.”
While Trump acknowledged that the “UK will have something to say about it, obviously,” he insisted that a reunified Ireland “would be a great thing.”
Trump also said he and the Irish prime minister are “friends” and described relations between Washington and Dublin as being better than ever before.
Speaking at the US ambassador’s residence later in the day, Trump acknowledged that his remarks could prove controversial, conceding that “it’s one of those questions where no matter what you say, there’s no good answer.”
Earlier this year, Trump similarly suggested that there should be a “merger” between the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland, citing what he described as a good rapport between Martin and Deputy First Minister of Northern Ireland Emma Little-Pengelly.
Trump’s predecessors in the White House supported the status quo that was established by the US-brokered 1998 Belfast Agreement, also known as the Good Friday Agreement. The accord largely ended roughly three decades of political violence in Northern Ireland between the Irish Republican Army and several other smaller groups, which sought reunification with Ireland, loyalist groups that wanted the region to remain part of the UK, and British security forces.
The agreement explicitly provides a path to Irish reunification should a majority in Northern Ireland express support for it. This would require the secretary of state for Northern Ireland to call for a referendum on the issue.
In a post on X on Saturday, Gavin Robinson, the leader of the Democratic Unionist Party, decried Trump’s latest remarks.
“President Trump knows better than most that elections matter… Northern Ireland is part of the United Kingdom because that is the settled democratic will of its people,” the politician wrote.
He expressed confidence that Northern Ireland “will continue to choose the UK and the security it offers.”
Speaking during his first visit to Northern Ireland last month, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham likewise stated that a referendum on Irish reunification was “off the table.”

Americans are increasingly sympathetic to Palestinians and critical of President Donald Trump’s handling of key foreign policy issues, according to a recent Quinnipiac University poll released ahead of the US midterm elections.
The poll found that 38% of registered voters said their sympathies lay more with Palestinians, compared with 35% who said they sympathize more with Israelis. Another 27% did not offer an opinion.
The result marks an all-time high for Palestinians and an all-time low for Israelis since Quinnipiac began asking the question in December 2001.
The poll also showed that 48% of voters believed the US is too supportive of Israel, while only 8% said Washington is not supportive enough. Some 34% considered the level of US support for Israel about right.
The findings come as Trump faces broad disapproval over his overall performance. Only 33% of voters approve of his handling of the presidency, compared with 59% who disapprove.
His ratings on foreign policy were similarly weak, with 33% of voters approving and 60% disapproving. On Iran, 29% approved of his handling of the situation, while 65% disapproved.
Voters also expressed caution over the US military presence in Iran. Thirty-nine percent favored keeping US forces there while negotiating a peace deal, while 30% supported withdrawing without a negotiated agreement. Twenty-two percent wanted military operations increased until Iran surrenders or agrees to a deal.
Voters gave Democrats an 11-point advantage over Republicans in the race for control of the House, with 49% favoring Democrats and 38% favoring Republicans.

Theatre audiences still show up. So why do so many shows fail to make money?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Theatre audiences still show up. So why do so many shows fail to make money?
Recent cancellations of major musical theatre productions, including Waitress and Beetlejuice, have raised an obvious question: has Australian theatre become too expensive?
It's tempting to blame the audience. As people contend with higher mortgages, rent and bills, a night at the theatre seems easy to cut. But that doesn't mean everyone has.
The Australian Bureau of Statistics' 2025 General Social Survey found 22.8 per cent of Australians aged 15 and over had attended a theatre performance in the 12 months prior. That's more than 5 million people.
So if people are still going to the theatre, why is it getting harder to make the numbers work?
Growing audiences aren't enough
We reviewed the 2024 and 2025 financial statements of major theatre companies, and found a striking pattern. Even though more money is coming through the door, companies are still struggling to break even.
Queensland Theatre grew its mainstage audience by 5.6 per cent in 2025 and box-office revenue by 42 per cent, compared with 2024 figures — yet recorded a $989,000 deficit in 2025.
Bell Shakespeare increased its income from $10.96 million to $11.47 million over the same period, but expenses rose faster — from $10.99 million to $12.87 million.
Sydney Theatre Company, operating at a much larger scale, generated $28.75 million in revenue from continuing operations in 2025 — but still had an underlying operational deficit of $8.76 million. One-off funding and increased fundraising ultimately helped turn this into a $786,418 comprehensive surplus.
Even if a company can get a considerable amount of people through its doors, this doesn't guarantee it'll turn a profit.
Theatre companies also fund work beyond the stage. Queensland Theatre's Scene Project takes scripts into regional communities for young people to explore acting, directing and storytelling. The project, funded by the Rekindle Foundation, reached almost 4,000 students in 2025.
This demonstrates how grants and philanthropy can also support education and artist development in a way the box office alone cannot.
What a ticket price doesn't tell you
A $100 ticket doesn't buy $100 worth of theatre.
Take a professional company production with 11 actors (a rare luxury for publicly funded theatre companies), four weeks of rehearsals and a four-week season. How much might this cost?
Based on minimum wage conditions laid out in the Media Entertainment & Arts Alliance's (MEAA) Performers' Collective Agreement 2026, paying the performers alone would set the company back at least $154,400. That's before they have paid the director, stage manager, designers, technicians and crew.
Then there are other costs that audiences rarely see. Venue hire, performance rights, insurance, workers' compensation, sets, storage, transport, accommodation and marketing all add to the bill — often before anyone knows whether enough people will buy tickets.
Theatre producer Suzanne Jones said the latest Australian production of The Book of Mormon cost $11.5 million just to reach opening night.
Why don't the numbers add up?
In 1966, economists William Baumol and William Bowen identified a key driver behind theatre's ongoing financial woes.
Over time, most sectors have leveraged manufacturing and technology to raise productivity. Live theatre can't do this.
For instance, automation has dramatically reduced the labour required to manufacture a car, without changing what a car does. Theatre can't replicate this.
A company could, in theory, "increase productivity" by casting six actors instead of eleven, or trimming a two-hour play down to 90 minutes. But that doesn't make the same production more efficient; it makes a different production.
The cost of wages, venues and materials keep rising with the rest of the economy, while the product of theatre stays stubbornly human. This is what Baumol calls the "cost disease". Any gain in efficiency comes at the cost of the thing itself.
Companies can use smaller casts and simpler productions, such as Sydney Theatre Company's recent one-man production of An Iliad. But there is a limit to this. Eventually, cutting costs means losing the very thing we're trying to save.
So who should pay?
Companies can cut costs, but only so far. Ticket prices can be increased, but that eventually turns the cost problem into an audience problem. And public funding alone is unlikely to solve theatre's structural economic issues.
The realistic solution is a combination of all three.
Producers are calling on the Australian government for an equivalent of the United Kingdom's theatre tax-relief scheme. This scheme allows UK theatre companies to claim close to 50 per cent in tax deductions for theatre productions.
That's worth taking seriously, even if a conventional tax deduction does little for companies that are charities or not-for-profits (with little taxable profit).
Another option could be a refundable theatre production incentive. Australia already provides 30–40 per cent offsets for eligible screen production expenditure.
A similar incentive for theatre would allow small and not-for-profit companies to benefit, even when they have little or no tax to pay. An incentive set at 30 per cent of eligible expenditure, for example, could return $30,000 on a $100,000 production. Having a cap in place would ensure it isn't swallowed by the biggest commercial shows.
On the audience side, the MEAA has proposed a government-funded cultural pass for young people, to the value of up to $200, to help boost theatre attendance.
Philanthropy also has a role to play, as Queensland Theatre's Scene Project demonstrates.
None of this removes the need for public funding, and none of it alone solves the problem. But spreading the load is more realistic than expecting theatre companies to simply keep cutting costs. Ultimately, there still needs to be an actor, on a stage, before an audience.
Sixty years since Baumol identified the "cost disease", we still haven't found a more efficient way to produce theatre without turning it into something it's not.
Linda Merewyn Lorenza is a senior lecturer and Robert Vanderburg is a lecturer CQUniversity. This piece first appeared on The Conversation.

====================================================================================================

Nick Rogers's leafy suburb is ground zero in Australia's battle over trees
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Will building more homes to solve the housing crisis cost us our trees?
As we build more homes to tackle the housing crisis some worry trees will become collateral damage. But as our climate changes, isn't now the time we need trees most?
Nick Rogers was working from home when it happened. Outside his window, several hard-hatted men appeared at the base of a robust red flowering gum. "I thought, well, they're just doing the annual trim," says Rogers, a middle-aged architect from Melbourne. "Then they began to chop down the entire tree."
At some point, Rogers, outraged about the destruction of a tree that had watched over his street for decades, stood up from his desk, joined the men wielding chainsaws on the nature strip and tried to act casual. He wanted to know who had sent them. By the time they had downed tools, an activist was born.
The story Rogers tells goes like this: he discovered the local council was suddenly enforcing a policy that he claims no one knew they had — removing established, healthy street trees to ensure roads are free of overhanging branches below 4.5 metres from "curb to curb" rather than just the centre of the road. Now standing in council's way is a plucky group of residents led by Rogers who possesses the ability to build a sassy website and organise. They're demanding consultation and a policy rethink to save what they consider their suburb's greatest asset: its trees.
The community campaign Save Banyule's Trees might seem insignificant. One note in the constant cacophony of tussles between residents and local government playing out across Australia on any given day. But a reckoning over trees is looming. The future of our cities, their liveability, their ability to ameliorate heat, their ability to improve our wellbeing is at stake. And Rogers's leafy Melbourne suburb, Heidelberg, is ground zero.
For the love of trees
When the Melbourne City Council assigned trees email addresses so residents could alert them about maintenance issues, they instead received messages of love and camaraderie addressed to the trees. Thousands of them — so many it made headlines worldwide.
"Dear Rose Gum, Over the past year I have cycled by you each day and want you to know how much joy you give me" and, "You are just outside my work and you make me happy :)" and, "Dear Moreton Bay Fig, You are beautiful. Sometimes I sit or walk under you and feel happier. I love the way the light looks through your leaves" and so on.
Everyone loves trees, I'm told by urban planners, arborists and researchers. Yet they go on to say everyone loves trees until they block a view, break a pipe, upend a foundation or stand in the way of development.
In Victoria, trees are the nucleus of so much neighbourly conflict the state's dispute settlement centre says it receives, on average, around 2,500 enquiries relating to tree disputes per year. The centre tells me the only dispute type more voluminous than trees is fences. The Victorian Law Reform Commission even spent several years inquiring into how neighbourhood tree disputes should be dealt with legally, although its recommendations have never been implemented.
Beyond neighbour disputes, councils have struggled to curb illegal tree removal and vandalism on private and public land. The fight has been heated along Sydney's coveted waterfront, where hundreds of trees from Mosman, to Castle Cove, to Monterey, to Brighton-Le-Sands, to Lane Cove, have been cut or poisoned in the name of a sea view.
Most of these cases go unsolved; perpetrators are hard to identify, yet last month a gardener was fined $187,500 for the illegal removal of nearly 300 trees in a Lane Cove case, which the local council dubbed "the worst act of environmental vandalism" in the area's history.
But a new fault line over trees is emerging. As governments push to densify Australian cities, some worry trees are becoming collateral damage at a time when we need them the most — as our climate changes.
Since the industrial revolution and the slums that followed, trees' significance in cities has been recognised, says Dr Joe Hurley of RMIT's Centre for Urban Research. What emerged as a push for the "garden city" is now being articulated differently, says the professor of sustainability and urban planning.
These days, trees are being labelled infrastructure. "Saying, actually, this is not just a nice to have, it's an infrastructure that's critical in the same way that the wires are that bring us the power, that the pipes are that bring us the water and take away the effluent, that the roads are and the rail are that enables our movement," Hurley says.
Canopy trees are one ingredient in a broader green infrastructure movement, where vegetation is re-introduced to cities via roofs, facades, streets and parks. The greening aims to combat the urban "heat island" effect, improve air quality, support biodiversity, help manage stormwater flow and improve citizens' mental wellbeing.
Governments and planners are increasingly measuring "canopy coverage" — which Hurley defines as "the area of cover that the crowns of trees have in urban landscapes" — to assess tree abundance and guide targets for increasing their numbers. These "urban forest strategies" are being rolled out across the country. But will their targets survive the push to build more houses?
Trees vs houses
One rainy, winter afternoon I meet Rogers near Heidelberg's red brick train station. He points to the hospital across the road and says that, during World War II, train carriages were modified to ferry wounded returning soldiers from the city to the hospital. On such an austere day, it's possible to imagine the ragged, broken men disembarking at what was then the edge of Melbourne. Theirs was the generation that built the postwar suburbs with large backyards, often peppered with trees, that now holds a swathe of the city's tree canopy.
Banyule council, which encompasses the Yarra River's serpentine curves in Melbourne's east, implemented an "urban forest strategy" in 2023. It aims to achieve 30 per cent canopy coverage across its suburbs by 2050, and 45 per cent across footpath and local roads, with no loss in areas that exceed that target. Council estimates have current canopy coverage at 29 per cent, spread unevenly between its wealthier suburbs, sitting at 40 per cent, and its traditionally more working-class areas, sitting at 15 per cent. Council points out more urbanised areas are lagging behind those with "larger residential lots and established vegetation".
As Rogers walks me through hilly streets, lined with gnarly, towering gums, he outlines the dilemma he believes the city is facing: How will the local council wed its commitment to canopy trees with other policies such as road management? And if they can't do that, then how will they deal with the wave of development heading for the suburbs? "There's not a strategic vision in the council of stitching all the competing parts together," Rogers says.
For its part, Banyule Council says its approach to managing street trees "has not changed". It says it must prune trees or, as a last resort, remove them to keep 4.5m of clearance on "any part of the road" (a 2025 council report says "over traffic lanes"). Debating the finer details of road clearance and tree pruning might seem foolish, until the conversation turns to where canopy trees will grow in a more urbanised city.
When a mature street tree is removed, it is replaced with "at least one suitable tree to support council's long-term canopy objectives" a council spokesperson said. Yet canopy trees take decades to reach maturity. The time spent waiting, without trees providing the same benefits, is known as "canopy debt".
"The local council is squeezed from state government just saying 'densify, densify, densify'." Rogers says. "And then the state government's planning department has a very laissez-faire, non-prescriptive way of rolling out densification." The area is one of Melbourne's 60 designated activity centres, and some areas have been rezoned for medium and high-density housing between six and 16 stories.
Banyule council says the "more significant issue for canopy outcomes" is the state's streamlined planning controls for townhouses and mid-rise developments up to six stories. The council says it has also advocated for more lenience when it comes to tree pruning around electrical wires — something the state government has previously rejected.
Rogers pauses beside a temporary chain-link fence. On the other side is a construction site, where a row of black and white townhouses is nearing completion. It has replaced a house on a large block with multiple trees.
"We're going to lose most of our large trees on our blocks that have been zoned for medium density housing, which is going to make our cities a lot worse," he says. "And what comes along with that is there are then applications to take down trees that get in the way of car access onto medium density properties and that's always given priority. We're going to end up with these barren hot suburbs that are going to be unpleasant to live in."
Last year, the Victorian government introduced regulations to enhance protections for the city's canopy coverage. Removing large canopy trees on residential land requires approval and in some instances replacement. Some critics concerned about tree loss say planning provisions don’t include minimum requirements for deep soil and permeable surfaces, which they see as crucial for the health of canopy trees over time.
But exactly how trees thrive is complicated, says Dr Greg Moore, a senior research associate at The University of Melbourne. "Trees are remarkably resilient," the horticulture expert says. "If you don't have deep soil and you don't have the tree roots exploring a much larger volume, then you probably need a permeable paving. If you've got a permeable surface, then you probably don't need to have as deep a root mass. So, I don't think there's a simple answer to this."
Still, he says a fight for space, above and below the ground, is taking place. "You're battling to have sufficient space above ground in many places for the canopy to achieve its full potential, but you're also battling for space below ground, particularly in public spaces such as nature strips that are now being used for all sorts of utility services."
The battle for space
YIMBY Melbourne argues the solution to the battle for space is to plant more street trees. "Building more homes is not without tradeoffs," the advocacy group says on its website, "densification of our city's under-utilised land will require the removal of trees from private backyards in order to build new, denser buildings for people to live in." They're calling for 60 street trees to be planted per 100 new dwellings.
The HIA, Australia's residential building industry peak body, says canopy coverage provisions are "challenging" and "can reduce development efficiency, lower housing yield and, in some cases, make projects unviable to proceed". It's calling for "industry to determine the most appropriate response for each site" and for canopy coverage to be focused on the public realm.
The HIA also raises concerns about the costly maintenance that canopy trees require and questions whether they are needed on residential land. While "tree canopy can help reduce urban heat", they say, are canopy tree requirements on residential lots an "effective way of reducing urban heat"?
So, could we do away with our backyard trees?
"The future of the outdoors is at stake," Hurley says. Creating liveable, resilient cities, he argues, is about getting the right mix of canopy coverage between private and public space. "The most important benefits around urban cooling, biodiversity, mental wellbeing come from an abundant, distributed urban forest."
Both Hurley and Moore argue the public realm alone can't sustain the number of trees cities need. Trees cool not only by shading, but through evapotranspiration, Moore says.
"We don't have enough streets and parks [even] if we fill them all full of trees … to actually provide the green infrastructure that would be part of a really vibrant and healthy city living," Hurley says. The 30 per cent target that many councils have set couldn't be reached by relying solely on public space, he adds. "So, the private realm is very fundamental to canopy cover."
Thirty per cent canopy coverage is considered the bare minimum to substantially lower daytime temperatures. "Studies say we actually need at least 40 per cent canopy cover to substantially lower daytime air temperatures," RMIT urban planning expert Thami Croeser has previously told ABC.
Canopy coverage decreased in Greater Melbourne between 2014 and 2018 by about 0.3 per cent, Hurley's research shows. Elsewhere, a 2022 evaluation of Adelaide's canopy coverage found it decreased by around 10 per cent in a decade. And recent data shows Greater Sydney's canopy coverage increased by 0.2 per cent in a year – at that rate it would take more than 250 years to reach the city's ambitious 40 per cent coverage target.
Melbourne's decrease isn't only caused by development, Hurley says. Changes to backyard use, from adding pools or garages or removing a tree for a view, were a major factor. "Where we see the loss — and the loss in most cases outweighs the gain — is in areas with higher base canopy cover in the private realm."
Doing density better
Hurley argues that we don't have to accept that we must choose trees above housing, or density over trees. "We cannot let ourselves accept that as a binary choice," he says. There is another way: it's about densifying differently, he says — deciding where to densify, and what forms that will take. He questions why we are willing to lose vegetation for developments which give us very little additional housing, such as subdivisions or renovations. Where vegetation is lost, he says, it should be for maximum numbers of houses.
For a long time, urban designer Leanne Hodyl has considered the question: "How do we make really high-density environments more liveable?" She sees floor area ratios (FARs) –a planning rule that limits the shape of a building on a piece of land — as key. Controlling how much floor area a developer can build, but giving them flexibility in how they build it, can allow space on site for permeable surfaces and soil deep enough to grow canopy trees, Hodyl says. To achieve more green space on sites, she argues, we must not be afraid to sometimes build up rather than out.
In other parts of the world, FARs are commonplace, says Hodyl. But in Melbourne we're "still wrestling with whether they're a useful tool or not".
Without such controls, Hodyl warns, density may not be done well. And she recently released a report advocating for them. "There's a misalignment between the drive of state governments across Australia to just deliver more and more and more housing," she says. "I don't feel that there's enough discussion about what type of housing we need and want. It's been fast tracked, accelerated, it hasn't been properly consulted on, and it's missed some huge opportunities to actually do density well."
Yet for every urban planner warning of impending disaster if density is done poorly, there are groups pushing for regulations, such as FARs, to be loosened.
In Banyule, Rogers holds up a photo of the trees that used to stand a few metres from where we're standing beside a row of townhouses under construction. He maintains he's not a NIMBY. He doesn't have a problem with density, he says, rather "with the way we do density". "We will strip mine our cities for amenity and then we'll look back at them in 50 years and go how did that happen?"

They had seized Mocha the day before after heavy fighting.

Nazili said on Friday that government forces had begun shelling areas in Mocha, and called on citizens not to use the Taiz-Mocha and Mocha-Dhubab roads.
The fall of the city to the Houthis on Thursday drove many residents to flee to Aden, where the internationally recognised government is based.
On Friday, Houthi media said two Saudi strikes hit Mocha's airport, while a local official said the city's seaport was hit by six missiles of unknown origin.
News site Axios reported that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman had twice called US President Donald Trump to request American strikes on the Houthis last week.
But on Saturday, Trump told reporters that "the Houthis called us and they don't want to fight with us".
He didn't say if Washington would take action, but added "everything's gonna work out fine and dandy" in the region.
The United States previously conducted a seven-week bombing campaign against the Houthis, starting in March 2025, in response to the group's repeated attacks on international shipping in support of Hamas in the war on Gaza.
That effort ended with a negotiated ceasefire, though the Houthis kept up their missile and drone attacks targeting Israel.
More recently, the group has resumed attacks on ships in the Red Sea after declaring a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis' ground offensive, launched last week, has killed more than 500 people, according to sources on both sides.
It has also displaced about 76,000 people, the UN migration agency said on Saturday, a figure that had quadrupled since last week.
Yemen's civil war began with the group's takeover of the capital Sanaa in 2014, and was paused by a 2022 truce that fell apart in July.

Anthropic CEO urges AI industry to slow down

Berk Kutay Gokmen
12 September 2026•Update: 12 September 2026
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei urged artificial intelligence (AI) companies on Saturday to reduce the speed of AI development as concerns continue to grow about the potential dangers of the technology.
In an essay released Saturday, Amodei expressed concern about whether humans will be able to maintain control over AI models capable of improving themselves. He also pointed to a recent incident involving AI agents that independently carried out cybersecurity attacks as another reason for concern.
“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” Amodei wrote. “Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain.”
“AI brings risks, and because it is such a powerful technology, these risks are serious… They include the risk of losing control of AI systems, misuse of AI for cyberattacks and bioterrorism, and serious economic disruption. A race to the bottom, spurred by commercial incentives, can make these risks more acute,” he added.
Earlier this week, an Anthropic researcher announced that he was leaving the company because of concerns that Anthropic and rival firms were not developing AI systems responsibly.
Jacob Coxon, who had also worked at Anthropic competitor OpenAI, said the companies appeared to be prioritizing competition with one another over ensuring the safety of their AI products.

====================================================================================================

Weightlifting offers large antidepressant effects for young women with anxiety, regardless of intensity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
18:00:52 UTC
03:00:52 KST

A recent study suggests that both standard and low-intensity strength training can help alleviate depressive symptoms in young women who experience high levels of anxiety. The findings provide evidence that weightlifting is a viable option for improving mental health, regardless of how much physical effort is involved. The research was published in Journal of Affective Disorders.
Generalized anxiety disorder involves severe, persistent worry that interferes with daily life. Some people experience symptoms that mimic this condition but fall just short of an official diagnosis, known as subclinical or analogue anxiety. Women are twice as likely as men to experience anxiety and depression, and these conditions often occur together. While medication and talk therapy are standard treatments, they can present barriers like high costs or unwanted side effects.
Lead author Darragh O’Sullivan, an exercise psychology researcher at the University of Limerick, Ireland, explained the focus on this demographic. “We also expanded on our previous research by focusing on anxious young women, as women are [generally] less involved in muscle-strengthening exercise, and therefore may have greater potential for improvement,” O’Sullivan told PsyPost.
“Women are also at higher risk of Generalized Anxiety Disorder, Major Depressive Disorder, their comorbidity, and experience greater disability from their comorbidity, and therefore may benefit from early interventions, such as exercise, to treat mild symptoms,” O’Sullivan added.
As an alternative, physical exercise has emerged as a potential treatment. Strength training, which involves exercising with weights or resistance to build muscle, has shown particular promise. A 2018 meta-analysis indicated that strength training reliably reduces depressive symptoms across various populations. Building on this, a study covered by PsyPost in 2023 found that an eight-week weightlifting program lowered depressive symptoms in young adults when compared to a group placed on a waitlist.
However, comparing a workout program to a waitlist leaves a gap in our understanding. It is difficult to tell if the physical exertion is what helps, or if participants just benefit from getting out of the house, interacting with a coach, and expecting to feel better. To separate the physical benefits from the psychological boost of receiving attention, scientists needed to compare standard strength training against a very low-effort workout.
The current research was designed to test whether the actual intensity of the weightlifting changes how much a person’s mental health improves. “Although our previous trial demonstrated that guidelines-based resistance exercise training can result in large antidepressant effects when compared to a waitlist control, a key limitation of waitlist controls is that they cannot control for important factors like social contact or expectations for improvement,” O’Sullivan noted. “We therefore expanded on that by comparing the same resistance exercise training intervention to a low-intensity sham resistance exercise training attention control.”
The researchers recruited 55 young adult women with an average age of 22. All participants met the criteria for subclinical generalized anxiety disorder and were not currently engaged in regular strength training. After a brief familiarization period, the women were randomly divided into two groups for an eight-week program. Both groups completed twice-weekly, one-on-one supervised sessions consisting of exercises like squats, bench presses, and deadlifts.
The primary difference between the two groups was the amount of weight lifted. One group performed a moderate-to-high intensity routine, lifting loads set at 70 to 80 percent of their maximum capacity. The second group acted as a control condition, performing the exact same exercises but lifting only 20 percent of their maximum capacity. The authors tracked depressive symptoms using a standard 16-item questionnaire at multiple points during the study and one month after the program ended.
The results indicated that both groups experienced massive drops in their depressive symptoms. In the higher-intensity group, symptom scores fell by an average of 54 percent. Meanwhile, the low-intensity group saw their scores drop by 43 percent. The difference in mental health improvement between the two groups was not statistically significant.
This suggests that a low-intensity workout also yields a strong antidepressant effect for this population. As expected, physical strength changes did differ between the groups. The higher-intensity group increased their overall lifting strength by 41 percent, compared to a 21 percent increase in the low-intensity group. For both groups, the psychological benefits were largely maintained a month after the supervised training concluded.
The strong benefit seen in the low-effort group was somewhat unanticipated by the research team. “The magnitude of the antidepressant effect of low-intensity resistance exercise training exceeded our expectations, but is likely reflective of what is still a substantial change in exercise activity, from not engaging in resistance exercise training to completing low-intensity resistance exercise training twice per week for 10 weeks,” O’Sullivan said.
These results stand in slight tension with a 2024 meta-analysis covered by PsyPost. That review found that higher exercise intensity is generally linked to greater reductions in depression, though it focused on clinical major depression rather than subclinical anxiety in young women. On the other hand, the new findings are consistent with research covered by PsyPost in 2026. That earlier study looked at older women and similarly found that weightlifting reduced depressive symptoms regardless of whether the participants lifted heavy or light weights.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The researchers point out that the low-intensity group might have actually received a mild physical training effect, rather than just acting as a psychological control. Because the low-intensity group did gain some physical strength, it is difficult to completely separate the psychological benefits of participating from the physical benefits of the movement itself.
Additionally, the study relied on self-reported questionnaires to track mental health changes. Such surveys can sometimes be influenced by a participant’s expectations or desire to show improvement to their trainers. The sample was also restricted to young adult women with a specific anxiety profile. This means the findings might not naturally extend to men, older adults, or people with a formally diagnosed clinical disorder.
Moving forward, the scientists suggest testing these programs in larger clinical settings. They hope to compare weightlifting directly against standard treatments like talk therapy or medication.
“Both higher- and lower-intensity resistance exercise training can result in large reductions in depressive symptoms in anxious young women,” O’Sullivan concluded. “Young women can benefit from even low-intensity resistance exercise training which requires less physical effort, but we do recommend gradual progression to higher intensity for additional health benefits.”
He added, “For those that are not involved in any resistance exercise, anything is better than nothing, including for mental health.”
The study, “Resistance exercise training compared to a low-intensity sham for depressive symptoms in young women with analogue generalized anxiety disorder: A randomized controlled trial,” was authored by Darragh O’Sullivan, Jennifer M. Rice, Mark Lyons, Brett R. Gordon, and Matthew P. Herring.
