How America misunderstood Iran’s monarchy - and the Pahlavi legacy - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:46:48 UTC
01:46:48 KST

American perceptions of monarchy and kingship differ profoundly from those in the Middle East.
The United States separated itself from the British monarchy with the Declaration of Independence on July 4, 1776, and formally established that separation with the signing of the Treaty of Paris in 1783.
In American political culture, the king is associated with opposition to democracy. Yet this deeply negative perception is fundamentally different from the historical reality of countries such as Iran, as well as from the experience of Europe.
In 1979, virtually the entire American media establishment lined up to praise a dictator like Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini while condemning the West’s friend, America’s loyal ally, and Iran’s late patriotic monarch, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi.
Neither the American media, much of which was influenced by Islamist and Marxist terrorists, nor Washington political figures – many of whom were in contact with Khomeini’s entourage and with terrorist organizations and groups connected to the KGB and the Soviet Union – had any meaningful understanding of Iranian culture or the Iranian tradition of kingship. They did not understand how much legitimacy and value the Pahlavi legacy possessed throughout Iran.
From the day Reza Shah the Great became king in 1905, following the removal of the Qajar dynasty by the Constituent Assembly and the formal establishment of the Pahlavi dynasty, until January 1979 (a period of approximately 53 years) neither the American media nor American political figures made a serious effort to understand the meaning of Iranian kingship, Iran’s ancient culture and civilization, or the monarchy’s cultural relationship with Iranian society.
Iran’s beloved and patriotic king hosted the celebration of the 2,500th anniversary of the founding of the Persian Empire by Cyrus the Great from October 12-16, 1971. From the United States, vice president Spiro Agnew attended the celebrations as the representative of president Richard Nixon, a close friend of the shah. Regrettably, the American media produced almost nothing about this ancient history beyond pointless criticism and the repetition of arguments advanced by Marxist-Leninist leftists, radical Islamists, and Khomeinists.
Nearly half a century later, American media and American political figures, Republican and Democrat alike, still seem unable to explain why, in a stadium filled with 100,000 people, despite decades of regime propaganda against the monarchy and the patriotic Pahlavi kings, the name of Reza Shah still shines and people still chant “Javid Shah” – “Long Live the King.”
The very root and meaning of the word “shah” in Iranian literature is associated with purity, truthfulness, and righteousness. Does anyone have a problem with the endurance of truth and righteousness?
Pahlavi is the most popular figure in Iran
Why doesn’t anyone ask: Although the entire propaganda machinery of the Shi’ite mullah regime, the thugs and hooligans of the Islamic Left (the so-called reformists), and the Marxist Left have been relentlessly anti-Pahlavi and anti-monarchy, Pahlavi nevertheless remains the most popular and credible political figure and political brand in Iran?
The historical reality is that Iranian culture, literature, and history are extraordinarily rich, belonging to one of the world’s oldest civilizations, with a history stretching back thousands of years.
Iranian mothers and grandmothers still tell their children and grandchildren stories of kings and kingdoms. How the king of Iran went to war against the kings of Greece and ancient Rome and defeated them. How Nader Shah the Great marched into India and returned with diamonds and was greater than Napoleon. Or stories of Cyrus, Darius, and countless others.
Iranian literature is interwoven with these stories. Hafez asks: “This land was the city of friends and the soil of the kindhearted. What became of kindness? What became of the kings?” This was among the poetry sung in concerts only a year or two after 1979, when the war with Iraq began.
Its meaning was unmistakable: Iranian culture, Iranian society, and the entire country had lost a pillar, a father, and a guardian, while Iran had descended into the darkness, terror, misery, poverty, and disorder of religious despotism.
The foundation of Iranian monarchy represents the unity of Iran’s ethnic communities, the endurance of law, the guardianship of the country, the protective umbrella over its culture, and the embodiment of Iranian civilization. The shah is the guardian of the law and the coordinator of the country. In Iranian literature, culture, civilization, and history, no one speaks of a supreme leader or a president.
Since 1979, each of those figures has been more corrupt, more notorious, more savage, more deceitful, and more disastrous than the one before him – a catastrophe in the fullest meaning of the word.
The concept of a republic is alien to Iranian culture. And it is shameful that no one seems to have such objections to the world’s most important democratic monarchies, including the United Kingdom, Japan, Sweden, Norway, Denmark, the Netherlands, Belgium, Spain, Luxembourg, Australia, and Canada (the latter two as Commonwealth realms represented domestically by governors-general). Yet some insist on prescribing abstract, imaginary, and philosophical formulas for Iran and Iranians.
Americans have little knowledge, understanding, or comprehension of the history of Iranian kingship. Today, American students are taught in school about the negative aspects of monarchy in US history, and may unconsciously generalize that perception to monarchies everywhere. This creates a one-sided cultural lens that fails to provide a complete picture of the broader historical reality.
Their view has almost always been negative. Yet, ironically, some politicians in the Trump administration have recently begun to recognize and gradually accept that perhaps the best form of government for Iran is a monarchy, comparable in some respects to Saudi Arabia and Dubai, where Mohammed bin Salman and Mohamed bin Zayed govern their countries effectively. There is something in the shifting sands of the Middle East that differs from Western standards, and the existence of a monarch can contribute to a country’s growth, progress, and development.
One can only hope that the White House will gradually recognize this point and historical reality: with the present scale of poverty, shortages, public dissatisfaction, militarization, and the suffocating security atmosphere, Iran is witnessing the beginning of the end of the Shi’ite mullah regime and its Islamic caliphate. Iran’s problems have become so enormous that any one of them could provide the spark.
Soon, protests may erupt across the country against a ruling establishment that occupies, represses, plunders, and destroys Iran. This time, no one may be able to contain the fire of the Iranian nation’s anger and desire for retribution.
Perhaps the only person capable of saving Iran from civil war and a bloodbath is Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi, under whose leadership Iran could witness a bloodless transitional period after the collapse of the regime and before the ballot box.
The evidence suggests that the regime has entered its final months. This savage regime is taking its last breaths and cannot overcome the magnitude of these crises. Iranians are being killed, arrested, executed, dismissed, disillusioned, driven to suicide, and blinded (the list goes on), as they contend with the absence of electricity, water, gas, Internet access, and fuel; soaring prices, poverty, and rage.
These are not merely news headlines. They summarize the daily lives of the Iranian people.
The train of Iranian civilization and history was driven toward the bottom of the abyss of destruction in 1979. Yet there is still a small spark alive. Once again, as Iranian youth declared in January 2026: “This is the final battle, and Pahlavi will return.”
One can only hope that the White House – rather than indulging once again in the temptation of losing another diplomatic gamble with the savage mullahs, and accepting the humiliation and indelible stain that would follow, will stand behind the Iranian people – and, as Israel has done, meet with the true representative of the Iranian nation and the genuine face of the opposition, Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi. By doing so, they may help bring history back to life.

How Iran’s Khomeinist Left reinvented itself as the ‘Reformist’ hard core of power - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:46:31 UTC
01:46:31 KST

The transformation of the Khomeinist Left into “Reformists” was neither an intellectual evolution nor a moral reckoning, nor an attempt to confront or atone for past crimes.
It was a calculated political deception, comparable to a blood-soaked mafia boss who stages his own death, changes his name, reconstructs his face, and returns to the scene, this time dressed as a “savior.”
Post-1979, the Khomeinist Left emerged as a violent, ideologically rigid force blending religious zealotry with leftist ideology. Far from mere participants, they were the direct executors of state repression and the systematic elimination of opponents.
These figures were not peripheral to power; they were its operational core.
State power, security, and censorship
Sadegh Khalkhali became the symbol of revolutionary brutality. As head of the revolutionary courts established after 1979, he oversaw extrajudicial and summary executions of senior Pahlavi officials, including military commanders and political figures.
Mohammad Mousavi Khoeiniha, the godfather of the Khomeinist Left, orchestrated the 1979 takeover of the US Embassy in Tehran and the hostage-taking of its diplomats, locking Iran into permanent confrontation with the international community.
Saeed Hajjarian, later branded the “architect of reform,” was originally a key architect of the Islamic Republic’s security and intelligence apparatus.
Mir-Hossein Mousavi, prime minister throughout the 1980s, governed during a period marked by mass executions and political repression.
Mohammad Khatami, who became the Culture and Islamic Guidance minister in 1982, was responsible for the extensive censorship of literature, art, film, and the press during the 1980s.
Later, as president, Khatami became the international face of “dialogue” and “tolerance,” without ever offering a serious public accounting of his role in enforcing cultural suffocation during that decade.
Regional and global operations: Blood beyond Iran’s borders
The record of the Khomeinist Left was not confined to domestic repression.
Seyyed Ali-Akbar Mohtashamipour represents the ultimate manifestation of this ideology through the regime’s proxy network. For a revolutionary movement, national borders are arbitrary.
This worldview is illustrated by the genesis of Lebanon’s Hezbollah.
In a supreme historical irony, Mohtashamipour, later championed as an Iranian “Reformist,” orchestrated this project as Iran’s ambassador to Syria from 1981 to 1985 (1360-1364), with the explicit directive of planting Khomeinist ideology in Lebanon.
At the time, Amal was the mainstream Lebanese Shia force and showed no desire for Tehran’s ideology. Utilizing limitless IRGC cash and weapons, Mohtashamipour engineered a bloody internal schism within Amal.
Radical factions loyal to Ruhollah Khomeini were armed to eliminate moderate rivals. From the ashes of this engineered civil war, Hezbollah emerged not as an indigenous Lebanese party, but as the IRGC’s first foreign franchise.
The October 1983 suicide bombing of the US Marine barracks in Beirut, which killed 241 Americans, was carried out under his direction.
Mostafa Tajzadeh
Under Khatami’s tenure as minister, Mostafa Tajzadeh served as deputy for International Affairs at the Culture and Islamic Guidance Ministry (1984-1988). He managed cultural relations and Iran’s cultural houses abroad.
The cultural houses were originally established during the Shah’s era to promote Iranian culture and the Persian language.
Under Tajzadeh’s watch, they were transformed into centers for exporting the ideology of the Islamic Revolution, supporting terrorist operations, and promoting Shia sectarianism.
He currently acts as a controlled-opposition figure, pretending to oppose the regime. His reported imprisonment merely makes the performance appear more genuine.
Khomeini’s death and the birth of a political disguise
Following Khomeini’s death in 1989, the Khomeinist Left lost its dominant position within the ruling hierarchy, but was never dismantled. Instead of accountability, it chose reinvention.
No trials.
No confessions.
Not even a single apology to the Iranian people.
By 1997, the same figures behind the 1980s atrocities reclaimed power under a new label: “Reformists.” With softened rhetoric, victimhood, and the systematic erasure of historical memory, they rebranded themselves.
This so-called Reformism was not a rupture with the past, but the same power structure repackaged.
Who is the real ‘hard core of power?’
Perhaps the true “hard core of power” in Iran is not limited to today’s hardliners, but lies even more deeply within yesterday’s Khomeinist Left and today’s Reformists, a political current uniquely skilled at:
• Redefining itself without transforming its essence;
• Changing its language while preserving its power;
• Portraying itself as a victim after decades of executing repression.
• And, when necessary, discarding even the regime’s religious facade to preserve the core of authority.
The distinction between “hardliners” and “reformists” obscures a deeper continuity within the Islamic Republic’s political establishment.
One faction defends revolutionary principles; the other advocates reform. Yet both derive their existence from the same underlying power system.
Changing political language does not constitute a change in political essence.
The Islamic Republic abroad
A significant part of the Islamic Republic’s lobbying network in Western think tanks, universities, and media has been cultivated by figures associated with the so-called Reformists.
Mohammad Javad Zarif played a prominent role in building ties with Western political, academic, and media circles. Westernized and fluent in Western political rhetoric, they promote the regime’s narratives, whitewash its crimes, and sanitize its image.
In effect, there are two Islamic Republics: one inside Iran, and another operating abroad through lobbyists, academics, journalists, and public intellectuals who function as an extension of its propaganda apparatus.
This external network resembles the German American Bund, which served as a vehicle for Nazi propaganda and influence in the United States.
The siloviki analogy
Given the so-called Reformists’ security backgrounds, they can be compared to Russia’s siloviki, political figures with roots in the Soviet security apparatus who helped transform the Soviet Union into the Russian Federation without communism, while preserving much of the underlying power structure.
Many naïve Western observers initially welcomed this transformation, and later Russian President Vladimir Putin, believing a fundamental break with the past had occurred.
The war in Ukraine, an existential war for Europe, should have dispelled that illusion.
The Islamic Republic’s so-called Reformists may be even more dangerous than Russia’s siloviki because their political project is intertwined with religious ideology and a history of Islamist terrorism.
Any expectation of genuine transformation from individuals whose political DNA is rooted in security, violence, and terrorism could therefore be a grave mistake, potentially more dangerous than the miscalculation made with Putin.
Putin is homicidal, but not suicidal. That distinction allows the logic of mutually assured destruction (MAD) to function.
The Islamic Republic, however, is driven by an ideology of religious martyrdom and revolutionary violence. Treating such a system as if it were governed by the same assumptions of rational self-preservation could have catastrophic consequences.
Conclusion
Reformism in Iran was not a genuine project of reform. It was a security-driven survival strategy, a politics of endurance built on collective amnesia, social exhaustion, and the deliberate removal of the bloodshed of the 1980s from public memory.
The faces changed.
The language changed.
The political branding changed.
But the networks, personnel, institutional experience, and their relationship with the Islamic Republic’s power structure remained.
Until this deception is exposed, every new rebranding, whether secular, nationalist, or even “pro-transition,” risks being nothing more than a new name for the same old clique.
The lesson is simple: changing the label, rhetoric, or political faction does not change the regime or its DNA.
The writer is the communications director to Prince Reza Pahlavi and an Iranian journalist who previously served as editor-in-chief of news at Manoto TV, a UK-based Persian-language television network.

EU has never sanctioned Russia’s nuclear sector. Activists say that gap just let Rosatom into German plant, and they’re suing to close It
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:42:18 UTC
01:42:18 KST

A German environmental group is going to court to stop Russia's state nuclear corporation from helping run a nuclear-fuel plant on German soil. BUND Niedersachsen has sued the state of Lower Saxony to overturn a July permit allowing the Lingen plant to produce Russian-designed fuel under a license from Rosatom, arguing that the arrangement gives Moscow access to critical infrastructure in the middle of its war on Ukraine.
The case turns on a gap in Europe's sanctions. Germany approved the deal not because it wanted Rosatom in Lingen, but because the European Union has never sanctioned Russia's civilian nuclear sector, leaving no legal grounds under German nuclear law to refuse, according to the Ministry for the Environment, Energy and Climate Protection of Lower Saxony.
BUND wants a court to override that logic. The July permit allows Advanced Nuclear Fuels, a subsidiary of France's Framatome, to expand the 45-year-old plant to build hexagonal fuel assemblies for Soviet-designed VVER-1000 reactors under a license from TVEL, Rosatom's fuel division, the trade journal Nuclear Engineering International reported.
BUND warns of Russian access
The group frames the deal as a security breach dressed as an energy contract.
Russia is continuing its war of aggression against Ukraine, and dangerous sabotage attempts are increasing in Germany, said Olaf Bandt, head of BUND's national organization.
"The EU is trying to stop the Russian shadow fleet. At the same time, Russia's Rosatom is gaining access to critical infrastructure in Lingen," he added.
Because both production and part of the quality control run on Rosatom-supplied equipment, Bandt argued, the process could be manipulated.
Susanne Gerstner, who leads BUND in Lower Saxony, said Rosatom's role was never fully disclosed in the application and that the operator hid material information from the public.
The permit came with limits
Lower Saxony's Green environment minister, Christian Meyer, has said he personally opposes doing business with Rosatom but that, absent sanctions, he had no legal basis to reject the application, which a federal security assessment had cleared.

Hungary’s new PM pledges to restore adoption rights for same-sex couples
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:41:17 UTC
01:41:17 KST

Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar said Saturday that his government would move to change legislation introduced under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán that effectively barred same-sex couples from adopting children. Until late 2020, same-sex couples in Hungary, a member of the European Union, could adopt if one partner submitted the application as a single person.
Orbán’s government then changed the law so that adoption applications by single people required approval from the minister responsible for family affairs, a requirement that in practice blocked same-sex couples from adopting. “We can say unequivocally that we will change this system,” Magyar said.
Asked about the issue during a briefing with reporters, the prime minister said such decisions should not be left to politicians.
“It should not be a minister, a politician, who makes the decision in cases like these, but professionals who are capable of determining the conditions under which a young child can have a life that allows them to become a happy person in society,” he said.
Magyar defeated Orbán after 16 years in power in a landslide election victory in April. If carried out, the adoption reform would mark a significant step toward reversing restrictions imposed on LGBTQ rights during Orbán’s tenure.
Orbán, who presented himself as a defender of “Christian values” against Western liberalism, oversaw legislation banning legal gender changes on official documents and effectively preventing same-sex couples from adopting children.
His government also prohibited schools from teaching material deemed to “promote homosexuality or gender change.”
It additionally defended a controversial law widely criticized as anti-LGBTQ that allows citizens to anonymously report people accused of “questioning the role of the family and the institution of marriage.”
The erosion of LGBTQ rights during Orbán’s 16 years in power had a profound impact on Hungary’s LGBTQ community.
Shortly before the April election, the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled that Orbán’s government had seriously violated EU law through rules banning or restricting access to LGBTQ-related content, measures the court said marginalized gay and transgender people.

The 80-year-old oligarch has brazenly promoted his family’s golf business since returning to the White House for his second stint as president in January last year.
Last summer, he welcomed then-UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer and EU chief Ursula von der Leyen to his plush resort at Turnberry on the west coast of Scotland.
Trump then inaugurated another golf course bearing his name in the town of Balmedie, near Aberdeen on the northeast Scottish coast.

Security arrangements for the visit are reportedly costing Ireland 20 million euros (US$23.2 million) and comes as the country grapples with a massive policing operation for its six-month presidency of the EU.
Trump’s trip to Doonbeg — a remote, coastal site in County Clare that the Trump Organization purchased in 2014 — adds an extra layer of complexity to the security effort.

Photo: CNA
This is the first time the festival, on its fourth edition, would feature a theme country and hold a month-long “artist in residence” program.

Coming from Kaohsiung, Croter’s illustration style is realistic and rich in detail.
Yang, who studied in Brussels, is experienced in using vivid blocks of color to simplify lines and compositions.
Chang said she chose not to bring the materials she is accustomed to, as she looks forward to improvising during the program.
Having visited art organizations across Taiwan, Tourette said new encounters and exchanges are the best part of the program.
The festival featured collaborations with six Taiwanese artists in 2024 and last year, Tourette said.
The collaborations with Taiwan were “beautiful coincidences” that led to this year’s Illustration Festival, Tourette said.
The festival was first held in 2023, with each edition inviting about 30 international artists to participate.

“We hope that through the art festival and such a brilliant, international collaboration with Taiwan, we can shed light on the value of artists,” he added.

China has warned that it could cancel a planned US-China leaders’ summit if Washington approves new arms sales to Taiwan, a Japanese media outlet quoted sources as saying yesterday.

Photo: AFP

In December last year, the Trump administration announced an arms sales package to Taiwan worth about US$11 billion, setting a new record for the value of a US arms sale to Taiwan, it said.

China is yet to officially announce plans for Xi’s visit to the US.

Russian drive on Donetsk region tests Kyiv’s new commanders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:36:43 UTC
01:36:43 KST

Ukraine is bracing for months of fierce fighting over key strongholds in the eastern Donetsk region that are at the heart of Russia’s war aims, in the first major test for Kyiv’s incoming top general Mykhailo Drapatyi and his new commanders.
Moscow’s larger forces have been inching toward the so-called “fortress belt” cities of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, the capture of which would bring Russia closer to its goal of seizing the entire industrialized Donetsk region.
The human toll has already been high, and, despite renewed diplomatic contacts, military analysts expect Russia to intensify its offensive as winter approaches.
A visit to Kyiv last week by US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner revived dormant peace talks, but there has been no sign of a breakthrough.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said he expected the war to continue through the winter.
The looming battle for Donetsk is shaping up to be one of the most consequential phases of the war this year. For Russian President Vladimir Putin, capturing the remainder of the region would mark a major political and military victory.
For Ukraine, holding it is critical to protecting the backbone of its eastern defenses and validating a command shake-up aimed largely at halting Russia’s slow but persistent advance.
Recent appointments under the reform-minded Drapatyi, 43, who replaced Oleksandr Syrskyi in July, have put respected and proven commanders in charge of defending the region.
The new command inherits a relatively stable frontline as the pace of Russian gains remains slow, military analyst Emil Kastehelmi said. However, he warned that the outcome on the battlefield was unpredictable.
“It’s a situation which can still go many ways, and many scenarios are still on the table,” said Kastehelmi, cofounder of the Finland-based Black Bird conflict analysis group.
Ukraine has routinely dismissed Putin’s demands that it surrender the 15 percent to 20 percent of the Donetsk region that Russia has been unable to take by force.
Zelenskiy described its fate as “the question of this war.”
CREEPING CLOSER
Russian forces are less than 15km from Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, the belt’s two main cities.
Both are under worsening strikes by killer drones and guided bombs, regional officials have said.
“In just ... months, they have gradually gone from thriving cities to places where it’s frightening just to walk down the street,” said Andriy Derun, a military manager at leading Ukrainian charity Come Back Alive, which supports the armed forces.
This month and the next could see the year’s most intense fighting, with Russia potentially trying to stage new mechanized assaults, Carnegie Endowment for International Peace senior fellow Michael Kofman said.
“As the weather conditions deteriorate, drones become less effective,” Kofman said. “And that’s usually where Russians try to return mobility to the battlefield.”
Ukraine had developed a solid defense against such attacks, he said, pointing to a failed Russian assault in July near the besieged city of Dobropillia.
NEW COMMANDERS
Overseeing the defense of Donetsk would be two of Ukraine’s best-known commanders: Andrii Biletskyi of the Third Army Corps and Denys Prokopenko of the National Guard’s First Corps Azov.
The two commanders have been credited with building disciplined and technologically advanced forces numbering in the tens of thousands.
Earlier this year, Biletskyi’s corps stabilized part of the front near Sloviansk, the northern anchor of the fortress belt. Prokopenko’s Azov thwarted a major Russian assault last year near Dobropillia that had threatened to break Ukrainian lines.
Pavlo Palisa, Zelenskiy’s military adviser, said promoting the commanders was “entirely logical,” because they were proven leaders who “enjoy respect and authority.”
Derun said they would be supported by air assault colonel Emil Ishkulov, another new-generation commander who is popular among troops for prioritizing soldiers’ lives. His 11th Army Corps covers Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.
Drapatyi’s predecessor Syrskyi had been criticized for what some observers said was a Soviet-style tolerance for heavy losses and micromanaging even small sections of the front.
Kofman said Drapatyi appeared to be delegating more authority to the operational-level commanders — a shift he said was aimed at making eastern defenses “a lot more cohesive.”
BUILDING ON MINOR GAINS
Ukraine enters the autumn campaign aiming to build on modest gains this year.
Kyiv said it clawed back more than 700km2 of territory in the southeast during a months-long “precision” counterattack.
Kastehelmi pointed to what he said were signs of a successful operation by Biletskyi’s Third Army Corps near the strategic town of Lyman to cut a Russian salient.
The extent remained unclear, he added.
In a video posted on Monday, Biletskyi — standing in the picturesque monastery town of Sviatohirsk, west of the salient — taunted Putin over his recent claim that Russian forces had captured it.
“This is a rear area for our corps,” he said.
Yet Ukraine’s army still lacks the manpower to stage large-scale offensive operations. Drapatyi and new Ukrainian Minister of Defence Yevhenii Khmara have yet to fix a draft system hobbled by corruption and mismanagement.
Putin said earlier this month that Russia was winning the war and that he had no doubt the Ukrainians would “crumble.”
Yet analysts said Russia has not found an effective solution to Kyiv’s drone-based defenses.
“Generally it’s difficult to see how the Russians would be able to achieve success beyond the tactical level,” Kastehelmi said.

Rugby continues to seek its US beachhead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:36:43 UTC
01:36:43 KST

Rugby players might be muscular, broad-shouldered athletes built to be seen, but some of the sport’s biggest stars barely turned any heads as they walked around Baltimore, Maryland, this week.
“We had a few people recognize us, not me necessarily but the guys I walk with,” South Africa number eight Jasper Wiese said before yesterday’s Test against New Zealand.
That anonymity captures the challenge, and the opportunity, facing rugby as it looks to capture a slice of the lucrative and crowded US sports market where the NFL, with its massive TV ratings and giant business deals, commands unmatched attention.
Photo: AP
Many of rugby’s decisionmakers are undaunted and hoping to harness what could be a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to grow the game and its fanbase in the US given the showcase events happening on American soil within the next decade.
Rugby sevens are part of the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, and the US is hosting the men’s Rugby World Cup in 2031 for the first time before hosting the women’s tournament two years later.
USA Rugby has more than 100,000 members across youth, high school, college and senior club levels, a number the organization would like to see reach 500,000 by the time the World Cups are held in the US.
“Where it needs to go, we’ve got a long ways and a lot of work to do,” USA Rugby CEO Bill Goren said.
LEARNING CURVE
Yesterday’s match, at the 71,000-seat home of the Baltimore Ravens, saw the All Blacks and Springboks continue a century-old rivalry as part of the sport’s plan to better position itself for a breakthrough in the US.
Rugby is hoping to capture fans in a landscape where the “Big Four” North American professional sports leagues, the NFL, MLB, NBA and NHL, dominate revenues, media rights and cultural impact. Soccer has gained popularity in the US, which co-hosted this year’s World Cup.
Bob Dorfman, a sports marketing analyst, said rugby’s growth in the US hinges on a reliable sponsorship pipeline and securing regular TV exposure, while persuading millions of sports fans to learn and make room for another game.
“It’s not an easy sport to learn, a lot of complicated rules,” Dorfman said. “It’s so close to American football that I think American football fans who might be the most likely to get into rugby are so wrapped up in the NFL that who has time to really follow another sport?”
ALL LEVELS
Goren, who ran Major League Rugby’s marketing and business operations as deputy commissioner of the North American league before moving to USA Rugby, has a blueprint.
Part of the plan is to ensure all levels of rugby in the US promote the game in the same direction, building opportunities and clear pathways that make it easier for a curious person to find a place to play.
“What it’s going to take is a number of people coming together, alignment throughout our community ... aligning to promote, drive the game, build the opportunity for people to enjoy the game,” Goren said. “Today, it’s a challenge.”
Success on the field of play and household names can go a long way, he added.
Ilona Maher did her part at the 2024 Paris Olympics when she exploded in popularity on social media while helping the US to bronze in rugby sevens. Maher understood the need for rugby to connect with a younger audience and gained fans through her posts about body positivity and femininity in the athletic form, plus her cheeky Olympic village flirting.
PLENTY OF WORK
Major League Rugby co-president Alexander Magleby is hoping Saturday’s game gives Americans a chance to fall in love with rugby fans, similar to how they did with soccer supporters during the World Cup, when Scotland and Norway fans created some of the tournament’s more memorable moments.
“If people love soccer fans, they’re absolutely going to love rugby fans,” Magleby said. “And so this is an opportunity to take over another city in that regard, which is super cool.”
There is plenty of work to be done to get rugby firmly on the map. As South Africa and New Zealand players prepared for their sold-out match, it was clear that rugby has work to do in a crowded US sports marketplace.
“I think it’s a bit hard to sell it to America as a sport because they don’t know rugby like we do, and maybe they don’t appreciate [the game] as much as we do,” South Africa’s inside center Damian de Allende said. “But the best way to sell it is to have them come to the stadium and enjoy the experience, and see us play as the two best teams in the world. That’s the best rugby product they can experience right now in America, so to have the Springboks play New Zealand is the best way to sell the sport.”

Now a teenager, she headlines China’s bid for Asian Games domination and has Olympic glory in her sights. The 13-year-old school girl with a pixie hair cut stunned the sporting world last year with a series of eye-popping times. Taiwan’s existence and culture are painful for China, Minister of Culture Li Yuan (李遠) said in a radio interview in France, describing Taiwan as “a mirror that reveals the true nature of things.”
Speaking to Radio France Internationale (RFI) on Friday, Li said China has been unable to achieve what Taiwan has demonstrated and therefore strongly wished Taiwan did not exist.
Responding to China’s frequent emphasis on the grandeur and long history of Chinese culture, Li said he found such rhetoric difficult to understand, as genuine culture is reflected in people’s everyday lives and does not need to be deliberately defined or promoted.
Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Culture via CNA
“A truly strong culture does not need to boast about itself, nor does it need to fear how others perceive or treat it,” Li said in Chinese.
Li began a European tour on Sunday last week, with the first stop in Britain, where he visited cultural institutions and witnessed the forging of a partnership between the National Museum of Taiwan Literature and the UK’s National Centre for Writing.
He left Britain on Thursday for France, where he attended events related to the Taiwan-France Cultural Award, including the judging of the award and the presentation ceremony.
He is scheduled to return to Taiwan on Wednesday.
During the European visit, Li also met with cultural and literary figures and discussed further cooperation in areas including literature, comics and digital arts.
In France, he visited a planned cultural facility in Saint-Denis and discussed potential cooperation with Taiwan in digital art, including joint exhibitions, co-productions and artist development.

Taiwan naturalizes 400 foreign professionals amid talent drive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:36:39 UTC
01:36:39 KST

A total of 400 foreign “high- level” professionals have been naturalized as Republic of China (Taiwan) citizens over the past decade as the government has eased nationality rules to attract talent from a wider range of fields, the Ministry of the Interior said yesterday.
The 400th high-level professional, who works in the electronics industry, was approved for ROC citizenship on Aug. 26, the MOI said.
The MOI quoted the newly naturalized citizen as saying that Taiwan is a leader in fields such as semiconductors, electronics manufacturing, artificial intelligence development and energy technology.
Photo: Huang Hsin-po, Taipei Times
He also said Taiwan has built a comprehensive high-tech ecosystem that allows top professionals like him to develop their careers, while the country’s high quality of life also attracted him to become a member of Taiwanese society.
The MOI did not disclose the new ROC citizen’s original nationality.
According to the MOI, high-level professionals are experts in various fields, including technology, economics, education and academic research, culture and the arts, and sports, whose naturalization is expected to “serve the interests of the ROC.”
Over the past 10 years, 170 of the high-level professionals naturalized as ROC citizens were from other Asian countries, 128 from the Americas, 76 from Europe, 13 from Oceania and 13 from Africa, the MOI said.
Among the 400 high-level professionals, 149 came from the fields of education and academic research, making it the largest group, followed by 85 in economics, 61 in technology, and 50 in culture and the arts, the MOI said.
The data showed that the naturalized professionals came from a wide range of backgrounds and areas of expertise, the ministry said.
The latest high-level professional to become an ROC citizen is the 400th to benefit from Taiwan’s efforts to ease restrictions under the Nationality Act.
In December 2016, the act was amended to allow high- level foreign professionals to retain their original nationalities after obtaining ROC citizenship.
In May 2024, the act was again amended to reduce the residency requirement for high-level professionals applying for naturalization from five years to two.
The MOI said Taiwan has various channels through which foreign talent can apply for naturalization. High-level professionals who already hold a Plum Blossom Card, for example, can apply for ROC citizenship after a review and do not need to renounce their original citizenship after naturalization.
As many countries compete for talent, Taiwan is determined to create a friendly legal and living environment to attract more outstanding foreign professionals to develop their careers and settle in the country, the MOI said.

====================================================================================================

Status is not a tool for intimidation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:36:38 UTC
01:36:38 KST

A recent incident in which a public representative took their young daughter to an emergency room and loudly berated medical staff has sparked outrage in the medical community. Behind the confrontation lies a longstanding workplace dilemma in the medical field — the unrealistic expectation that healthcare workers should exhibit unlimited tolerance and understanding.
During peak election season or periods of overcrowding in emergency departments, politicians always pay lip service to the vital importance and hardworking nature of healthcare workers. Yet whether someone truly respects the medical profession is often clearest when they or a family member falls ill. While it is entirely understandable for parents to feel extremely anxious when their children are sick, everyone in an emergency department is grappling with their own anxieties and fears. A largely empty emergency room waiting area does not mean that medical staff are not tending to critically ill patients. A doctor’s repeated verification of medications, dosages and administration methods is an essential part of ensuring patient safety.
New regulations on workplace misconduct that took effect in July explicitly require employers to establish mechanisms for filing complaints, conducting investigations and protecting employees. The Medical Care Act (醫療法) has also long prohibited the obstruction of medical services through violence, coercion, public insult or other unlawful means. For years, healthcare settings have placed excessive emphasis on asking frontline workers to “understand the emotions of patients’ families,” but, this “understanding” has devolved into a justification for demanding that healthcare staff unconditionally endure verbal abuse and even humiliation.
Elected representatives wield considerable social resources, powerful public voices and political influence. Even without explicitly invoking their titles, the psychological pressure they exert when they raise their voices at frontline medical workers is far greater than that imposed by ordinary members of the public.
Respect for medical professionals should not merely be a campaign slogan for politicians. Before demanding that the government improve the medical workplace environment or calling on society to treat healthcare workers better, politicians should bear in mind that, upon entering a hospital, they are simply another participant in the medical system. Neither power nor status should be used as a tool to intimidate or oppress frontline healthcare workers.
Lu Chun-wei is a dermatologist and assistant professor at Chang Gung Memorial Hospital.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher

16:36:37 UTC
01:36:37 KST

The bodies of passengers killed in a ferry fire off the Philippines arrived at a port near the resort town of Coron yesterday morning, as the country’s coast guard said the death toll of 35 would grow.
Tents were set up to accept 30 bodies brought from the M/V June Aster, which ran aground near the tourist hotspot after a fire erupted on Wednesday evening and tore through the vessel “in seconds.”
Philippine Coast Guard spokeswoman Commodore Noemie Cayabyab yesterday told news conference the remains would be turned over to police forensic investigators for “proper disposition and identification” before allowing local authorities to inform family members.
Photo: AP
“Currently, we are focused on the retrieval, and after that, we will proceed with the investigation,” she said, confirming that the bodies had been found in the ship’s economy accommodation area.
Police investigators were seen arriving at the port shortly after the news conference ended.
Asked how many bodies remained aboard the ship, she said authorities would provide an update later in the day.
Cayabyab on Friday evening said that the first transfer had been capped at 30 bodies due to the capacity of the patrol vessel transporting them and that additional cadavers remained on the ferry.
Five others had been confirmed dead in the immediate wake of the fire.
Photos released by the Philippine Coast Guard showed rows of body bags being placed into a small ship alongside men in hazmat suits.
Thirty passengers and 13 crew have so far been rescued, while 54 people remain unaccounted for.
On Friday, Cayabyab had told a radio station the fire had begun in the cargo hold, then tore through the ship within seconds.
“From the time that they heard the loud explosion, the appearance of smoke, and then fire. It spread very quickly,” she said of survivors’ accounts.
“Everything happened in seconds,” she said, adding that those who made it off the ship had not even had time to put on life jackets.
Myra Cabilan said she had flown to Coron to find her missing brother, 40-year-old Rammel Gonzaga, who had taken the ferry from Manila on a business trip with his brother-in-law.
“His wife had just given birth a month ago. He was so happy he was given a daughter,” Cabilan said. “At dawn, I still believed he survived, but he’s still missing. I have lost hope.”
Hundreds of people desperate for news about the incident left comments on the Facebook page of a local mayor, searching for relatives, friends and even a dog.
The ferry’s manifest listed 134 crew and passengers, but two had not boarded, the coast guard said.
The ferry was also carrying goods, an electric vehicle, a pickup truck and motorcycles.
The archipelago nation of 116 million has a long history of disasters involving the inter-island ferries that ply its seas.
Many rely on cheap and poorly regulated boats and ships for transport between the country’s more than 7,000 islands, despite regular accidents.
In January, a triple-decker ferry carrying more than 340 people sank off the southern Philippines, killing at least 52 people.
The M/V Trisha Kerstin 3 sank along nearly the same route where 31 people died in 2023 after a fire broke out aboard the Lady Mary Joy 3 ferry.
On Thursday, the company that owns the M/V June Aster, Atienza Interisland Ferries Inc, said it was fully cooperating with the investigation.

MOA to relax seed, seedling sale rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:36:36 UTC
01:36:36 KST

Seed and seedling business operators without a fixed place of business could apply for a plant seed enterprise registration certificate at the end of this month at the earliest, the Ministry of Agriculture (MOA) said.
The Plant Variety and Plant Seed Act (植物品種及種苗法) stipulates that seed and seedling businesses cannot operate without such a certificate, and those who want to apply for the certificate need to own a fixed place of business.
Those who sell seeds or seedlings without a certificate could be fined by local authorities, the act states.
Photo: Taipei Times
The ministry said it has asked local governments to allow businesses without the certificate to sell seeds or seedlings as long as the products are edible, or for ornamental or educational purposes.
Given the booming online demand for seeds and seedlings, requirements for the certificate would be relaxed, it said.
The act has long been criticized for its vague wording. The situation continued until a horticultural operator allegedly filed multiple reports to several local governments regarding online seed and seedling sellers that were operating without a certificate.
Such reports caused concern among the tens of thousands of plant sellers in Taiwan, the ministry said.
In June, it issued an administrative interpretation to local governments, saying that registration certificates are not required for the sale of seeds or seedlings that are edible, or for ornamental or educational purposes.
To ensure sellers’ rights, the ministry’s Agriculture and Food Agency announced it would revise the Requirements and Facility Standards for the Qualification of Plant Seed Enterprises (種苗業者應具備條件及設備標準) to align with the trend of e-commerce, allowing seed and seedling sellers without a fixed place of business to apply for the certificate.
Regulations on applicants’ plant nursery area would also be changed: from a required 1,000m2 or more to allowing local governments to decide on the size, according to the plant’s species or seedling’s characteristics.
Vegetable and Seedling Industry Division section chief Fu Li-chung (傅立忠) said the regulatory change aims to make local administrative work more flexible.
It would allow local governments to grant certificates to online sellers that do not have a physical place of business, or those who propagate seeds or seedlings at small scales, he said.
The agency said it would consult experts and academics about formulating more specific regulations on business types and crop items.
Such regulations would be aimed at critical cash crops, the quality of which must be strictly maintained to ensure farmers’ revenue, it said.
Draft revisions regarding the relaxation of restrictions for the certificate application have a 14-day notice period, the ministry said.
If no disagreement is put forward during the period, the revised act and requirements would be implemented by the end of this month at the earliest, it added.

Philippine’s Teodoro reads letter from Beijing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:36:36 UTC
01:36:36 KST

At a security conference in Seoul this week, Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr was handed a note, apparently from a Chinese military attache, restating Beijing’s position on the 2016 South China Sea arbitration. Teodoro did not pocket it. He read it aloud to the room, commenting on it line by line, then thanked the sender for the gift and added, in Tagalog, that China should show some shame and decency. The audience applauded.
The note itself is worth more scrutiny than the theatrics it produced.
“China’s position on the South China Sea arbitration is clear, consistent and firm,” it declared, four words asserting nothing, followed by a claim that the 2016 tribunal ruling was “illegal, null and void.” This is the same tribunal established under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), a convention China ratified in 1996 and then simply refused to accept the results of once it lost. The ruling found the “nine-dash line” has no basis in international law, and that Beijing’s claims to historic rights inside it were extinguished once UNCLOS took force. The note did not contest this, because no counterargument exists in the convention. Instead it called the ruling a violation of “fundamental principles of international law,” a phrase doing the work a citation would do. It named no principle, cited no article and engaged no part of the tribunal’s text, because the verdict was “illegitimate.”
Within a day, Guancha, a nationalist outlet fluent in saying what the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs cannot say on the record, accused Teodoro of “putting on a show.” Prominent nationalist commentator Hu Xijin (胡錫進), a former editor at the state-backed Global Times newspaper, who has built a second career performing outrage on cue, decided the Philippines had “become so arrogant” because China had “treated the Philippines as an equal.” That is, a former state propagandist argued that Manila’s offense was insufficient gratitude for being treated as a sovereign country.
This is the standard playbook, and it barely varies by target: Whoever objects to Beijing’s territorial claims is reframed as rude, insolent or ungrateful, so the actual dispute, a binding ruling China has ignored for a decade, never has to be argued on its merits. Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokeswoman Mao Ning (毛寧) supplied the closing note, telling reporters she was “not sure what exactly happened,” before pivoting to the approved line that the Philippines had “unilaterally initiated” and “abused” the arbitration process. A ministry precise enough to sanction Teodoro by name in June, as it did, does not lose track of its own attache’s paperwork by accident.
The pattern extends well beyond one shoal. Lithuania opened a trade office bearing Taiwan’s name and had its exports to China cut off entirely. Taiwan is told its elected government’s claim to sovereignty is itself the provocation. Japan and Australia get the same treatment whenever they decline to defer. In each case Beijing behaves as though it alone gets to certify which entities qualify as states, where their borders run, and how much sovereignty they may exercise before that exercise becomes an insult.
Teodoro’s contribution was not defiance so much as refusal to perform the usual diplomatic evasions. He read the note exactly as written and let it indict itself. Unaccustomed to having its talking points repeated back to it in front of an audience that could see through them, Beijing did what it always does: called the honesty a performance, and hoped nobody asked what was actually being performed.
Clive Hazell is a Kaohsiung-based writer and educator. A 30-year-resident of Taiwan and Japan, he writes on geopolitics, culture and East Asia.

EDITORIAL: Alliances, security, cooperation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:36:34 UTC
01:36:34 KST

On Tuesday, two delegations of Japanese lawmakers came to Taiwan to meet President William Lai (賴清德) at the Presidential Office. The first, led by Haruo Kitamura of the Conservative Party of Japan, represented the Diet Members’ Association for Peace and Stability in the Taiwan Strait cross-party parliamentary group; the second was led by former Japan Innovation Party (JIP) leader Nobuyuki Baba, head of the JIP’s Japan-Republic of China Friendship Study Group. The JIP is a junior coalition partner of Japan’s ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP). Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is president of the LDP.
Kitamura called Taiwan Japan’s “most important friend” and said that peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait are “vital to Japan’s very survival.” He called for economic and security cooperation between the two countries and referenced the passage of a Japanese version of the US’ Taiwan Relations Act (TRA).
Baba spoke to Lai about the need for cooperation between Tokyo and Taipei on regional security issues; Lai said that he believed the visits would help advance former Japanese prime minister Shinzo Abe’s vision of a free and open Indo-Pacific.
As the heads of delegations of Japanese lawmakers, neither Kitamura nor Baba represented the Japanese government. However, the utility of parliamentary groups is that they can reveal things that official government representatives are prohibited from saying.
A member of Kitamura’s delegation, JIP lawmaker Hei Seki, took advantage of that extra flexibility. On Wednesday, he spoke at the Taiwan-Japan Foreign Affairs and Defense Forum in Taipei, calling for Taiwan to be included in a triangular alliance of the US, Japan and Taiwan to ensure regional stability in the face of challenges created by aggression from the Chinese Communist Party (CCP). More controversially, he said that he supports the restoration of diplomatic relations between Taiwan and Japan, and seconded Kitamura’s call for a Japanese TRA. He also took the opportunity on Friday to travel to Kaohsiung to visit the bronze statue of Abe in the grounds of the Baoan Temple (保安堂) in the municipality’s Fengshan District (鳳山). This was not just sightseeing; there was a purpose behind his visit. It was Abe who had linked CCP military aggression against Taiwan to an existential threat to Japan.
There is little love lost between Seki and the CCP. Chinese by birth, his Japanese name is a transliteration of his Chinese name Shi Ping (石平). During the Cultural Revolution, his parents were sent to the countryside for “political re-education.” He moved to Japan in 1988, the year before the Tiananmen Square crackdown, became a naturalized Japanese citizen in 2007 and has served in the Japanese House of Councilors since last year.
On Sept. 8 last year, the CCP placed sanctions on him, citing the spreading of “fallacies” about Taiwan, Xinjiang, Tibet and Hong Kong, freezing his assets in China and prohibiting him and his family from entering China, Hong Kong or Macau.
When he arrived in Taipei’s Songshan Airport in January this year, he said that his ability to enter Taiwan demonstrated that Taiwan is not part of China, affirming its status as an independent country.
Seki has called the sanctions a badge of honor. Tokyo protested the sanctions as a form of intimidation.
The CCP’s resort to intimidation tactics was also called out on Tuesday by Philippine Secretary of National Defense Gilberto Teodoro Jr at the Seoul Defense Dialogue.
If Seki’s visit to the Abe statue in Kaohsiung hinted at the importance of regional stability in the face of CCP aggression, Teodoro’s was more explicit, and fully in line with Manila’s approach of “assertive transparency” to expose China’s destabilizing behavior. In terms of the messages sent, the Japanese delegations’ visits and Teodoro’s reaction are not unrelated. They link the need for transparency and recognition of the Chinese threat to regional stability, as well as the importance of showing a united front against it.
Tokyo and Manila are cooperating on shoring up regional stability. Japanese lawmakers are visiting Lai and talking of the need for security cooperation. Economic cooperation is part and parcel of this relationship. A Japanese TRA would be helpful; restitution of diplomatic recognition is perhaps a bridge too far, at least for now. When Seki talks of alliances, they should probably think about inviting Manila to the party, too.

European Union eyes battle over ‘pervert’ AI glasses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:36:30 UTC
01:36:30 KST

Calls are growing louder in Europe for action against “pervert” smart glasses after secretly filmed footage of girls and women appeared online — with a petition in Britain demanding a ban on their sale.
Anyone wearing smart glasses can take photos, film videos, listen to music, make phone calls, translate text or interact with an artificial intelligence (AI) assistant, with sales now hitting millions.
The devices grabbed attention this summer after a marketing tie-up between Kylie Jenner, beauty mogul and member of the Kardashian dynasty, and tech giant Meta.
Photo: Reuters
Since smartphones are now embedded in daily life, “big tech” is increasingly looking to glasses as the next big thing in wearable technology, helped by AI’s advances.
A 2013 push by Google failed to take off, but Meta’s smart spectacles, developed in partnership with Ray-Ban maker EssilorLuxottica, have fared much better.
Meta sold about 7 million pairs last year, up from a total of 2 million in 2023 and 2024. Others, including Google and Snap, are also preparing to roll out AI-powered glasses.
However, with exponential growth came the backlash.
Worries reached a peak in the summer in Europe, especially in Britain which saw intense media coverage of so-called “pervert glasses” alongside reports that Meta is developing a facial recognition feature to be integrated into the devices.
In one case, a 17-year-old girl told British broadcaster Channel 4 News last month how she had been approached by a man who covertly recorded her and their interaction.
Meta said it has taken multiple steps to prevent tampering with the blinking LED light intended to show other people the device is recording — a key concern of critics.
“These investments are already having a deterrent effect,” it said, saying that companies offering to disable the LED lights had shut down as a result.
In the meantime, Norway’s capital Oslo banned the glasses in schools this week as the government mulls regulating their use and considers a ban on features that enable facial recognition in public.
There are similar calls for the EU to take up the issue, while France’s National Commission on Informatics and Liberty data protection watchdog has urged “vigilance.”
A Swedish designer, Mateusz Pozar, launched a “Ban Ray” site earlier this year, providing signs to ban smart glasses from venues and selling stickers.
Pozar said he started the site after his girlfriend was approached by two men wearing the glasses and recording her, which “freaked her out.”
He said he wanted a discussion about how “we as a society feel about this technology” before it becomes ubiquitous.
“This is a lever to have a discussion about privacy, personal rights, control over my data,” he said.
Pozar also pointed to his concerns about data extraction after reports about Kenya-based workers who reviewed graphic content captured by Meta’s AI glasses.
Slovakian Member of the European Parliament Veronika Cifrova Ostrihonova said that she raised the issue with the bloc’s executive after the first cases of women being secretly filmed, seeking to know if the glasses comply with data protection and AI rules.
“I am still awaiting an answer,” the Slovak lawmaker said.
“We need clear EU rules to protect and strong enforcement to make sure new technologies don’t come at the expense of our fundamental rights,” she said.
The European Commission said national data protection authorities were “responsible for monitoring and enforcing” privacy rules.
The EU executive would not be drawn on what further action it could take, but the independent European Data Protection Board commissioned a report expected in autumn looking at the glasses’ “social acceptability.”
That report would guide the European Parliament, where Member of the European Parliament Alex Agius Saliba said there were concerns across the political spectrum.
“We must act as soon as possible,” he said.
“For me, they are still pervert glasses,” Saliba said.
“As things stand today, we should definitely go for a ban” until they are proven safe, he added.
A “Stop Smart Glasses” campaign launched in Britain and Ireland, with a petition and call for supporters to contact stores to stop their sale.
The petition has more than 9,100 signatures so far. The British government must respond if it reaches 10,000.
One of the campaign’s founders, teacher Guy Holder, said he had several concerns about the glasses including their effects on girls and women and a broader “invasion” of public spaces that could lead to “total surveillance.”
“We are also concerned more broadly about an atmosphere in which it feels like anybody can film anybody without their knowledge or consent,” he said.

Taiwan temple culture showcased in Poland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:36:29 UTC
01:36:29 KST

Taiwan’s traditional temple culture was showcased in the Polish city of Lodz on Friday, drawing crowds with traditional music, deity processions, performances and a Taiwan-themed market.
Organized by the National Cultural Association of Taiwan (NCAT), the Taiwan Day event saw Taipei Gong Le Xuan and the Lei Sheng Art Group recreate the lively atmosphere of a Taiwanese temple square for local audiences.
Taipei Gong Le Xuan, a century-old Taiwanese Beiguan music ensemble, performed traditional music alongside a deity procession led by the Lei Sheng Art Group, a Taiwanese traditional performing arts group specializing in folk religious and temple performances.
Photo: CNA
Taipei Gong Le Xuan member Chen Li-ting (陳俐廷) said some of the group’s members were traveling overseas for the first time and had initially been nervous about how local audiences would respond to the traditional music.
However, the unfamiliar sounds drew considerable interest from Polish visitors, with many stopping to watch and record the performances on their phones, Chen said.
The troupe’s deity figures and traditional instruments also drew interest, with visitors taking photos and trying their hand at playing the instruments after the performances.
A Taiwan-themed market at the venue featured Taiwanese food, drinks, handicrafts and cultural activities, giving visitors an opportunity to experience aspects of Taiwan’s traditional and everyday culture.
Taiwan’s representative to Poland, Jeff Liu (劉永健), who attended the event, said it provided an opportunity to promote Taiwan’s culture overseas and introduce Taiwanese traditions and everyday life to Polish audiences.
Also attending the event was Lodz Deputy Mayor Adam Pustelnik, who said the event seamlessly blended Taiwanese culture with local Polish traditions and sentiments.
The event in Lodz is part of a tour of Austria, Hungary and Poland organized by the NCAT between Sept. 5 and 19, which features other aspects of Taiwanese culture such as contemporary dance.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:36:19 UTC
01:36:19 KST

Big Foe made another big run at the US Open but again could not break through to his first Grand Slam final.
Frances Tiafoe got knocked out in the semi-finals on Friday night by fellow American Ben Shelton. This was his third trip to the semi-finals at Flushing Meadows in five years, after getting this far in 2022 and 2024.
“It’s hard,” Tiafoe said after losing 4-6, 6-3, 6-3, 7-5. “As you look at it, obviously I’ve been in this position a lot now — thankfully, but also it’s tough. I wanted to be in a Grand Slam final. Obviously it was a big match.”
Photo: AFP
Tiafoe won the first set Friday night to the delight of a packed house at Arthur Ashe Stadium but could not overcome 20 aces from his hard-serving opponent.
“[Tiafoe is] like a big brother to me,” Shelton said. “To be honest, every time that we get to take this court together, Arthur Ashe, and play each other is super special. This is where we want to be: at the tail end of this tournament.”
The 28-year-old Tiafoe, a DC area local and a fan favorite for his personality and exciting style of play, got a standing ovation from the crowd leaving the court after the four-set defeat.
“I just want to win it,” Tiafoe said. “The love is incredible, man. It’s something that gives me definitely tears in my eyes from a kid starting how I did, and the love I have here is crazy. Every match I play, from everyone, all the staff, the security guards — everyone really wants to see me do the thing.”
Tiafoe improved drastically from his performance at the US Open a year ago, when he lost to Jan-Lennard Struff in the round of 32. He was feeling “really, really bad” about himself at that time.
This time, he beat Daniil Medvedev and came back from down two sets against Alex Michelsen in the quarterfinals, but falling short left him with a familiar, empty feeling.
“These last couple weeks have been great weeks, but I haven’t been able to finish,” Tiafoe said. “And that’s probably going to be the next thing for me.”

Philadelphia ready for season opener with DC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:36:17 UTC
01:36:17 KST

The Philadelphia Eagles hope for a distraction-free start to the season today against the visiting Washington Commanders.
Of course, this is Philly, where the next controversy is always right around the corner, but for now the focus is squarely on football entering this early encounter between NFC East rivals.
Meanwhile in Washington, a city where bipartisan battles are the national pastime, fans and analysts are divided over whether fans are going to see the 12-5 Commanders of 2024 or the 5-12 version from last season.
Photo: AFP
As so often happens in the NFL, quarterbacks and coaches under the biggest spotlights.
Eagles signal-caller Jalen Hurts and head coach Nick Sirianni are 5-0 in season openers. Sirianni attributes his Week 1 success to building good practice habits throughout training camp.
“I think people get it confused, and they think practicing hard has to be long,” Sirianni said Wednesday.
With AJ Brown now with the Patriots, Hurts has a new undisputed No. 1 wideout in receiver DeVonta Smith. He has a new offensive coordinator in Sean Mannion, a healthy Saquon Barkley and one of the NFL’s best offensive lines.
To replace Brown, the Eagles drafted Makai Lemon in the first round and acquired Dontayvion Wicks from Green Bay.
Despite being a three-time Pro Bowl selection and Super Bowl MVP by the age of 28, Hurts still has his share of doubters entering his sixth full season as the starter. He refuses to let the outside noise divert his attention.
“I’m truly focused on being the best that I can be right now,” he said. “That’s where my energy is. There’s a lot of change. I’m focused on this offense. I’m focused on building with Sean [Mannion] and being at my best.”
Defensively, the Eagles locked up star tackles Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis with big contracts this offseason and gave edge rusher Jonathan Greenard a four-year, US$98 million deal.
Greenard’s season debut would have to wait at least one more week as he is out for this game after missing training camp with an injury and returning to practice Wednesday on a limited basis.
Third-year head coach Dan Quinn is 2-3 against Philadelphia since taking over in Washington, which includes the 55-23 loss in the NFC Championship Game after the 2024 regular season. Quinn has two new coordinators with David Blough at the offensive controls and Daronte Jones taking over a defense that allowed 26.5 points per game last year.
“The best teams I’ve been part of have a strong connection in the locker room first,” Quinn said. “This team is just connected, maybe more quickly than we’ve had.”

Police arrest woman who allegedly shot lover’s wife
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:36:14 UTC
01:36:14 KST

A woman surnamed Yi (易), suspected of ambushing and shooting her boyfriend’s wife in Taipei on Friday, was arrested yesterday in New Taipei City’s Sanchong District (三重), police said.
The victim, a 50-year-old woman surnamed Chao (趙), was shot by a suspect dressed in a black down jacket, baseball cap and face mask at about 2pm while she was leaving her residence, police said.
The suspect fired two shots at close range, with one bullet striking Chao in the abdomen, they said, adding that one bullet was jammed in the firearm.
Photo copied by Liu Ching-ho, Taipei Times
Chao remained conscious and was rushed to National Taiwan University Hospital for emergency treatment.
After reviewing surveillance footage, investigators concluded that many of the suspect’s movements and physical characteristics were consistent with those of a woman, they said.
The shooter fled in a vehicle, which was registered to Chao’s husband, a man surnamed Chen (陳), they said.
Chen was arrested at the Taian Service Area on National Freeway 1 at about 6pm on Friday, they added.
Chen denied any involvement, police said, adding that they are still searching for the firearm used in the shooting.
The two suspects were transferred to prosecutors on suspicion of contravening the Controlling Guns, Ammunition and Knives Act (槍砲彈藥刀械管制條例) and attempted murder.
Yi had allegedly been dropped off in the New Taipei City’s Jhonghe (中和) or Yonghe (永和) district after the shooting, police said.
She allegedly changed clothes, boarded the Taipei Metro at the Nanshijiao Station and was last seen in Sanchong District (三重), where she was arrested at about 10am yesterday at a friend’s home, they said.
Yi and Chen allegedly met in an online chatroom, developed a romantic relationship and then lived together, with Chen providing her with financial support, police said.
Chen frequently complained about his wife after the latter returned from China several months ago, Yi was quoted by investigators as saying.
He allegedly said that his wife had forced him out and prevented him from seeing their children, causing him to harbor resentment and eventually plot her murder, the police said.
Yi said Chen persuaded her to carry out the shooting and in March took her to a shooting range in Tainan after purchasing a firearm online, they added.

Houthis take over strait vital to global shipping
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:36:13 UTC
01:36:13 KST

The Iran-backed Houthis yesterday controlled Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast after capturing three strategic islands in a lightning offensive the previous day, cementing their hold on a vital shipping corridor linking Europe and Asia.
The developments are likely to deepen the Middle East war’s impact on international commerce as Saudi Arabia shut down an oil pipeline following attacks, and after months of Iran’s blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.
Following a week-long offensive that has killed hundreds, government officials said the Houthis seized the Yemeni side of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the southern gateway to the Red Sea and the Suez Canal.
Photo: AP

Almost all households have Internet access: survey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:36:12 UTC
01:36:12 KST

Smartphone and Internet access in Taiwan exceeds 90 percent even among the lowest-income households, a survey released by the Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics (DGBAS) showed.
The latest Survey of Family Income and Expenditure, which compared the top 20 percent of income earners with the bottom 20 percent, found Taiwan’s highest and lowest-income households show the largest disparity in ownership rates for cars, computers and dehumidifiers, while basic home appliances, mobile phones and Internet access have become nearly universal across income levels.
The survey found that Taiwan has largely achieved digital inclusion, with more than 90 percent of low-income households having access to mobile phones and Internet connectivity.
Prepared by reporter Kao Chia-ho
While car ownership has remained stable since 2017, with a national penetration rate of about 60 to 61 percent after first surpassing 50 percent in 1996, ownership rates differ sharply by income level, the survey showed.
More than 95 percent of households in the highest income bracket own a car, compared with 39 to 42 percent of households in the lowest income bracket — a gap of more than 50 percentage points, indicating that the high price of vehicles and maintenance costs remain significant barriers for low-income households.
More than 96 percent of high-income households own a home computer, compared with 34 to 43 percent of low-income households.
Dehumidifier ownership ranges from 65 to 70 percent among high-income households, compared with 40 to 44 percent among low-income households, suggesting that low-income families prioritize essential needs over quality-of-life appliances.
In contrast, basic appliances such as color televisions and washing machines maintain near-universal adoption at 98 to 99 percent across all income groups.
Mobile phone ownership exceeds 90 percent in the lowest income group and approaches 100 percent in the highest group, while Internet access equipment showed a similar pattern, with more than 91 percent of low-income households connected online, almost matching the rate among wealthier families.
Mobile phones and mobile Internet services have replaced many of the household technologies that once dominated daily life, the survey showed.
Mobile phone ownership rose to 98.04 percent last year from 86.15 percent in 2005, surpassing televisions, which stood at 97.65 percent, to become the most common household device in Taiwan, the survey showed.
Cable television subscriptions, once the dominant source of living-room entertainment, peaked at an 86.36 percent adoption rate in 2017, up from 54.15 percent in 1995, but declined to 80.44 percent last year as streaming services gained ground.
Devices such as video cassette recorders have disappeared from Taiwanese homes, while digital camera ownership fell to 5.7 percent from 51.7 percent over 15 years.
Similarly, the landline telephone penetration rate, which peaked at 97.55 percent in 2005, dropped by more than 24 percentage points to 73.76 percent last year.
CONTINUED ON PAGE 3
DGBAS data on household consumption patterns also showed that Taiwanese spending habits have undergone significant changes over the past three decades.
While basic expenses such as food, clothing, housing and transport have declined or stagnated as a proportion of overall budgets, spending on healthcare, dining out and lodging has grown rapidly, the data showed.
The share of spending on food, beverages and tobacco fell to 15.36 percent last year from 19.53 percent in 1995, while expenses on clothing and footwear dropped to 2.57 percent from 4.6 percent.
Spending on housing services, utilities and fuel edged down to 24.09 percent from 25.13 percent, while transportation and communications slipped slightly to 11.39 percent from 11.47 percent, indicating stable spending patterns for housing and commuting needs.
In contrast, the share of spending on restaurants and accommodation surged to 14.19 percent last year from 8.16 percent 30 years ago, while healthcare spending also rose sharply to 14.08 percent from 9.96 percent over the same period.
DGBAS officials attributed the rise in dining and travel spending to the growing number of dual-income households and single-person households, saying that dining out has become normal, as cooking at home takes longer.
People are also increasingly willing to spend on specialty restaurants, as well as domestic and overseas travel, and hotel stays, reflecting a growing preference for lifestyle and leisure experiences, they said.
The increase in healthcare expenditure is largely driven by Taiwan’s rapidly aging population, they said.
As more households care for elderly family members, spending on nutritional supplements, out-of-pocket treatment for chronic illnesses, long-term care and caregiving services has become a growing financial burden, they added.

The concept of a “social battery” is a metaphor used to describe the amount of energy an individual has for social interaction. Like a physical battery, this energy runs low over time and requires periodic recharging. __1__ Understanding these patterns helps individuals manage their social lives more effectively.
In general, a social battery functions differently between introverts and extroverts. Extroverts tend to focus on the outside world and often gain energy from social interaction, sometimes even feeling recharged by it. Introverts, by contrast, are more inward-focused and may feel drained by too much socializing. __2__ This difference reflects a variation in temperament rather than a lack of social skills. It shows how people respond to social environments in different ways.
Photo: AdobeStock I 照片：AdobeStock
Several factors can drain a person’s energy. These include the people they interact with, the type and quality of interaction, and the size of the group. For example, large gatherings, noisy environments, and long periods of socializing without breaks can be particularly tiring. __3__ Internal stressors like anxiety can also affect how quickly energy is depleted.
When a person’s social battery is low, they may feel tired, stressed, irritable, or less interested in talking. They may feel a strong urge to leave and find a quiet, familiar space. While these feelings can be intense, having a smaller social battery is not a medical diagnosis. __4__ To recharge, individuals may spend time alone or take part in calming activities such as reading, yoga, or gardening. Recognizing personal limits and taking breaks are essential to maintaining a healthy balance between social life and personal well-being.
「社交電池」這個概念是一種隱喻，用來描述一個人從事社交互動時所擁有的精力多寡。就像實體電池一樣，這種能量會隨著時間逐漸耗盡，且需要定期充電。每個人的電量消耗速度以及恢復精力的方式都不一樣。了解這些模式有助於人們更有效地管理自己的社交生活。
一般而言，社交電池在內向者與外向者之間的運作方式有所不同。外向者往往會關注外在世界，且常常從社交互動中獲得能量，有時甚至會因此感覺充了電。相較之下，內向者較為關注內在，且太多的社交活動可能會讓他們感到疲憊不堪。他們通常是透過靜態或獨處的活動來恢復能量。這種差別反映的是性格上的差異，而非缺乏社交能力。這顯示出人們對社交環境的反應方式各不相同。
有幾個因素會消耗一個人的能量。這些因素包括他們互動的對象、互動的類型與品質，以及群體的規模。舉例來說，大型聚會、吵雜的環境，以及長時間沒有休息的社交活動，都可能特別容易讓人感到疲累。此外，社交壓力（例如不對等的權力關係）可能會加劇這種疲憊。如焦慮等內在壓力源也可能會影響能量消耗的速度。
當一個人的社交電池電量不足時，他們可能會感到疲倦、壓力大、易怒，或較不想與人交談。他們可能會極度想要離開現場，並尋找一個安靜且熟悉的空間。雖然這些感受可能相當強烈，但社交電池較小並不是一種醫學診斷。它只是反映了一個人如何體驗社交互動。為了充電，人們可能會花時間獨處，或從事如閱讀、瑜伽或園藝等讓人放鬆的活動。認識個人的極限和休息對維持社交生活與個人身心健康之間的良好平衡不可或缺。
What Did You Learn?
(A) It simply reflects how someone experiences social interaction.
(B) They often regain energy through quiet or solitary activities.
(C) People with the condition may choose to be alone, where they feel safe.
(D) People differ in how quickly their battery drains and how they restore it.
(E) Furthermore, social stress, such as unequal power dynamics, may increase this exhaustion.
答案：
1. D 2. B 3. E 4. A
