Modi-Xi-Putin bonhomie, car diplomacy, gala dinner, Pahalgam condemnation and New Delhi Declaration: Brics Summit key takeaways
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:30:46 UTC
01:30:46 KST

Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Russia President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping, Iran President Masoud Pezeshkian (PTI Image)
NEW DELHI: India hosted the 18th Brics Summit in New Delhi on September 12-13, bringing together leaders of the expanded 11-member grouping for discussions on global conflicts, terrorism, trade, energy, technology, climate change and reform of international institutions. India used its 2026 chairship to push a people-centric agenda centred on resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability.The summit was marked by high-level bilateral meetings, visible displays of bonhomie among leaders and efforts to bridge differences over the conflicts in West Asia and the Black Sea region. PM Modi held separate meetings with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, while leaders also participated in the Brics Business Forum and other summit engagements.
From PM Modi and Putin travelling together by car inside the Bharat Mandapam complex to PM Modi and Xi sharing warm moments and the leaders participating in a gala dinner and cultural engagements, the summit combined diplomacy with symbols of Brics unity.Also read - 'Global South must be rule-shaper, India ready to take lead': PM Modi at Brics SummitThe summit adopted the New Delhi Declaration, a 45-page document containing 140 points that brings together the grouping's positions on terrorism, unilateral military action, West Asia, global governance, trade, sanctions, energy, finance and development.
PM Modi-Xi bilateral: Boundary question and reset in ties
PM Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping held a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of the summit, with both sides stressing the importance of viewing India-China relations from a strategic and long-term perspective.The two leaders committed to seeking a fair, reasonable and mutually acceptable solution to the boundary question. PM Modi stressed that differences should not become disputes and highlighted the importance of mutual respect, mutual sensitivity and mutual interest.The discussions also covered peace and tranquillity along the border, economic relations, trade imbalances, supply chains and people-to-people exchanges. The meeting came as New Delhi and Beijing seek to stabilise bilateral ties while continuing to manage differences over the boundary.The Modi-Xi meeting was one of the summit's most closely watched engagements, given the strategic importance of India-China relations and their simultaneous participation in an expanded Brics framework.
PM Modi-Putin meeting: Ukraine, West Asia and $100 billion trade target
PM Modi held an over 45-minute bilateral meeting with Putin on the eve of the summit, reviewing the India-Russia strategic partnership and discussing regional and global developments.The two leaders discussed the impact of the Russia-Ukraine conflict and the West Asia crisis on maritime trade and the safety and security of Indian seafarers. PM Modi reiterated that dialogue and diplomacy remained the way forward in resolving conflicts and said India was ready to contribute to peace efforts.Five Indian seafarers have died in the Black Sea amid the Russia-Ukraine hostilities, making maritime safety an important concern for New Delhi.The two sides also discussed defence, energy, critical minerals, civil nuclear cooperation, fertilisers, infrastructure, technology and industrial cooperation. India and Russia agreed to work towards taking bilateral trade to $100 billion by 2030.Putin also invited PM Modi to Russia for the 24th India-Russia Annual Summit. The dates will be finalised through diplomatic channels.
Car diplomacy: PM Modi and Putin travel together
After their bilateral meeting, PM Modi and Putin travelled together in the same car inside the Bharat Mandapam complex before attending the Brics Business Forum.The unusual visual quickly became one of the defining moments of the summit, highlighting the close nature of the India-Russia relationship amid continuing geopolitical pressure on Moscow and India's effort to maintain strategic autonomy.PM Modi later highlighted the growing India-Russia economic relationship, including the participation of companies from both countries at the INNOPROM industrial exhibition held at Bharat Mandapam.
PM Modi presented Putin with a Russian translation of the Thirukkural, the classical Tamil work attributed to poet-saint Thiruvalluvar."Two thousand years ago, Thiruvalluvar wrote the Thirukkural. It includes the entire gamut of human life. It has been translated into the Russian language. I am confident that the people-to-people contact will increase with the translation of the Thirukkural into Russian, which will play a big role in strengthening our relations," Modi told Putin.The gift was presented as a cultural bridge between India and Russia and reflected the emphasis placed by India on people-to-people links during its Brics chairship.
PM Modi-Pezeshkian talks: West Asia and regional peace
PM Modi met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the summit, with the two leaders discussing India-Iran relations, Brics cooperation and the conflict in West Asia.PM Modi reiterated India's position that disputes must be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy and stressed the need for lasting peace and stability in the region.The discussions also covered freedom of navigation and commerce and the safety and well-being of seafarers, issues that have acquired greater importance amid disruption to shipping routes in the region.The meeting followed the leaders' earlier interaction on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Summit in Bishkek. India also stressed the importance of expanding bilateral trade channels and pursuing a long-term and mutually beneficial relationship with Iran.
PM Modi, Xi, Putin and leaders showcase Brics unity
The summit was accompanied by a series of high-profile visuals showing leaders of the expanded grouping interacting informally.PM Modi was seen greeting Putin and Xi together, holding their hands and sharing smiles. In another visual, Modi walked alongside Putin, Xi and Pezeshkian.Also read - Big reunion at Brics: PM Modi, Xi & Putin meet for 3rd time in 3 yrs; PM shares photoPM Modi was also seen holding hands and walking alongside Pezeshkian and other leaders during the Brics Business Forum. The images were widely seen as a demonstration of the grouping's effort to project unity despite differences among members on major geopolitical issues.The presence of leaders from Russia, China, Iran, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Brazil, South Africa and other member states underscored the diversity of interests represented within the expanded grouping.
Gala dinner: Leaders gather for cultural evening
The Brics leaders also attended a gala dinner hosted during the summit, providing an informal setting for interactions between heads of government and state.Also read - Gucchi marmik, millet pulao, khumb galouti: What's on the Brics gala dinner menuThe cultural programme and dinner formed part of India's effort to showcase its heritage alongside the formal diplomatic agenda. The event brought together leaders who had spent the summit discussing contentious issues ranging from wars and terrorism to trade and global governance.The informal interactions added a softer dimension to a summit otherwise dominated by difficult geopolitical negotiations.
Banyan tree plantation: Symbol of Brics unity
A symbolic tree plantation ceremony was also organised during the summit, with Brics leaders participating in the planting of a Banyan tree.The Banyan tree, known for its extensive roots and interconnected branches, was presented as a symbol of continuity, resilience and interconnectedness. The gesture complemented India's 2026 Brics theme of "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability".Also read - PM Modi, Brics leaders take part in joint tree plantation at Bharat Mandapam: WatchThe plantation also reflected India's attempt to connect the summit's diplomatic agenda with sustainability and environmental cooperation.
Brics Business Forum: Trade, investment and technology
The Brics Business Forum brought together heads of state, ministers and business leaders to discuss trade, investment, finance, technology and development.PM Modi highlighted the economic weight of the expanded grouping, saying:"Today, BRICS nations represent 50 per cent of the world's population, 40 per cent of its GDP, and over 25 per cent of global trade. Moreover, while global GDP has grown approximately two-and-a-half-fold over these years, the combined GDP of BRICS nations has expanded nearly four-and-a-half-fold. In other words, the economic strength of BRICS has grown at nearly twice the pace of the rest of the world.""The growing scale, speed, and optimism of BRICS are clearly evident among us. This forum, hosted in India, is the largest BRICS Business Forum to date," the Prime Minister added.Also read - Brics New Delhi Declaration adopted: Terrorism, conflict resolution, tariff concerns addressed; key pointsPezeshkian called for Brics to convert its economic potential into practical cooperation through trade, investment and joint financing."We believe that the true strength of BRICS is not confined merely to the size of its members' economies; rather, it becomes more apparent when these capacities are transformed into a network of trade, investment and joint financing – a transition from potential cooperation to operational one," he said.Putin stressed the importance of business-to-business relations and economic partnerships, arguing that they could help create more resilient international economic relations.
Putin attacks trade restrictions, backs new growth platform
At the Business Forum, Putin criticised what he described as attempts by Western competitors to regain their former economic leadership."We have always been told that competition is a sacred cow, something that must not be touched," Putin told a BRICS business forum event. "Yet, unfortunately, today your Western competitors are trying by any means necessary to regain their former leadership.""This competition is sometimes assuming unsightly forms," he said. "They even include direct physical attacks or the destruction of industrial and logistical facilities, pipelines, and so forth."Putin also criticised restrictions on international transport corridors, shipping and trade and called for Brics to contribute to building "a new, sustainable platform for global growth".
India-Russia economic partnership gets push
The summit also provided an opportunity for India and Russia to discuss expanding economic cooperation amid Western sanctions and geopolitical uncertainty.The two countries discussed the Programme for Economic Cooperation 2030 and cooperation in infrastructure, energy, technology, defence, critical minerals and civil nuclear energy.The sides also explored industrial cooperation in railways and tunnelling, the steel value chain and greater access to the Russian market for Indian exporters.India continues to maintain strong energy ties with Russia, while seeking to expand trade beyond traditional sectors.
Brics pushes practical cooperation across sectors
India's 2026 chairship focused heavily on converting Brics into a platform for practical cooperation rather than limiting it to political declarations.More than 350 meetings and high-level engagements were organised across approximately 30 cities during India's chairship. These covered political and security cooperation, economic and financial cooperation, and cultural and people-to-people exchanges.PM Modi said: "It gives me immense pleasure to welcome and greet you all to India. India’s BRICS chairmanship is based on a people-centric and humanity-first approach. Resilience, innovation, cooperation, and sustainability have been our priorities.""Alongside these priorities, we have placed special emphasis on connecting BRICS cooperation with the common people. With this vision in mind, more than 350 meetings were organised. We had the opportunity to welcome your teams to approximately 30 cities..."
Agriculture: Digital farming and climate resilience
Brics countries agreed on new mechanisms to strengthen agricultural cooperation.These include Centres of Excellence on agro-ecology for research and knowledge sharing on natural, organic and regenerative farming, a Brics Network on Digital Agriculture using artificial intelligence, geospatial intelligence, IoT-enabled monitoring and advanced data analytics, and BRICS AGRIN, a voluntary framework covering agricultural inputs, seeds and genetic resources.The initiatives seek to promote climate-resilient farming and greater technology-driven cooperation among member countries.
Health: Lifestyle, traditional medicine and mental health
The Brics Mission for Healthy Lifestyle was launched along with a roadmap for joint cooperation for 2026-2029, focusing on preventive approaches to obesity and other non-communicable diseases.Members also agreed to establish an Expert Working Group on Traditional, Complementary and Integrative Medicine, covering research, evidence generation, academic exchange, quality standards and protection of traditional knowledge.Mental health cooperation was also strengthened through the Brics Training Hub Network and Network of Centres of Excellence, with NIMHANS India as the coordinating centre.
Energy: Smart grids and storage
Brics adopted guiding principles on energy storage and smart grids and launched a Digital Centre of Excellence for Smart Grids and Energy Storage.The initiative will provide a platform for knowledge sharing, capacity building, policy and regulatory cooperation and pilot projects among member countries.The summit also placed emphasis on energy security, diversified energy sources and equitable energy transitions.
MSMEs and startups: New platforms for businesses
India pushed stronger cooperation for micro, small and medium enterprises and startups.The Brics MSME Cooperation Portal will connect MSMEs, technology centres, trade associations, financial institutions and policymakers across member countries.A Brics Incubator Network will connect startups with incubators in other member countries, while the Brics Startup Innovation Fund is intended to support early and growth-stage startups.
Logistics and global supply chains
Brics members agreed on a Logistics Supply-Chain Cooperation Framework aimed at improving resilience, sustainability and connectivity.The grouping also advanced cooperation on global value chains through the GVC Action Plan 2026-2030, including a Technical Council and joint study.The initiatives are intended to reduce vulnerabilities caused by fragmented supply chains, improve connectivity and promote economic diversification.
Urban mobility and climate-resilient infrastructure
The summit also advanced cooperation on sustainable urban development.A Brics Urban Mobility Hub was established as a platform for technical cooperation and knowledge sharing. Members also adopted voluntary principles on climate-resilient urban infrastructure.An Urban Research and Knowledge Network was established to facilitate cross-border research, peer learning and institutional cooperation.
Skilling, youth and sports technology
India also advanced cooperation on skills and employment through BRICS CONNECT, a voluntary network covering capacity building, social security, women's workforce participation, employability and digital public infrastructure.The Brics Youth Cooperation Framework 2026 was adopted to provide greater continuity and structure to youth cooperation.Sports technology cooperation was institutionalised through a working group focusing on technical information, research, institutional experience and best practices.
Science and research cooperation
The Brics Science and Research Repository was welcomed as a structured platform for sharing scientific knowledge among member countries.The initiative is intended to strengthen research collaboration and facilitate greater exchange of scientific information across the expanded grouping.
Brics 2026: A wider and more diverse grouping
Brics currently comprises 11 countries: Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the UAE.The expansion has significantly widened the grouping's geographical reach across Asia, Africa, the Middle East and Latin America. It has also brought together countries with different political systems, economic priorities and positions on major international conflicts.India's chairship therefore focused not only on expanding cooperation but also on finding consensus among members with competing interests.
New Delhi Declaration: Key outcomes
The summit concluded with the adoption of the New Delhi Declaration 2026, following intensive negotiations among members. The 45-page declaration contains 140 points and represents India's central diplomatic outcome from its 2026 chairship.The declaration addresses terrorism, conflicts, global governance, trade, sanctions, energy, finance, development and the interests of the Global South.
Terrorism: Pahalgam attack explicitly condemned
The declaration strongly condemns terrorism in all its forms and manifestations and calls for "zero tolerance for terrorism".It specifically condemns the April 22, 2025, Pahalgam terrorist attack, in which 26 people were killed. The declaration also condemns cross-border movement of terrorists, terrorism financing and safe havens.Brics reaffirmed that terrorism cannot be associated with any religion, nationality, civilisation or ethnic group and called for those involved in terrorist activities and their support to be held accountable.The grouping also called for progress towards the adoption of the Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism under the UN framework.
West Asia: Ceasefire, diplomacy and two-state solution
The declaration expresses deep concern over the continuing escalation in West Asia and calls on all parties to exercise maximum restraint.It stresses dialogue, consultation and diplomacy as the means to address conflicts and calls for the protection of civilians and humanitarian assistance.On Gaza, Brics called for the upholding of a ceasefire, unhindered humanitarian aid and an end to forced displacement of Palestinians. It reaffirmed support for a two-state solution based on the internationally recognised 1967 borders.
Unilateral war condemned
The declaration condemns unilateral military action without naming any country.The language assumes significance because Brics includes members with differing positions on the major conflicts in West Asia and the wider international system.The consensus was reached after negotiations continued into the early hours of Saturday, with India working to bridge differences between members and produce a common position.
UN reform and greater Global South representation
Brics reaffirmed its support for comprehensive reform of the United Nations, including the Security Council.The grouping called for greater representation of developing countries in global decision-making and a more democratic, representative and inclusive international system.China and Russia reiterated support for the aspirations of India and Brazil to play a greater role in the UN, including the Security Council.
Trade: Opposition to tariffs and protectionism
The declaration expresses concern over unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures that distort international trade and create uncertainty for businesses and supply chains.Brics reaffirmed support for a rules-based multilateral trading system centred on the World Trade Organization.The grouping also called for the restoration of a fully functioning two-tier binding WTO dispute settlement mechanism.
Brics voiced opposition to unilateral coercive measures that it considers inconsistent with international law and the principles of the UN Charter.The declaration calls for such measures to be eliminated and highlights their impact on international economic relations.The position reflects a longstanding Brics push for a more balanced international economic and political order.
Local currencies and cross-border payments
The declaration supports greater use of local currencies in cross-border payments and trade settlements among Brics countries.Members acknowledged ongoing work on interoperability between payment and messaging systems and efforts to facilitate trade settlements and investment in local currencies.The initiative forms part of the wider Brics effort to strengthen financial resilience and cooperation.
Energy security and transition
The declaration calls for stronger energy security through diversified energy sources, resilient infrastructure and stable markets.It also supports just, orderly, equitable and inclusive energy transitions while recognising the differing circumstances and priorities of member countries.Brics backed cooperation involving renewables, nuclear energy, hydropower, hydrogen, fossil fuels and other low-carbon technologies.
Women and inclusive development
The declaration recognises women as leaders, decision-makers and drivers of economic growth and social transformation.It highlights women's participation in governance, entrepreneurship, employment and peacebuilding and calls for greater financial and digital inclusion.The grouping also emphasised skills development and access to productive and social services.
Tackling organised crime and illicit financial flows
Brics expressed concern over illicit financial flows linked to drug trafficking, firearms trafficking, terrorism financing, human trafficking and organised crime.The grouping called for stronger cooperation between member countries to trace and disrupt criminal proceeds and tackle transnational criminal networks.
The larger message from New Delhi
The New Delhi Declaration combines a strong political message on terrorism, unilateral military action, West Asia and global governance with a broad economic and development agenda.
For India, the outcome represents an effort to demonstrate that the expanded Brics can reach consensus despite major geopolitical differences. The declaration also places India's priorities of resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability at the centre of a wider agenda covering trade, technology, energy, health, agriculture, finance and development.The summit therefore ended with two parallel messages: Brics wants a stronger collective voice in global affairs, while India wants that voice translated into practical cooperation that reaches businesses, communities and ordinary people.

As Russia targets gas stations, Kyiv draws up plans for possible fuel shortages, Klitschko says
Kyiv authorities don't have the resources to build shelters at every gas station, while the city also faces a shortage of weapons needed to intercept Russian drones and missiles, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Sept. 11.
Klitschko's remarks come as Moscow has stepped up its attacks on Ukraine's capital, including at least four strikes on gas stations over the past week. Kyiv has faced near non-stop drone attacks in recent days, killing and injuring civilians.
According to the mayor, protecting gas stations from Russian attacks is a "complicated issue."
"The issue of protection is a question of air defense. Speaking with the military, I can say that, unfortunately, we have a shortage of means of destruction — those missiles that work against drones, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles. There is a problem with this," Klitschko told reporters on the sidelines of the Yalta European Strategy (YES) conference.
The Sept. 10 attack marked the first time Russian troops targeted a gas station in Kyiv, after similar attacks had largely been concentrated in frontline areas. The expanding campaign is disrupting fuel distribution, potentially affecting both civilians and military personnel who rely on passenger vehicles.
Klitschko said authorities have stockpiled fuel for the winter and in case of emergencies. The reserves will help keep generators running during possible power outages, he added, as many expect Russia to again seek to cripple Ukraine's energy grid ahead of winter.
"We are working through various plans," Klitschko said. "We must be prepared for different scenarios, including a bad one."

AI, jets, drones: IAI chairman Boaz Levy describes future battlefield, air force - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:27:31 UTC
01:27:31 KST

In a special interview for the Maariv podcast, Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI) Chairman and father of the Arrow missile defense system, Boaz Levy, described how he views the battlefield of the next decade: heavily reliant on space, artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, robotics, drone swarms, and missiles - and primarily requiring seamless connectivity between all bodies operating during wartime, from the IDF to hospitals and emergency rescue forces.
Levy began with space. When asked if IAI has plans to "conquer space," he replied: "I thought we already conquered it. IAI is a space superpower. This needs to be understood."
According to him, the roots of this movement lie in the late 1970s, following the peace agreement with Egypt and the withdrawal from the Sinai Peninsula, which created a significant intelligence gap. "The way to bridge this gap was through technological means. IAI came up with the idea of: 'Let's launch a satellite into space with sensors that would observe from above."
At the time, he noted, only the United States and the Soviet Union possessed similar capabilities. "And along comes little Israel, with extraordinary Israeli chutzpah, and says: We are going to do it."
"Putting more eyes in the sky mid-war"
Levy pointed to the Ofek satellites as one of the main expressions of Israel's transformation into a space superpower. During the war, he said, they provided the IDF with intelligence capabilities that enabled precise strikes and advanced operational planning. "Today it is no longer a secret that a pilot sitting in the cockpit receives an image taken from a satellite, which tells him where to fly and where to aim, and afterward it also tells him whether he hit the target or not," he said.
In just one single year and during an active war, Israel launched three satellites: the "Dror" communications satellite and two "Ofek" reconnaissance satellites. "This demonstrates the capabilities of a superpower. In the middle of a war, we put more eyes in the sky and deployed another communications unit." The growing number of observation satellites creates a massive data pool, Levy added, which serves as the foundation for artificial intelligence systems.
When asked about a plan to deploy a larger constellation of small satellites to allow the defense establishment to continuously track areas of interest from Iran to Turkey, he replied that it is not a fantasy.
"I wouldn't use the term 'flood.' We are not talking about infinite quantities; we are talking about many satellites; it is a plan." For the operational user, there are two main questions: how frequently a specific target can be observed, and at what resolution. "We are working on a technological solution that will allow intelligence, using space sensors and the most sophisticated AI-based algorithms in the world, to know exactly what is happening in our areas of interest at any given moment."
Levy emphasized that the plan has already received government approval and is in execution. Funding comes partly from IAI's research and development budgets and partly from the Defense Ministry. As more budget is allocated, the program will advance faster. "Israel needs to be a space superpower, at least among the top three in the world. I think we are approaching that big time," he said.
The next battlefield: Fewer soldiers, more robots
For Levy, the next major shift is not just in platforms but in how militaries think and operate. "We are talking about a world of autonomous capabilities. We need to reduce the burden on the soldier in the field by increasing the use of robots. We have seen the beginnings of this in the current war."
Alongside robotics, highly advanced sensory capabilities and enormous databases are required. "We need to have very advanced sensing capabilities, with very large data pools, that will allow these AI algorithms to analyze." He offered the example of a radar scanning the same sector of terrain for years. "The moment you see a change, you can dive backward into this data and deduce what is going to happen moving forward. That is the greatness of AI." IAI is already building these databases and establishing dedicated units of professionals who know how to integrate AI tools into operational systems.
When asked what the next war will look like, Levy was blunt: "We've learned that wars no longer happen on the border. There is no line you can call a frontline where the war takes place." The Yom Kippur War model - where citizens in Tel Aviv lived far from the front - no longer applies. "Look at Ukraine, look at Israel. The next wars are happening in cities."
The implication, he said, is that the military is no longer the only body operating during combat. "There are civilians, security forces, rescue forces, hospitals, banks. Everyone relies on the same database." Levy argues that an ambulance, a rescue helicopter, and a military force need to operate on the same data network and share the same situational picture. "Everyone sits on the same planning basis, and everyone needs to know how to cooperate."
The technology to enable this already exists, he noted. "From here, we need to receive budgets and more budgets. I know it's difficult. This war has cost the State of Israel a lot of money and will cost more, but if we don't invest today, we won't have the answer tomorrow."
Asked to picture the battlefield 10 or 20 years from now, Levy used the metaphor of playing on multiple chess boards simultaneously. "Think of Israel facing Yemen, Iran, Syria, Lebanon. This whole business is becoming very, very complex in terms of decision-making."
The future lies in a world of sensors, munitions, autonomous systems, and spatial control. All systems must "talk" to each other, share data, and select the optimal response at any given moment based on the threat and available resources. "The data must flow from the same information pool to everyone, and at any given moment, for any given scenario, the system must find the optimal response based on the sensors and the effectors or munitions it possesses."
Technologically, this is not science fiction, Levy added. "It’s all relatively uncomplicated mathematics and computing tools that already exist today. We just need to connect them together to create the future solution."
The drone threat occupies a significant place in the conception of the future battlefield. Levy admitted Israel began addressing it "a bit later than perhaps we should have," partly because of budget constraints and shifting priorities. The first step in dealing with a drone is detection. "If I don't know it's there, I can't do anything about it. I think today we know how to provide a perfect response regarding the detection of drones."
After detection comes interception. Levy noted several possible layers: kinetic means, electronic warfare, and lasers. "The answer needs to be all of the above. When you are talking about large quantities, about swarms, things coming from various places, you need a resilient and robust solution. Such a solution must integrate several technologies working together." He added that MAFAT (the Defense Ministry's Directorate of Defense Research and Development) is currently working on an integrated national-level solution, with defense industries presenting their capabilities and integrating into the overarching response.
Levy also addressed the long-standing debate over whether Israel needs an independent missile corps. "I don't think the question is really whether to have a missile corps or not. A missile corps is a means. Does Israel need missiles that will provide a response in certain situations? Yes." The recent war, he said, illustrated the need for missiles. "Missiles give you superiority at a given moment."
The question of who operates them - the Air Force, ground forces, or a separate corps - is secondary in his view. "That is a marginal question; it doesn't matter. The real question is whether orders and requirements will truly be issued here to develop such missiles."

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei calls on AI companies to slow down AI development amid superintelligence risks.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:24:46 UTC
01:24:46 KST

Amodei's announcement came days after the AI company revealed that its models were being used for cyberattacks, propaganda campaigns and dangerous biological research.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Saturday called on artificial intelligence (AI) companies to slow down the development of the powerful technology, as concerns mount over the risks of "superintelligent" computer systems.
Superintelligence is the theoretical point when AI's capabilities exceed human intelligence.
His comments came a few days after AI researcher Jacob Coxon, who left OpenAI to join Anthropic, decided to leave the industry, accusing both US companies and industry giants of "gambling with our lives" in the race to develop models capable of self-improvement.
"We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain," wrote Amodei in a post on his personal website.
"AI brings risks, and because it is such a powerful technology, these risks are serious."
"Not building the technology deprives humanity of benefits or simply places AI in the hands of authoritarian powers, while building it too fast is reckless. We have sought a middle way," said Amodei, who co-founded Anthropic, which developed AI model Claude, with his sister Daniela in 2021.
"But over the last few months, I have become convinced that fully addressing the risks requires even more prudence," added the Anthropic chief executive.
Amodei's statement echoes another call by Anthropic in early June to slow or suspend development. Then in late July, Sam Altman, head of Anthropic rival OpenAI – developers of ChatGPT – said developers might need to voluntarily pump the brakes on their rapid advances to give society a chance to catch up.
Around the same time as the June statement, more than 1,000 employees at cutting-edge AI companies, including Amodei himself, signed a petition calling on the US government to help "deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development."
OpenAI had revealed that during testing, the AI models broke out of their confined environment, connected to the internet and infiltrated Hugging Face, a site developers use to store and share code.
Earlier this week, 27-year-old Jacob Coxon, sounded the alarm after spending the past three years pre-training AI models, first at OpenAI and then, this year, at its rival Anthropic, which he considered more cautious in its approach.
Pretraining is the stage where AI models absorb vast quantities of data of all different kinds, from pictures to videos to voice recordings, which help it understand things to then be able to generate images or answer user prompts on chat platforms.
"Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives," said Coxon in a chain of posts on X on Tuesday.
"The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade," he added.

USA Approves $4 Billion Military Loan for Poland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:20:08 UTC
01:20:08 KST

The United States has signed a $4 billion loan agreement with Poland under the Foreign Military Financing (FMF) program for the purchase of American weapons.
Poland’s Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defence, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, announced the signing of the agreement.
News of the agreement’s preparation first emerged in June 2026. Under the agreement, Poland received a loan guarantee from the U.S. government, which will enable the Polish state-owned bank BGK to raise funds for the Polish Armed Forces Support Fund (FWSZ).
The funds raised will be used to co-finance contracts already concluded and to finance new agreements for the procurement of U.S. defense equipment.
The funds will likely be used, in particular, to expedite the delivery of Apache helicopters and to order additional F-35s.
“The allocation of $4 billion to Poland under the Foreign Military Financing (FMF) program is another important step in the modernization of the Polish Armed Forces. The agreement signed today strengthens the strategic partnership between Poland and the United States, accelerates the implementation of previously concluded contracts (in particular, regarding Apache helicopters), and enhances Poland’s defense capabilities,” said Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz
In total, since the beginning of 2022, Poland has concluded six FMF agreements with the United States totaling $19.08 billion. The first direct loan of $2 billion was finalized on September 25, 2023, the second for the same amount on July 1, 2024, and the third for $3.08 billion on October 1, 2024. Subsequently, the United States provided three loan guarantees of $4 billion each: on December 5, 2024 and on July 25, 2025.
The FWSZ is a special government instrument created for the rapid and large-scale modernization of the Polish army. The fund’s total annual budget for 2026 is planned at 77.2 billion zlotys ($19.9 billion).
The main feature of the fund is that it is financed primarily through loans and bond issuances. This creates Poland’s so-called ‘off-budget debt,’ as these expenditures are not included in the country’s official state budget.
As of September 2026, the fund had accumulated significant debt, which is growing rapidly due to constant borrowing. The fund’s actual debt already stands at 118.9 billion zlotys (approximately $30.6 billion), and by the end of 2026, this amount could reach 157.5 billion zlotys ($40.6 billion).
Overall, the fund’s total debt is expected to exceed 300 billion zlotys (about $77.3 billion) by 2029.
Despite the enormous amount of funds, the Fund is also known for regularly failing to meet its spending targets. For example, in the first half of 2026, the fund spent only about 14 percent of the amount planned for the year. And in 2025, the FWSZ was able to use about 79 percent of the planned funds.

War Books to be rewritten by the end of this year
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
17:15:40 BST
01:15:40 KST

The government has committed to rewriting the War Books by the end of this year as part of an accelerated Home Defence Programme, with defence planning feeding into the work, according to a written answer published on Friday.
Louise Sandher-Jones, Parliamentary Under-Secretary and Minister for the Armed Forces, was responding to Stuart Anderson, the Conservative MP for South Shropshire, who had asked what progress has been made on ensuring plans under the programme meet needs in the event of escalation to war. She said the Ministry of Defence continues to update its own homeland defence and transition to war plans while playing a significant role in the wider Cabinet Office-led programme.
On the acceleration announced in July, she said: “A key element of this is the commitment to re-write, by the end of this year, the War Books. Defence planning is informing our input to these War Books as we support the Home Defence Programme focus on resilience and preparedness in the face of the range of threats and risks that the UK faces.”
Because homeland defence is an inherently whole-of-government effort, she said, the department is working closely with others to ensure all plans align in meeting needs in the event of escalation to war. The War Book is one of the oldest instruments of British government planning, originating before the First World War as a single volume setting out precisely which departments would take which actions, in which order, on the transition from peace to war.
The concept was maintained through both world wars and the Cold War, covering everything from the requisitioning of shipping and the imposition of censorship to the dispersal of government and the mobilisation of reserves, with each department holding its own chapter and the whole coordinated centrally. The practice fell away after 1991, when the prospect of a transition to general war ceased to shape Whitehall planning.
The Defence Readiness Bill
Running alongside the planning work is a legislative element, since the Strategic Defence Review committed the government to a Defence Readiness Bill, which the minister said is being developed in close partnership with the rest of government for introduction within this Parliament.
Luke Pollard, Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, set out its intended scope in a separate answer the same day, responding to Helen Maguire, the Liberal Democrat MP for Epsom and Ewell, who had asked about broadening it to cover national resilience and other risks in the national risk register. He said: “The legislation will help ensure the Government has the powers needed to respond to sub-threshold and hybrid threats, while providing a framework of reserve powers that could be activated during a national crisis or escalation towards conflict.”
On the question of scope, he said work is under way across government and that consideration is being given to how the legislation can support wider national resilience objectives. The risks being planned against continue to be informed by the National Risk Register, the public-facing version of the National Security Risk Assessment.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told the Commons this week that he would report back to the House with plans for a national conversation about the threat, saying the aim is to raise awareness without raising alarm, after being asked whether Britain should run a public awareness campaign of the kind seen in Finland and the Baltic states.

Ukraine’s Third Army Corps won’t just hold Donetsk fortress cities. It’s building mission to pull civilians out of them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:13:47 UTC
01:13:47 KST

The Ukrainian soldiers simultaneously perform defensive, logistical, and humanitarian functions. Ukraine’s Third Army Corps is launching a separate AB3.HUMANITARIAN initiative to evacuate civilians from frontline settlements. This means saving families, elderly people, children, people with disabilities, from Russian attacks, and those who often have no way to leave on their own.
Recently, the 3rd Army Corps, led by Andrii Biletskyi, the Azov founder, has been tasked with stabilizing the Donetsk front, where Russia is battering the fortress cities that have held since 2014. As that fighting grinds toward towns like Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, the civilians still living in them have to be moved, often under fire.
Robots and boats reach cut-off towns
The corps says its soldiers already regularly pull residents out of settlements near the front. The hard part is the routes: roads watched by Russian drones, approaches too dangerous for a bus or an ambulance. To work them, the evacuation teams use ground robots, armored vehicles, motorboats, and whatever else the terrain demands, reaching places that an ordinary rescue cannot.
Unmanned ground vehicles have become a fixture of Ukrainian evacuations, part of a wider shift in which the military ran more than 100,000 robot logistics and evacuation missions in the first eight months of 2026.
A fund pays for more trips
Making it a formal mission is also about money. The corps' own Staff Fund is opening financing for the vehicles and equipment that the evacuation teams need. The corps expects this dedicated support to enable it to run more trips, into more places, more often, than volunteer improvisation allowed.
The corps urges people to leave early
The appeal underneath the announcement is blunt.
"Take care of yourselves and your loved ones, and leave in good time, because the lives of our people are the most precious thing," the corps wrote.
The plea matters because many who remain on the front line are the least able to move on short notice, and the window to reach them narrows every time the front creeps closer, while roads get more dangerous.

Will the Houthi attacks activate the Mecca Pact?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:06:48 UTC
01:06:48 KST

Will the Houthi attacks activate the Mecca Pact?
If there is a Saudi request, Pakistan and Turkiye will intervene, but direct involvement in the Yemen war is unlikely.
Yemen’s Houthi rebels have captured Mocha port and now threaten to control the main waterway of the Bab al-Mandeb strait. They have also attacked several cities in Saudi Arabia, wounding about 70 people, including women and children.
The repeated attacks against Saudi energy, civil, and defence facilities, combined with the maritime blockage by Iran and its Yemeni partner the Houthis, directly raise the question of the Mecca Pact’s operationalisation between Saudi Arabia, Turkiye, and Pakistan.
The Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia can activate the mutual defence agreement. If that happens, what could a Pakistani and Turkish intervention look like?
The answer to this question necessitates some crucial background first.
The US – the main security partner of the Gulf states – has signalled for a while now that it expects regional countries to take primary responsibility for their own defence and deterrence, with US help remaining critical but limited.
That posture is already visible on the ground. Since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran, the US has not been able to provide comprehensive defence for its regional partners. On several occasions, it has even failed to stop attacks on its own bases in the Gulf.
With US presence receding and Washington emphasising regional burden-sharing, Gulf states have had to look into a new defence architecture. In September 2025, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed their first mutual defence agreement, which expanded in August this year to include Turkiye and became the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement.
The three countries have since established a joint secretariat, with its headquarters in Riyadh, with Pakistan taking the chairmanship for an initial three-year term.
The pact remains in a gestation period. It does not publicly identify the thresholds or scenarios under which a member would move to direct military intervention. Its organisational and institutional structure, including rules of engagement, mechanisms of consultation, and collective defence and deterrence, are yet to be formally developed.
Now, back to the question of how the pact will be operational if a member state is attacked.
Earlier this week, Pakistan’s Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said that an unprovoked aggression against Saudi Arabia, or a spillover of the Yemen conflict into the kingdom, would make the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement operational, adding that “there should be no doubt in this.”
Asif, however, did not share specific details on what shape that operationalisation would take. Last month, Turkiye’s Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan clarified that the Mecca Pact would work the same way as NATO: If a member state is attacked, it must actively request and define the specific type of help it needs.
NATO’s Article 4 allows for a member to call alliance consultations and exchange of information. Article 5 requires mutual assistance from allies, but it leaves each state to decide the nature of that assistance.
In 2012, after Syria shot down a Turkish warplane, Ankara invoked Article 4 for consultation and requested specific defence assistance. Instead of demanding direct military intervention, the Turkish government explicitly asked for Patriot missile defence batteries. NATO approved the request and deployed the systems to protect Turkish airspace.
In this context, if the Mecca Pact is to be operationalised, it would have to be Saudi Arabia that defines the type of military assistance and involvement that it needs. If, for example, Riyadh makes an actual request for Pakistani direct military intervention, beyond materiel and intelligence support, Islamabad would be obliged to comply. But the request, and the scale of the response, would still likely need to be defined and agreed in a consultation meeting.
For now, none of this has been tested as Riyadh has not invoked the pact with either Pakistan or Turkiye.
In the meantime, diplomatic efforts have intensified, with Pakistani Field Marshal Asim Munir and Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud talking to Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.
Islamabad has also publicly urged Iran to rein in the Houthis from attacking Saudi Arabia and threatening the Bab al-Mandeb, and has reminded Tehran of Pakistan’s commitment to Riyadh’s defence through the pact. Ankara would likely play its own part in diplomatically restraining the Houthis and Iran.
If diplomacy fails and Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia or the Bab al-Mandeb continue, Turkiye and Pakistan would likely expand the air and technological support they already provide. Islamabad already has an air squadron of about 16 JF-17 Thunder multirole aircraft, defence systems, and thousands of troops deployed in Saudi Arabia.
But a direct military operation by Pakistani forces inside Yemen remains unlikely at the moment. Given the disastrous and lasting impacts of its participation in the Afghan war against the Soviet Union on behalf of the US, Pakistan would be far more wary of joining a war against Iran and its allies, for fear of spillover into its western border provinces’ economy, domestic security, sectarian balance, and societal harmony. Pakistani leaders would find it hard to build domestic consensus for direct attacks on the Houthis or a fight with Iran.
The likely scenario is that Pakistan would increase joint diplomatic pressure on Iran to restrain the Houthis, further augment its support for Saudi defence, and push for a multinational naval coalition to secure the Bab al-Mandeb. Adopting this restraint would still keep the essence of the Mecca Pact intact, while putting more weight behind regional de-escalation.
The new security architecture that agreements like the Mecca Pact are setting up will take years to mature. Until the mechanisms and rules of collective response develop, Pakistan’s existing bilateral defence relationships with Saudi Arabia and other Arab partners will continue to focus on defence needs.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

====================================================================================================

Different video game genres alter brain activity and enhance cognition in unique ways
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:00:51 UTC
01:00:51 KST

Playing different types of video games can improve a person’s cognitive abilities and alter how their brain operates at rest. A new study reveals that fast-paced action games and turn-based strategy games both enhance mental performance, but action games lead to more pronounced and long-lasting neural adaptations. The research was recently published in the journal Brain Sciences.
As video games have grown into a dominant form of global entertainment, researchers have increasingly investigated their potential to shape the brain. Past studies have suggested that regular gameplay can boost attention, memory, and executive function. Executive function refers to a set of mental skills that include flexible thinking and self-control.
Researchers Jingqing Lu, Dezhong Yao, and their colleagues at the University of Electronic Science and Technology of China wanted to understand how distinct game genres uniquely influence the brain. Different genres require vastly different mental resources to succeed. Fast-paced action games demand rapid reflexes, hand-eye coordination, and the simultaneous monitoring of multiple visual targets. Turn-based strategy card games focus on long-term planning, probabilistic reasoning, and keeping track of past moves.
The researchers designed a study to compare these two specific gaming experiences. They aimed to track how dedicated practice alters performance on mental tests and changes the brain’s baseline electrical activity. To measure this baseline activity, they used electroencephalography, commonly known as EEG, to record electrical signals while participants rested with their eyes closed. Resting-state EEG provides an objective measure of the brain’s intrinsic activity and structural efficiency when not actively engaged in a task.
The researchers recruited 68 college students who did not regularly play video games. They randomly assigned the participants to play either an action game, League of Legends, or a strategy card game, Legends of the Three Kingdoms. Each participant played their assigned game for one hour a day, five days a week, over a span of 20 weeks.
To track changes, the research team tested the participants at six different points over 30 weeks. This timeline included a baseline test, mid-training assessments, a post-training test at 20 weeks, and a final retention test 10 weeks after all training had stopped. At these sessions, participants completed three computer-based cognitive tasks. The researchers separately recorded their resting brain activity during these testing weeks.
The first task evaluated distributed spatial attention, which is the ability to monitor multiple locations at once without moving the eyes. Participants had to remember the location of a quick visual cue. They later had to identify a symbol that appeared in that exact spot on a screen.
Over the course of the training, both groups became faster and more accurate at this spatial attention task. However, the action game group experienced a much larger boost in accuracy than the strategy game group. This advantage for the action game players remained robust at the final 10-week follow-up.
The second assessment was a spatial working memory task. It required participants to observe a grid of flashing squares and recall if a current square matched one that flashed several turns earlier. Working memory acts as a temporary mental workspace for holding and processing information on the fly.
Participants in both the action and strategy groups responded faster on the working memory task as their training progressed. Both groups maintained their initial accuracy levels as their speed improved. The action game players consistently demonstrated higher overall performance throughout the testing period.
The final task measured executive function by presenting participants with colored arrows. The participants had to press buttons based on specific rules that pitted the color of the arrow against the direction it was pointing. This forced them to suppress their instinctive reactions and follow the changing logical rules.
In this executive function test, both groups substantially reduced their reaction times without sacrificing accuracy. The researchers observed that differences in accuracy between the two groups were not statistically significant. This indicates that both game types provided a similar enhancement to the speed of cognitive processing.
During the EEG sessions, the researchers looked at specific frequencies of brainwaves. They focused on slow-moving delta and theta waves, as well as functional connections in the alpha band. Delta and theta waves are associated with neural adaptability and readiness. Alpha-band connections indicate how efficiently different brain regions communicate with one another.
The physiological data showed that both groups developed increased delta and theta wave power over the 30 weeks. They also showed a reduction in alpha-band connectivity. A decrease in alpha connectivity suggests that the brain is streamlining its networks. It appears to cut out redundant pathways to process information more efficiently.
The action game group exhibited much stronger brain wave changes than the strategy game group. Ten weeks after the training ended, the action game players had notably higher slow-wave activity than their strategy game counterparts. They also displayed much lower alpha connectivity. These physiological shifts closely mirrored the action group’s superior performance on the attention and memory tasks.
While these results highlight the mental benefits of gaming, the findings apply specifically to the structured environment of the experiment. The participants only played for one hour a day. They avoided extreme gaming habits that could lead to fatigue or behavioral issues. The study also focused exclusively on young, healthy college students.
The way video games affect the brains of children, older adults, or individuals with cognitive impairments might look entirely different. Additionally, the researchers relied on self-reported logs and limited account data to verify that participants were not playing other video games during the study. This method relies on honesty and memory, which can introduce errors.
The researchers also did not track the participants’ academic workloads during the testing phases. Heavy coursework or stressful exams could have independently influenced their mental fatigue or cognitive performance. Future research will need to incorporate broader age groups and track daily stress levels to fully understand how digital environments shape human brain function.
The study, “Effects of Video Game Type on Cognitive Performance and Brain Functional Connectivity: A Longitudinal EEG Study,” was authored by Jingqing Lu, Ruifang Cui, Lijun Jiang, Chenyu Mu, Weiyi Ma, Diankun Gong, and Dezhong Yao.

====================================================================================================

Number of UK anti-migrant vigilante groups surges in last 18 months
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:00:38 UTC
01:00:38 KST

At least 28 anti-migrant vigilante groups have formed in the UK in the last 18 months, ranging from unauthorised street patrols claiming to protect women and children to groups harassing migrants in France and blocking ports.
From Belfast to the south coast of England, the number of active groups has surged since the summer of 2025, according to analysis by the Guardian, amid widespread concerns over fresh disorder after black-clad vigilantes, many of them wearing balaclavas, blocked roads in Portsmouth and Dover last weekend.
Often arguing that they are filling gaps left by the police or taking action on migration that the government is unable to, the groups range from small-scale community patrols near asylum-seeker accommodation to those attempting to stop migrants crossing the Channel from France.
They include Scots Active, which conducts late-night patrols around Glasgow city centre claiming to protect the public from migrants, sometimes wearing balaclavas and stab-proof vests. It says its activities help ensure the safety of women and girls. It was one of two groups banned from TikTok earlier this year after reportedly sharing footage claiming to expose migrant hotels.
Another is the British Security Project, a self-styled civilian safety group that has described itself as the “tip of the spear in mass deportation under a Rupert Lowe government”. It recruits “visible deterrent patrol” volunteers via its website and social media platforms, and responds to reports from the public about incidents claiming to involve migrants. It aims to “provide 124,000 security personnel to public spaces by 2035”, according to its Facebook page.
When the Guardian contacted the group for comment, a spokesperson said it was neither vigilante nor anti-migrant. “The British Security Project is a developing non-profit community protection organisation committed to lawful, peaceful and accountable volunteer action,” they said. “It has no police or immigration-enforcement powers, does not permit people to be targeted because of their nationality or immigration status, and expressly prohibits vigilantism, intimidation, racism and unlawful discrimination.”
Members of another group, Raise the Colours, made several trips to France in 2025 to try to stop migrants crossing the Channel in small boats. They filmed themselves claiming to have slashed dinghies on French beaches. France subsequently banned 10 members from the country.
Members of far-right Patriot Platform blocked roads near Dover for several hours last Saturday, disrupting traffic to and from the port. Kent police initially said they had received no warning, but later admitted officers had failed to act on calls made on Friday evening.
On Sunday, about 200 black-clad men gathered in Portsmouth after 120 asylum seekers rescued from a dinghy were brought ashore there. They blocked roads and allegedly assaulted several police officers.
The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, urged police on Thursday to curb the activities of such groups, telling senior officers to make full use of their powers.
The rise in vigilante groups is a recent phenomenon, overwhelmingly happening in the last year. Of the 31 active groups the Guardian was able to establish initiation dates for, 28 were set up since last summer, with a spike in August 2025 after Raise the Colours’ flag operation and unrest at an asylum hotel in Epping. Setup dates were taken from online activity on Facebook and Instagram, domain name registrations and media reports.
To classify as anti-migrant vigilantes, the Guardian considers that a group must have taken the law into its own hands in the name of opposing migrants or asylum seekers. Groups limited to more conventional protests and far-right political parties were not included.
In a campaign of intimidation last summer, a vigilante group called the Belfast Nightwatch First Division was involved in targeting dark-skinned males in the city, challenging them to produce identification documents.
Dr Julia Ebner, an expert on extremism at the University of Oxford, said the figures showed a rapid shift in the ways anti-migrant activists were mobilising which was particularly striking.
“At the heart of most vigilante groups is the claim that the authorities are incapable or unwilling to protect a country’s citizens,” she said. “This is a dangerous dynamic, because when trust in authorities is undermined this can quickly translate into justifications of running their own policing operations or even violent campaigns – all supposedly for a good cause.
“Another underlying narrative that is not new but has been amplified across social media is the idea that ‘our’ women and children are threatened by men of migrant backgrounds. There is also a performative aspect of vigilante movements: uniforms, patrols and security equipment can project authority and legitimacy even when the groups themselves are relatively small.
“This can help far-right movements recruit new members and produce visually appealing social media content to increase their public profile and expand their followership.”
 Alex MacKinnon, a researcher at Hope Not Hate, said vigilantism had long been part of far-right activism, but that there had been a dramatic increase in extremists’ grassroots efforts in the last 18 months.
 “While vigilante groups typically purport to protect the wider community, the majority do not properly vet their members, resulting in several being exposed for their violent criminal histories,” he said.
“Furthermore, they regularly engage in intimidatory behaviour, as seen in Patriot Platform’s Dover demonstration. Vigilante groups of this type often promote aggressive anti-migrant agendas, using ‘community protection’ as a cover for racist thuggery.” 
 In response to the Guardian’s analysis, the National Police Chiefs’ Council said it was important for the public to report concerns about crime and safety.
“Police officers are specially trained to respond to a wide range of incidents safely and lawfully,” a spokesperson said. “While we understand people may want to protect their communities, taking enforcement into your own hands can be dangerous, and could compromise a police investigation.”

Türkiye also welcomed the Iraqi government’s condemnation of the attacks and its immediate launch of an investigation to clarify the incident and identify those responsible.

Russia refuses to stop attacking Ukraine during peace negotiations, Lavrov says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:00:32 UTC
01:00:32 KST

Moscow will not pause the full-scale invasion of Ukraine while conducting negotiations for a peace settlement, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said on Sept. 12.
Lavrov's comments come the same day that President Volodymyr Zelensky said he would be willing to meet face-to-face with Russian President Vladimir Putin for peace talks at the G20 leaders' summit in Miami in December.
Speaking to the Russian news outlet Vesti, Lavrov claimed the Kremlin was open to talks — while pouring cold water on the idea of a ceasefire or a Putin-Zelensky summit in Miami.
"We are still ready for negotiations, but the (war against Ukraine) will not be stopped during this period," Lavrov said.
"We have already had this experience and have drawn conclusions," he added, perhaps referring to the previous periods of brief, limited truces that Russian forces nonetheless violated.
Regarding Zelensky's invitation to meet Putin at the G20, Lavrov reiterated the Kremlin's standard excuse: insisting the leaders can only meet in Moscow.
"On this matter, I believe (Kremlin Spokesperson) Dmitry Peskov has already spoken. An invitation was sent to (Zelensky). If he wants to meet, then he should come," Lavrov said.
read also
After refusing even a temporary ceasefire or a leader-level meeting in a noncombatant country, Lavrov went on to emphasize the level of "goodwill" Moscow was displaying in the peace process.
"This is already a huge gesture of goodwill on our part, because (Zelensky) has not yet canceled his decree banning contacts with Putin and his team," Lavrov claimed. "So, we are not lacking in goodwill, while he, it seems, lacks good intentions."
Zelensky and Putin have not met in person since before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
While Zelensky has expressed willingness to sit down with Putin on a number of occasions, he has ruled out Moscow as a venue for peace talks. He has not, however, demanded the Russian president visit Ukraine.
Instead, Zelensky has repeatedly proposed meeting in a third country — a proposal the Kremlin has consistently denied.
Kyiv has also insisted that negotiations take place during a cessation of hostilities, and has said it is willing to uphold an unconditional ceasefire if Russia is willing to do the same.
Lavrov and Zelensky's comments follow a renewed U.S.-led effort to resume negotiations between Kyiv and Moscow. U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited both capitals for separate talks with the Russian and Ukrainian governments in September, though the discussions did not produce a breakthrough.
At the end of the latest round of talks, the U.S. envoys said they hoped to resume trilateral negotiations with all parties present. Zelensky has affirmed the need for trilateral talks, and the Kremlin has said it isn't ruling out this format — though no future talks have been announced.
