Britain’s sanctions on Israeli settlements reveal hypocrisy of its ‘occupation’ policy - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
14:38:05 UTC
23:38:05 KST

So the gloves are off.
The British government has banned trade with Israeli communities in Judea and Samaria, prohibited settlement goods, and restricted related services.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband went further, accusing “settler terrorists” of carrying out “ethnic cleansing.”
Chief Rabbi Ephraim Mirvis called it “a dark day for British Jews.” He is right.
The announcement came three days before Rosh Hashanah. During the High Holy Days, synagogues across Britain will be packed. Their congregants will gather behind security guards, locked doors, and barriers, conscious that simply attending Jewish worship can make them a target.
For me, this is personal. We are approaching the first anniversary of the horrific terrorist attack at Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation on Yom Kippur. Two worshipers were killed and others seriously injured, including a friend of my son. The synagogue is less than a mile from my former home.
As another Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur approach, I fear for family and friends who will be especially vulnerable. God forbid that there should be another attack.
The British government will insist that its policy targets settlements, not Jews. But ministers cannot ignore the atmosphere in which their words are heard.
British Jews now feel less secure
At a moment of acute anxiety, branding Israelis as perpetrators of “ethnic cleansing” and turning Israel into a pariah makes British Jews feel less, not more, secure.
The timing is deplorable for another reason. Israel is weeks away from an election. President Isaac Herzog has called the move gross interference in Israel’s democratic process.
Whatever London intended, sanctions imposed during an election campaign will inevitably influence it and may strengthen precisely the politicians Britain opposes.
Israel’s response was swift. It announced the closure of the British Consulate in east Jerusalem and barred 12 British politicians and activists from entering, including Jeremy Corbyn, Diane Abbott, John McDonnell, Zarah Sultana, and every Green Party MP.
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich had demanded the expulsion of the British ambassador. National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir suggested that Israel recognize Argentine sovereignty over the Malvinas, known in Britain as the Falkland Islands, and sanction Britain until its own “occupation” ends.
This sounds like political theater, but it raises a fair question: When is an occupation not an occupation? Apparently, when Britain is doing the occupying.
London calls Judea and Samaria “occupied Palestinian territory.” Jewish communities beyond the 1949 armistice lines are treated as inherently illegal. Yet the Falklands, controlled by Britain since 1833 and claimed by Argentina ever since, are called a “British Overseas Territory.”
There are important differences. Falkland Islanders voted overwhelmingly to remain British, while Palestinians do not want Israeli rule. But the United Nations still recognizes a sovereignty dispute over the islands and calls for negotiations.
Britain says history, security, and the wishes of the present population matter. That is a reasonable argument. It is simply one Britain rarely permits Israel to make.
The Chagos Islands are even more uncomfortable.
Britain separated them from Mauritius, forcibly removed their inhabitants, and retained Diego Garcia for a vital British-American military base. In 2019, the International Court of Justice said Britain’s administration was wrongful and should end rapidly.
Britain did not leave. It eventually agreed to recognize Mauritian sovereignty while leasing Diego Garcia back for 99 years.
Then US President Donald Trump reversed his support, called the deal an “act of GREAT STUPIDITY,” and Britain put it on indefinite hold.
London therefore understands that international rulings do not make security needs and strategic geography disappear. When British interests are involved, there can be delay, compromise, and special arrangements. Israel is offered condemnation and sanctions.
Judea and Samaria were not the sovereign territory of a Palestinian state when Israel captured them from Jordan in 1967. The pre-1967 boundary was an armistice line, not a permanent border.
The Jewish connection to Hebron, Shiloh, and Beit El is thousands of years old.
None of that erases Palestinian rights or ends the legal argument over settlements. E1 is sensitive, and its consequences deserve serious discussion.
But this history cannot honestly be reduced to the single word “occupation,” and sanctions cannot substitute for negotiation.
Only last year, Britain recognized a Palestinian state whose final borders, capital, government, and security arrangements had not been agreed with Israel. Now it is using economic punishment to advance its preferred territorial outcome.
There is also a widespread suspicion that this is partly about British politics. The Labour party is losing support on its Left to the Green Party. The Greens immediately welcomed the sanctions and demanded more.
The measure looks less like peacemaking than political positioning designed to stem that flow of votes. The result is a policy announced before the Jewish New Year, during an Israeli election campaign, and against the warnings of British Jewish leaders. It has provoked retaliation, damaged diplomatic relations, and increased the anxiety of a community already living behind guarded doors.
Closing the British Consulate is a serious escalation, and expelling the ambassador would sacrifice a useful diplomatic channel. Israel should instead keep him in Jerusalem and ask him a simple question: Why are Britain’s territorial disputes historical, strategic, and complicated, while Israel’s can be reduced to one condemnatory word?
Britain is entitled to defend its interests. It is not entitled to deny that Israel has history, interests, and security needs of its own.
An occupation, it seems, is only not an occupation when Britain is doing the occupying.
The writer is a rabbi and physician. He writes and teaches on Jewish ethics, leadership, and resilience. His work appears on rabbidrjonathanlieberman.substack.com and youtube.com. @rabbidrjonathanlieberman

BRICS summit: Iran, UAE, others urge restraint over Middle East escalation

The BRICS group of nations unanimously adopted a joint declaration on Saturday, expressing "deep concern" over the war in the Middle East and urged maximum restraint, advocating for a "multilateral approach" that respects national viewpoints.
The declaration, adopted on the first day of the BRICS leaders' annual summit in New Delhi, comes at a time when US and Iran have resumed tit-for-tat strikes against each other, after a pause in fighting for much of August.
The BRICS bloc includes both Iran and Washington-ally United Arab Emirates, which was expected to make clinching a joint statement consensus a particularly challenging task for host New Delhi.
A call for exercising 'maximum restraint'
"We express deep concern over the continued escalation of tensions in the Middle East...call for exercising maximum restraint...avoiding actions that could further aggravate the situation," the 'New Delhi Declaration' said.
The declaration also reiterated the commitment of member nations to a peaceful resolution of international disputes "through dialog, consultation, and diplomacy."
In addition, they voiced concerns about the rise of "unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures" that distort trade, against the backdrop of US sanctions against Tehran amid its war with the country, and against Russia over its conflict with Ukraine.
BRICS includes Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates.

No signed Hormuz deal expected yet from Oman, Gulf States meeting on Monday, Iranian official says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
14:37:22 UTC
23:37:22 KST

A meeting between Iran and Gulf states planned for Monday in Oman will be a chance to discuss issues including the Strait of Hormuz, but is not expected to yield a signed agreement over the blockaded waterway, a senior Iranian official said on Saturday.
Iran has been negotiating for months with Oman, which controls the opposite bank of the strait, over a deal that would govern transport through it. Oman has long said other Arab countries in the Gulf support its negotiations.
Tehran announced on Friday that it was planning to attend a meeting with Gulf countries in Oman on Monday. Oman has not officially announced the meeting, and other regional states have so far remained silent. Bahrain said on Saturday it would not attend meetings with Iran.
The Kingdom of Bahrain said it will not attend the meeting to discuss the Strait of Hormuz until diplomatic ties between the two countries are restored, according to state media.
Oman called for meeting over Strait of Hormuz
The Iranian official, who discussed the plans on condition of anonymity, said Monday's meeting was called at Oman's initiative, and would provide a forum to discuss other regional issues as well as Hormuz.
According to the Iranian official, Iran still wants an agreement that would allow it to collect fees from ships that use the strait, which Oman rejects.
Around a fifth of global oil supplies transited the strait before the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February, launching the war.
Global oil prices have surged over the past week after the United States and Iran both fired on tankers in the strait, and Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen advanced near another crucial Middle East conduit for oil, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula.
Iran sees possible meeting as a path to open the Strait
Speaking to the semi-official Tasnim news agency on Saturday, an unnamed Iranian official source said any understanding between Iran and Oman does not provide for the immediate reopening of the Strait of Hormuz but establishes the basis on which it could reopen.
The source said the arrangement would be a step toward Iran exercising sovereignty over the strait and that its reopening depended entirely on the United States meeting Tehran's conditions.

‘Why the hell are they laughing?’ Mamdani, AOC clip at 9/11 memorial sparks uproar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

A four-second clip from New York’s ceremony marking the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks has ignited a political storm after Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez were filmed smiling and speaking while the names of victims were being read aloud.
The footage, taken from a broadcast of Friday’s ceremony at Ground Zero, shows Mamdani standing beside Ocasio-Cortez, the progressive Democratic congresswoman widely known as AOC, as the two briefly talk and smile. Moments earlier, the broadcast had shown a young man crying beside the memorial, and the abrupt transition between the images quickly drew criticism from conservative politicians and commentators.
The ceremony lasted roughly four hours, and their conversation could not be heard. Michael Ragusa, who previously served as security chief for former New York Mayor Rudy Giuliani, said the suggestion that the pair had been laughing during the ceremony was misleading. He said he had been standing near them and that Ocasio-Cortez was simply greeting Mamdani.
“The camera just caught her greeting him hello,” Ragusa wrote on X. “Multiple other politicians were laughing and joking behind me. Republicans and Democrats.”
Footage from other portions of the ceremony showed Mamdani standing silently with a serious expression.
CNN reported that it had contacted representatives for Mamdani and Ocasio-Cortez for comment. The brief interaction nevertheless prompted a fierce online debate, with Republicans accusing the two New York Democrats of behaving inappropriately during the solemn ceremony and others arguing that the viral clip stripped the moment of its context.
Texas Sen. Ted Cruz shared the footage, writing: “How the hell do you laugh while the names of those murdered on 9/11 are being read aloud?”
Former New York State Assemblymember Yuh-Line Niou, who also attended the ceremony, dismissed the criticism as “ridiculous talking points.”
Niou noted that many politicians do not remain for the entire ceremony, while Mamdani “stayed for every name and even stayed after to talk to families for 45 minutes.” Ocasio-Cortez also remained until the end, she said, adding that the brief interaction occurred when the congresswoman approached Mamdani to say hello.
Niou, who said she has attended the Ground Zero ceremony every year for a decade, also pushed back on the suggestion that attendees remain visibly grief-stricken throughout the hourslong event.
“My friends and neighbors are not crying for 6 hours straight,” she wrote. “We are greeting each other, hugging each other, laughing at the memories and the jokes the families tell remembering their loved ones.”
Conservative television personality Meghan McCain, daughter of the late Republican Sen. John McCain, was among those criticizing the footage, asking on social media why the two were laughing.
The controversy came during an already politically charged anniversary for Mamdani, New York City’s first Muslim mayor.
Before the ceremony began, Mamdani approached Giuliani, who led New York during the September 11 attacks, and the two shook hands. The encounter drew attention because Giuliani had only days earlier said Mamdani’s presence at the memorial offended him and compared the mayor to the September 11 hijackers.
Aides said Mamdani and Giuliani “exchanged pleasantries,” with Giuliani telling the current mayor that running New York was a difficult job. A Giuliani representative later said the former mayor told Mamdani he was praying for him.
Asked afterward what the two had discussed, Mamdani declined to elaborate.
“He came over and we both extended our hands and exchanged pleasantries,” Mamdani said, according to remarks released by his office. “I think the focus for all of us is a focus on the families, a focus on first responders and to be here and hear the names of all those who were stolen from us 25 years ago and how the families have persevered through that time.”
Later Friday, Mamdani spoke at an interfaith memorial service at St. Nicholas Greek Orthodox Church and National Shrine, which was destroyed in the September 11 attacks and later rebuilt.
“Those who attacked our city, they did so because they thought they could break us at the fractures,” Mamdani said. “They thought they could frighten us, they could make us feel alone, they could leave us on our knees.”
“How wrong they were. How quick we were to stand back up.”

In Germany, one of the suspects in the sabotage at Leipzig Airport was linked to the GRU of the Russian Federation
Kyiv • UNN
German investigators suspect Russian and Belarusian citizens of attempting to blow up a Ukrainian aircraft with a drone. One of them may be linked to the GRU
German investigators have identified two main suspects in an attempted act of sabotage at Leipzig/Halle Airport. One of them, a Russian citizen, is believed to have links to Russia’s military intelligence agency, the GRU. Welt am Sonntag reports, as cited by UNN.
Details
According to the publication, the suspects are Russian citizen Oleg L. and Belarusian citizen Andrei K. Investigators believe the Russian may have been responsible for organizing and providing logistical support for the operation, including supplying the perpetrator with explosives. One of the key pieces of evidence in the case was DNA traces found on components of equipment that was likely used to control drones. The matches were found in law enforcement databases in Finland and Lithuania.
Investigators currently know that Oleg L. entered Germany via Turkey, then traveled around the country before flying from Berlin to Serbia. According to German intelligence services, he is currently in Russia.
Investigators consider the second suspect, Andrei K., a possible direct perpetrator. According to media reports, he entered the Schengen Area via Latvia approximately one week before the attack. The man also remains at large. Investigators are also examining a possible connection between Andrei K. and a fire at a home improvement store in the Polish city of Łódź in the summer of 2024. Polish law enforcement previously treated that incident as possible sabotage with a Russian link.
What happened at Leipzig Airport
The incident occurred on August 4. According to investigators, a drone carrying explosives deliberately flew toward a Ukrainian Antonov transport aircraft and struck its wing. At the time, the aircraft was carrying approximately 25,000 liters of aviation fuel. According to a journalistic investigation, the drone may have been carrying around 1.8 kg of Semtex explosives. An explosion was avoided, likely because the detonator became detached upon impact.
Investigators believe that at least several drones may have been used in the operation. According to law enforcement, one of them may also have been involved in damaging a DHL cargo aircraft.
Germany’s Federal Prosecutor General’s Office is investigating the case on suspicion of attempting to cause an explosion and dangerously interfering with the operation of air transport.
Germany’s Response
At the beginning of September, the German government officially stated that it considered Russia responsible for the attempted act of sabotage at Leipzig/Halle Airport. Chancellor Friedrich Merz said that the operation had allegedly been prepared in Russia over several months, and that a major disaster and loss of life had been avoided only by chance. In response, Berlin announced a number of diplomatic and political measures against the Russian Federation, including the closure of Russian institutions and increased pressure במסגרת its sanctions policy.
Moscow rejected the accusations.
Reminder
Earlier, we reported that Germany was expelling more than 150 Russian diplomats and their family members following the sabotage in Leipzig.

Drones Strike Russian Aviation Plant Servicing Tu-95 Bombers and Chemical Giant in Tolyatti

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Exilenova+ on September 12, satellite fire-detection data and footage shared by local residents showed several fires in Taganrog, including near the Beriev Taganrog Aviation Scientific and Technical Complex.
The facility specializes in maintenance and modernization of Russia’s A-50 airborne early warning and control aircraft, Be-series amphibious aircraft used by the Russian Navy, and Tu-95MS/MSM strategic bombers. Russia uses Tu-95 bombers to launch Kh-101 air-launched cruise missiles against Ukraine.

Another fire was recorded near Taganrog’s automobile plant, according to satellite observations and reports from local residents.
In Tolyatti, Samara region, drones targeted the KuibyshevAzot chemical plant, according to monitoring group Exilenova+. A fire was reported on the plant’s premises following the attack.
KuibyshevAzot produces ammonia, ammonium nitrate, urea, ammonium sulfate, nitric acid, caprolactam, and polyamide products. The company is among Russia’s major producers of nitrogen fertilizers and caprolactam, a chemical used in the production of polyamide plastics and synthetic fibers.

In Malyn, an extracurricular education school damaged in a Russian bombing attack at the beginning of the full-scale war reopened its doors, enabling nearly 400 children to continue taking part in extracurricular activities. The EDUHUB opened in Zhytomyr, meanwhile, gives nearly 4,000 early childhood education teachers access to modern teaching practices. ESTDEV designed both projects so that their impact would extend beyond individual buildings and institutions and create models that could also be used in other regions of Ukraine.
“Alongside military, financial and political support for Ukraine, it is also important to invest in Ukraine’s future. Tanks help Ukraine defend its freedom today, but education helps build the country Ukrainians are fighting for. Both the EDUHUB education centre and the Malyn extracurricular education school are laying the foundations for educating the generations that will shape Ukraine’s future,” Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said.
With an investment of nearly €2.4 million from ESTDEV, the war-damaged building of the Malyn extracurricular education school was restored, while the school’s curriculum, teachers’ skills and institutional management were also updated in cooperation with Estonian experts. Nearly 1,000 young people, teachers and parents were involved in the development of the Malyn school. Teachers also took part in training courses and study visits to Estonia to learn about modern teaching methods. Both teachers and parents were able to participate in trauma-awareness training to better support children and young people affected by the war.
The EDUHUB early childhood education competence centre opened in Zhytomyr gives more than 4,000 kindergarten teachers in the Zhytomyr region access to support in applying modern teaching practices. The centre was established with the support of ESTDEV, Liechtenstein and the City of Tallinn, in cooperation with Zhytomyr City Council and the Tallinn Teachers’ House.
“When rebuilding Ukraine, it is not enough simply to restore buildings damaged by the war. Alongside rebuilding the physical environment, we must also strengthen the people, institutions and systems that help society recover from the crisis, continue developing and prepare for accession to the European Union. Both the Malyn extracurricular education school and EDUHUB are good examples of how infrastructure reconstruction and substantive development can go hand in hand,” said Andrea Kivi, Executive Director of the Estonian Centre for International Development (ESTDEV).

BRICS New Delhi declaration rejects sanctions, nuclear threats and terrorism
The BRICS nations on Saturday called out “unilateral coercive measures,” condemned terrorism, and called for the peaceful resolution of global disputes through dialogue and diplomacy in their summit declaration.
The declaration adopted by the BRICS leaders at their 18th summit in New Delhi reaffirmed the bloc’s “opposition to unilateral coercive measures that are contrary to international law” and the UN charter, and called to eliminate them.
The leaders of emerging and developing countries pointed out that sanctions and secondary sanctions have “far-reaching negative implications” including for human rights and food security, and disproportionately affect the poor and vulnerable.
The BRICS leaders repeated their earlier calls to reform the UN and other global institutions to reflect the new global realities. The New Delhi declaration stressed that no single country or group of countries should have a monopoly over senior positions in the UN – which was formed in the aftermath of World War 2.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi made the same point while addressing the leaders, saying a “rapidly changing world can no longer be governed by outdated institutions.”
⚡️ Seeds of Solidarity: BRICS Leaders Plant Saplings in Delhi#BRICS2026#BRICSIndia2026#IndiaBRICSChairshiphttps://t.co/jFFeLBM3e6pic.twitter.com/67iS09utSz
— RT_India (@RT_India_news) September 12, 2026
Importantly, China and Russia, the two BRICS members who are also permanent members of the Security Council, reiterated their support for “Brazil and India to play a greater role in the UN, including its Security Council.”
BRICS, which started as a five-member grouping two decades ago, has now expanded to 11 full members, raising its economic size and global influence.
The adoption of the 45-page declaration is itself seen as a success for Indian diplomacy, which was able to unite Iran and the United Arab Emirates – on different sides of the Middle East conflict – behind the document.
The presence of Chinese President Xi Jinping in New Delhi – after seven years – along with Russian President Vladimir Putin, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has added to the gathering’s gravitas amid rising global tensions and economic turbulence.
The BRICS leaders condemned all acts of terrorism as “criminal and unjustifiable, regardless of their motivation” – a point that host India has repeatedly made at various global fora. The declaration specifically condemned the terrorist attack in Jammu and Kashmir in April last year, in which 26 civilians were killed. India clashed with nuclear-armed neighbor Pakistan with drones and missiles following that attack.
The BRICS countries also called out the unilateral blockade of Cuba, and expressed concern over deliberate attacks on civilian infrastructure and peaceful nuclear facilities in violation of resolutions by the International Atomic Energy Agency.
While the document does not mention the Ukraine conflict, it says ”nuclear safeguards, safety, and security must always be upheld, including in armed conflicts, to protect people and the environment from harm” – an obvious reference to the Zaporozhye Nuclear Power Plant, which has seen attacks by Ukrainian forces endangering its safety.
The BRICS nations opposed the forced displacement of the Palestinian people from “Occupied Palestinian Territory,” and any geographic or demographic changes in the Gaza Strip. They further called on Israel to withdraw its forces from all Lebanese territories.
The next BRICS summit will be held in China.

Farage’s Reform UK gets second record £36 million donation in 48 hours

Cryptocurrency billionaire Christopher Harborne said on Saturday he had donated £36 million (US$49 million) to Britain’s anti-immigration Reform UK, matching an already record contribution to Nigel Farage’s party a day earlier as it prepares for the next election.
The donation gives the veteran Brexit campaigner’s party £72 million from two donors in less than 48 hours at a time when it is confronting allegations about irregularities in its funding, which it denies.
The figure exceeds what either the governing Labour Party or the opposition Conservatives spent during last year’s election campaign, according to Electoral Commission figures. The funds will help Reform, whose lead in opinion polls has slipped over the funding allegations, win over voters before the next election, which is due by 2029.

Delo’s donation on Friday had already dwarfed the previous record of £10 million that British businessman John Sainsbury, who died in 2022, had left to the Conservatives, according to the Electoral Commission’s online database.

Drones targeting the East-West oil pipeline were launched from Iraq: who is behind the attack
Kyiv • UNN
UAVs attacked the East-West oil pipeline after being launched from Maysan province. Saudi Arabia postponed its response pending Baghdad's investigation.
Iraqi authorities confirmed that the drones that attacked Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline were launched from the territory of the southern province of Maysan. Baghdad launched an investigation, while the leadership of local security agencies began removing officials from their posts. Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia is refraining from retaliatory strikes for now. This is reported by Associated Press News, according to UNN.
Details
According to Iraqi authorities, the attack was carried out from a facility in Maysan province, which borders Iran. Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zaidi ordered the immediate establishment of the circumstances surrounding the drone launch and the identification of those involved in the strike.
Amid the investigation, the leadership of the province’s security agencies has already been removed from office, including the commander of the operations command and the chief of police of Maysan. Iraqi authorities have also closed two important border crossings with Iran — Shalamcheh and Chazabeh. At the same time, the specific group that may have carried out the attack has still not been officially named. No one has claimed responsibility for the strikes. An association of pro-Iranian armed formations in Iraq denied involvement and promised to cooperate with the investigation.
Meanwhile, U.S. President Donald Trump said that Iran was likely involved in the attack, although no public evidence supporting this version has been presented so far.
Saudi Arabia said that, following an appeal from the Iraqi prime minister, it had agreed not to launch a retaliatory strike at this stage and to give Baghdad time to investigate. At the same time, Riyadh stressed that it reserves the right to take measures to protect its territory and critical infrastructure.
Context
The attacks on Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline occurred in the areas of Riyadh and Medina. Following the strikes, Saudi authorities suspended its operation for security reasons. According to preliminary data, the pumping stations that ensure the pipeline’s operation may have been damaged.
The approximately 1,200-kilometer-long East-West oil pipeline connects oil-producing regions in eastern Saudi Arabia with the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea. It is particularly important for oil exports amid problems with shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
In recent months, about 4–5 million barrels of oil per day have been transported along this route. Amid the attacks and escalating tensions around the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, oil prices exceeded $100 per barrel this week.
The situation surrounding the attack has also intensified questions about Baghdad’s control over pro-Iranian armed groups. Iraqi authorities had previously stated their intention to secure their disarmament, but a number of formations refused to comply with the relevant demands.
As of September 12, the specific perpetrators of the attack, the number and type of drones used, the extent of the damage to the oil pipeline, and the timeline for the full restoration of its operation remain unknown.

Trump says a unified Ireland would be ‘fantastic’ during Irish visit
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham maintains that a poll is ‘off the table’ as there isn’t enough popular support for Northern Ireland to leave the UK.
United States President Donald Trump has said that a unified Ireland would be “fantastic”, in remarks made during a visit to Dublin that were not welcomed by government ministers in London.
Trump’s comments on Saturday came weeks after British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said a referendum on Northern Ireland leaving the United Kingdom was “off the table”.
Recommended Stories

- list 3 of 3EU remains divided over trade sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements
“Well, I don’t want to cause any problems, but I will tell you, I’d love to see it unified,” Trump told reporters, while sitting next to Ireland’s Prime Minister, Micheal Martin.
“It’s going to happen eventually … I think it would be a fantastic thing,” he said.
“Now the UK will have something to say about it … but I think it would be a great thing,” he added.
Martin declined to respond to reporters’ questions to comment on the US president’s remarks.
Following Trump’s comments, a spokesperson for Burnham said his position on Irish unification remained unchanged.
Responding to questions from members of parliament on Wednesday about a potential poll in Northern Ireland, Burnham said: “I am not aware that there is majority public support for another referendum, and until that changes, there will not be one”.
Under the terms of the 1998 Good Friday Agreement (also known as the Belfast Agreement), a referendum on leaving the UK can be held only at the discretion of the British government.
The accord ended three decades of violence known as The Troubles. The sectarian conflict involved mostly Catholic nationalist paramilitaries seeking a united Ireland, mostly Protestant unionist paramilitaries wanting to remain part of the UK, and British troops.
Gavin Robinson, leader of the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP), Northern Ireland’s main unionist party, said that Northern Ireland’s future was a matter for its people to decide, not Trump.
“President Trump knows better than most that elections matter. Northern Ireland’s constitutional future will be decided by the people of Northern Ireland, not by commentary in London, Dublin or Washington.”
While polls show a comfortable majority in Northern Ireland favour remaining in the UK, the gap has narrowed slightly since Britain’s departure from the European Union pushed unity higher up the political agenda.
Trump also met Irish President Catherine Connolly, who was elected head of state last year. When Trump last visited Ireland as president in 2019, Connolly, an outspoken politician with left-wing foreign policy views, protested at Shannon Airport in western Ireland.
During Trump’s current visit, some supporters had urged her to speak out against US military actions around the world and defend Ireland’s neutrality.
Anti-Trump protests
Anti-war and anti-Trump protests were held in Dublin and some were planned for later in western Ireland, near Trump’s golf course in Doonbeg.
Reporting from the capital, Al Jazeera’s Milena Veselinovic said Dubliners had a “laundry list” of reasons for protesting against Trump’s visit.
“They feel that the Irish government should not be, in their words, rolling out the red carpet for someone like Trump, who they say is a cause of instability in the world and has been enabling Israel’s actions in Gaza … and destabilised the whole of the Middle East.”
Irish people are also protesting against the high cost of hosting Trump, including security, which they say could pay for other things, such as healthcare and social issues, added Veselinovic.

BRICS to seek reform of institutions of global economic governance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
14:19:57 UTC
23:19:57 KST

NEW DELHI, September 12. /TASS/. Reforming the system of global economic governance is one of BRICS’ priorities, member states said in the New Delhi Declaration adopted at the group’s 18th summit.
"With the growing share of emerging markets and developing economies (EMDEs) in global output and growth, reform of global economic governance remains a consistent BRICS priority," the document reads.
"We will continue to strengthen coordination among BRICS members to make international financial institutions more representative, transparent and accountable," the leaders added.
They reiterated "the urgent need to reform the Bretton Woods Institutions (BWI) to make them more agile, effective, credible, inclusive, fit for purpose, unbiased, accountable, and representative, to enhance their legitimacy."
"BWI governance structure should be reformed to reflect the transformation of the global economy since their establishment. The voice and representation of EMDEs in the BWI must reflect their relative position in the global economy. We also reiterate our call for improved management procedures, including through a merit-based, inclusive and transparent selection process that would increase regional diversity and representation of EMDEs in the leadership of the IMF and the World Bank," the declaration added.

In Canada, Ukrainian Pilots Prepare to Fly Gripen Fighter Jets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
14:18:51 UTC
23:18:51 KST

Ukrainian military pilots are undergoing training at the International Pilot Training School in Canada to eventually fly fighter jets, including the Gripen and F-16.
This was announced by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky after a meeting with Ukrainian pilots.
According to him, this training is part of the preparation of a new generation of pilots who are expected to strengthen Ukraine’s combat aviation.
“The pilots are training to be ready to fly modern fighter jets, including the F-16 and Gripen, and to strengthen Ukraine’s combat aviation,” the president noted.
Zelensky thanked Canada, the instructors, and the training center for training Ukrainian military personnel.
The president had previously announced that 21 Ukrainian pilots are currently undergoing training in Canada.
Photos from the meeting released by the Office of the President show that the Ukrainians are conducting training flights on L-39 aircraft and using modern simulators for Western fighter jets.
Canada allocated up to 389 million Canadian dollars for the training of Ukrainian aviation personnel between 2024 and 2029.
The program includes, in particular, the Fighter Lead-In Training phase, during which pilots master Western procedures, tactics, and skills necessary for their subsequent transition to modern Western fighter jets, specifically the F-16.
The first Ukrainian service members arrived in Canada for training in September 2024. The training includes not only pilots but also specialists in the maintenance and operation of aviation equipment, which is necessary for the future operation of the aircraft.
As part of the program, Canada also provides access to simulators and other training resources. In particular, Ukrainian military personnel can use F-16 simulators to practice flight and tactical scenarios without using actual aircraft.
As a reminder, back in December of last year, Ukraine and Sweden discussed the start of training for Ukrainian pilots and technical personnel for Gripen fighter jets.

Philippine ferry fire death toll jumps to 76
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
14:16:57 UTC
23:16:57 KST

The death toll from a Philippine ferry fire jumped to 76 on Saturday after the coast guard confirmed the discovery of 41 more bodies aboard the burnt-out vessel.
The remains will be transported to a port in Coron, Palawan, coast guard spokesperson Commodore Noemie Cayabyab said in a statement.
AFP watched hours earlier as disaster agency workers carried coffins to a cemetery in the resort town, intended for the temporary burial of victims of the fire that tore through the M/V June Aster on Wednesday.
The first 30 bodies arrived by sea earlier on Saturday as forensic specialists began the painstaking process of identifying the remains.
The confirmed death toll now stands at 76, including five bodies recovered in the immediate wake of the incident. The ship sits grounded about 7.5 kilometres (4.5 miles) off the coast.
One-metre (three-feet) deep graves have been dug to hold the victims' remains until DNA testing is completed, Kristine Ablana, a tourism official serving as an official spokesperson, told reporters on Saturday.
Relatives will be brought to identify personal items that may have belonged to family members.
"Once someone is able to verify... that this photo or these belongings are indeed those of their relative, they will be asked to provide a DNA sample," Ablana said.
Thirty passengers, including two Chilean nationals, and 13 crew have been rescued, according to the coast guard. Around a dozen people are believed to remain unaccounted for.
'Happened in seconds'
Cayabyab said in a radio interview that the fire had begun in the cargo hold, then tore through the ship within seconds.
"From the time that they heard the loud explosion, the appearance of smoke, and then fire. It spread very quickly," she said of survivors' accounts.
"Everything happened in seconds," she said, adding that those who made it off the ship had not even had time to put on life jackets.
Near the pier where the bodies were to be returned, an emotional Josenit Mayo, 40, told AFP her daughter had been aboard the ferry, returning from the capital Manila for a family visit.
"She told me 'Mom, I want to go home as I'm missing my siblings,'" Mayo said. "She insisted she was lonely."
Myra Cabilan told AFP she had flown to Coron to find her missing brother, 40-year-old Rammel Gonzaga, who had taken the ferry from Manila on a business trip with his brother-in-law.
"His wife had just given birth a month ago. He was so happy he was given a daughter," Cabilan said, fighting back tears.
"At dawn, I still believed he survived. But he's still missing. I have lost hope."
Hundreds of people desperate for news about the incident have taken to leaving comments on the Facebook page of a local mayor, searching for relatives, friends and even a dog. The archipelago nation of 116 million has a long history of disasters involving the inter-island ferries that ply its seas. Many rely on cheap and poorly regulated boats and ships for transport between the country's more than 7,000 islands, despite regular accidents.
In January, a triple-decker ferry carrying more than 340 people sank off the southern Philippines, killing at least 52 people.

BRICS nations urge 'maximum restraint' in Middle East war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
14:16:35 UTC
23:16:35 KST

Breadcrumb
BRICS nations urge 'maximum restraint' in Middle East war
Members of the 11-nation BRICS group including China, Russia, Iran and India called for calm in the Middle East at a summit in New Delhi on Saturday, overcoming earlier divisions to issue a joint statement.
Chinese President Xi Jinping, who joined Russian, Iranian, Indian and other leaders in the Indian capital, told the summit that the war in the Middle East "does not serve the common interests of the international community".
Foreign ministers of the BRICS grouping failed to agree on a joint statement when they met in New Delhi in May, with Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates divided over the war that began with US-Israeli strikes on 28 February.
But leaders issued a statement on Saturday after intense diplomatic efforts by host India, as the bloc seeks to bolster its global influence and address conflict, trade turbulence and energy security.
"We express deep concern over the continued escalation of tensions in Middle East/West Asia," the joint statement said, adding the countries "call for exercising maximum restraint, as well as avoiding actions that could further aggravate the situation".
BRICS was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by Western powers.
"We have to transform this pyramid of privilege into a platform of partnership," Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi told Xi, Russian President Vladimir Putin, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and other leaders.
Modi, opening the two-day summit, called for a system "where every country has a voice, every member has a stake and humanity's development is at the centre of every effort".
He told leaders that BRICS nations "represent 50 percent of the world's population, 40 percent of global GDP and more than 25 percent of global trade".
But finding balance in the bloc is a tough diplomatic task.
India maintains cordial relations with Iran and Israel, but is also careful to strike a delicate balance in its ties with Washington.
Iran's Pezeshkian attended the summit shortly after warning that the Middle East does not need the United States to be a "regional policeman", with the two countries at war and tensions threatening the vital Strait of Hormuz.
Pezeshkian met with Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed on the summit sidelines.
India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the US-Iran war in part by turning to Russia, despite Moscow's war in Ukraine and pressure from Washington and other Western capitals.
Modi embraced Putin before talks on Friday. Putin, who last visited India in December 2025, is one of New Delhi's most important strategic partners.
'Handling differences'
But the summit's other major focus is China.
Xi's visit is also being closely watched because it is his first to neighbouring India since 2019, and the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the nuclear-armed rivals.
Xi was given a red-carpet welcome, with an honour guard of soldiers and traditional dancers in colourful dresses, and greeted with a handshake by Modi at the summit venue.
Xi and Modi later met, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported, without providing further details.
His visit comes six years after a deadly military clash along their disputed Tibetan border, with ties gradually improving through restored flights, visas and high-level contacts.
Beijing said ahead of his visit that it was "ready to work with India... by strengthening communication, enhancing cooperation, and properly handling differences".
The underlying territorial dispute remains unresolved, and both sides retain heavy military deployments along their roughly 3,500-kilometre (2,175-mile) high-altitude border with Tibet.
"They are looking for 'early and substantial harvest' when it comes to the border issue," said Pradeep Taneja, a China-India expert at the University of Melbourne.
"You cannot have a build-up of your forces on the border... but at the same time say 'we should continue to have people-to-people relations and economic relationships'."
Deep mistrust remains, with their contested Himalayan frontier, a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry continuing to complicate ties.
Dozens of Tibetans protested in New Delhi on Friday - exiles, like their Buddhist leader the Dalai Lama, who has lived in India since fleeing a Chinese crackdown in 1959 - waving placards against Xi's visit.

suspended metal grid ceiling meets translucent and reflective surfaces inside french café
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
14:15:38 UTC
23:15:38 KST

Raw Metal and Pale Blue Accents Give Mellow Cafe Its Identity
Mellow Cafe is an unbuilt interior concept for a compact takeaway coffee shop in Mulhouse, France. Developed by Wrong Door Studio, the project explores how a small commercial footprint can become a distinctive hospitality experience through a clear spatial strategy, expressive materials, and carefully integrated functional elements. The concept is built around efficiency and intuitive customer flow. Rather than filling the limited space with decorative elements, the design uses the architecture itself to organize the experience, from ordering and preparation to pick-up and product display. Functional zones are visually integrated into the interior, allowing the 31-sqm space to remain open, legible, and uncluttered.
The material palette combines raw industrial references with a softer, almost weightless atmosphere. Stainless steel forms the main working surfaces and custom counters, while textured metal panels and grid structures introduce depth without visually reducing the space. A suspended metal grid ceiling becomes one of the defining elements of the interior, integrating lighting and technical components into a single architectural system. Translucent and reflective surfaces interact with the predominantly neutral palette, while pale blue accents appear throughout the space in furniture, signage, shelving details, and graphic elements. These subtle interventions give Mellow Cafe its visual identity without competing with the functional character of the interior.
Lighting Becomes Part of the Architecture at Mellow Cafe
The designers at Wrong Door Studio treat lighting as part of the architecture rather than an additional decorative layer. Illuminated signage, linear lighting integrated into shelving, and luminous ceiling panels create a graphic rhythm across the space. A projected digital menu further reduces physical visual clutter and reinforces the deliberately minimal approach. The project also extends the spatial identity into smaller details, from the suspended speakers and product displays to the pick-up counter and branded packaging, creating a consistent experience across architecture, furniture, graphics, and customer touchpoints. Rather than attempting to disguise its compact dimensions, Mellow Cafe uses them as the starting point for the design. The result is a precise, contemporary hospitality concept where industrial materials, digital elements, and functional architecture come together to give a small takeaway space a strong and recognizable identity.
Mellow Cafe is a takeaway coffee shop concept in Mulhouse, France
Wrong Door Studio designs the 31-sqm interior around efficiency and intuitive customer flow
the compact layout organizes ordering, preparation, pick-up, and product display
stainless steel forms the main working surfaces and custom counters
grid structures introduce texture without visually reducing the space
textured metal panels add depth to the compact interior
a suspended metal grid ceiling integrates lighting and technical components
pale blue accents appear across furniture, signage, and shelving details
reflective surfaces add another layer to the compact cafe interior

French officials investigate if malicious act caused train derailment
- Published
Officials in northern France are investigating whether the derailment of a passenger train on Friday evening was the result of a malicious act.
"At this stage, the leading theory is that a piece of rail was present on one of the tracks, potentially causing the derailment. The reason for its presence is unknown," prosecutor Sébastien Gallois said on Saturday.
Local media say 186 passengers were on board the train that was operating between Rouen and Caen in Normandy.
Forty-four people were treated for injuries, including an 18-year-old woman who was airlifted to hospital in a critical condition.
"The train's 'black box' has been seized. Several interviews are scheduled, and a court-appointed expert has been called in," prosecutor Gallois said in a press release.
"The main victim is still in hospital but her life is no longer in danger. The other victims have received care and treatment; they have either been discharged or are about to be."
The Rouen prosecutor's office earlier said the train driver had tested negative for drugs and alcohol.
The train derailed near Cléon, just south of Rouen, shortly before 20:00 (18:00 GMT), and some 140 firefighters and other emergency teams were immediately deployed to the crash scene.
"Suddenly there were a few jolts, and then after about three seconds it got stronger and stronger," Louis, a passenger on the train, told ICI Normandie radio.
"I couldn't stay in my seat anymore. The windows partially shattered, the stones from the track came into the carriage. It was really shocking. I'm still shaking," he added.

PANDA child advocacy and rehabilitation center opens in Kyiv region
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
17:12:52 EEST
23:12:52 KST

The PANDA Center for the Protection, Advocacy and Recovery of Children, dedicated to the memory of staunch child rights advocate Denys Monastyrsky and established based on the Barnahus model, has begun operating in one of the communities of Kyiv region, the Kyiv Regional Military Administration and the Ministry of Justice reported.
"Children should not have to face war, cruelty or pain. But when tragedy strikes, our main human task is not simply to find those responsible, but to protect the child's psyche and not hurt them a second time. A warm, safe space has been created here, where psychologists, medical professionals, lawyers and law enforcement officers come together around the child," Kyiv Regional Military Administration Head Tymur Tkachenko, who attended the center's opening on Saturday, wrote on Telegram.
According to him, more than 13,000 children in Kyiv region have found themselves in difficult circumstances, and more than 11,000 of them have suffered as a result of the war.
National Police Deputy Head Andriy Nebytov also attended the opening of the center.
"At the center, police officers, medical professionals, psychologists and social workers will provide comprehensive assistance to children who have suffered from violence, human trafficking and war crimes. The center will operate according to the international Barnahus model: necessary investigative procedures and assistance will be provided in a single safe, child-friendly environment to prevent the child from being traumatized again," the National Police said in a statement on Telegram.
According to the National Police, about 800 children have suffered from sexual violence, rape, sexual harassment and sexual abuse this year alone. Another 65 children have been recognized as victims of human trafficking.
"We must not only ensure that those responsible are inevitably punished. It is fundamentally important to return the child to a normal life," Nebytov said.
Ukraine's Justice Minister Denys Maslov, who also attended the event, explained that one of the key problems in the child protection system for children who have experienced violence is that a child often has to recount their painful story again and again to different specialists – an investigator, doctor, psychologist, and so on.
According to him, Ukraine is working to change this approach. This involves implementing the Barnahus model, which makes it possible to bring the necessary procedural actions together in a single child-safe environment. The main principle is to minimize repeated traumatization and create conditions in which the child does not have to repeatedly recount what they experienced.
The PANDA Center has 30 places for the safe accommodation of children and is capable of assisting about 500 children per year. It is equipped with specialized rooms for interviewing children, observation and conducting forensic medical examinations.
"This model should become the standard. We are working on this together with the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine, the Ministry of Social Policy, Family and Unity of Ukraine and the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Ukraine. The Ministry of Justice will also cooperate with the PANDA team to study this experience and further scale it up across Ukraine," Maslov said.
"For our region, this project is fundamental. Integrating the Barnahus model at our regional center for social and psychological rehabilitation is a joint decision and responsibility for the benefit of high-quality rehabilitation of children," Tkachenko stressed.

The body of 23-year-old Itai Parson, a member of Yamam, Israel Police’s elite counterterrorism unit, was found Saturday after a three-day search off the coast of Haifa. Parson, a Haifa resident, entered the water Thursday for a dive at the city’s Student Beach and did not return.  
Police said Parson had initially enlisted in the Israeli Air Force’s pilot training course in January 2023 before transferring that August to compulsory service in the Border Police. After completing his combat training, he entered a specialized undercover training track and was later assigned to Yamam’s observation and drone team. He began permanent service in December 2025. He is survived by his parents, four siblings and his partner.
“After three days of intensive and continuous operational activity, the missing man was located today,” Carmel District Commander Brig. Gen. Boaz Samucha said. “From the moment the report was received, Israel Police deployed hundreds of officers, fighters and volunteers who worked without interruption day and night, at sea, in the air and along the coastline,” he said.
Samucha said specialized units, technological equipment and a range of operational capabilities were used throughout the search, alongside emergency and rescue organizations. “Israel Police shares in the family’s grief and embraces them at this difficult time,” he added.
A relative of Parson who was out on a kayak initially alerted rescue forces. Searches were halted late Thursday and resumed early Friday morning, with Police Commissioner Dani Levy also arriving at the Haifa coastline.
The Israeli Navy later joined the operation, with members of the Shayetet 13 naval commando unit and Yaltam, the Navy’s underwater missions unit, taking part in searches at sea. Parson had been free diving without breathing equipment.
Police said virtually every available search capability was deployed, including drones, a police helicopter, light aircraft, boats, jet skis, mounted officers and off-road vehicles.
“We searched along the coastline and in the water, day and night and from the air,” police said.
The operation also included Border Police personnel, marine police, mounted units, canine teams, police rescue volunteers, Israel Fire and Rescue Services’ Lahava special unit, Haifa Municipality personnel, United Hatzalah, civilian security teams, volunteer divers, beach lifeguards, Magen David Adom, Yedidim and ZAKA volunteers.

====================================================================================================

Russia can’t be isolated as long as it has the Far East
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
14:09:43 UTC
23:09:43 KST

Russia can’t be isolated as long as it has the Far East
The Eastern Economic Forum has evolved from a regional investment showcase into one of the key platforms where Russia’s eastward strategy acquires tangible economic substance. Its central idea revolves around the fact that closer relations with Asia require more than diplomacy and trade alone: they need the development of Russia’s own Far East – its ports, industries, transport corridors, cities, and technological base.
The 11th Eastern Economic Forum, held in Vladivostok in early September, centered around the theme of ‘Development for the Benefit of People,’ reflecting the understanding that the region’s future is to be a major center of economic growth, modern industry, and international cooperation, with living standards and human capital the heart of development policy.
The Forum’s program included more than 150 events bringing together government officials, business leaders, academics, and experts, including those from abroad. Representatives of more than 80 countries had expressed interest ahead of the event, and the final figures showed over 9,300 participants from 78 states. These included 18 countries whose governments currently pursue policies regarded by Moscow as unfriendly towards Russia.
This goes to show that political tension between governments does not eliminate commercial or professional interest in working with Russia. The Forum demonstrated that even amid sanctions, geopolitical rivalry, and the fragmentation of global markets, there remains considerable demand for direct engagement with Russian institutions and businesses. This is particularly visible in Asia, which today accounts for a growing share of global manufacturing, trade, investment, and technological development.
Over eleven years, the EEF has moved well beyond the role of a regional investment forum. Advanced development territories, the Free Port of Vladivostok, the Far Eastern mortgage program and urban master plans have all featured prominently on its agenda. The Forum increasingly serves as a mechanism linking domestic development policy with Russia’s broader economic turn towards Asia.
Russia’s pivot East begins at home
Development of the Russian Far East has become inseparable from the eastward pivot in the country’s foreign policy. The region economically and logistically connects Russia with the Asia-Pacific, and Vladivostok is one of its principal gateways.
This process begun well before the West’s attempts to 'isolate' Russia. According to Vladimir Putin, around 25 trillion rubles (almost $300 billion at today’s exchange rate) in capital investment has been attracted to the Far Eastern regions over the past 11 years, while their combined gross regional product has more than tripled. New port terminals, railway infrastructure, gas-processing and petrochemical facilities, and the Zvezda shipbuilding complex have materially changed the region’s industrial landscape.
Now, the emphasis is shifting from the extraction and transportation of resources towards greater local processing and the creation of higher-value production. Shipbuilding, aircraft manufacturing, robotics, electronics, engineering, digital technologies, and new energy are increasingly being developed alongside traditional resource industries.
This gives Russia’s eastward strategy a dual character. Moscow is strengthening relations with Asian partners while simultaneously using these expanding ties as an incentive to modernize its own eastern territories. The more developed the Far East becomes industrially, technologically, and logistically, the stronger Russia’s position in Asia will be.
Investment deals give weight to strategy
The practical orientation of the Forum was most evident from the agreements concluded during the event. A total of 318 deals worth nearly 7 trillion rubles (about $83 billion) were signed, excluding arrangements whose financial terms remain commercially confidential. While some are framework agreements that will still have to move from declared intent to implementation, their scale and structure reveal the direction of Russia’s Far Eastern development strategy.
International connectivity remains one of its central pillars. Among the notable initiatives was the proposed Mohe-Nayba transport corridor, designed to create an additional link between Yakutia and China. Other agreements concerned the development of the Arctic and the Trans-Arctic Transport Corridor. Such projects are important not only for regional infrastructure: they improve Russia’s access to Asian markets and strengthen its role as a major transport space connecting different parts of Eurasia.
Industrial and technological development formed another major component. Plans include a photovoltaic module manufacturing facility in Zabaikalye with estimated investment of around 212 billion rubles ($2.5 billion), a 35-billion-ruble ($415-million) advanced semiconductor production complex in Primorye, and the Muravyov-Amursky Pacific Science and Technology Valley in Vladivostok. Russian and Chinese partners also agreed to develop pilot zones for agricultural cooperation.
Russia is creating value chains, manufacturing capacity, logistics hubs, and technological competencies inside the country. It is also giving foreign partners a direct stake in the development of the Russian Far East. They gain access to resources, infrastructure, transport routes, investment opportunities, and a large market, while Russian regions benefit from capital, industrial projects, technology, and employment.
Working with the world majority
During the plenary session, Vladimir Putin was joined by Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto, Mongolian Prime Minister Nyam-Osoryn Uchral, Myanmar Vice President Nyo Saw, and Chinese Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang. Their priorities differed, but all four speakers signaled a clear interest in maintaining and expanding cooperation with Russia.
Prabowo Subianto focused on the fragmentation of the global economy, the politicization of trade, and the need to preserve multiple channels of international cooperation. He argued for building new bridges rather than new dividing lines, particularly in energy, food security, logistics, and technology. Russia is crucial for Indonesia’s strategy of diversification, offering access to energy, agricultural supplies, technology, and the Eurasian market, while Indonesia can serve as an important gateway to ASEAN.
Mongolia’s approach is shaped largely by geography. Prime Minister Nyam-Osoryn Uchral stressed the importance of cooperation with Russia and China and highlighted the potential of transport, transit, and energy projects linking the three countries. Closer ties with Moscow can bring his country infrastructure investment, greater energy security, and transit revenues; Mongolia, in turn, can provide Russia with an additional route towards China and deeper connectivity across Eurasia.
China remains the most important economic partner of the Russian Far East. Ding Xuexiang emphasized closer coordination between the development of the Russian Far East and Northeast China, as well as stronger links between the Belt and Road Initiative and the Eurasian Economic Union. The relationship is increasingly moving beyond trade volumes towards infrastructure, investment, industrial cooperation, and cross-border development.
Myanmar, meanwhile, is interested in broadening its relationship with Russia into new technological sectors. Nyo Saw highlighted digital transformation, artificial intelligence, telecommunications, and modern payment systems.
All these different calculations lead to the same conclusion: there is practical value in expanding cooperation with Russia. Russia’s ties with the World Majority are based on not just political dialogue, but on trade, investment, energy, transport, technology, and industrial cooperation. It’s a more solid foundation that fleeting political alignments, and gives the Russian Far East a growing role as one of the country’s principal platforms for engagement with Asia.

Russian Court Disqualifies Liberal Yabloko Party List in Tomsk

A regional court in western Siberia’s Tomsk region disqualified the candidate list of the liberal Yabloko party ahead of upcoming regional assembly elections, the party said on Friday, Sept. 11, according to The Moscow Times.
The ruling leaves the northwestern Novgorod region as the only remaining area in Russia where Yabloko candidates remain on the ballot. Authorities have now invalidated or denied registration for the party’s electoral slates across seven Russian regions.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The Tomsk Regional Court ruled in favor of a complaint filed by the right-wing Liberal Democratic Party of Russia (LDPR). The LDPR accused Yabloko of campaign finance infractions, copyright infringements, and using prohibited social media platforms.
Yabloko rejected the allegations, characterizing the case as a “copycat” lawsuit orchestrated amid systematic administrative pressure ahead of next week’s vote, and announced plans to appeal the decision. Seven Yabloko candidates running in single-member constituencies in Tomsk remain registered on the ballot.
Nationwide disqualifications and legal risks
The decision in Tomsk follows a broader wave of legal actions targeting Yabloko candidates across the country.
At the federal level, Russia’s Supreme Court in August revoked the registration of Yabloko’s national candidate slate for the State Duma elections, granting a lawsuit initiated by the nationalist Rodina party that alleged electoral irregularities and foreign funding.
Russia’s War in Ukraine Has Cost Poland’s Economy More than €100 bln, Estimate Shows
While candidates in single-member districts were initially permitted to run, Yabloko stated on Wednesday that courts in several regions have received last-minute challenges seeking to remove local nominees. If the courts uphold these suits, 17 single-member district candidates could be stripped of their registration, reducing the party’s nationwide representation to 104 individual constituency races.
The systematic exclusion from regional ballots also endangers Yabloko’s legal standing as a registered political party. Under Russian election law, political parties risk losing their official registration if they fail to field candidate lists in at least 20% of regional legislative elections or participate in 10% of gubernatorial races within a seven-year cycle.
Founded in 1993, Yabloko is Russia’s oldest liberal political party and the only officially registered party in the country campaigning openly on a pro-peace platform advocating an immediate ceasefire in Ukraine.
Crackdown on anti-war figures and leadership
The regional disqualifications come amid an ongoing domestic crackdown against anti-war politicians and political dissent under wartime censorship statutes.
On Aug. 17, Russia’s Supreme Court formally upheld its ban on Yabloko’s federal parliamentary slate. Concurrently, the Pskov City Court sentenced Yabloko deputy chairman Lev Shlosberg to 11 years and one month in a penal colony over public remarks criticizing the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Shlosberg was convicted of “discrediting” the Russian armed forces and disseminating military “fake news” following public comments calling for a ceasefire during an online broadcast.
Despite the disqualifications and legal risks, Yabloko chairman Nikolai Rybakov has stated that the party intends to maintain its operations in Russia, emphasizing that public demand for an end to the war remains significant despite increasing state restrictions on independent political participation.

According to South African police, the men are alleged to have targeted more than 100 women in the US, defrauding them of more than $6m through online romance or love scams.
Among the alleged victims were pensioners and businesspeople who were reportedly targeted through sophisticated online relationships.
“Through the coordination of Interpol South Africa, the six will today be transported from a correctional facility in Cape Town to Cape Town international airport, where they will be handed over to officials from the FBI and the United States Secret Service, who arrived in South Africa this morning,” said police spokesperson Katlego Mogale.
A recent operation by Interpol targeting west African organized crime groups led to the arrest of 58 people and the identification of 263 suspects linked to various criminal networks involved in similar crimes, the multinational police body said last month.
The operation aimed to disrupt money laundering, identify high-value targets, seize assets, and support arrests and prosecution.
In South Africa, authorities raided seven locations in the city of Johannesburg linked to a syndicate that ran romance and investment scams targeting retirees in English-speaking countries.
In that operation in South Africa, police arrested 39 people, seized $2.67m and froze more than 250 bank accounts, Interpol said.
