The oldest evidence of regular psychoactive substance use has been found on an island in Indonesia
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
16:40:07 EEST
22:40:07 KST

The oldest evidence of regular psychoactive substance use has been found on an island in Indonesia
Kyiv • UNN
Sulawesi hunter-gatherers may have consumed betel nuts 25,000 years ago. Scientists found traces of them on severely damaged teeth.
Hunter-gatherers on the Indonesian island of Sulawesi may have regularly consumed betel nuts as early as 25,000 years ago. This is indicated by research conducted by scientists from Griffith University, Live Science reports, writes UNN.
Details
Researchers examined heavily damaged teeth belonging to two people who lived on Sulawesi during different periods. One man died approximately 25,000–16,000 years ago, while the other person died around 7,600–6,300 years ago. Both were approximately 40–50 years old at the time of death.
The teeth displayed characteristic grooves, and analysis of the samples confirmed the presence of traces of betel nuts. The seeds of the Areca catechu palm contain arecoline, a neuroactive substance that affects the nervous system.
They may have used it as a painkiller
According to one of the study's authors, Adam Brumm, ancient people may have sucked on whole betel nuts to numb their mouths and ease toothache. At the same time, this practice likely only worsened the condition of their teeth.
On one of the teeth, the groove was so deep that it exposed the inner pulp cavity.
It must have been incredibly painful
Approximately 4,000 years ago, the inhabitants of Sulawesi were already mixing betel nuts with slaked lime to produce a stimulant. A similar practice still exists in parts of South Asia and Oceania.
It now seems likely that betel chewing in the form in which we know it developed from a much simpler and more ancient practice — sucking on a whole nut
The study's findings were published in the scientific journal Science Advances.

The Nashville airport is to be renamed after Dolly Parton, a board of commissioners voted on Friday, in tribute to the Smoky Mountain singer who is estimated to bring $1.8bn each year to Tennessee through her Dollywood theme park.
The decision ensures that Parton, who died last month at 80 years old, will be memorialized with her name on an airport, although the renaming process will take time to complete.
In her lifetime, Parton did not think the idea, which came about last year, would come to fruition.
“I think that’s probably more of a joke than anything,” Parton told the Tennessean. “I mean, it does sound like a lot of fun to say: ‘Your flight is departin’ from Nashville’s D Parton.’”
The move to rename gained traction last month when the Nashville mayor, Freddie O’Connell, and the Tennessee governor, Bill Lee, threw their support behind the name change.
“Dolly Parton’s extraordinary life is forever woven into the fabric of our state,” Lee said in a statement, recognizing what he called her “Volunteer spirit”.
“It is fitting that Nashville international airport would bear the name of our state’s favorite daughter and greet travelers with the enduring legacy of Dolly’s music, generosity, faith and kindness,” Lee added.
After the airport’s commissioners voted in favor of the change, Lee said it was an “important step to honor her remarkable legacy” as “Dolly has always helped the world fall in love with Tennessee”.
The name change is likely to be pricey since it will require new signage across the entire 4,500-acre (1,700-hectare) property, and updates to an airport monuments, merchandise, shuttle buses, uniforms, business cards, legal contracts and leases.
Although the new airport name in her honor has not been decided, Tennessean columnist Alejandro Ramos argued last month that the case for the change “is larger than music” because of her contributions to the state of Tennessee and to international literacy through her Imagination Library charity.
“Parton’s songs helped make Tennessee recognizable around the world. But her deepest legacy may be what she did with the success that followed. She accumulated the kind of fame, wealth and influence few people ever experience. Then she repeatedly turned those resources outward,” Ramos wrote.
The Metropolitan Nashville Airport Authority said in a statement: “While a final name has not yet been determined, we are working closely with the appropriate parties to thoughtfully determine how Dolly Parton’s name and legacy will be incorporated”.

Gujarat earthquake, Nepal floods &amp; more: What is it about the date 26?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
13:40:01 UTC
22:40:01 KST

Gujarat, the tsunami, 26/11, and now Nepal. Some of the disasters etched deepest into public memory have one oddly specific thing in common: they happened on the 26th.The coincidence surfaced again after the August 26 catastrophe in Nepal, where a glacier collapse unleashed a wall of mud, rock and water through the Himalayan valleys, killing more than 1,300 people and leaving thousands missing. As images of the destruction spread, so did an old question: what is it about the 26th?But is the date really unusually deadly, or are we simply very good at finding patterns once we know where to look?
When nature struck on the 26th
The natural disasters alone would be enough to build a legend around this date. The Gujarat earthquake of January 26, 2001, Republic Day, struck Kutch with such force that it killed close to 20,000 people and injured more than 160,000, flattening entire towns like Bhuj and Anjar. Three years later, on December 26, 2004, a magnitude 9.1 undersea earthquake off Sumatra sent a tsunami crashing into the coastlines of Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, part of a disaster that killed or left missing roughly 228,000 people across the Indian Ocean rim. The following July, on July 26, 2005, Mumbai received close to 944 mm of rainfall in 24 hours, a deluge that killed more than a thousand people across Maharashtra and brought the city to a standstill for days.
Gujarat earthquake of 2001
The pattern isn't confined to Indian soil, or even to this century. Turkey's Erzincan earthquake killed an estimated 32,700 people on December 26, 1939. The Skopje earthquake of July 26, 1963 killed around 1,070 and left 200,000 homeless. Iran's Bam earthquake, which levelled a 2,000-year-old citadel city, struck on December 26, 2003, killing roughly 31,000 people. Indonesia's Yogyakarta earthquake killed more than 5,700 on May 26, 2006, and the Hindu Kush earthquake of October 26, 2015 shook Afghanistan, Pakistan and parts of northern India simultaneously.
When the 26th turned man-made
Where the 26th gets stranger is that it isn't only earthquakes and floods, events with no human author. It has also coincided with some of the worst disasters humans have caused deliberately or through negligence.The most seared into Indian memory is November 26, 2008, when ten Lashkar-e-Taiba gunmen launched coordinated attacks across Mumbai, laying siege to the city for nearly three days and killing 166 people. It is remembered simply as 26/11, a date that needs no year attached to be understood. It wasn't an isolated instance of terrorism landing on this date, either, the Ahmedabad serial blasts of July 26, 2008, one of the deadliest terror strikes on Indian soil that year, fell on the same date. Outside India, the Kabul airport bombing of August 26, 2021, carried out during the US-led evacuation from Afghanistan, killed at least 183 people, including 13 American service members.
Lashkar-e-Taiba gunmen launched coordinated attacks across Mumbai
Industrial and nuclear disasters share the date too, and this is where the list stops looking like a coincidence confined to any one country or cause. Reactor No. 4 at Chernobyl exploded during a botched safety test on April 26, 1986, in what remains the worst nuclear accident in history. More than four decades earlier, on April 26, 1942, a gas and coal-dust explosion at China's Benxihu colliery killed 1,549 miners through carbon monoxide poisoning, one of the deadliest mining disasters ever recorded.
Crashes, collisions and the 26th
Then there is a third category that rarely makes it into casual conversations about the 26th, but rounds out just how wide its reach is: ordinary transport disasters, the kind that don't need an earthquake or a bomb, just a broken rail or a failed engine part.India's Khanna rail disaster, a derailment and collision caused by a broken rail near Punjab's Khanna town, killed 212 people on November 26, 1998. The Aurangabad air crash, when flight IC-491 went down while approaching the Maharashtra airport, killed 55 of 118 people aboard on April 26, 1993. Overseas, Lauda Air Flight 004 crashed in Thailand on May 26, 1991, after an uncommanded thrust-reverser deployment sent the Boeing 767 out of control, killing all 223 people aboard.
The date that refuses to be just a number
Laid end to end, the list stops looking like a curated coincidence and starts looking almost deliberately comprehensive — quakes, tsunamis, floods, terror attacks, a nuclear meltdown, a mine explosion, a rail crash, an air crash. Nearly every disaster category a newsroom covers has, at some point, chosen the 26th.
So, is the 26th actually cursed?
There's a statistical explanation for this, and it's less exciting than a curse. The British statistician David Hand has spent years studying coincidences like this, he calls it the law of truly large numbers. Basically, if disasters are happening somewhere in the world almost every day, and a month only has 28 to 31 possible dates, some date was bound to end up looking busier than the rest. It just happened to be the 26th. It could as easily have been the 9th.Then there's confirmation bias, which does a lot of the heavy lifting here. Once you start looking for disasters on the 26th, you notice every one that fits and forget the ones that don't. Bhopal's gas leak, India's worst industrial disaster, happened on the night of December 2-3, 1984. The Uttarakhand floods were in June 2013. The Balasore train collision that killed nearly 300 people was on June 2, 2023. None of these are anywhere near the 26th. Nobody brings them up when the "jinx" comes up, because once you believe a pattern, you stop counting the exceptions.
Uttarakhand floods of 2013
Numerology adds a third layer, and in India this one actually sticks with people. Add up 2 and 6 and you get 8, a number some numerology traditions link to upheaval and karmic reckoning. For anyone who already believes in that system, a disaster landing on the 26th isn't a coincidence: it's confirmation.
There's no actual link between a calendar date and earthquakes, floods or violence. But belief doesn't need a mechanism. It just needs enough stories that fit, and the 26th has no shortage of those by now.
What the 'jinx' really tells us
So what does the list really tell us? Not that the date is cursed; just that disasters don't check the calendar, and over a long enough stretch of history, every date ends up with its own body count. The 26th's list happens to include some of the most consequential disasters of the last century, ones big enough that they changed building codes, early-warning systems, even how countries think about security. That's really why the date sticks in memory. Not the number itself, but what it forced people to rebuild afterward.

When Statecraft Becomes Transaction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
13:40:00 UTC
22:40:00 KST

Executive Order (EO) 14422, signed Aug. 27, 2026, counts icebreakers. The US Coast Guard supplies nine of the 11 icebreaking vessels on the Great Lakes and clears the commercial lanes without charge, the order observes; the United States has spent nearly four billion dollars on the freshwater ecosystem in a decade, and Canada far less. From that ledger the order draws its conclusion. Because the deepest water lies on the American side, “the United States claims most of the Lake’s volume.” Lake Ontario “becomes” Lake America.
Read the inference slowly, because it does not hide: contribution establishes ownership; ownership licenses the name.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The EO presents the inference as settled policy, restating a January 2025 EO on names as a commitment to recognize “the extraordinary contributions of the American people” by naming landmarks for shared achievements.
The earlier EO’s stated policy said nothing like that. Instead, it spoke of honoring “visionary and patriotic Americans” in the nation’s past. In the older document, contribution names what a patriot gave; in the newer one, what a nation has paid in.
Ten days after the lake order, President Trump began posting maps of New Mexico with “Mexico” struck through in red, an image the White House amplified and the state’s governor refused to entertain. No constitutional route exists for renaming a state, and none was attempted.
Russia’s War in Ukraine Has Cost Poland’s Economy More than €100 bln, Estimate Shows
                                                                                                                                                                         
But naming has never been only about names. It announces who holds the standing to say what a thing is.
None of this argues against bargaining: diplomacy bargains, as it must. European governments underinvested in their own defense for three decades, and an administration that forces allies to buy usable capacity rather than rent American cover is right about that. I grant that fully, and once, because what follows does not depend on denying it. What follows depends on a distinction between a method and a metaphysics.
An alliance, though, is not a subscription willy-nilly reducible to a method. Its worth lies partly in goods that never appear on an invoice: interoperability built over decades, intelligence relationships unavailable at market, and the deterrence produced when an adversary believes a commitment will hold under pressure.
The last item is the strange one. It exists only in the enemy’s mind, and it thins the moment the enemy suspects that the commitment itself is subject to continual repricing.
On assistance to Ukraine, at least, the ledger has shifted decisively. NATO’s Ankara Declaration of July 8, 2026 records that European allies and Canada now finance the vast majority of security assistance to Ukraine and pledges €70 billion ($81 billion) in equipment, assistance, and training for 2026, with at least equivalent levels promised for 2027. Burden-shifting has produced substantial results. The strategic question it was supposed to answer sits exactly where it sat.
Territory is one object of the war in Ukraine – it is not the war itself. The Charter of the United Nations treats the territorial integrity and political independence of states as constitutive of international order rather than as negotiable holdings, and the Secretary-General has called Russia’s full-scale invasion a clear violation of it.
Putin’s own account of his aims will not fit inside a real-estate frame. At the St. Petersburg forum on June 20, 2025, he grounded a claim on a premise about peoplehood: Russians and Ukrainians being one people, and so “all of Ukraine is ours.” Putin then supplied the operative rule: “wherever a Russian soldier sets foot, that’s ours.”
Set that beside the Lake Ontario EO… and something uncomfortable surfaces: because the largest constituent of the Russian Empire was Russia, because both Russia and Ukraine have a shared history, then “all of Ukraine is ours.”
Of course, one cannot justifiably claim that Trump’s EO and Putin’s nationalism are moral equivalents – that would be grotesque. However, the grammar of naming based on power and “possession” is the same. Each converts a prior claim (contribution in one case and kinship in the other) into title. In the Lake Ontario EO, title then licenses a name; in Putin’s historical argument, naming and genealogy serve as evidence of title.
What separates them is what each is prepared to do to make the title hold. Russia invaded a sovereign state, annexed its territory, and denies its separate political existence; nothing in an executive order about a lake belongs to that category, and an argument that blurred the distinction would deserve to fail. Yet the parallel is narrow. It is also instructive, because the same grammar deceives its user in both cases.
Putin’s longer argument, set out in his 2021 essay on the historical unity of Russians and Ukrainians, rests on genealogy – and carries its own refutation. The essay concedes that the medieval word behind Ukraine’s name appears in 12th-century sources “referring to various border territories.” Various: plural, relative to more than one center. Having granted that the word named several frontiers, the essay proceeds as though it had named one, and as though naming a frontier settled who owns it.
I decline to litigate whether Kyiv’s baptism under St. Volodymyr in 988 outranks Moscow’s first appearance in the chronicles in 1147. Why? To litigate is to concede the premise: that antiquity conveys title. Sovereignty is not an inheritance, and etymology is not a deed.
A negotiating framework of this kind fails here, and it fails on its own terms. If a rational actor accepts a sufficiently good offer, then everything turns on what counts as good, and instrumental rationality supplies no common scale. Putin need not be deranged to refuse terms Washington considers generous. A leadership may rank strategic depth, imperial standing, and the denial of a neighbor’s independent existence above sanctions relief and reconstruction contracts and rank them consistently for 20 years. A negotiator can handle the priceable dimensions of such a conflict with skill and still be working on the wrong problem. A scale calibrated for one quantity returns a number for anything you set on it. The number is not false; it is beside the point.
Early on Sept. 8, 2026, ending a three-day pause on strikes observed while American envoys visited Moscow and Kyiv, Russian ballistic and cruise missiles and drones struck Kyiv and the surrounding region, killing and injuring civilians and damaging more than 50 sites in the capital, among them residential buildings, dormitories, and schools.[12]Later that day, the Kremlin’s readout of an hour-long call described Trump pressing for a swift end to the war, which would open “impressive and far-reaching” prospects for restored relations, with particular benefit to trade.
Ukraine’s foreign minister answered in 10 words: “His ballistic missiles speak louder than his words on diplomacy.” An offer denominated in trade normalization reached a party that had spent that same morning demonstrating what it values more.
Rhetorical domination compounds the difficulty, and its record can be checked. George C. Edwards III, surveying Trump’s public discourse, catalogs the branding and delegitimizing of opponents, the fueling of fear, and the stoking of division, and arrives at a finding easy to skip past: the rhetoric diminished the president’s capacity to govern.
Consider the clearest instance: on July 31, 2025, Dmitry Medvedev, answering a warning from Trump, invoked the “Dead Hand,” the Cold War-era system reputed to launch automatically should Russia’s leadership be destroyed – though he called it fabled even as he brandished it. The following day, Trump announced on Truth Social that he had ordered two nuclear submarines repositioned. That is, a social-media post moved strategic assets.
Whatever that is, it is not the pricing of interests; it is a contest over who is seen to yield, conducted with the instruments of nuclear deterrence. The same instinct shows in Vice President JD Vance’s assigned part, which Reuters described in 2025 as an attack-dog role, exercised in Munich and then in the Oval Office against President Zelensky.
Any comparison with Medvedev stops well short of equivalence: Vance has not invoked a doomsday system.
Moscow, meanwhile, has folded nuclear risk into the bargaining environment. The doctrine Putin approved on Nov. 19, 2024 reserves the right to answer with nuclear weapons a conventional attack creating a “critical threat” to Russian or Belarusian sovereignty or territorial integrity, where the 2020 formulation had spoken of a threat to the state’s very existence.
Analysts read the change differently: the Arms Control Association sees a lowered and blurred threshold, while the United States Institute of Peace argues the amendments codify guidance already operative and mark no real departure. Either reading serves the point, since ambiguity is the instrument.
A negotiator who prices deliverables cannot price this, because its worth to Moscow lies in its staying unresolved. Beijing repeats that nuclear weapons must not be used and nuclear war must not be fought. The statement matters and may constrain Moscow. It also remains a Chinese position serving Chinese interests, and expecting Beijing to enforce Western assumptions about tolerable Russian conduct would reproduce the original error at a higher level.
The danger begins not with bargaining but with the elevation of a partial truth into a master category. The objects of statecraft are not homogeneous: political communities have histories, identities, jurisdictions, and common goods; alliances embody commitments and serve strategic goods; sovereignty is a juridical status, not merely possession of territory. None is commensurable without remainder in a single metric.
Putin’s characteristic move is civilizational absorption: Ukraine’s independent political identity is subordinated to an alleged antecedent unity of peoplehood, history, and imperial space.
The Trump administration’s recurrent vocabulary is different (assets, leverage, contributions, burdens, and deals), but it raises an analogous question: does bargaining remain an instrument ordered toward political goods that exceed exchange value, or does the logic of the bargain become the measure of those goods themselves? Treat an alliance as a subscription, and its members learn to calculate cancellation.
Sovereignty includes territory and exceeds it, the way a marriage may include a shared address without being constituted by it. Each of these realities has a transactional dimension; none is exhausted by one. The error lies not in using a category that captures something real, but in allowing a partial category to become an exhaustive ontology. At that point, the category no longer merely guides policy; it governs what its user can see.
Which returns us to the issue of Lake Ontario. Federal maps will print the new name, since an executive order can compel that much, and the water will keep crossing a border that no order can move. There is the difficulty in miniature: a name can be assigned; the thing declines to be renamed.
Washington may yet win real concessions from Moscow, and nothing here forecloses it. But a settlement built on the assumption that Moscow must eventually want what Washington would want in its place is the same category mistake, now committed where the cost of error is counted in cities.
The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.

Russia Launches Large-Scale Missile and Drone Attack Across Ukraine, Killing at Least Four
Russia launched a large-scale overnight missile and drone attack across Ukraine on September 12, killing at least four people and injuring civilians in Odesa, Kryvyi Rih, Zaporizhzhia, and the Kyiv region.
Odesa and the surrounding region were the primary target of the attack, the Ukrainian Air Force reported. At least 17 people were injured in Odesa, including a five-month-old baby, after a Russian strike significantly damaged a multi-story residential building, according to Odesa City Military Administration head Serhii Lysak.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Emergency and municipal crews were deployed to the damaged building, while an operational headquarters was established to assist residents.
In Kryvyi Rih, a Russian ballistic missile struck an industrial facility, killing one person and injuring two others, according to Dnipropetrovsk regional authorities. Another man was reported missing. The two injured men, aged 54 and 58, were hospitalized, with one reported in serious condition and the other in moderate condition.
Five apartment buildings, a primary healthcare center, three educational facilities, and several businesses were also damaged in Kryvyi Rih. The city was later targeted by attack drones.
Russia also struck a residential area of Zaporizhzhia with a drone, destroying at least one house and starting fires, regional defense officials reported. Rescue workers recovered the bodies of a 64-year-old woman and a 37-year-old man from the rubble. A 59-year-old woman was injured.
Authorities in the Kyiv region reported further damage from Russian attacks involving jet-powered drones. One person was killed and three others, including a child, were injured over the previous 24 hours.
Damage was recorded in the Brovary, Obukhiv, Bucha, Boryspil, and Vyshhorod districts. At least 15 sites were affected, including seven private homes, vehicles, warehouses, hangars, and a power line.
According to the Ukrainian Air Force on September 12, Russia began the overnight attack at around 6 p.m. the previous evening and used ballistic missiles, eight sea-launched Kalibr cruise missiles, six Kh-59/69 guided air-launched missiles, and 129 drones.
The drones included Shahed-type attack UAVs, S8000 Banderol drones, and decoys. They were launched from areas around Kursk and Oryol in Russia, as well as from temporarily occupied Donetsk region and Hvardiiske in temporarily occupied Crimea.
Russian ballistic missiles were launched from Russia’s Voronezh and Rostov regions and from temporarily occupied Crimea, while the Kalibr missiles were fired from the Black Sea.
As of 8:30 a.m., Ukrainian air defenses had destroyed or suppressed 110 aerial targets, including six Kalibr cruise missiles, two Kh-59/69 missiles, one S8000 Banderol drone, and 101 Shahed-type and other drones, the Air Force said.
Russian missiles and attack drones were recorded hitting 20 locations across Ukraine, while debris from intercepted targets fell at four additional sites.
Ukraine used combat aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare systems, unmanned systems, and mobile fire groups to repel the attack. The Air Force said Russian drones remained in Ukrainian airspace after the initial interception figures were released.
Earlier, on September 11, Russian drones struck gas stations in Kyiv’s Obolonskyi and Dniprovskyi districts, injuring at least two people. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko also reported a second strike on a gas station in the Obolonskyi district.

An attempted drone attack targeting a Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft at Germany’s Leipzig/Halle Airport on Aug. 4 failed only because a detonator wire snapped, leaving approximately 1.8 kilograms of Semtex concealed in a vegetable tin can unexploded, German newspaper Welt am Sonntag reported.
According to investigators, the plot involved three unmanned aerial vehicles. Two drones crashed during launch due to unexplained technical failures, while the third successfully reached the Ukrainian cargo plane inside the airport’s security perimeter but did not detonate.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Investigators assessed that an explosion would have caused catastrophic structural damage to the transport hub, noting that the Antonov transport plane held roughly 25,000 liters of jet fuel at the time of the incident.
German security agencies have identified two primary suspects: Belarusian national Andrei K. and Russian citizen Oleg L. Investigators assessed that Oleg L. coordinated logistical operations on behalf of Russia’s military intelligence service, the Main Directorate of the General Staff (GRU).
Logistics, entry route, and GRU connections
Investigation records show that Oleg L. entered Germany through Berlin-Brandenburg Airport via Turkey before traveling to Serbia and subsequently returning to Russia.
Although German security agencies possessed preliminary intelligence regarding his potential ties to the GRU at the time of his arrival, authorities did not establish physical surveillance on him during his stay in the country.
Ukraine Strikes Russian Drone Command Posts and Supply Depots
Forensic investigators traced the suspects through DNA evidence recovered from work gloves abandoned near a radio antenna used to operate the drone. The DNA profile matched records held in Lithuania and Finland, where Andrei K. had prior documentation linked to petty criminal offenses.
Polish prosecutors have separately tied Andrei K. to a major summer 2024 arson attack on a home improvement hypermarket in Łódź, which Polish authorities formally classified as an act of state-sponsored sabotage directed by Russian intelligence services.
Investigators determined that the Semtex used in the Leipzig plot was smuggled across Europe through Bulgaria and Serbia hidden inside hollow vehicle compartments of commercial freight trucks.
Upon arrival in Germany, the explosive charges were buried in ground caches in areas surrounding Leipzig/Halle Airport. German federal police later located several hidden caches after analyzing telemetry and GPS data retrieved from a vehicle rented by the suspects.
Diplomatic expulsions and mutual facility closures
The investigative disclosures follow diplomatic fallout between Berlin and Moscow over the attempted airport sabotage.
On Sept. 1, the German federal government attributed the Leipzig/Halle incident directly to Russian intelligence agencies, accusing Moscow of deploying contract operatives to target critical logistics infrastructure utilized by NATO and Ukraine.
In response, Berlin ordered the closure of Russia’s consulate general in Bonn – mandating the departure of roughly 60 Russian diplomats and staff by Sept. 18 – and terminated its intergovernmental operating agreement for the Russian House cultural center in Berlin.
German intelligence officials assessed that approximately one-third of the personnel at the Bonn consulate were affiliated with Russian intelligence agencies.
On Sept. 7, the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs launched reciprocal measures, ordering the closure of the German Consulate General in St. Petersburg and terminating all branches of the Goethe-Institut cultural organization in Moscow, St. Petersburg, and Yekaterinburg.
Russian authorities ordered German consular staff in St. Petersburg to vacate the country by Sept. 18 and gave the Goethe-Institut until Sept. 13 to shut down operations.
Western allies have characterized the airport incident as a major escalation in hybrid warfare against European aviation and critical infrastructure, with French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte warning that allied nations will respond to attacks on European territorial integrity and democratic stability.

Researchers find a Wordle strategy that wins 99% of the time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
13:35:56 UTC
22:35:56 KST

Researchers find a Wordle strategy that wins 99% of the time
A mathematical strategy that prioritizes information over lucky guesses can solve Wordle 99% of the time.
- Date:
- September 12, 2026
- Source:
- Binghamton University
- Summary:
- Researchers at Binghamton University have developed a mathematical strategy that can solve Wordle with a 99% success rate. Instead of simply guessing words packed with common letters or choosing the most likely answer, the method uses Shannon entropy, a measure from information theory, to identify guesses that reveal the most useful information. Each guess is designed to rapidly shrink the pool of possible answers, even when the guessed word itself seems unlikely to be correct.
- Share:
Millions of people open Wordle each day hoping to solve its five-letter puzzle before their six guesses run out. Now, researchers at Binghamton University, State University of New York, say mathematics can dramatically improve the odds.
By applying information theory, the team developed a strategy that solved 99% of Wordle puzzles in simulations. The key is surprisingly counterintuitive. Instead of always trying to guess the answer as quickly as possible, the method favors words that reveal the greatest amount of useful information.
How Wordle Turns Every Guess Into a Clue
Wordle gives players six attempts to identify a hidden five-letter word. The game begins with no clues, so the first guess can be any valid word.
After each attempt, Wordle uses colors to show how close the player is:
- Grey means the guessed letter does not appear in the secret word.
- Yellow means the letter is in the secret word, but it is in the wrong position.
- Green means the letter is both correct and in the correct position.
Players use those clues to narrow the possibilities with each new guess. The game ends when all five squares turn green or when the player uses all six attempts without finding the answer.
That process of progressively reducing possible answers makes Wordle a natural problem for information theory, a branch of mathematics concerned with measuring and communicating information.
The Math Behind a 99% Wordle Strategy
The research team, led by Assistant Professor Congyu "Peter" Wu, focused on a concept known as Shannon entropy.
Shannon entropy is a mathematical way of measuring uncertainty. In simple terms, it can help determine how much useful information a particular choice is expected to reveal. The concept was developed as part of modern information theory and is widely used to study how efficiently information can be transmitted, stored, or processed.
In Wordle, that means asking a different question. Instead of simply choosing the word that seems most likely to be correct, the researchers looked for guesses that would eliminate the greatest number of possibilities.
"Let's say you're at a certain guess. The previous guesses will eliminate a whole bunch of options, and based on the remaining options, guessing some words will send you into a trajectory where information gain is speedier," said Wu, a faculty member at the Thomas J. Watson College of Engineering and Applied Science's School of Systems Science and Industrial Engineering.
A word that appears unlikely to be the final answer can therefore still be extremely valuable if its letters help divide the remaining possibilities into smaller groups.
"A subtle but important insight from the paper is that a guess doesn't have to be the most likely answer; it simply has to be informative," said Donald Stephens, a doctoral student at Binghamton University. "By applying Shannon entropy, the objective shifts to maximizing the expected reduction in uncertainty rather than the probability of being right. In practice, this approach can lead to solving the puzzle in fewer guesses."
Why the Best Guess Can Look Wrong
To a human player, some of the strategy's recommendations might initially seem strange or even random. But the goal is not necessarily to solve the puzzle immediately. It is to make each guess reveal enough information to make the next decision easier.
For example, when several possible answers remain, choosing a word that tests a useful combination of letters could eliminate many of them at once. Even if that word has little chance of being the actual solution, the feedback it produces may point much more clearly toward the correct answer.
Using the strategy during a real Wordle game would require running a separate script or program. After each guess, the player would enter Wordle's color-coded feedback into the program. The software would then calculate the next guess expected to provide the most information.
Information Beats Common Letter Guessing
The researchers compared their approach with a more conventional strategy centered on frequently used letters (e.g., "A," "E," "R").
The difference was substantial. In simulations, the information theory method successfully solved 99% of Wordle puzzles. The common letter strategy solved 90%.
That result highlights an important distinction between simply choosing letters that appear often and choosing guesses that provide the greatest amount of new information. Common letters can certainly be useful, but the mathematical approach continually adjusts its choices based on what has already been learned.
A Classroom Project Becomes Published Research
The work did not begin as a formal research project. Instead, it grew out of a class assignment in which Wu challenged students to demonstrate how information theory could be used to solve a real problem.
The students chose Wordle, turning a popular daily puzzle into a practical test of mathematical decision-making.
Co-author Talal Aladaileh said that the project's evolution from a classroom exercise into a published paper reflects the rigor, depth, and quality of the School of Systems Science and Industrial Engineering program at Binghamton.
"The courses here don't just teach concepts; they push you to apply them in ways that have real, lasting impact," Aladaileh said.
Wu said the project demonstrates how information theory can move beyond simply describing uncertainty and instead become a tool for making better decisions.
"What is especially creative and valuable about the team's intellectual contribution," Wu said, "is that it transformed a static measurement (Shannon entropy) in a scientific domain into a dynamic solution that helps accomplish a popular task better, which showcases the team's deep understanding of class material and their talent as engineers."
The paper, "Solving Wordle Using Information Theory," was published in the Northeast Journal of Complex Systems.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Binghamton University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Talal Aladaileh, Donald Stephens, Mallak Alqaisi, Congyu Wu. Solving Wordle Using Information Theory. Northeast Journal of Complex Systems (NEJCS), 2026; 8 (1) DOI: 10.63562/2577-8439.1146

German investigators reportedly link Leipzig airport attack to Russian military intelligence
German security agencies can now identify with a high degree of probability two suspects following the drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport, with one of them linked to Russian military intelligence.
Source: European Pravda, citing German media outlet Welt am Sonntag
Details: Welt am Sonntag gained access in recent weeks to classified, previously unknown investigation materials and spoke to senior security officials.
The editorial team knows the suspects' full names, as well as details of their entry into Germany and departure from the country. This evidence formed the basis for Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul and Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt to accuse Russia of carrying out the attack at a joint press conference a week and a half ago. Russia has denied any involvement.
Leipzig/Halle Airport was attacked with an explosive drone on the evening of 4 August. The device was found near a Ukrainian transport aircraft and defused. Investigators found the remains of two more drones near the airport. Security sources said the two main suspects are Belarusian citizen Andrei Ka. and Russian citizen Oleg Le. German security services believe Le. was responsible for planning and logistics for the attack. He is believed to have links to Russian military intelligence.
Investigators say Le. entered Germany via Türkiye through Berlin Brandenburg Airport (BER). He later left through the same airport for Serbia. Le. is now in Russia. Welt am Sonntag reported that investigators already knew when he arrived that the Russian citizen is linked to Russia's military intelligence. However, he was not placed under surveillance after entering Germany.
Two of the three drones used in the attack were reportedly destroyed during take-off. The reason for this remains unclear. The third drone reached the Antonov aircraft but failed to explode. Investigators say the plan was to use a total of around 1.8 kg of Semtex explosive. The Antonov aircraft targeted in the attack was carrying about 25,000 litres of kerosene. Investigators believe that had the explosive charge detonated, it would have caused a powerful blast and destroyed part of the airport.
Previously unreleased surveillance footage obtained by Welt am Sonntag shows a drone lying directly next to the Antonov aircraft. Investigators say the explosive device had been hidden in a vegetable tin. The explosion was avoided because the detonator broke off.
The outlet's investigation reveals how investigators tracked down the suspect. Forensic experts found fragments of a glove with traces of DNA on the structure of an antenna which law enforcement officials believe was used to control the drone. These DNA traces had previously been registered in Finland and Lithuania, where Ka. has convictions for ordinary criminal offences. In Finland, he has also been charged with theft, among other offences.
Polish authorities have also linked Ka. to a fire at a DIY store in the city of Łódź, Poland, in the summer of 2024, which prosecutors in Łódź are also treating as sabotage. Polish investigators say the trail in that case also leads to Russia. Ka.'s emergence in connection with the Leipzig attack is seen as further evidence of Russian supervision.
The authorities believe the explosives used in the Leipzig attack probably entered Germany via Bulgaria and Serbia. Investigators believe they were transported in hidden compartments in lorries and later concealed in underground caches. Police found several potential hiding places near Leipzig airport after analysing data from a rented car used by the suspects.
Background:
- It was reported earlier that German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt is planning a package of measures covering protection against drones and sabotage targeting critical infrastructure and cyberattacks, as well as the detection of spies and potential terrorists.
- On 1 September, Germany directly accused Russia of a hybrid attack at Leipzig airport in early August and announced countermeasures.

Breadcrumb
Charity Commission issues regulatory guidance to Board of Deputies of British Jews after ICJP complaint
The UK's Charity Commission has issued regulatory guidance to the Board of Deputies Charity Foundation's trustees over claims made about protests against the "Great Israeli Real Estate" event held at Edgeware United Synagogue in June.
The move comes after the International Centre for Justice for Palestinians (ICJP) filed a complaint to the commission, highlighting that the Board of Deputies of British Jews had claimed that the protests had taken place on "bogus grounds".
The protests against the real estate event took place due to the organisers' advertising of illegal settlement land for sale - a matter highlighted by rights groups, including Amnesty International.
The Board of Deputies characterised the anti-settlement protests as an attempt to "harass and intimidate members of the Jewish community".
The ICJP highlighted that material distributed at the event referred to several illegal settlement developments on Palestinian land -- a fact acknowledged by the organisers, who later apologised.
The pro-Palestine legal group raised the complaint after the Board of Deputies did not correct its statements.
“The Board of Deputies dismissed a lawful protest against the marketing of property in illegal Israeli settlements as being based on “bogus grounds”. But the evidence proved otherwise: promotional materials for properties in illegal settlements were distributed at the event, and the organisers were subsequently forced to apologise," Shaima Dallali, ICJP’s Legal Researcher, said.
“Palestinians are being driven from their land while that same land is marketed to buyers abroad, including in the UK. These are not ordinary property exhibitions. They are part of the economic infrastructure that sustains Israel’s unlawful occupation and settlement enterprise. Those who protested were challenging precisely the activity that the UK government is now moving to prohibit," she added, saying that the Board of Deputies must "correct the public record".
In its guidance, the Charity Commission noted that the claims about the protesters appeared to have been made by The Board of Deputies of British Jews Limited, rather than the charitable foundation, however deemed it appropriate to issue the guidance to the charity's trustees.
According to the ICJP, the Commission reminded the trustees of a charity being, "or perceived to be, closely associated with a company, particularly in relation to public statements and communications".
The regulatory action comes as the UK moves to impose sanctions on Israel's illegal settlements and ban trade from them. The sanctions, announced by UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband on Tuesday, was welcomed by pro-Palestine groups and sections of the UK Jewish community.
The Board of Deputies of British Jews said it viewed the announcement with "deep regret", saying that it will be "felt particularly acutely by British Jews".

Trump says he'd like to see Ireland 'reunified' as he meets Taoiseach Martin in two-day official visit

Unknown Publisher

22:33:48 KST

The US president criticised Europe over trade, energy and immigration, and called relations with European allies "disappointing" over their response to his Iran war efforts
US President Donald Trump said on Saturday that a unified Ireland would be “fantastic,” wading into a complex and politically charged subject during a two-day visit to a major tournament at his private Irish golf course.
At a meeting with Irish Taoiseach Micheál Martin in Dublin, Trump said he would love to see the reunification of the Republic of Ireland with the UK’s Northern Ireland.
“I don’t want to cause any problems but I’d love to see it unified," Trump offered when asked for his opinion on the issue by a reporter. "It’s going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now.
“I think it would be a fantastic thing," he said, adding that "the UK will have something to say about it, obviously.”
Competing visions of Northern Ireland — whether it's Irish or British — drove decades of violence in Northern Ireland that left some 3,600 people dead. Previous US presidents have avoided commenting directly on the subject, even those, like Joe Biden, with strong ancestral and emotional ties to Ireland.
When Ireland, long dominated by its bigger neighbour Britain, became a self-governing Roman Catholic-majority country a century ago, a six-county region in the north with a Protestant majority remained part of the United Kingdom.
Northern Ireland was split between two main communities, nationalists — most of them Catholic — who desired union with the rest of Ireland, and largely Protestant unionists, who wanted to stay British.
Tensions eventually exploded in the Troubles, unwinding three decades of violence involving paramilitary groups on both sides and British troops.
A 1998 peace accord that Washington was instrumental in brokering largely ended the violence, but left Northern Ireland’s ultimate status unresolved.
The peace accord allows for a vote on unification if it appears likely a majority of people would vote for it.
Newly-appointed UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said point blank on Wednesday that there won’t be another referendum on reunification unless there is an evident desire for one.
“I am not aware that there is majority public support for another referendum, and until that changes, there will not be one,” said Burnham.
Trump also held talks Saturday in Dublin with his Irish counterpart Catherine Connolly and will address US and Irish business leaders at the US ambassador's official residence, before traveling to his oceanfront golf club in Doonbeg, on the other side of the country, to watch the Irish Open golf championship.
Connolly is a left-wing politician who was among those who protested when Trump visited Ireland in 2019, during his first term in office. She is now Ireland's elected head of state, which is a largely symbolic and ceremonial position.
A supporter of the Palestinian cause, she has in the past criticised US policy in the Middle East and called the Republican president a “bully” in his dealings with other states, pressuring of them and approach to foreign policy and bilateral relations.
The Irish president met Trump at the end of a red carpet at her official residence in Dublin. They shook hands and chatted before going inside. He emerged alone a few minutes later and saluted as an Irish Defence Forces band played the US national anthem and inspected an Irish Army guard of honour.
Trump rebukes European allies
The US president also lashed out at European allies as he spoke in a joint press conference with Martin following the meeting, slamming them for what he says has been a notable decline in their societies.
"I hate to see what's happening with Europe. I hate to see what's happening on trade, energy, and immigration," he said. "Ooh... that immigration, what you're doing to yourselves, you're just killing yourselves."
He also criticised Washington's relationship with European allies as "disappointing" following many nations' unwillingness to help the Republican president with his Iran war efforts, and the chaos that ensued with the closure of a strategic waterway, the Strait of Hormuz.
The US president however said that his country is maintaining a working relationship with all its allies in the continent.
Trump’s visit is the latest example of blending his official duties and personal interests.
Trump plays golf about every weekend at clubs he owns in Florida, New Jersey and Virginia. His attendance at the Irish Open continues his trend of appearing at high-profile sporting events — and having a hand in organising some of them in ways that benefit his family business.
His clubs in Doral, Florida, and Bedminster, New Jersey, have each hosted professional golf tournaments this year.
The Irish Open is the second European Tour event to be held at a Trump property this year. The Nexo Championship was held last month at Trump's golf course in Aberdeen, Scotland.
Last year, Trump went to Scotland for five days to play golf at his club in Turnberry and later inaugurated a new Trump golf course in Balmedie, Aberdeenshire.
During that visit, he held talks with the then-UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to discuss his controversial global ‘reciprocal’ tariff policy.

US Space Command Should Always Be Led by a Guardian
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
13:33:00 UTC
22:33:00 KST

General Stephen Whiting took command of U.S. Space Command in January 2024, and if customary three-year tenures hold, his tour would end in January 2027. The question now before the President and Senate is who should follow him?
Whoever they choose, it has to be a Guardian—and so should every successor thereafter.
The reason is operational, not parochial: Guardians are the military professionals best prepared to integrate spacepower into global, multi-domain operations, and the Space Force exists to generate the nation’s combat-ready space forces.
Space is no longer an uncontested domain, merely enabling others; it is a warfighting domain and capable of delivering decisive effects. U.S. Space Command’s job is to secure space superiority to preserve access to space capabilities, and plan, execute, and integrate military spacepower into multi-domain global operations. Its commander therefore must be more than familiar with space-enabled capabilities. The position demands mastery of orbital warfare, space domain awareness, command and control, electromagnetic and cyber dependencies, counterspace threats, and the integration of space effects across every geographic combatant command. Guardians are the only service members who train from accession through senior command around that full mission set.
By law, the Space Force must provide freedom of operation for the United States in, from, and to space; conduct space operations; and protect U.S. interests in space. That statutory responsibility matters. Other services have space expertise to support their missions, but Congress made the Space Force uniquely responsible to organize, train, and equip forces for prompt and sustained space operations.
A Guardian commanding U.S. Space Command brings both the depth to fight for space superiority and the breadth to lead Soldiers, Sailors, Airmen, Marines, and allied forces as a joint team. Jointness is not achieved by rotating a command among services for the sake of balance; it is achieved by selecting the officer best prepared to accomplish the assigned mission.
When U.S. Space Command was re-established in August 2019, President Trump selected General John “Jay” Raymond, soon to be the first Space Force Guardian, as the commander. But this was a temporary one-year arrangement, as Gen. Raymond was also named the first Chief of Space Operations after the Space Force was created four months later. President Trump selected Army General James Dickinson to lead U.S. Space Command from August 2020 to January 2024. When Gen. Dickinson assumed command, the Space Force was still in its first year. No pool of seasoned Guardians existed to compete for the position.
That’s no longer the case. In 2023, President Biden nominated and the Senate confirmed Gen. Whiting for the position. Since then, the Space Force has continued to develop Guardian leaders with the critical operational experience, expertise, and an unparalleled understanding of space as a warfighting domain. Gen. Dickinson’s selection was a sound transitional exception, not a precedent for an enduring Army-Space Force rotation.
The Space Force now has multiple positions and pathways to prepare its senior leaders for the responsibilities of Commander, U.S. Space Command.
First is Combat Forces Command, which traces its lineage to Space Operations Command and Air Force Space Command, where Gen. Whiting and Gen. Raymond, respectively, commanded before taking the reins of U.S. Space Command. Lt. Gen. Gregory Gagnon is, the current commander of CFC. His predecessor, Lt. Gen. David “Rock” Miller, is still serving, now as Deputy Chief of Space Operations, Strategy, Plans, Programs and Requirements on the Space Force staff.
Second are the Space Force’s component commands, which present the service’s forces to different combatant commands. These component commanders range in rank from colonel to 3-star general in Lt. Gen. Dennis Bythewood at Space Forces-Space. These positions build essential experience in integrating space effects into combat operations and provide Guardians with a distinct expertise in integrating space effects with those of all domains to achieve national objectives terrestrially and in orbit. That pipeline now produces leaders who have both commanded space forces and integrated their effects across the U.S. military, the precise combination U.S. Space Command requires. 
The Army’s June 2026 decision to create its own Space Operations Branch, along with U.S. Space Command’s relocation to Huntsville will understandably fuel an Army case to lead Space Command in the future. But neither development changes the underlying command requirement: to deliver space superiority in support of national objectives in all domains.
The Army branch is designed to improve Army component access to space-enabled capabilities at the tactical edge; it does not displace the Space Force’s responsibility for space warfare or its much broader mission set.
Likewise, while Redstone Arsenal’s Army space expertise will be valuable to U.S. Space Command, that expertise is both technical and geographical. It has little to do with governance. Locating a combatant command on an Army installation does not justify an Army claim to command it.
Some might argue that a Guardian commander would somehow make U.S. Space Command less joint. This is specious. The command will continue to employ capabilities and personnel from every service and work with the intelligence community, allies, and commercial partners. But to ensure space superiority, the officer heading U.S. Space Command must be able to make time-critical decisions to protect, defend, and employ space combat power under attack. At that level, the domain expertise inherent to Space Force Guardians is not a mere parochial preference; it is an operational warfighting requirement. Jointness does not require rotation for rotation’s sake. It requires the right commander for the mission.
The President should make the institutional logic explicit: future commanders of U.S. Space Command should come from the Space Force. The Senate should reinforce that standard in confirmation.
Doing so would align operational command with the service Congress created to protect U.S. interests in space. It would also sharpen accountability for space superiority and preserve, rather than diminish, the command’s joint character.
The move to Huntsville should deepen U.S. Space Command’s and the Space Force’s partnership with the Army, but should not blur responsibility for leading the nation’s space warfighting enterprise. Gen. Whiting’s successor should be a Guardian. So should every commander who follows.

Are the UK sanctions on Israel real progress, or more illusion?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
13:30:00 UTC
22:30:00 KST

The United Kingdom, joined by Canada and France, announced this week that they are taking action against Israeli settlements in the West Bank. It’s an announcement that is at once groundbreaking and insufficient.
Specifically, the UK said it would suspend export licenses for weapons materially supporting Israel’s illegal occupation; ban imports of Israeli settlement goods, and; sanction private companies providing services–including financial services–that enable settlement expansion.
Those are, without a doubt, positive steps. They break with the long-standing western practice of empty condemnations of settlement activity without establishing any consequences if Israel continues that activity.
The fact that the sanctions the UK announced could include firms that provide services that support the expansion of settlements is also a meaningful and groundbreaking step. It widens the scope of actions that can be taken to prevent settlement expansion to areas that are much easier to influence than Israeli settlers themselves, especially in the field of finance.
In explaining these sanctions to the House of Commons, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband bolstered accusations of war crimes against Israel and even described its actions on the West Bank as “ethnic cleansing.”
That is perhaps the most important development here. A major ally of Israel, one which is often said to have its own “special relationship” with the United States, is supporting the decision of the International Court of Justice that declared Israel’s occupation of the West Bank and Gaza illegal.
That could profoundly change the international discourse regarding the politics around not just settlements but the occupation as a whole.
These are unquestionably good things, and represent real progress, coming from a sector that has been so complicit with Israeli crimes and so hypocritical in ignoring the yawning gap between British rhetoric on the issue and its actions.
But the enthusiasm in some quarters over this announcement is overblown. There is a need to pump the brakes and prepare for a much greater push that can capitalize on this promising first step, address its shortcomings, and create something impactful.
What’s missing in the UK statement
Obviously, we cannot expect the United Kingdom to go from a regressive, genocide-enabling policy to one that promotes real justice and hope in one day. Since that is too much to ask, we need to be clear-eyed about what is still needed, not to chastise Miliband or his new boss, Prime Minister Andy Burnham, but to encourage and push them to go much further.
The exclusive targeting of settlements means that expansion will be more costly for Israel and that settlement enterprises themselves would face barriers to their income.
That’s great, but it is also already international law and, ostensibly, the policy of both the UK and the European Union. The problem is not the rules, it’s their enforcement.
The sanctions on settlements will not go into effect for six to nine months, and we can be sure that legal and political challenges will be mounted by Israel and its British supporters to maximize the delay.
During that time, the momentum and political urgency driven by this announcement could fade. If it becomes less politically convenient to enforce the sanctions, it would be very much in keeping with long-standing British and European practice to ignore them.
Then there is the matter of the efficacy of sanctioning only the settlements, not the state.
Back in June, the Global Echo Litigation Center released an illuminating report detailing the many ways settlement products evade regulations on labeling their point of origin accurately, making it more difficult to police their sale. It’s a system that is easily gamed.
As I reported at the time, “For years, it’s been widely known that Israel exports products, chiefly agricultural, from its settlements on the West Bank and the Golan Heights under a ‘Made in Israel’ label. It does so even though it is legally required by the European Union and the United Kingdom to label such products as being from settlements.”
Given the volume of world events and the speed of the news cycle these days, it is easy to imagine that, in nine months or more, the burden of policing false labeling and other deceptive practices would be more than the UK would want to undertake.
It’s also important to note that the ban on weapons is somewhat selective. One of the most crucial items Israel imports from the UK, albeit indirectly, are components of the F-35 fighter jet, a plane commonly used for airstrikes in Gaza. Those components were excluded from the weapons ban.
Indeed, Miliband’s wording on weaponry in general was very vague. “We will now also refuse all license applications for arms and other exports that materially contribute to the occupation…”
Like cutting off money to the settlements, arms sales are fungible. Many arms Israel uses in military operations which are not covered by this ban are also used in the settlements. Such laws, which already exist in the UK, the EU, and the United States, have not been barriers to Israel arming itself to the teeth through western largesse. Nothing in Miliband’s statements indicates a fundamental change in that travesty is certain.
The false separation between the Israeli state and Israeli settlements
Israel has long since stopped trying to pretend that the settlement project is not fully part of state activities. The Israeli army openly escorts settlers on their pogroms. The Knesset retroactively legalizes so-called “outposts” that settlers simply put up on Palestinian land. Indeed, the military regularly confiscates Palestinian land, labeling them “closed military zones” or some other title before breaking ground on new settlements there.
Yet Miliband insists on limiting the penalties to the settlements themselves. He intends to sanction ”particularly violent settlers,” but not the Israeli leaders—up to, and including, the prime minister—who enable their activities.
His speech to the House of Commons explaining this “reset” in UK policy toward Israel was prefaced by a long-winded exposition of his love for Israel. But more concerning was his explicit refusal to target the state that is, after all, intentionally pursuing the policies that are bringing these sanctions.
“The sanctions regime will target illegal settlements and settlement expansion, not Israel,” Miliband said. “We will continue to support important and valued trade with green line Israel precisely because we support the two-state solution, including security and prosperity for Israel. For this reason, I wholeheartedly oppose the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions or BDS campaign.”
That strategy is doomed to fail. Beyond the question of enforcement of these new rules, sanctioning the settlements simply doesn’t have much impact. Settlement exports are a very small part of trade between the UK and Israel.
In 2025, according to the UK government’s reports, trade between the two countries totaled approximately $8.1 billion. While it is impossible to know exactly how much trade was done with the settlements because of the evasion practices discussed above, UK records show only about $8 million of imports from Palestine, which includes the West Bank, whatever drips out of Gaza, and the settlements.
Clearly, the trade from settlements is tiny. But the fact is that the settlements are not isolated from Israel. Many firms operating in the settlements are simply parts of larger Israeli companies. Most financing for those companies isn’t specifically sent to a “settlement” business.
Settlers themselves are not worried about this. They know they can find alternative recipients for their goods or, failing that, other ways to make a living. The unending support of the state reassures them, and they’re right to feel that way.
Limited vision
Miliband’s fear of this UK action being seen as a contribution to the BDS movement is also irrational. Whether he likes the movement or not, these are the sort of sanctions BDS activists want to see put in place, although they certainly want them broader, targeted at the state, and with more bite.
His approach to presenting these sanctions reflects another potential flaw in their implementation.
The sanctions were prompted not by a realization that years of UK policy in Palestine and Israel had dismally failed to make any progress toward ending the occupation or stabilizing the region.
No, they were prompted by Israel pushing the envelope, as it has so often done. The government of Benjamin Netanyahu knows well that construction in the E-1 corridor—which would, if completed, bisect the West Bank and shatter the last remaining illusion that a two-state solution is possible—is a red line for the Europeans, and would be so for a more rational American government as well. They also know that the escalated settler violence has prompted negative reactions around the world.
Netanyahu and his cronies are trying to see what they can get away with. Issuing tenders for construction in E-1 is something Israel has threatened to do for decades. They’ve always been forced to back off.
But they have, in the last few years, been able to get away with actions they had previously thought too provocative, such as the complete destruction of Gaza and the genocide of the people there. They have even managed to finally talk the United States into a suicidal war with Iran.
So why not see if they can finally get away with cutting the West Bank in half and putting paid, once and for all, to any Palestinian aspirations for a state?
These sanctions are Britain’s response to that. Even the United States, which routinely screams almost as loud as Israel at any hint of pressure on its Israeli ally, has been relatively quiet about this.
While the Christian Nationalist Ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee threatened potential consequences, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who actually matters in this regard, sounded a more conciliatory note: “We heard their arguments as to why,” Rubio said. “But look, we share the goal of stability. We don’t want to see some uptick in violence or an uptick in conflict or tensions in the West Bank at a very tenuous time in the region. But beyond that, as of this moment, we don’t have any further comment.” Neither he nor Donald Trump have said anything more.
This indicates that they are waiting to see if Israel backs off of the construction in E-1 in response to British pressure. There’s a good chance that this will happen, and, if it does, an equally good chance that the UK will back off from its sanctions.
That’s by no means inevitable. By invoking the ethnic cleansing of the West Bank and stating its support for the ICJ’s 2024 ruling, on top of recognizing the State of Palestine last year, the UK has made real progress.
But it’s not irrevocable progress, and Miliband’s own words contain both the promise that something can really change here, and the possibility that Britain will back off, especially if Israel agrees not to take any more steps in E-1 for a while and confines its killing and terrorizing of Palestinians to its security forces instead of the settlers.
Supporters of Palestinian rights—in the UK, the United States, and Europe—can all contribute a lot to pushing the Burnham government forward rather than back. One thing this recent announcement does show is that having been supported by Canada and France, if the UK does take more positive steps, they will be magnified by others.

EU Eastern Border Irregular Crossings Drop 47%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
13:25:00 UTC
22:25:00 KST

Irregular crossings into the EU via the bloc’s Eastern Land Border route fell by 47% in the first eight months of 2026, the EU’s border agency said, as eastern member states continue to fortify their frontiers.
Frontex recorded just over 4,000 detections along the route between January and August, according to preliminary data released on Friday.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The route covers parts of the EU’s eastern external frontier, including Poland’s borders with Belarus and Ukraine.
Ukrainians, Afghans and Estonians were the three most commonly detected nationalities on the route, Frontex data showed.
The sharp decline came as irregular migration into the EU fell across almost all major routes, with nearly 75,000 crossings detected in the first eight months of the year, down 35% from the same period in 2025.
Frontex did not provide a specific explanation for the decline on the Eastern Land Border route. It linked the overall fall across the EU to sustained cooperation with partner countries and preventive measures in key departure states.
Eastern borders reinforced
The fall comes as Poland and other countries on the EU’s eastern flank continue to strengthen their borders amid concerns over irregular migration and security threats from Russia and Belarus.
Poland has extensively reinforced its border with Belarus in recent years, adding physical barriers and electronic surveillance systems following a migration crisis that Warsaw, Brussels and its allies have accused Minsk of deliberately orchestrating.
Most Ukrainian Refugees in Poland Plan to Return Home, Survey Finds
The country is also building East Shield, a 10-billion-złoty (€2.3 billion) defense program designed to fortify roughly 800 kilometers of its eastern and northern borders with Belarus and Russia’s Kaliningrad exclave, respectively.
Other countries along the EU’s and NATO’s eastern flank, including the Baltic states and Finland, have also moved to reinforce their frontiers with Russia and Belarus.
How other routes fared
Across the EU, the Eastern Mediterranean remained the busiest migration route, with more than 24,200 crossings recorded in the first eight months of the year, down 25% year-on-year.
The Central Mediterranean recorded around 19,400 detections, down 55%, making it the second-busiest route.
The Western African route saw the sharpest decline, with detections down 58% to around 5,100.
The Western Mediterranean, which includes routes toward mainland Spain and its Balearic Islands, was the only major route to record an increase, with detections rising 34% to around 15,900.
The figures exclude the large-scale movement of people from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in late July, as Frontex said many of those who crossed returned to Morocco without being registered.
Despite the decline in arrivals, more than 1,800 people have died in the Mediterranean so far this year, according to the UN migration agency, IOM.

Train derailment in France injures 44, police suspect sabotage
Authorities suspect sabotage caused a train derailment in northwestern France that injured 44 people after a piece of rail was found on the track.
The regional train was carrying 186 passengers from Rouen to Caen when it derailed Friday evening in Cleon. One carriage tipped onto its side while four others left the tracks.
An 18-year-old woman was among the injured and was evacuated by helicopter to Rouen University Hospital, police said.
A spokeswoman for the French national police communications service, known as SICOP, told The Associated Press the piece of rail found on the track was "probably" linked to the derailment. She spoke on condition of anonymity because she wasn't authorized to be publicly named in line with police policy.
"The reasons for its presence are unknown and will have to be determined by the investigation," Rouen prosecutor Sebastien Gallois said, according to Agence France-Presse.
Investigators were working to establish whether the circumstances were accidental or involved sabotage, the service said. The prosecutor's office remained cautious about drawing conclusions, according to police.
Cleon Mayor Melanie Delacour said the victims were "in a state of shock."
"The windows of the carriages that remained upright shattered, and because of the train's speed, stones flew into the carriages," she told AFP.
France's previous rail disasters include the July 2013 derailment at Brétigny-sur-Orge, south of Paris, which killed seven people.
In November 2015, a high-speed TGV train carrying out tests derailed at Eckwersheim, near Strasbourg, killing 11.
More recently, a crash involving two high-speed trains at Adamuz in southern Spain killed 46 people and injured more than 100 in January, according to the Andalusian regional government.
