U.S. Space Force taps California startup for orbital nuclear reactor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
12:58:35 UTC
21:58:35 KST

- The U.S. Space Force awarded Antares a $161 million contract to develop a nuclear reactor for spacecraft, the largest such award to date.
- Antares' Mark-0 reactor reached criticality in June 2026, becoming the first private reactor to do so under the DOE's Reactor Pilot Program.
The Office of the Assistant Secretary of the U.S. Air Force for Space Acquisition and Integration has awarded a $161 million Strategic Breakthrough contract to Antares, a California nuclear startup, to advance a reactor design meant to power spacecraft. The company describes it as the largest Department of War award to date focused specifically on nuclear power in space.
The award covers two related efforts. Antares will run a nuclear ground demonstration of a reactor design called R1-S, then work toward integrating that reactor with a spacecraft ahead of an eventual flight. Separately, the company plans to power an operational ground-to-space asset using Mark-1, an electricity-producing reactor scheduled to begin testing in 2027.
“Space has been core to the Antares thesis since the company was founded,” said Jordan Bramble, CEO and co-founder of Antares. “This partnership with the Space Force turns that long-held vision into a codified space mission. Fission will unlock strategic capabilities that are impossible today.”
Most satellites today run on solar panels and batteries, which limit how much power is available onboard and how freely a spacecraft can maneuver without draining its reserves. A compact nuclear reactor would give a satellite continuous, high-output power instead, supporting heavier onboard computers, more aggressive orbital maneuvers, and power-hungry equipment such as directed-energy systems or electronic-warfare gear.
Antares already has a notable first to its name in this space. On June 4, 2026, the company’s Mark-0 reactor reached criticality, the point at which a nuclear reaction becomes self-sustaining, at Idaho National Laboratory. The test, conducted with the Department of Energy, the laboratory and nuclear fuel maker BWX Technologies, with the U.S. Army observing as a potential future user, made Antares the first private company to bring an advanced reactor to criticality under the Energy Department’s Reactor Pilot Program. It was also the first newly designed reactor to reach criticality at the Idaho site in more than 50 years.
That same reactor line feeds into more than one military effort. Data from the Mark-0 test is being shared with the Department of War’s Project Pele, a long-running program to build a transportable microreactor for military use, and Antares is also a supplier under the U.S. Army’s separate Janus Program, which is installing microreactors at bases including Fort Benning, Georgia.
Antares tied the new Space Force award to a presidential directive the company calls Executive Order 14369, “Ensuring American Space Superiority,” part of a broader government push, outlined in a policy document known as NSTM-3, to fly a nuclear reactor in space as early as 2028 and place one on the lunar surface by 2030.
Antares, founded in 2023 and based in Torrance, California, has raised more than $600 million and operates additional facilities in Idaho Falls, Idaho, and Aiken, South Carolina. The company has not disclosed a target launch date for the R1-S demonstration, named which spacecraft or mission it might eventually support, or said how the $161 million award is divided between the ground demonstration and the Mark-1 testing effort.

BRICS nations see unilateral tariffs, non-tariff measures as threat to global trade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
12:53:39 UTC
21:53:39 KST

NEW DELHI, September 12. /TASS/. BRICS nations see unilateral tariffs and non-tariff measures as a threat to global trade, according to the New Delhi Declaration adopted at the group’s 18th summit.
"The proliferation of trade-restrictive actions that are inconsistent with WTO rules, whether in the form of indiscriminate rising of tariffs and non-tariff measures, or protectionism under the guise of environmental objectives, threatens to further reduce global trade, disrupt global supply chains, and introduce uncertainty into international economic and trade activities, potentially exacerbating existing economic disparities and negatively affecting prospects for global economic development," the document reads.
The member states voiced "serious concerns about the rise of unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures which distort trade and are inconsistent with WTO rules."
"We will work together to enhance the WTO’s responsiveness to trade disruptions and the needs and priorities of emerging markets and developing economies," as well as to strengthen the multilateral trading system.

Greek firm gives old military jeeps a modern makeover
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
12:50:58 UTC
21:50:58 KST

- ELVO has demonstrated the first modernized Mercedes G-Class jeeps under a program to upgrade the Greek Army's 30-year-old vehicle fleet.
- The refit adds a new engine, camera systems, anti-drone protection and other upgrades rather than replacing the vehicles outright.
ELVO, Greece’s main military vehicle manufacturer, has shown off the first Mercedes G-Class “jeeps” modernized under a new refit program built to extend the life of the Greek Army’s aging vehicle fleet rather than replace it outright. The vehicles being upgraded are roughly 30 years old.
ELVO is fitting a new engine and automatic transmission, electric air conditioning and a redesigned interior with adjustable, suspension-equipped seats. On the outside, the vehicles get 360-degree day and night camera systems, all-LED lighting, an anti-drone protection net, thermal and visual camouflage, reinforced windshields built to resist rioters, and mirrors that won’t shatter. The vehicles are built to U.S. and NATO-aligned military standards known as MIL-STD, and ELVO says they can also be configured to carry weapon systems.
The approach reflects a broader shift some militaries are making as vehicle budgets tighten. Rather than retiring an entire fleet and buying new replacements, ELVO is retrofitting vehicles already in service, vehicles it has direct experience with since it supplied more than 10,000 Mercedes 290GD and Mercedes 240 jeeps, along with over 12,000 Steyr trucks, to Greece and Cyprus over the decades.
“ELVO is redefining what military vehicle modernization can deliver,” said ELVO General Manager Antonis Vitetzakis. “By combining our deep engineering expertise with the latest technologies, we can bring existing fleets into the modern era, combining decades of operational service with new capabilities while maximizing the value of investments our customers have already made.”
ELVO, based in Thessaloniki, has spent more than 50 years building vehicles for the Greek military, including the Leonidas family of armored personnel carriers and Steyr-based trucks. The company also holds a certified production and assembly line for Leopard 2 HEL tanks, the Hellenic Army’s variant of the German-designed Leopard 2. In August 2025, Israeli-founded holding company SK Group acquired full ownership of ELVO, marking the group’s first operational base in Europe.
The G-Class refit lands amid a broader expansion at ELVO this year. In May 2026, Rheinmetall signed a memorandum of understanding with ELVO to assemble military trucks and specialized systems for the Hellenic Armed Forces. In September, ELVO said separately that it would invest 40 million euros, roughly $46 million, to expand its Sindos manufacturing plant and add drone production capacity, drawing on unmanned systems technology from SK Group, a project expected to create about 300 jobs.

Webinar on fertility preservation for people over 30 set for October
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
12:48:13 UTC
21:48:13 KST

Webinar on fertility preservation for people over 30 set for October
TEHRAN – Royan Institute will host a specialized webinar on October 1 to help individuals make informed decisions about their reproductive health, focusing on fertility preservation options and strategies for single women and men over 30.
The rising age of marriage and delayed childbearing have made reproductive health, awareness of one’s fertility status, and knowledge of available fertility preservation options more important than ever, IRNA reported.
Nevertheless, understanding age-related changes and recognizing opportunities to preserve fertility and extend their reproductive timeline can play a significant role in empowering individuals to make informed decisions about their future childbearing.
Titled ‘Fertility preservation in modern era, opportunities and strategies for single women and men over 30’, the specialized webinar will examine various aspects of male and female fertility, covering topics such as the impact of aging on fertility, the assessment of fertility status and capacity, the importance of understanding one’s fertility status before delaying childbearing, and the methods for preserving reproductive cells.
It will also discuss the medical considerations associated with fertility preservation methods, the factors that influence the success of these methods, as well as the opportunities and limitations facing individuals who postpone childbearing for any reason.
Policies, programs for infertility treatment
To address infertility, which is known as one of the main challenges of health and population in the country, the government has adopted different measures, including infertility insurance to lower high-cost and out-of-pocket expenses of infertility treatment.
Covering the services associated with fertility treatment, the insurance organizations have played a key role in infertility treatment since the Iranian year 1400 (2021), IRNA reported.
The covered services include the costs of tests, medications, and assisted reproductive methods, like IVF and intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI), which have facilitated access to specialized services and encourage couples to have regular health visits.
In government centers, 90 percent of the treatment costs, which are based on subsidized rates, are covered, while in private centers, 90 percent of the costs, which are based on free rates, are covered.
Currently, 150 medical centers are providing health services to infertile couples, out of which 120 centers are under the coverage of health insurance.
Over the past Iranian year (March 2025 – March 2026), the health insurance reviewed a total of 107,374 claims and reimbursed 9.98 trillion rials (around 6.743 million dollars) to medical centers.
The health insurance also paid 11.16 trillion rials (almost 7.541 million dollars) for prescribed medications to infertile couples. Since the Iranian year 1400, the health insurance has invested 37 trillion rials (about 25 million dollars).
Apart from insurance, the government has taken other measures to boost fertility, such as developing specialized infertility treatment centers in metropolises and deprived areas, considering incentive policies for infertile couples, like financial support and granting loans for treatment, implementing national projects, and comprehensive programs on family health and population to promote childbearing and reduce infertility.
Equipping medical centers with advanced facilities for in vitro fertilization (IVF), providing counselling and psychological services, are among other actions taken to help infertile couples.
Demographic shifts in Iran
With older adults already accounting for 13 percent of Iran’s population and the country’s fertility rate continuing to decline, demographic shifts are accelerating. Current projections indicate that within the next 25 years, nearly one-third of Iran’s population will be aged 60 and above.
Iran is aging, and this demographic shift will place significant pressure on the healthcare system, pension funds, social support agencies, and the national economy. To prevent the consequences of an aging population, the country is pursuing policies aimed at boosting the youth population and incentives for childbearing.
Aging is a natural process of the life cycle, but the way society approaches this life phase today will shape the living conditions of future generations.
An aging population entails more than just an increased demand for healthcare services; the rising number of elderly individuals also drives a growing need for care services, rehabilitation, home-based care, environmental adaptations, and social welfare services, which will alter the pension system and pose serious challenges to it.
Demographic shifts make action more urgent than ever. Actions need to be taken now to be able to address the livelihood and well-being of the elderly in the years to come. The interval between the current situation and advanced aging offers an opportunity for policymaking and structural reform; failing to act would result in consequences that are significantly more challenging to address.
Fortunately, Iran is in a population window of opportunity – a period when a large proportion of the population is of working age; the country has 15 to 20 years before the demographic window begins to close.

Tiny nuclear reactors headed to a Georgia U.S. Army base
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
12:46:43 UTC
21:46:43 KST

- The U.S. Army selected Fort Benning, Georgia, to host three Radiant Industries microreactors under the Janus energy resilience program, announced August 26, 2026.
- The three 1-megawatt units will provide backup power to Lawson Army Airfield and other critical infrastructure if the regional grid fails.
The U.S. Army has selected Fort Benning, Georgia, as one of five military bases that will host nuclear microreactors under a new Pentagon energy resilience initiative called the Janus Program, Army officials announced August 26, 2026.
Fort Benning will pair with California-based Radiant Industries to install three of the company’s one-megawatt Kaleidos microreactors, adding a combined 3 megawatts of power tied directly into the base’s electrical grid.
The reactors are meant to protect against a specific vulnerability. Fort Benning, home to the Army’s Maneuver Center of Excellence, relies mainly on commercial utility power, backed up by diesel generators that depend on fuel deliveries vulnerable to disruption during a crisis. Lawson Army Airfield, the base’s main launch point for deploying airborne infantry, Rangers and other maneuver units worldwide, needs uninterrupted power for runway lighting, air traffic control and secure facilities to keep flights moving on short notice. If the regional grid goes down, the microreactors are designed to keep those systems running independently.
A microreactor works on the same basic principle as a full-scale nuclear plant, splitting atoms to generate heat that produces steam and spins a turbine, but at a fraction of the size. Radiant’s Kaleidos units are self-contained and roughly the size of a commercial bus, skipping the large cooling towers and support buildings traditional reactors require. The company says each unit is designed to run for up to five years without refueling and has a 20-year operational lifespan, and Radiant, not the Army, will own and operate the reactors, handling fueling and eventual spent-fuel management under Army regulatory oversight.
“The Fort Benning microreactors are not like older, traditional nuclear plants that need giant cooling towers or millions of gallons of water to prevent an accident,” said Dr. Ed Locke, master planner for Fort Benning’s Directorate of Public Works and the installation’s Janus Project lead. “These microreactors are self-contained and walk-away safe.”
Locke said the design includes passive safety features that automatically reduce reactor power and remove heat without relying on outside electricity, cooling water or an operator stepping in, a system he described as governed by the laws of physics rather than active controls. Fort Benning has identified candidate parcels of land for the three units but has not finalized a site, and officials say they are looking for a location isolated from water sources and everyday facilities while still close enough to connect to the base’s power grid.
The Janus Program launched in October 2025 through the Defense Innovation Unit, pairing the Department of War with commercial nuclear power companies across a group of military installations, of which Fort Benning is one of five announced so far. Radiant has said separately that it holds an Army contract worth up to $750 million to deploy 15 microreactor units across those Janus sites. That deal is distinct from an earlier agreement the company signed with the Department of the Air Force in April 2026 to install a Kaleidos reactor at Buckley Space Force Base in Colorado, part of a different, earlier effort called the Advanced Nuclear Power for Installations program that also includes companies such as Oklo, X-energy, BWXT and Kairos Power.
“Energy resiliency is not a luxury, it is a foundation of power projection and combat readiness,” said Maj. Gen. Colin P. Tuley, commanding general of the Maneuver Center of Excellence and Fort Benning. “Integrating microreactors into our critical infrastructure ensures that our flight lines, command nodes, and combat training pipelines remain fully mission-capable, regardless of external disruptions to the regional utility grid.”
The Army is targeting 2028 for the first Janus microreactors to become operational, and Fort Benning’s exact site selection remains under evaluation.

Chinooks deploy police in Scottish training exercise
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
13:46:40 BST
21:46:40 KST

Police Scotland officers flew aboard RAF Chinook helicopters between force headquarters during a joint training exercise with military personnel and the emergency services on Friday, the Ministry of Defence stated.
Exercise Tartan Kukri brought together Police Scotland, the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service, the Scottish Ambulance Service and military units, and sits within the wider Exercise Kukri Dawn, a routine RAF-led exercise running from 2 to 18 September which trains new Chinook aircrew by replicating operational scenarios.
Squadron Leader Paul Day, Chinook Flight Commander, said: “This is the culminating exercise for our trainee Chinook pilots and crewmen before they progress to operational flying duties. Operating in the demanding conditions found here in Scotland, alongside our civil partners and the British Army, provides realistic, high-quality training that develops the skills, experience and confidence our crews need for future operations.”
Lieutenant Colonel Doug Mackay, Joint Regional Liaison Officer Scotland, said: “This exercise is a valuable opportunity for Defence to work in close cooperation with our Emergency Services colleagues in a challenging and fast-moving scenario, improving our interoperability and gaining mutual understanding of each other’s organisations and way of working. Tough, realistic training is key to operational success on the day.”
The specialist teams involved included Police Scotland firearms officers, Counter Terrorism Policing officers and the Major Incident Support and Coordination Unit, alongside 43 Commando Fleet Protection Group Royal Marines, 2nd Battalion The Royal Regiment of Scotland, Military Provost Staff, the Scottish Ambulance Service Special Operations Response Team, Scottish Fire and Rescue Service National Inter-agency Liaison Officers, RAF Chinook crews and Tactical Support Wing personnel from 28 Squadron.
The RAF was based at Police Scotland headquarters at Tulliallan, with officers flown from there to the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service headquarters at Cambuslang, where they joined the Royal Marines and 2 SCOTS in a scenario-based exercise using blank firing ammunition.
According to the department, the exercise also tested the process for the safe handling, triage and handover of individuals between military and police personnel, with the aim of ensuring smooth coordination between the two. The partnership reflects the principles of the Joint Emergency Services Interoperability Programme, which sets out how emergency services should work together to save lives and reduce harm.
A previous Exercise Kukri Dawn took place in March, with joint police and defence activity centred on Murrayfield Stadium in Edinburgh.

Fighting across the front remained intense, with Ukrainian forces recording 237 combat engagements during the latest reporting period. The heaviest Russian assault activity was reported in the Pokrovsk and Kostiantynivka sectors, where Russian forces carried out 29 and 22 attacks, respectively.

'Zero tolerance' on terror: Brics declaration strongly condemns Pahalgam attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
12:40:15 UTC
21:40:15 KST

Prime Minister Narendra Modi delivers closing remarks during the BRICS Session on 'Inclusive Global Governance and Strengthening Multilateralism', at the 18th BRICS Summit at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi
NEW DELHI: The Brics countries have strongly condemned the Pahalgam terrorist attack in Jammu and Kashmir that killed 26 people, reaffirming their commitment to combating terrorism in all its forms and calling for “zero tolerance” towards the menace.The condemnation was included in the New Delhi Declaration 2026, adopted at the 18th Brics Summit in New Delhi on Saturday.The declaration also opposed double standards in countering terrorism and called for concerted action against all UN-designated terrorists and terrorist entities.“We express strong condemnation of any acts of terrorism as criminal and unjustifiable, regardless of their motivation, whenever, wherever and by whomsoever committed,” the declaration said.It specifically condemned “in the strongest terms” the terrorist attack in Jammu and Kashmir on April 22, 2025, during which 26 people were killed and several others injured.
Brics reaffirms stand against cross-border terror
The Brics declaration reaffirmed the grouping’s commitment to combating terrorism in all its forms and manifestations, including the cross-border movement of terrorists, terrorism financing and safe havens.The grouping said terrorism should not be associated with any religion, nationality, civilisation or ethnic group.
It also stressed that those involved in terrorist activities and their support must be held accountable and brought to justice in accordance with relevant national and international law.The declaration called for “zero tolerance for terrorism” and rejected double standards in countering terrorism.It also emphasised the primary responsibility of states in combating terrorism, while stressing that global efforts to prevent and counter terrorist threats must comply with international law, including the UN Charter and relevant international conventions and protocols.Brics welcomed the activities of its Counter-Terrorism Working Group and its five subgroups, which operate on the basis of the Brics Counter-Terrorism Strategy, Counter-Terrorism Action Plan and the Counter-Terrorism Working Group Position Paper.The grouping also called for the expeditious finalisation and adoption of the Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism under the UN framework.The declaration further stressed the importance of countering extremism and radicalisation, particularly among younger generations, and called for greater cooperation among Brics countries and their competent authorities, including through the sharing of best practices.
Pahalgam attack and India’s response
On April 22, last year, 26 civilians were killed in a terrorist attack in the Baisaran meadow area near Pahalgam in South Kashmir, a major tourist destination.The victims were segregated by the attackers based on religion before being shot in front of their families, triggering widespread outrage.Security forces launched search operations in the surrounding areas following the attack, while investigations were expanded to trace the terrorist network and its logistical support.India responded with “Operation Sindoor” on May 7, 2025, carrying out precision strikes on terror infrastructure in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir.The operation marked a major escalation with Pakistan, followed by a four-day conflict that ended with a ceasefire on May 10, after Islamabad’s request.In the aftermath, Indian armed forces launched “Operation Mahadev” and tracked down and eliminated the three attackers involved in the Pahalgam killings.
Declaration backs India, Brazil for greater UN role
Beyond terrorism, the New Delhi Declaration reaffirmed Brics' support for comprehensive reform of the United Nations, including the UN Security Council, with greater representation for developing countries.China and Russia, as permanent members of the UN Security Council, reiterated their support for the aspirations of India and Brazil to play a greater role in the UN, including its Security Council.The declaration called for greater and more meaningful participation and representation of emerging market and developing countries, as well as Least Developed Countries, in global decision-making processes.On Security Council reform, Brics said the process should make the body more democratic, representative, effective and efficient while increasing the representation of developing countries.“We stress that the UN Security Council reform is to lead to the amplified voice of the Global South,” the declaration said.The grouping also called for equitable geographical representation in the UN Secretariat and other international organisations, particularly at senior and decision-making levels.
Brics raises concerns over trade measures
The declaration also expressed serious concern over unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures, saying they distort trade, threaten global supply chains and create uncertainty for international economic activity.Brics reaffirmed its support for reform of the World Trade Organization and called for an open, equitable, transparent, fair, inclusive, predictable and rules-based multilateral trading system, with the WTO at its core.The grouping also advocated the immediate restoration of an accessible, effective and fully functioning two-tier binding WTO dispute settlement mechanism and called for the appointment of new Appellate Body members without further delay.
On unilateral coercive measures, Brics condemned sanctions that it said were contrary to international law and reiterated its opposition to unilateral coercive measures, including those not authorised by the UN Security Council.The New Delhi Declaration was adopted during the 18th Brics Summit, being hosted by India on September 12-13 under its 2026 chairship. India’s Brics chairship is guided by the theme “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability.”

From Monday morning until the end of Sunday Sept. 20, 92-, 95-, and 98-octane unleaded gasoline will cost NT$31.2 (US$0.98), NT$32.7, and NT$34.7 per liter respectively. Premium diesel will cost NT$29.9 per liter, Liberty Times reported.

The energy company said it will have absorbed NT$19.85 billion in oil price rises from the start of the Iran War on Feb. 28 until Sunday. The move formed part of a government policy to limit the impact of energy price rises on local civilians and businesses.

====================================================================================================

Ukraine combat experience shapes Redwire’s new drone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
12:33:32 UTC
21:33:32 KST

- Redwire says more than 250 Penguin drones supplied to Ukraine have shaped its approach to maintenance, training, electronic warfare and aircraft upgrades.
- An undisclosed NATO country has ordered the new Penguin Mk3 under a multi-year contract valued in the high eight figures.
Russia’s war against Ukraine has turned unmanned aircraft from a supporting capability into one of the central elements of modern battlefield operations. It has also forced drone manufacturers to confront a problem that peacetime testing cannot fully reproduce: how to keep an aircraft useful when tactics, electronic warfare threats and operational requirements can change within weeks or even days.
Redwire Defense Tech has been dealing with that challenge through the deployment of its Penguin fixed-wing unmanned aircraft in Ukraine since 2022. The company says the platform’s combat experience has influenced not only the aircraft itself, but also the way Redwire approaches training, maintenance, engineering support and the introduction of new configurations.
According to Redwire, one of the main lessons from Ukraine is that endurance, range and payload are only part of what determines whether a tactical drone remains useful in combat. Repair times, operator workload, local support, the ability to reconfigure the aircraft and the speed at which manufacturers can respond to battlefield changes have become equally important.
In an interview with The Defence Blog, Josh Stinson, co-president and chief growth officer of Redwire Defense Tech, discussed how sustained operations in Ukraine changed the company’s assumptions about tactical drones, what Redwire has learned from operating in a contested electromagnetic environment, and how those lessons are shaping the Penguin family and its future NATO deployments.
Q: Redwire has delivered more than 250 Penguin aircraft to Ukraine since 2022. Looking back at that experience, how has daily combat use changed your understanding of what it means to build a drone for an actual war rather than for a procurement specification?
A: Ukraine has reinforced that an aircraft is only useful when it is available to the unit, in the configuration needed, at the moment it is needed. A procurement specification can measure endurance, payload and range. It cannot fully capture repair turnaround, operator workload, training quality, reliability, ease of reconfiguration or the speed at which engineering and support teams must respond to a truly dynamic and rapidly evolving environment.
Redwire’s Penguin UAS has deep eastern European roots and is built for survivability in the weather extremes of the region. Its engineering, production and flight operations are anchored in Latvia, and Redwire maintains a significant presence in Ukraine for support service, Maintenance, Repair, and Overhaul (MRO), training, and engineering work. In country support allows our team to engage directly with operators and their operational reality. Most importantly, Ukraine is not a test range. It is a sovereign European country defending itself, and the consequences of design and support decisions are immediate. That creates a higher standard: build for repeated operation, recovery, repair, continual adaptation, and return to service under pressure.
Q: Which assumptions about tactical drones that appeared reasonable before 2022 proved incomplete or wrong once the Penguin entered sustained operations in Ukraine?
A: Ukraine’s use of uncrewed systems has revolutionized modern warfare and provided the operational advantage to a lesser equipped military, proving that with the right technology, David can stand up to Goliath. The impact of this extends far beyond Europe. Ukraine’s utilization of drones has forever changed warfare for everyone, challenging previously held axioms of maneuver force application.
Another incomplete assumption was that requirements would remain relatively stable after a system entered service. In Ukraine, the threat, operating environment and tactics continue to evolve—and so must the technology supporting the warfighter. A tactical UAS therefore cannot be treated as a finished product at delivery.
Ukraine also demonstrated that airframe performance alone does not equal operational capability. Training, maintainability, logistics, configuration control, local support and the ability to integrate new mission equipment are all part of the capability. Endurance, range, high altitude capabilities, and sensor performance remain essential, but they must be balanced with operational footprint, ease of use and adaptability. The most valuable system is not simply the one that performs best during a controlled demonstration. It is the one operators can employ repeatedly, support locally and adapt in response to adversary innovations and as the mission changes.
Q: Ukrainian and foreign drone manufacturers have faced powerful Russian electronic warfare, particularly against navigation and communication links. Has Redwire encountered the same challenge with the Penguin, and how has it changed the way you approach the aircraft’s design and continued development?
A: Penguin operates in a heavily contested electromagnetic environment where there is also risk of kinetic interception and other counter-UAS capabilities. This is the battlespace all UAS in Ukraine must survive, and it would be misleading for any manufacturer to suggest immunity from electronic warfare. For operational-security reasons, we do not discuss specific configurations, countermeasures or mission performance.
The central lesson is that navigation and communications cannot be treated as guaranteed resources. Development must consider how the complete system, including the aircraft, mission equipment, software, procedures and operator, functions when conditions are degraded or rapidly changing. This has reinforced our emphasis on modularity, mission adaptability and growth capacity. Electronic warfare is not a problem solved permanently by one feature. The adversary adapts, so the more effective tactic is to design an aircraft and support model that can also adapt quickly and incorporate new technology as innovative solutions emerge.
Q: Another challenge in Ukraine is that operational experience and information do not always move quickly between different military units. Has this affected your ability to collect feedback, identify common problems and deliver updates to Penguin operators?
A: Feedback from a distributed force does not arrive as a single, clean dataset, and one unit’s experience may reflect its mission, configuration, terrain or operating methods rather than a fleet-wide issue.
Our response has been local presence. With the help of a translator, our Chief Technology Officer even had a virtual meeting with a Special Operations Forces (SOF) commander in a bunker in Ukraine where they discussed the changing tactics on the ground and how our engineers might mitigate risks or adapt our capabilities to overcome those challenges.
Redwire has an office in Ukraine where our team works directly with warfighters, while our Riga-based Flight Operations team trains Ukrainian personnel and maintains recurring contact with operators. We have training facilities in both Latvia and Ukraine. These interactions create multiple opportunities to hear questions from end users firsthand, identify recurring themes and provide actionable feedback to our engineering teams. That does not eliminate the friction inherent in wartime communication, but it shortens the route between Ukrainian operators, regional support personnel and the engineers developing the system.
Q: Can you share an example of a request or observation from a Ukrainian operator that directly changed the Penguin? What did that experience teach your engineering team?
A: The Penguin deployed in Ukraine today is not the same UAS fielded four years ago, and that is the result of direct engagements like the anecdote about our CTO having a virtual meeting with a Special Operations Forces commander in a Ukrainian bunker. Our more sophisticated Penguin Mk2X can fly significantly higher than it did in 2022, which aids in protecting the asset from targeting by First-Person View (FPV) drones during Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance missions.
Another documented example we can discuss is how Ukrainian experience changed the way Penguin training and fielding are approached. Our Riga team has developed training around the challenges operators face in real missions, with ongoing operator feedback passed to engineering. The programme is tailored to the aircraft configuration and mission rather than relying on a standard, one-size-fits-all course.
The lesson for our engineers is that usability, documentation and training are not activities that begin after a design is complete. They are engineering inputs. A technical improvement has limited value if an operator cannot employ it confidently, understand its behaviour or maintain the system under wartime conditions.
Q: Operating and supporting more than 300 aircraft during a war is very different from managing a limited peacetime deployment. What challenges emerged only after the Ukrainian fleet reached this scale?
A: Scale changes the nature of sustainment. A minor maintenance issue, unclear procedure or commonly needed component can become a fleet-level availability concern when multiplied across hundreds of aircraft and several operating units. Training consistency, configuration management, spare-parts planning, technical documentation, repair throughput and the communication of updates all become as important as production.
That experience has reinforced the need for support close to the customer. Our presence in Ukraine, our Flight Operations organisation in Riga and our wider European engineering and sustainment capabilities allow us to respond regionally rather than treating support as a distant export function. The central lesson is that the aircraft must be capable of continually evolving to meet the warfighter’s most urgent needs, but that is only one part of delivering operational capability. A manufacturer must also help operators sustain, repair and continually adapt the fleet.
Q: Which lessons from Ukraine are now built into the Penguin Mk3, and what will its NATO customer receive that Redwire could not have developed from testing and peacetime operations alone?
A: It is important to distinguish between the Penguin series’ combat experience and the specific Mk3 configuration. We do not assume that a new model is automatically combat proven. Rather, Mk3 has been developed using lessons accumulated through years of operational and combat use across the Penguin family.
The most important lesson is to design for change in response to an ever-shifting battlespace. Mk3 incorporates enhanced modularity, mission adaptability and growth capacity. Its public configuration includes fully automated VTOL, multiple payload bays, increased payload capacity, continuous power for mission equipment, winter-operating provisions and a compact logistics model that can be deployed by a two-person crew. Programme execution and long-term sustainment for NATO customers will be supported through Redwire’s European operations.
Testing can demonstrate whether an aircraft meets a performance requirement. Sustained combat operations reveal which issues recur, how quickly configurations must evolve, what operators need under pressure and what is required to sustain a distributed fleet. NATO customers will receive both the aircraft and a European support model informed by those operational realities.

Tallinn to open exhibition of Masayoshi Sukita's David Bowie portraits
Starting 9 October, the Poco Art Museum will present Japanese photographer Masayoshi Sukita's solo exhibition dedicated to pop‑music legend David Bowie — marking the first time Sukita's work is shown in Estonia.
The exhibition features more than one hundred photographs highlighting the 40‑year creative partnership between Bowie and Sukita. The show arrives in Tallinn from its previous European tour stop in Gothenburg.
"'Bowie x Sukita' has travelled through some of the world's largest museums and cultural institutions. Its arrival in Tallinn is the strongest confirmation yet that Poco has reached an international level, operating alongside the world's leading art institutions. And more importantly: the Tallinn public deserves access to world‑class art in their own city," said Poco founder Linnar Viik.
Masayoshi Sukita encountered Bowie in an unusual way: he did not speak English, and Bowie did not speak Japanese. But upon seeing a Bowie poster on a London street in 1972, Sukita immediately knew he had to photograph him. Sukita followed Bowie across the world — from Tokyo press conferences to Berlin studio sessions, the streets of Kyoto and concert stages in New York.
"Bowie x Sukita x Poco" will remain open until 25 April next year.

Warehouses of Ammunition Manufacturer EMCO Catch Fire in Bulgaria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
12:29:01 UTC
21:29:01 KST

On the night of September 12, a massive fire broke out at the warehouses of EMCO, an ammunition manufacturer, in Bulgaria.
This was reported by the NOVA television channel, citing one of the company’s directors, Slavcho Dimiev.
The fire broke out at an ammunition warehouse near the village of Horishni Verpishcha, not far from Tsareva Levada. A series of explosions was heard at the scene after the fire started.
There are 11 warehouses in the area. The fire began in one of them and then spread to two neighboring ones.
The nearest settlement is located more than a kilometer from the scene. No casualties have been reported so far.
The area was cordoned off by police and firefighters, and the BG-Alert system was activated to warn the public.
Due to the risk of further explosions, firefighters assessed the extent of the damage using a drone.
This is the second fire at the warehouses of the Bulgarian company EMCO in the past month. On August 10, a similar incident occurred at an ammunition warehouse near the village of Belitsa. A similar fire in the manufacturer’s warehouse occurred in June 2023.
The Bulgarian company EMCO is one of the country’s largest private defense enterprises and specializes in the manufacture of a wide range of weapons and ammunition, both Soviet and NATO standards.
The company’s factories produce artillery shells, including 122 mm, 152 mm, and 155 mm calibers; 122 mm rocket-propelled shells for Grad-type multiple launch rocket systems; as well as tank rounds and rounds for grenade launchers.
The company also manufactures mortars and corresponding mines in 60 mm, 82 mm, and 120 mm calibers, unguided air-to-ground missiles and aerial bombs, as well as hand grenades and specialized pyrotechnic devices.
In addition to manufacturing ammunition, EMCO modernizes light artillery and anti-aircraft systems, anti-tank weapons, and performs major repairs on light armored vehicles.

Egyptian president urges protection of international navigation amid regional tensions
Unknown

12:26:54 UTC
21:26:54 KST

Hussien Elkabany and Rania Abushamala
12 September 2026•Update: 12 September 2026
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi called Saturday for maintaining the stability and freedom of international navigation amid escalating tensions in the Middle East.
“The current developments in the Middle East and their negative repercussions on the global economy, trade and energy flows, and supply chains affirm the close link between security and development,” Sisi said in his speech at a closed session of the BRICS summit in the Indian capital New Delhi.
“Given its strategic location and pivotal role in global trade, Egypt recognizes the importance of maintaining the stability and freedom of international navigation,” he added in his comments carried by a presidency statement.
“We must continue building on what has been achieved within BRICS and utilize our countries’ potential by establishing specific projects and programs that support the Sustainable Development Goals, diversify sources of growth, enhance productivity, and narrow development and technological gaps,” he said.
Sisi also expressed Egypt’s desire to assume the BRICS presidency “in the near future.”
He affirmed Cairo’s commitment to continuing close cooperation with member states to develop cooperation across all fields and transform their potential and capabilities into “tangible partnerships that support development and achieve common interests,” according to the statement.
The remarks marked Sisi’s second public call in just 24 hours for stability along international shipping routes.
During a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the summit on Friday, Sisi stressed “the importance of achieving stability amid the circumstances and crises facing the region, particularly regarding the waterways through which a massive volume of international trade passes via the Red Sea and the Suez Canal,” according to a presidency statement.
Sisi’s call came amid escalating tensions around major maritime chokepoints, as navigation through the Strait of Hormuz remains disrupted by the repercussions of the US-Iran war, which began in February.
The Iran-aligned Houthi group has also made advances toward the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, raising concerns about far-reaching consequences for navigation through the Red Sea and Egypt’s Suez Canal.

Why doing nothing is good for your brain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
12:25:32 UTC
21:25:32 KST

You finish a lecture, a meeting, a conversation with someone you care about. And what do you do? You reach for your phone. You stick in your earbuds. You fire up a podcast, a playlist or whatever algorithmic feed is currently consuming your life.
It feels productive. It feels like filling empty time.
But here’s what may be happening: you have interrupted your brain mid-sentence.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
When you learn something new, whether it is a colleague’s name or the material covered in a morning lecture, your brain does not simply file it away neatly. The memory is fragile at first, more like wet cement than carved stone. In the minutes and hours following new learning, the brain works to strengthen what it has taken in. This is known as memory consolidation, the process through which newly formed memories become more stable.
Research suggests that quiet rest can help this process. Two recent meta-analyses, drawing on dozens of studies, found that people generally retained more information when learning was followed by several minutes of quiet rest rather than an absorbing task. One of the reviews found that the effect varied considerably between groups and was weaker in healthy younger adults. However, the overall advantage has been detected as long as seven days after learning.
One leading explanation is that quiet rest gives the brain fewer competing demands and more opportunity to reactivate a new experience, like an internal highlight reel reinforcing what has just been learned. Researchers have found that increased coordination between the hippocampus and areas of the cortex during post-learning rest is associated with better later memory.
The precise source of interference remains uncertain. One experiment found that engaging in a task after learning was more detrimental than resting, but that the task’s attentional demands did not explain the difference.
Sleep isn’t the whole story
Decades of research have established that sleep supports memory consolidation. But some researchers argue that sleep may form part of a broader process rather than acting as an entirely unique memory state.
The opportunistic consolidation hypothesis proposes that the brain takes advantage of periods with little new information or interference to stabilize what it has recently learned. These periods can include overnight sleep, shorter bouts of sleep and quiet wakeful rest.
In one experiment, participants completed memory tasks and then spent 30 minutes sleeping, resting with their eyes closed or performing a distracting task. Sleep and quiet rest produced similar memory benefits over this short interval, while both were more beneficial than the distracting task.
Doing nothing is harder than it sounds
Achieving genuine quiet rest can be difficult. The memory-consolidation window may be disrupted by internal mental activity as well as external stimulation.
In one series of experiments, participants who spent the rest period recalling past experiences or imagining future events retained less of the newly learned material than those who rested without being prompted to think autobiographically. Participants who reported the most vivid thoughts also tended to show greater disruption.
Resting on the sofa, then, may work best when the mind settles too.
A recent study of adults without clinical anxiety adds a further complication. Moderate anxiety during quiet rest was associated with poorer memory consolidation, while lower and higher anxiety levels left new memories relatively intact. The study found only a modest overall advantage for rest and no significant difference in its main measure of recognition sensitivity, so the anxiety finding needs further investigation.
Even so, it raises the possibility that ordinary background worry can interfere with consolidation by pulling the brain into a vigilant state when it would otherwise be processing what it has just learned.
Exam pressure and a full inbox may therefore make effective rest harder to achieve.
A note of caution
This is not settled science. Translating laboratory findings into classrooms, offices and other everyday settings is difficult, and individual studies have sometimes failed to reproduce the expected benefit. The size of the effect also varies with age, the type of memory being tested and the characteristics of the participants.
A recent classroom study involving children aged ten to 12 found better word retention after ten minutes of quiet rest, although the benefit appeared only when the rest condition came first. Earlier research involving 13- and 14-year-olds found that rest supported memory over seven days, but the benefit was concentrated among children whose initial recall was lower.
We still do not know how reliably this can be applied in a school, during workplace training or in a care home. Nor do we know why some people benefit more than others.
What this means for real life
Quiet rest does not appear to require complete silence, closed eyes or a particular body position. A 2025 meta-analysis found that these factors did not significantly alter the average effect, although the evidence cannot yet tell us what the ideal real-world routine would look like.
For now, the practical implication is modest: after learning something you want to remember, consider leaving a brief gap before introducing more information.
It might mean waiting a few minutes after a lecture before reaching for your phone. It could mean travelling home after an important conversation without immediately putting on a podcast. It might involve spending the space between two tasks looking out of a window.
These are the moments we increasingly fill with new input. If the emerging evidence is right, leaving some of them empty may give the brain a better chance to hold on to what just happened.

BAGHDAD, Sept. 12 (Xinhua) -- Iraqi security authorities said Saturday that they have initiated administrative and security reorganization operations at several border crossings, which necessitate their closure, to investigate security breaches.
Necessary legal measures have been taken, and intelligence, investigative and audit efforts have been intensified to determine the circumstances surrounding the breaches and violations that occurred at these crossings and to devise appropriate solutions and remedies, the Security Media Cell, affiliated with the Iraqi Joint Operations Command, said in a statement.

The closures came after Ali al-Zaidi, Iraq's prime minister and commander-in-chief of the armed forces, dismissed the Maysan Operations Commander on Saturday after authorities confirmed attacks targeting Saudi Arabia had been launched from a site in Maysan province in southern Iraq.
The Saudi Foreign Ministry said Friday that its East-West Pipeline was attacked by several drones launched from Iraq, causing injuries and damage.
The ministry noted that at the request of the Iraqi prime minister, the kingdom had refrained from responding at this stage.
Saudi Arabia has invested heavily in the East-West Pipeline, which carries crude oil from its eastern fields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz. ■

Metinvest Group Chief Operating Officer Oleksandr Myronenko stressed that Zaporizhstal produced pig iron and steel for civilian needs. The attack damaged the main and auxiliary equipment of the blast furnace and open-hearth shops, as well as the plant's power system, networks and logistics infrastructure.
Since production processes at the plant had not been operating following the previous attacks, there is no threat of a man-made disaster, Zaporizhstal said.
The number of personnel at the plant was significantly limited.

Yemen government forces hit Houthis in strategic Red Sea city
DUBAI – Yemen’s Riyadh-backed government forces said on Sept 12 that they struck Iran-allied Houthi fighters in the strategic Red Sea city of Mokha.
Following a week-long offensive, the Houthis on Sept 11 captured Yemen’s Red Sea coast, cementing their hold on the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a vital artery for Saudi Arabian oil exports as the Strait of Hormuz remains closed amid the US-Iran war.
“The armed forces destroyed vehicles and weapons and killed members of the Houthi terrorist militia backed by the Iranian regime” near the port of the city of Mokha, the government news agency Saba reported.

The Houthis seized control of Mokha on Sept 10, with their attack driving many to flee to Aden, where the internationally recognised government is based.
On Sept 11, Houthi media said two Saudi strikes hit Mokha’s airport, while a local official said the city’s seaport was hit by six missiles of unknown origin.
The Houthi offensive, which started last week, has killed more than 500 people, according to sources on both sides.
It has also displaced about 46,000 people, the UN migration agency said on Sept 11.
It is part of renewed hostilities in Yemen’s civil war that began with the group’s takeover of the capital Sanaa in 2014. AFP

Russia’s War in Ukraine Has Cost Poland’s Economy More than €100 bln, Estimate Shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
12:19:00 UTC
21:19:00 KST

Russia’s war in Ukraine has cost the Polish economy more than €100 billion, according to the latest estimates from Poland’s state-run statistics office.
Statistics Poland announced on Wednesday that the country’s lost GDP value was estimated at 490.1 billion złoty (€113.4 billion) between 2022 – the year Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine – and 2025.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The value includes estimated losses of 126 billion złoty (€29 billion) in the country’s corporate sector and 292.1 billion złoty (€67.5 billion) in the household sector, the Polish state news agency PAP reported.
Paweł Kowal, chairman of the parliamentary foreign affairs committee, cited by PAP, said many countries are suffering “very significant losses” as a result of the war, largely due to the economic effects of international sanctions on Russia.
Kowal said: “The fundamental issue today, from the perspective of the legal interests of countries like Poland… is to find a way to calculate these losses.
“This does not mean we expect Russia to pay us these sums tomorrow, but we believe it is essential to establish such an account for… the post-war period and to demonstrate to others inclined to act against international law that methods exist to calculate costs not only for the country under attack,” he added.
EU Examines Funding for Ukraine-Led FREYJA Missile Defense System
War led to inflation
The head of Statistics Poland, Marek Cierpiał-Wolan, said conservative estimates indicate that one-third of inflation above the inflation target was caused by the escalation of the war in Ukraine, PAP reported.
“High inflation caused a sharp rise in nominal wages, but the pace of real wage growth slowed after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine,” he said, adding that real wages fell by 2% in 2022.
Cierpiał-Wolan also said that Moscow’s war in Ukraine led to additional Polish spending that otherwise would not have occurred, including tens of billions of euros in defense spending and aid for Ukraine.
Statistics Poland said the economic shock caused by Russia’s war also led to an estimated 426.5 billion złoty (€98.7 billion) reduction in Poland’s gross value added, a measure of the value created through the production of goods and services, PAP reported.

A Russian intelligence operative and a Belarusian petty criminal: Germany names the Leipzig bomb-drone suspects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
12:18:54 UTC
21:18:54 KST

German security services can now name two suspects in the drone attack on Leipzig/Halle airport with high probability, one of them attributed to Russian military intelligence, Welt am Sonntag reported, citing secret investigation files it obtained. The paper says that evidence is what allowed Berlin to blame Russia publicly a week and a half ago. Russia has denied any involvement.
The two men
The main suspects are a Belarusian citizen, Andrei Ka., and a Russian, Oleg Le., according to security sources cited by the paper. German investigators believe Le. was responsible for the preparation and logistics of the attack, and attribute him to the GRU, Russia's military intelligence agency.
Le. entered Germany through Türkiye, landing at Berlin Brandenburg airport, and later left from the same airport for Serbia. He is now back in Russia. Investigators knew at the point of entry that he was tied to the GRU's circle, and he was not surveilled afterward.
A drone beside a Ukrainian cargo plane is costing Russia its last consulate in Germany
What was on the drone
The attack used three drones at Leipzig/Halle airport on the evening of 4 August, and two were destroyed at launch for reasons still unclear. The third landed beside a Ukrainian transport aircraft and sat there for hours. About 1.8 kg of Semtex, built into a vegetable can, failed to fire because a detonator tore loose. The Antonov it reached held 25,000 liters of kerosene, and investigators estimate a detonation would have destroyed parts of the airport.
How the trail was found
Forensic technicians recovered glove remains with DNA traces from the antenna used to fly the drone, and those traces were already on file in Finland and Lithuania, where Ka. has a record for ordinary criminal offenses, including theft in Finland. Polish prosecutors separately link him to a hardware-store fire in Łódź in the summer of 2024 that they treat as sabotage directed from Russia, which fits the pattern European authorities have documented since 2022: Russian services hiring residents, often migrants, to burn warehouses and malls. The Leipzig explosives are thought to have crossed from Bulgaria through Serbia in truck cavities and gone into buried caches, and police found several suspected hiding places after examining the suspects' rental-car data.
Germany suspects Russian intelligence behind arson attack as hybrid warfare threat grows across Europe
What Berlin has done about it
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul and Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt blamed Russia at a joint press conference on 1 September, ordering the closure of Russia's last consulate in the country and scrapping the agreement behind Moscow's cultural center in Berlin. Russia's embassy claims more than 150 of its mission staff and their families must now leave Germany, and Moscow answered by closing the German consulate in St Petersburg and the Goethe institutes.
Four days after the attribution, German investigators suspected Russian intelligence behind an arson attack on a defense company.

Bulgaria: Fire at factory making munitions for Ukraine
September 12, 2026
Bulgarian authorities are investigating a fire at a munitions storage facility operated by arms maker EMCO.
Police say the blaze broke out Friday night and follows a similar incident at another EMCO site in August.
EMCO's munitions are used in Ukraine and sabotage has not been ruled out, video images of the fire broadcast locally showed it illuminating the night sky near the village of Tsareva Livada.
The full extent of the damage is not yet known but no casualties have been reported.
"At present there is no danger to the population," said local police, adding that employees had been evacuated and the area cordoned off.
EMCO has ruled out any possibility of human error in the incident.
Bulgarian authorities investigating
On Saturday, Bulgarian Interior Minister Ivan Demerdzhiev announced an investigation, saying, "We will review previous cases in which similar fires occurred in the warehouses of this company, as well as at other companies, in order to look for a possible connection or a similar pattern."
EMCO production facilities manager Slavcho Dimiev confirmed the fire as well, saying the site mainly stores ammunition, including a small quantity of medium-caliber rounds.
Dimiev told reporters additional security measures should be considered to protect arms facilities.
"If it is ultimately concluded that they [arms facilities] have been targeted," he said, "this is not an attack on a particular company alone; it is an attack on the national interest."
EMCO fire latest of several attacks attributed to Russia
NATO member-state Bulgaria has supported Kyiv's self-defense efforts since Russian forces invaded Ukraine on February 24, 2022.
And EMCO, like other European arms manufacturers, has been the target of repeated sabotage.
The company is run by Bulgarian arms dealer Emilian Gebrev, the survivor of an assassination attempt that authorities there say was carried out by Russian operatives. Three Russian nationals were charged over the incident.
In 2024, Bulgaria also issued arrest warrants for six Russian nationals that prosecutors say were involved in the destruction of EMCO arms depots storing munitions set for export to Ukraine and Georgia between 2011 and 2020.

Friday's fire at EMCO echoes a number of recent attacks targeting European arms makers supplying Ukraine.
On August 13, the KNDS Ammo Italy arms manufacturing facility outside Rome was rocked by an explosion. Although the Italian government said it had no reason to believe that Russia was behind the attack, the Franco-German defense company said the incident was under investigation.
On September 3, incendiary devices were thrown near the Munich headquarters of defense technology company Rohde & Schwarz.

In 2024, US and German intelligence uncovered a Russian plot to assassinate Armin Papperger, the CEO of Germany's largest arms manufacturer, Rheinmetall.
In all instances, Russia has denied involvement, calling accusations, European war mongering.

Mr Pollard said: “The Department has not had sight of the 2026 edition of the US Government Accountability Office report entitled F-35 Joint Strike Fighter: Update on Production and Modernization Efforts.”
The report exists and has been completed, but a GAO spokesperson told The Hill in July that it had been reviewed by the U.S. Department of War and marked as containing “Controlled Unclassified Information with no current plan to be released to the public”. The Pentagon declined to comment.
Congress mandated the annual review in statute, and the GAO has reviewed the programme every year for more than two decades, delivering a public verdict each time on cost, schedule, production and readiness. This is the first occasion on which the entire report has been kept from publication.
Controlled Unclassified Information is a handling designation, not a security classification, of course. Material marked that way is not secret in the ordinary sense, but its distribution is restricted, and in this case the restriction extends to a document whose public title has been published while its contents have not.
The 2025 report, the most recent to reach the public, gives a sense of what the withheld edition would have covered. It found that Lockheed Martin delivered 110 aircraft in 2024 and that every one of them was late, by an average of 238 days. Technology Refresh 3, the $1.9 billion suite of hardware and software upgrades on which the Block 4 modernisation depends, was running around three years behind schedule.
On Block 4, the GAO reported previously that the Department of War was redefining the subprogramme and expected it to comprise fewer capabilities than the original plan, deferring development of some to a future effort. The programme had told the GAO in 2018 that it planned to deliver 66 Block 4 capabilities by 2026, and by May 2024 the content had been revised and the completion date extended to 2029. Reporting on the same document put the cost growth at more than $6 billion above original estimates.
The same report carried a Department of War estimate putting the cost of Block 4, engine and power thermal management modernisation, and maintaining and operating the 2,470 planned aircraft across a 77-year life cycle, at more than $2 trillion. The GAO has separately reported that power and cooling shortfalls force the engine to work harder than its contractors intended, reducing its life expectancy, with programme officials estimating that the resulting wear has added $38 billion to the life cycle cost estimate.
What it means for Britain
Britain has been an F-35 partner since the earliest stages, at Level 1 alongside the United States, with British industry holding roughly 15 per cent of the workshare on every aircraft built, on paper at least. BAE Systems manufactures the rear fuselage at Samlesbury, Rolls-Royce produces the lift system for the short take-off and vertical landing variant, and Martin-Baker supplies the ejection seat.
Mr Pollard confirmed on the same day that discussions with the F-35 Joint Program Office are ongoing on procurement profiles and the delivery schedule for Britain’s next batch of aircraft, with delivery anticipated from the early 2030s. The Strategic Defence Review confirmed an intention to buy a further 27 aircraft, of which 12 are to be the F-35A conventional take-off variant to support Britain joining NATO’s dual capable aircraft nuclear mission.
A partner nation committing to further purchases while unable to see the most recent independent audit of the programme’s production performance is an unusual position.

“Garbage, shouting, and overflowing bins”: Ukrainians are massively complaining about the behavior of Hasidic Jews in Uman
Kyiv • UNN
After 52,000 Hasidic Jews arrived in Uman, Ukrainians reported garbage, overflowing bins, and the pilgrims’ loud behavior.
Ukrainians are massively complaining about the behavior of Hasidic pilgrims who came to Uman to celebrate Rosh Hashanah—the New Year holiday for all those who profess Judaism. People are sharing their impressions of the tourists on social media, reports UNN.
Details
The videos and photos garnering the most views show pilgrims leaving trash behind. Thus, a video from a carriage of "Ukrzaliznytsia" is circulating on social media; according to its author, pilgrims traveled in it. This is an Intercity train.
The footage shows a dirty sink in the restroom and numerous empty food boxes lying on the floor in the vestibule. In addition, the passengers left behind half-empty bottles of beverages (some had spilled onto the floor), dirty tissues on the seats, and snacks scattered across the floor.
Meanwhile, on the Threads social network, a user named Olha Doroshchuk published photographs from Uman itself. They show a great – great deal of household waste, among which pilgrims walk calmly. The few garbage bins and trash cans are overflowing with waste. In addition, the area around them is thickly covered with rubbish.
Ukrainians are also surprised by the behavior of Hasidic pilgrims in public. Many people have already found themselves in unpleasant situations. They say that the pilgrims often speak, laugh, and shout very loudly. And they do not respond to requests to be quieter so as not to frighten, for example, small children in the train carriage.
I was traveling by train to Lviv today, and at 1:30 a.m. about 100 Hasidim boarded our train. They laughed throughout the entire carriage in the middle of the night, threw trash right where they were standing, did not respond at all to remarks, and pretended not to understand what you were telling them. I wonder whether they behave the same way at home?
Context
A record number of Hasidim—52,000—arrived in Uman this year to celebrate Rosh Hashanah. According to Mikhail Zingerman, a representative of the Israeli police press service, the dangerous situation in Ukraine does not deter the pilgrims. On the contrary, many pilgrims believe that a pilgrimage to a country where a war is ongoing will have special significance for their spiritual growth.
These are the peculiarities of their faith
Why Hasidim travel to Uman on pilgrimage every year
Hasidic pilgrims travel to Uman because their spiritual mentor—the tzadik Nachman of Breslov—is buried there. In his will, he promised intercession before God and happiness to everyone who would come to his grave on Rosh Hashanah and pray there.

BRICS leaders oppose forced displacement of Palestinians from Gaza, urge conflict prevention amid wars in Iran, Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
12:08:13 UTC
21:08:13 KST

Saadet Gokce and Ahmad Adil
12 September 2026•Update: 12 September 2026
- Emerging economies bloc condemns imposition of unilateral coercive measures, economic and secondary sanctions
BRICS leaders on Saturday called for greater efforts to prevent and peacefully resolve conflicts amid the wars in Iran and Ukraine, while opposing any forced displacement of Palestinians from the Gaza Strip.
 
The calls were included in the New Delhi Declaration, unanimously adopted on the first day of the bloc's two-day summit in the Indian capital.
 
Expressing "deep concern" over continued violence in Gaza despite the October 2025 ceasefire agreement, BRICS leaders called for an end to "any policies aimed at forced displacement of Palestinians from the Gaza Strip."
 
The declaration also expressed "concern regarding arrangements that may prejudice the inalienable rights of the Palestinian people and legitimize or prolong occupation."
 
"We reaffirm that a just and lasting solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict can only be achieved by peaceful means and depends on the fulfilment of the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people, including the rights to self-determination and return," it said.
 
The bloc also rejected "any unilateral measures that seek to alter the legal and historical status of occupied Jerusalem."
 
"We urge full respect for the sanctity of all religious sites and holy places in the city and for the rights of all to access and to observe their religious rites without hindrance," the New Delhi Declaration said on Saturday.
 
The bloc also condemned attacks on the UN Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) installations and personnel, emphasizing that "such attacks are a violation of international law."
 
Noting the "current global context of polarization and distrust," BRICS members called on the international community to respond to challenges and related security threats through "politico-diplomatic measures to lower conflict potential."
 
The bloc also stressed the "need to engage in conflict prevention efforts, including through addressing their root causes."
 
"We encourage the active role of regional organizations in conflict prevention and resolution and support all efforts conducive to the peaceful settlement of crises," the declaration said.
 
BRICS leaders also expressed concern over the growing risks of nuclear conflict and called for disarmament, arms control and nonproliferation.
 
The declaration voiced "serious concern" over "deliberate attacks" on civilian infrastructure and peaceful nuclear facilities.
 
"Nuclear safeguards, safety, and security must always be upheld, including in armed conflicts, to protect people and the environment from harm," it said.
 
Condemn unilateral trade measures
 
The BRICS leaders noted that the multilateral trading system "has long been at a crossroads."
 
"The proliferation of trade-restrictive actions that are inconsistent" with World Trade Organization (WTO) rules, whether in the form of indiscriminate rising of tariffs and non-tariff measures," the statement said.
 
"We voice serious concerns about the rise of unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures which distort trade and are inconsistent with WTO rules," it added.
 
The BRICS bloc condemned the imposition of unilateral coercive measures that "are contrary to international law, and reiterate that such measures, inter alia in the form of unilateral economic sanctions and secondary sanctions, have far-reaching negative implications for human rights, including the rights to development, health and food security, of the general population of targeted states, disproportionately affecting the poor and people in vulnerable situations, deepening the digital divide and exacerbating environmental challenges."

Falklands Typhoons to be swapped for later aircraft

The four Tranche 1 Typhoons held by 1435 Flight in the Falkland Islands are to be replaced by four Tranche 2 aircraft drawn from the existing fleet during the rotation planned for late November to early December 2027, the Government have again confirmed.
Luke Pollard, Minister of State for Defence Readiness and Industry, was responding to Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative MP for Huntingdon, who had asked what steps have been taken to replace the aircraft when they are decommissioned in 2027.
Mr Pollard said: “The four Tranche 1 Typhoon aircraft currently assigned to British Forces South Atlantic Islands are scheduled to be replaced by four Tranche 2 Typhoon aircraft from the existing fleet during the aircraft rotation planned for late November to early December 2027. Following their return to the UK, the four Tranche 1 aircraft will be withdrawn from the Military Aviation Authority Register and enter the disposal process.”
He added: “UK F-35 Lightning remain available for global operational tasking in line with Defence priorities.”
Readers will note that this is, obviously, unconnected to the current tensions, but it’s important to remind people.
The same answer was given to a separate question from the same member asking what discussions have been held with the American counterpart and the F-35 Joint Program Office on the future use of the F-35B in the defence of the islands.
Tranche 1 Typhoons are the earliest production aircraft, delivered from the early 2000s and built to a standard that has not been carried forward through the upgrade programmes applied to later aircraft. They have been progressively retired since 2019, and the remaining airframes have largely been used for training and for the Falklands commitment, where the demanding requirement is quick reaction alert rather than the full spectrum of modern combat capability.
Tranche 2 aircraft carry a more capable radar, avionics and weapons fit, and have received successive capability upgrades including the Phase 3 Enhancement package covering Storm Shadow, Brimstone and Meteor.
The replacement therefore represents a capability improvement for the South Atlantic rather than a like-for-like swap, though it is drawn from the existing fleet rather than from new production, which means the aircraft come from elsewhere in the Royal Air Force’s order of battle.
