National document on Persian medicine governance being developed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
12:05:19 UTC
21:05:19 KST

National document on Persian medicine governance being developed
TEHRAN - The first expert meeting to develop the National Governance Document for Iranian Traditional Medicine was held with the aim of reviewing the sector’s overarching policies, bringing together senior officials, leading academics, and representatives of executive bodies.
The meeting was attended by Hossein Rezaeizadeh, the head of the headquarters for developing traditional medicine and medicinal herbs, university professors, and representatives of executive agencies, Mehr news agency reported.
The first part of the meeting focused on the country’s current status regarding medicinal plants and traditional medicine, the challenges inherent in the previous documents and their respective strengths and weaknesses, as well as novel policies and approaches for inclusion in strategic objectives of the new document.
Drawing on past experience, participants identified several key areas for strengthening the new document. These include benchmarking it against international frameworks developed by leading countries such as India and China; adopting more people-centered implementation indicators; prioritizing education while avoiding an excessive emphasis on credentialism in medicine; and leveraging the potential of health diplomacy.
The development of technological infrastructure, including medicinal herb refineries, the use of artificial intelligence (AI), market regulation, development of new pharmaceutical and therapeutic documentation, and scientific management of traditional herbal shops and guilds are among other discussed issues.
Other points highlighted by the participants included compiling a comprehensive statistical yearbook on medicinal plants; clearly defining the mandates of each relevant agency and ministry in line with their respective responsibilities; reviewing the composition of the headquarters council; restructuring executive operations; and reforming budget allocation mechanisms to enhance the effectiveness of the National Governance Document for Persian Medicine.
National research, technology network
The health ministry’s traditional medicine is developing a national research and technology network for Persian medicine to integrate scientific and technological efforts to enhance Persian medicine’s status and expand the value chain of medicinal plants.
The network will organize the country's research and scientific capacities in supplementary medicine and Persian medicine to meet the needs of the health sector and knowledge-based economy, Rezaeizadeh said in February.
It will serve as a platform for the development of a roadmap for technologies relating to indigenous knowledge to address the challenges, such as the lack of a structured link between traditional knowledge and modern technologies, the official further noted.
The network’s core areas are centered around biochemical, molecular, and microbiological research, animal studies, disease models, safety assessments, pharmacodynamics, and pharmacokinetics.
Developing interdisciplinary research and utilizing new technologies such as proteomics, metabolomics, microbiome studies, cellular models, bioinformatics data analyses, epidemiological studies, and advanced animal models are among other key pillars of the network to create synergy between traditional knowledge, biological, and data-driven sciences.
Iran’s commitment in traditional medicine
During the closing ceremony of the second World Health Organization (WHO) Global Summit on Traditional Medicine, Iran pledged commitments to advance the implementation of the Global Strategy for Traditional Medicine 2025-2034.
Co-organized by the WHO and the Government of India, the second global Summit on Traditional Medicine was held from December 17 to 19 last year in New Delhi, under the theme ‘Restoring Balance: The science and practice of health and well-being’.
Rezaeizadeh, Arman Zargaran, the advisor to the health ministry’s traditional medicine office, and Mohammad Fathali, the ambassador to India, attended the event.
Iran’s five commitments include launching a WHO collaborating center, launching a national platform for clinical trials, strengthening research and evidence, publishing in reputable journals, compiling five standard operating procedures (SOPs) for specialized Persian procedures, and integrating traditional medicine into the health system, the health ministry’s website reported.
The second WHO Global Summit on Traditional Medicine aimed to advance a global movement to restore balance for people and the planet, grounded in the science and practice of Traditional Medicine.
During the summit, Iranian officials took part in specialized discussions on traditional medicine. Zargaran was the first speaker to deliver a speech, titled ‘Codifying complexities: standardization in traditional medicine research’, at the parallel session 2A themed ‘Translating the WHO Traditional Medicine Research Roadmap into Global Action’.
Like many ancient medical systems, Persian medicine takes a holistic approach to health, emphasizing lifestyle factors such as adhering to a proper diet, moderate exercise, sufficient sleep, and mental/emotional balance.
According to Roshanak Ghods, an associate professor of Persian medicine at Iran University of Medical Sciences, many treatments in Persian medicine focus on restoring balance and boosting the body’s natural healing capacities.
“The knowledge accumulated over centuries of practice and research provides clinical insights and therapeutic approaches complementary to modern medicine”, she said. “Preserving this medical tradition and making it accessible ensures that people today can benefit from this time-tested system of natural healing and its unique principles, but of course, we also need the evidence on the effectiveness and safety of traditional and complementary medicine, based on suitable research methods for personalized medicine.”
Ghods’ vision is for a health-care system that combines traditional with conventional medicine, without prejudice. “Our goal for the future should be to provide personalized, patient-centered care that addresses the person’s mind, body, and spirit”, she said.

Forensic Medicine Organization seeks to enhance ties with ICRC
TEHRAN – Iran’s Forensic Medicine Organization has voiced its readiness to maintain and expand cooperation with the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), with a focus on strengthening joint efforts in scientific, educational, and operational fields, alongside the provision of equipment.
Highlighting the need to strengthen cooperation between the two organizations, Mehdi Foruzesh, the deputy head of the Forensic Medicine Organization’s Crisis Management Division, said the organization was ready to expand collaboration with the ICRC.
He also emphasized the organization’s considerable capabilities, particularly its highly skilled personnel across various fields, including the identification of victims of crises and disasters, IRIB reported.
The official made the remarks at a ceremony marking the handover of essential supplies and equipment to Iran’s Forensic Medicine Organization by Maruf Kandikov, the ICRC representative.
He noted that joint workshops and exercises with regional countries would facilitate the exchange of expertise and strengthen crisis preparedness, including the cross-border transport of deceased bodies.
The official highlighted the high capabilities of the Forensic Medicine Organization in managing crises and mass gatherings like Arbaeen, saying that apart from regional cooperation, boosting collaborations with the ICRC could help develop predetermined mechanisms for the identification, documentation, and transportation of dead bodies in cross-border incidents, which would facilitate the return of the remains to their families.
He also underlined the challenges the organization encounters in procuring laboratory consumables because of coercive sanctions, noting that the ICRC can help overcome the problem by establishing a secure, transparent, and controllable channel.
The official further called for the establishment of a joint expert working group to coordinate and institutionalize cooperation between the two organizations and identify the Forensic Medicine Organization’s needs.
As part of its humanitarian mandate to strengthen humanitarian response capacities in Iran, the ICRC donated 12 tons of essential supplies and equipment to Iran’s Forensic Medicine Organization, the ICRC website announced in a press release on September 20.
The donated items include administrative, as well as technical items needed to support the organization’s work, particularly in the identification of people who have died in natural disasters or armed conflicts, while ensuring that they are treated with dignity.
For his part, Kandikov commended the Legal Medicine Organization’s work to ensure the dignity of the dead and expressed hope that the donation would further strengthen its capacity for identification and helping families establish the fate of their loved ones. He expressed hope for the expansion of cooperation with Iran’s Forensic Medicine Organization.
The ICRC’s humanitarian forensic work aims to ensure the dignified management of the dead, support the scientific identification of human remains, and help clarify the fate of people who have died or gone missing in conflicts and emergencies.
In Iran, the ICRC has worked with the Forensic Medicine Organization and other national institutions for about two decades, providing technical support, training and equipment for the identification and repatriation of remains from the Iran-Iraq War of the 1980s.
Its work has also expanded to strengthening preparedness for mass-fatality incidents, including training in forensic anthropology and the dignified recovery and management of human remains. At the heart of this work is helping families learn the fate of their loved ones while ensuring that the dead are treated with dignity.
Another aspect of the ICRC’s work in Iran is facilitating networking opportunities between national institutions and the international forensic community to promote the exchange of expertise, methodologies and good practices on the search for and identification of missing and deceased persons affected by conflict, emergencies and migration.

Public perception of mobilization issues does not reflect actual situation — military psychologist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Public perception of mobilization issues does not reflect actual situation — military psychologist
This view was expressed by social and military psychologist Oleh Pokalchuk in an interview with Ukrinform.
According to him, the enemy has “200%” exploited the mobilization problems and, in essence, used them to form an anti-state movement based on instincts.
Pokalchuk noted that at this point, it is more important not to communicate about mobilization but to find other mechanisms, since human behavior is always governed by two factors—the expectation of reward and the fear of punishment.
“When this mobilization system was created, neither of these factors was present—and, consequently, the system fell apart,” said the social psychologist.
At the same time, Pokalchuk emphasized that public perception of mobilization issues does not correspond to the actual state of the process.
“You see, we assess and comment on mobilization issues as if they were a complete failure, but that is absolutely not true! It is happening; training centers are operating; the ‘18–24’ contracts are in effect. But when isolated incidents occur, we blow them out of proportion,” he stated.
According to the psychologist, Russian propaganda quickly picks up on such isolated cases, after which they create the impression that “everything is lost.”
“No, the process is underway. It will never run as smoothly as we’d like, but this system is changing,” Pokalchuk emphasized.
He added that mobilization had once become a political issue, but now, in his opinion, it has returned to the administrative and organizational realm.
As reported by Ukrinform, Russian propaganda continues to spread disinformation about alleged preparations for the mobilization of women in Ukraine.

Bridget Phillipson, the chair of the Labour party, said that Farage couldn’t “buy his way out of the sleaze and scandal he and Reform UK are drowning in – or the multiple police investigations that are ongoing into Reform’s dodgy finances”.
Rachel Millward, the deputy leader of the Green party in England and Wales, accused the prime minister, Andy Burnham, of “flip flopping” on a cap on domestic donations. Burnham, who previously appeared supportive of a cap, has faced lobbying from trade unions who fear restrictions would inhibit their ability to donate to the Labour party.
The Labour MP Stella Creasy tabled an amendment to the representation of the people bill, which is progressing through parliament and has its second reading in the Lords on Monday.
Creasy proposed an annual cap of £100,000 on most domestic donations. Although it attracted the support of 60 MPs from various parties, it was not put to a vote.
“The Labour party urgently needs to find a spine and support a tight cap on donations from individuals,” Millward said.
Duncan Hames, of Transparency International UK, said the donations made “an irrefutable case” for a cap, adding: “At this rate just two people could end up buying our democracy before the next election.”
The campaign group Spotlight on Corruption said the donations could have a “huge and damaging impact” and accused the government of “ignoring the very high risk of the Americanisation of our politics”.
Farage said that Delo and Harborne “know that we are the only party that can turn the country around and win the next general election – thanks to their generosity, we are now able to fight that election on a level playing field”.
Harborne said: “There will be a lot of media speculation regarding this donation. So what do I expect in return for my donations? Nothing. No peerage, no policy change, just a party that is ready for government.
“I have already accumulated enough wealth for the rest of my life. I am committed to putting that to work for Britain and humanity as a whole. I want the same as everyone else in Britain: for my children and grandchildren to have the chance to live happy and productive lives here and be rewarded for their hard work.
“At the next general election, people will have to vote for the party that they think will best get that done and I’m making a donation very clearly to the party that I believe will do so.”
Harborne is a citizen of the UK and Thailand, while Delo recently moved back to Britain from Hong Kong. As part of the new legislation, donations to political parties from Britons living abroad or those who have returned to the country within the past 12 months will be capped at £100,000 a year, with the rules backdated to March.
The Guardian asked Reform exactly how long each has been on the electoral roll. A spokesperson said: “All donations to Reform UK comply strictly with Electoral Commission rules and UK law. Both men are British citizens who are fully entitled to support political change in their own country, despite the establishment’s desperate attempts to silence opposition.”
Their donations have amplified concerns about the influence of “mega donors” on British politics.
Margaret Hodge, a Labour peer and former chair of the House of Commons public accounts committee, said she was “gobsmacked” to hear of Harborne’s donation and said it “reinforces the urgency of us dealing with the issue”. Hodge, who favours a cap, said there was now a “real danger” that British politics could be “captured by rich individuals”.
“There has been a reluctance on Labour’s side to confront this danger because of the trade unions,” she said. “This highlights what a lot of us have been saying – you have to tackle the issue. We can’t leave it alone. Self-interest shouldn’t dominate.”
Many senior Labour figures, including Hodge, believe union funds could be classified as a series of individual donations from members.
“Union members could tick a box saying, ‘I wish to contribute [to the Labour party]’, so it becomes an individual donation, rather than a union [donation],” Hodge said, adding that she believed this would “strengthen democracy” and challenge the power of union leaders.
However, this proposal is likely to be condemned by opposition parties and transparency campaigners.
Shaun Bowler, who runs the campaign group Wake Up GB, has proposed financing political parties through a government funded civic voucher, in which voters could choose to allocate a small sum to the party of their choice.
“The unions funded the Labour party to compete with Conservative funding,” he said. “If you take funding away from the Conservatives and everyone else, it’s a level playing field.”

How anxiety and face gender shape emotional processing in children
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
12:00:47 UTC
21:00:47 KST

As children grow, their brains develop distinct ways of processing facial expressions based on a mix of emotion and face gender. A recent study reveals that these neural responses grow more specialized with age, while elevated anxiety can alter how kids react to potentially threatening faces. The research was published in Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience.
Cultural norms and early experiences teach children to associate certain emotions with specific genders. Anger is often linked with male faces and interpreted as a sign of dominance or potential threat. In contrast, happiness is frequently associated with female faces and perceived as a sign of emotional warmth. When a facial expression violates these expectations, such as an angry female face or a happy male face, the brain must work harder to interpret the social cue.
The research team wanted to see how the developing brain manages these unexpected social signals. They focused on tracking specific patterns of electrical activity, known as brain waves. Alpha and beta brain waves are associated with attention and the filtering of sensory information. Gamma waves, which oscillate much faster, are linked to higher cognitive tasks, like blending different pieces of social and emotional information together.
The scientists also aimed to explore how anxiety affects these developmental trajectories. Anxious individuals often exhibit a specific pattern of attention when faced with a threat. They may initially focus heavily on a threatening cue before quickly looking away to reduce their own psychological distress. The research team, led by neuroscientists Hua Bai, Yasra Arif, and Tony W. Wilson at Boys Town National Research Hospital in Nebraska, set out to map these cognitive processes in youth.
The researchers enrolled a group of healthy children and teenagers between the ages of six and 17. The final analysis included data from 149 participants. While positioned inside a brain scanning machine, the participants viewed photographs of adult faces displaying angry, happy, or neutral expressions. Half of the faces shown in the experiment were male, and the other half were female.
The participants were instructed to press a button indicating the gender of each face, regardless of the emotional expression. While the youths performed this task, the researchers recorded their neural activity using a technique called magnetoencephalography. This non-invasive imaging technology measures the tiny magnetic fields produced by the electrical firing of brain cells, allowing researchers to track brain waves with high precision in real time.
The team also collected behavioral data during the task, such as how accurately and quickly the participants responded. Afterward, the researchers used specialized software to filter out background noise from the brain recordings, such as the electrical signals generated by eye blinks and heartbeats. Finally, the children aged eight and older completed a standardized self-report questionnaire to assess their daily anxiety levels.
The behavioral results indicated that response times varied depending on both the age of the participant and the combination of gender and emotion. The youths responded fastest to angry male faces. In contrast, angry female faces prompted the slowest reactions across the board. The researchers noted that these reaction times did not reach a level of statistical significance for the happy faces, meaning the age-related changes were specific to angry and neutral expressions.
When analyzing the brain wave data, the researchers noticed distinct patterns emerging within a fraction of a second. In regions of the brain responsible for visual perception and movement control, alpha and beta wave responses grew stronger in older children. These brain waves were especially active when participants viewed faces that violated social expectations, such as angry female faces and happy male faces.
The researchers found a specific association between these brain waves and reaction times for angry male faces. Older children showed increased alpha and beta activity in a brain region involved in motor planning and inhibitory control. The scientists proposed that as children age, they increasingly recruit this inhibitory network to control their physical responses to threatening cues, slowing themselves down just enough to process the information safely.
A different pattern emerged slightly later in the brain’s processing timeline, characterized by gamma wave activity. Older children displayed increased gamma activity in areas of the brain known for handling complex social and emotional information, such as the temporoparietal junction. This activity was particularly elevated when processing angry female faces, suggesting that the brain requires more integrative processing to make sense of unexpected social signals.
The team also observed age-related increases in gamma waves when participants viewed neutral faces. However, these responses were mixed, with some brain regions reacting more to neutral male faces and others to neutral female faces. The researchers attributed this lack of a consistent pattern to the inherently ambiguous nature of a neutral expression, which requires social interpretation regardless of the person’s gender.
Individual anxiety levels also altered how the brain processed these faces. Children reporting higher levels of anxiety displayed weaker early alpha and beta responses in visual processing areas when viewing angry male faces. This pattern aligns with behavioral theories suggesting that anxious youths instinctively suppress attention toward highly threatening social cues to manage their own distress. Meanwhile, responses to angry female faces remained consistently elevated across all anxiety levels.
The study focuses exclusively on typically developing children, meaning the results may not generalize to youths with clinical conditions like social anxiety disorder or autism spectrum disorder. The faces used in the experiment were also entirely composed of adults. Future studies could incorporate images of children and teenagers to test if youth react differently to the faces of their own peers.
The participant pool was predominantly White, which introduces the possibility of an own-race familiarity bias in how the faces were perceived. Because the study only evaluated participants at a single point in time, researchers cannot track how these brain patterns evolve within the same individual over the years. Longitudinal tracking would clarify how early brain responses shape social and emotional development long-term.
The study, “Facial expression processing is modulated by face gender and anxiety levels in developing youth,” was authored by Hua Bai, Yasra Arif, Jake J. Son, Nathan M. Petro, Grace C. Ende, Danielle L. Rice, Jason A. John, Anna T. Coutant, Erica L. Steiner, Ryan J. Glesinger, Hannah J. Okelberry, Brittany K. Taylor, Giorgia Picci, and Tony W. Wilson.

====================================================================================================

Deepfakes are wrecking influencers’ credibility, one fake ad at a time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
12:00:34 UTC
21:00:34 KST

Earlier this year, Emily Schuman, the creator of the lifestyle blog Cupcakes and Cashmere, saw a photo of herself she didn’t recognize on Instagram. In a sponsored ad, Schuman, who has more than 500,000 Instagram followers, is holding up a vial of GLP-1 drugs, advertising the telehealth company Gala. There was just one problem: Schuman had never heard of Gala and had nothing to do with the ad.
The ad was based on a digitally altered version of a selfie Schuman had taken in her car and posted on Instagram years earlier. Once her followers got wind, they flooded her inbox with questions about the sponsorship as it didn’t seem consistent with Schuman’s personal brand. Soon after, Schuman discovered this was just the beginning. There was also an Instagram post where an AI version of her with darker hair appears to apply foundation to promote a makeup brand called Meroda Cosmetics, and TikTok posts with generated images of her promoting the blood testing company Superpower.
“It’s so violating,” she said. The videos and images look “just like me, but the upside down version”.
Neither Gala nor Meroda responded to requests for comment. Superpower CEO Max Marchione said the TikTok post wasn’t a real ad, but instead came from a scammer his company later reported. “Whilst scamming isn’t new, AI has made this much worse,” he said.
As generative AI makes it easier to create text, code and media, it has also supercharged the creation of deepfakes, the synthetic photos and videos that can be nearly indistinguishable from reality. Influencers are some of the easiest people to impersonate due to the sheer amount of videos and images AI can learn from. The vulnerability represents a new workplace threat: influencers aren’t just competing for brand deals with other creators, but also fighting to preserve the credibility of their own likeness – the very asset that generates their income.
“Their brand is their business,” said Alice Marwick, the director of research at the Data & Society Research Institute, who published a recent paper on the rise of AI impersonation scams. “If their brand takes a hit, so does everything in their business life.”
On social media, impersonation schemes run a large spectrum, from deepfaked Elon Musk promoting a fraudulent cryptocurrency, to brands quietly scraping an influencer’s image to manufacture ads. Global consumers may have lost as much as $3.7bn due to deepfake scams in 2026, according to an investigation from the VPN-maker Surfshark’s research team. The investigation found that social media impersonations on social media accounted for about half of all losses.
Easy targets for deepfakes
Celebrities and influencers are often the easiest to impersonate because they “have hundreds of hours of footage and thousands of pictures of them online. So you can feed that into a model and produce a fairly convincing deepfake,” said Marwick. Taylor Swift, Oprah Winfrey, Kim Kardashian, Gwyneth Paltrow and Tom Hanks have all been deepfaked by AI to promote various products online.
But big celebrities aren’t alone. On Instagram, beauty influencer Arielle Lorre was deepfaked to promote a skincare brand. Fashion creator Jessi Caparella discovered altered images of herself on Pinterest redirecting traffic to affiliate clothing links. And deepfaked videos of OnlyFans creator Elaina St James were used to trick fans into sending money to fraudulent accounts. While the financial impact of these impersonation schemes is hard to pinpoint, creators say that deepfakes dilute their value, cost them the trust of their followers, and can be time-consuming to fight: even when one deepfake post is reported and removed, another one pops up in its place.
With AI, “impersonation is much easier and much more convincing … [so] scams can be operated at a much larger scale,” said Marwick. “It’s often really believable. And with every new frontier model, they get better and better.”
One reason for the rise of deepfakes may be a growing use of AI-generated marketing content in general. AI-generated or “virtual” influencers accounted for $1.37bn, or about 4% of all brand spending in 2026, according to research from marketing consultancy Digital Applied. Virtual influencers may not have the same authenticity as real people, but they are much cheaper, always available, and infinitely customizable, which makes them attractive for some brand campaigns.
While the ad industry has always blurred the line between real and fake with airbrushing, CGI and other digital editing tools, the rise of AI has allowed brands to generate content from nothing with minimal production costs. And for some brands, that means crossing the line into deepfakes.
Influencers are doing whatever they can to fight the issue. Molly Tranchin, a fashion influencer known as FashionVeggie with more than 500,000 followers on Instagram, recently filed a lawsuit against the underwear brand Eby. According to the lawsuit, Tranchin had a contract to create three marketing videos for Eby in exchange for a fee. Eby was entitled to one round of “reasonable edits” for Tranchin to revise. The lawsuit claims that instead of posting the videos Tranchin submitted – in which she posed “modestly covering her chest and breasts with her arms” – the brand instead posted a deepfake video of Tranchin in a different pose, “exposing her breasts and nipples through one of Eby’s sheer bras”.
Tranchin has since dropped the lawsuit over a lack of jurisdiction and plans to refile it in a different court, according to court documents filed last month.
Eby spokesperson Clara Spahr said the company couldn’t comment on the pending litigation but will address the claims through the legal process.
The fight for their likeness
Tranchin, whose lawsuit is ongoing, has the benefit of knowing exactly who to hold accountable for the deepfakes. Other creators are not as lucky.
When Schuman discovered the deepfaked ads using her likeness, she and her manager immediately reported them to Meta. She said many of her followers, who brought these ads to her attention, also reported them. But it took weeks of badgering before Meta removed the GLP-1 ad. The makeup ad still remains in circulation on Instagram, despite many attempts from Schuman to get it taken down.
Both Meta and TikTok explicitly prohibit using artificial intelligence or digital manipulation to replicate a person’s identity. But the reality is that these platforms’ personalization algorithms may inadvertently grease the wheels for these schemes.
Meta, for example, allows advertisers to use hyper-targeted audience slicing, meaning bad actors can quietly launch fraudulent ads, create new accounts if one gets flagged, and scale their reach rapidly. In response to complaints about rampant scams on its platforms, Meta introduced new tools this year, including stronger advertiser verification policies and an AI detection tool to prevent “celeb-bait”, or the impersonation of celebrities. But experts say these tools do not go far enough, and that the company lacks incentive to clean up its own ad ecosystem. Meta did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
“The reality is that platforms make a lot of money off scams,” Marwick said.
Meta made about $16bn from ads promoting scams or banned goods, accounting for about 10% of its revenue in 2024, according to a 2025 investigation from Reuters. That investigation also quoted an internal presentation from Meta’s safety team, which estimated that its platforms were “involved in a third of all successful scams in the US”.
Not only do deepfakes hurt brand deals for individual influencers, but they also challenge the entire influencer marketing ecosystem. They disrupt the already delicate premise that a real person trusts a product or brand, and therefore their followers should do the same.
Schuman said she is deciding whether or not she needs to retain legal counsel to help her fight off the deepfakes as they keep popping up. Besides reporting the offending posts and threatening legal action, influencers don’t have much recourse.
“That’s money and time lost,” Schuman said about hiring a lawyer. But the alternative is a hit to her reputation. “So it’s a lose-lose from all ways of looking at it.”

From socialist student to Trump proxy: the 25-year rise of Venezuela’s Delcy Rodríguez
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
12:00:33 UTC
21:00:33 KST

It was April 2002 and Delcy Rodríguez was a woman on a mission.
Venezuela’s then president, Hugo Chávez, had been temporarily toppled by a bungled coup and Rodríguez, a junior diplomat who had been studying at Birkbeck, University of London, decided to act.
Rodríguez, then 32, set about trying to convince two reporters from the BBC programme Newsnight to accompany her to Venezuela’s capital to tell the world about what had happened.
“She desperately wanted to get the story of Chávez and the coup out there on a big platform,” says one of those journalists, Meirion Jones, who engaged Rodríguez as their fixer and flew to Caracas with her.
As the trio travelled around the South American city trying to land an interview with Chávez – who by then had reclaimed the presidency after being briefly detained – Jones had no inkling that his Venezuelan field producer and interpreter might one day become president herself.
“She looked like she was still a student really … it was just impossible to imagine at that point that she would become president of Venezuela,” Jones says.
Yet that is precisely what Rodríguez, now 57, has become, albeit in extraordinary circumstances precipitated by Donald Trump’s decision to abduct Chávez’s authoritarian heir, Nicolás Maduro.
When US special forces snatched the unpopular Maduro on 3 January this year, he was widely expected to be replaced with María Corina Machado, the Nobel-winning opposition leader whose movement beat him in the stolen 2024 election.
Instead, Trump discarded Machado and backed Maduro’s vice-president, Rodríguez, who became Venezuela’s interim leader two days after the downfall of her boss.
Eight months later, Rodríguez is still in power – despite leading a country many now consider a US protectorate – and looks likely to remain there for the foreseeable future, with scant sign of fresh presidential elections being called.
“We are very happy with the president-elect that we have right now,” Trump said of the un-elected Rodríguez after announcing what he called “the biggest oil deal in world history”.
Imdat Oner, a former Turkish diplomat in Caracas, believes the deal has strengthened Rodríguez and dealt a big blow to those hoping for democratic change. “Delcy is winning … I see Delcy Rodríguez staying in the presidency for at least four or five more years,” he says.
The Delcy Rodríguez that Jones flew with to Caracas more than two decades ago was a well-connected but politically insignificant figure known fundamentally because of her father.
Jorge Antonio Rodríguez was a Marxist activist who died in police custody in 1976, when his daughter was seven, reputedly after being tortured while detained over the kidnapping of a US businessman.
“All the Chavistas knew who her father had been – but they didn’t really know who she was,” says Jones, who is now a freelance investigative journalist. “[But during our time in Caracas] she’d made herself known to all these people … and I think by the end of the trip she was starting to think: ‘Maybe there is an opening for me in politics in Venezuela.’”
Soon after, Rodríguez returned to Venezuela, landing jobs with its state oil company, PDVSA, and foreign ministry. By 2006, she had become Chávez’s chief of staff, although she fell out of favour after clashing with Venezuela’s then ambassador to Russia during a visit to Moscow.
That row interrupted Rodríguez’s rise but she was rehabilitated by Maduro when he became president after Chávez’s 2013 death. In the years that followed, as her country nosedived into hunger and authoritarianism, Rodríguez enjoyed a rapid ascent.
She served as foreign minister before taking charge of the country’s economy as petroleum minister, finance minister and Maduro’s vice-president. Her brother, a psychiatrist turned politician, Jorge Rodríguez, established himself as the head of the national assembly.
After Maduro’s capture, the siblings formed a powerful triumvirate, alongside the feared interior minister, Diosdado Cabello.
“Delcy is not Delcy. Delcy’s Delcy and her brother. They do everything in tandem … they don’t do anything without each other’s approval or consent,” says Andrés Izarra, Chávez’s communication minister who went into exile after falling out with Maduro.
Those who have encountered Rodríguez during her unlikely 25-year rise, from being a leftwing student in the UK to the pinnacle of power in Venezuela, paint her in dramatically different ways.
Admirers describe a pragmatic, witty and intelligent workaholic who they credit with helping Venezuela escape years of hyperinflation and believe can fulfil promises to revive the country’s decaying oil industry and economy.
“Venezuela under Delcy is going to have the best possible kind of technocratic care – and that’s what is needed right now … she’s going to get that oil moving,” says Greg Palast, the other journalist who flew to Caracas with Rodríguez for the BBC in 2002.
Palast believes Venezuela is “way better off” under Rodríguez than the incompetent Maduro, calling her a clever strategist who plays politics “on a four-dimensional chessboard”.
Detractors paint Rodríguez as a belligerent, power-hungry chameleon whose political leanings can change on a dime and who, as a key member of Maduro’s regime, was herself responsible for Venezuela’s slide into poverty and dictatorship.
“They’re evil, they are crazy and they are smart … they’re evil geniuses,” a prominent opposition politician, who asked not to be named, says of the Rodríguez siblings.
Izarra says his former friend is “very machiavellian” and has a taste for luxury.
Tom Shannon, a retired US diplomat who has worked with Venezuela since the 1990s, describes the multilingual Rodríguez as a “very smart, very articulate, very determined” and profoundly ideological person.
Shannon recalls being “intercepted” by Rodríguez – then foreign minister – after flying to Caracas to meet Maduro during Barack Obama’s second term.
Their conversation was wide-ranging. “But I remember very distinctly, at one point I raised the issue of human rights – our interest in especially seeing the release of certain people from prison,” Shannon says.
“She … turned to me, with a look almost of contempt, not for me, but for the subject I was raising and she said: ‘You might not know my story, but my father was a revolutionary member of an armed revolutionary movement in Venezuela who was arrested [and] tortured during interrogation and killed by the Venezuelan security services when I was a girl.’
“And she said: ‘This interrogation and the killing of my father took place during a time when, from your point of view, Venezuela was a democratic country governed by the rule of law. But I can tell you, the security services weren’t.”
Shannon adds: “It was very striking … it was evident to me that she saw her father as kind of a revolutionary north star, kind of a martyr point of reference – and I believe that’s still the case.”
He thinks Rodríguez’s objective in her new partnership with Washington is political survival “and to make sure that a revanchist, conservative, elitist, democratic opposition does not return to power”.
Speaking in the White House, Trump heaped praise on his unlikely Venezuelan partner. “Delcy is doing a very, very good job – very highly respected,” he told reporters.
Trump claimed Venezuela had only just escaped a “very nasty” regime and was not ready for elections. “You know, it’s very new. We took them out of a dictatorship, and we’re getting along great with the government,” he said.
Such comments will have been music to Rodríguez’s ears. “Delcy wants to survive,” says Oner. “And she knows that if she gives enough to the Trump administration, the Trump administration will allow her to stay in power.”

I think I finally understand why Fox News pays Jesse Watters the big bucks. The network star, famous for hot takes like men shouldn’t “eat soup in public”, has an incredible talent for inserting misogyny into absolutely any news story.
Take, for example, Donald Trump’s ludicrous announcement on Wednesday night that he will give every American adult $5,000 if Republicans retain control of the US Congress in November’s midterm election. That’s a story about apparent bribery, right? A story about fiscal recklessness and empty promises. A story about how the president, whose popularity is plummeting, is so out of ideas that he’s resorted (yet again) to dangling cash in front of voters.
Actually, says Watters, it’s none of the above; it’s just Trump behaving like a woman.
“That $5,000 check, Dana, that’s not a bribe,” Watters told Fox anchor Dana Perino on Thursday. “We’re calling it an enticement … It’s like a woman. Sometimes a woman can entice you, OK? Perhaps the Fox News host isn’t completely wrong. After all, I am a woman and I am about to entice you to look up the story about how Watters courted his much younger second wife. It’s very intriguing.
But back to this definitely-not-a-bribe $5,000 payment which the president calls a Trump “dividend”. I wouldn’t start spending it now, if I were you. The president, like his right-hand man Elon Musk, has a habit of making grandiose promises he doesn’t keep. Remember the Doge dividends floated last February? Those haven’t materialized. Nor have the tariff dividends that Trump made so much noise about. “People that are against Tariffs are FOOLS!” Trump said in a Truth Social post last year. “We are taking in Trillions of Dollars and … A dividend of at least $2000 a person (not including high income people!) will be paid to everyone.” Almost a year after that post, nobody has received a tariff dividend. I feel pretty confident saying there is a 0.00001% chance that anyone is going to get a $5,000 Republican celebration check. Let’s pretend that the president is a serious man who makes thoughtful policy proposals, rather than an opportunist who says whatever inane thing happens to pop into his brain in the moment. He may not end up issuing people celebration checks, but he has already gutted election security programs and attempted to limit voting access. The real story here isn’t $5,000 cheques, it’s the fact that America’s self-styled king seems intent on meddling with the election, and no meaningful checks and balances are stopping him.

US-China decoupling could benefit other countries, China trade war game suggests
The study suggests a complete severing of trade ties would hurt both superpowers while bringing temporary gains elsewhere
Chinese researchers have modelled a war game scenario suggesting that a complete economic decoupling between the US and China could, unexpectedly, yield dividends for most other nations.
However, the simulations carried an important caveat: any spillover benefits would be fragile. If those economies were subsequently to cut their own economic ties with China, their initial welfare gains would quickly turn into losses.
The study, co-authored by researchers from the Guangzhou Geological Survey Institute and the Bay Area International Business School at Beijing Normal University, was published in the peer-reviewed South China Journal of Economics.

AFU Gains Ground, Kuban Gets Pounded, NATO Trains Hard and Gives Russian Drone Free Pass
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

The most impressive pure war news this week probably was two days of damaging drone strikes in Russia’s southern Kuban region: warships hit, sea drones participating, air defenses hunted down and destroyed.
Russia is visibly shifting from periodic big strikes with five to six days of light drone raids over the rest of the week, to what looks like individually planned attacks designed to make more unlivable places the Russians want the civilians to be miserable. This is Kyiv, Odesa, Kherson, Sumy and Kharkiv. More civilians are getting killed and injured as a result.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
This week not only the Americans with their goofball “peace initiative” were in the news, NATO stepped on a rake as well by running an impressively big and complicated air defense practice exercise with lots of fighter jets and air watch aircraft and so forth, simultaneously with a Russian drone flying deep into Romania, quite unmolested by NATO. So if the Russians were deterred by training, then for sure NATO deterred Russia this week.
                                                                                                                                                                         
The Front
In general the trend of fighting seems to be shrinking Russian pressure in almost all sectors. Based on the field descriptions this is the textbook “we’ve just about run out of men to send on attack” phase. This is the fifth (!) Russian summer offensive when we’ve seen this happen.
Russian Ballistic Missiles Strike Zaporizhstal Steel Plant, Injuring 4
Zaporizhzhia sector – 1st Assault Regiment commander Dmyrtro “Perun” Filatov gave a Monday interview to TV24 and he said that in his sector Russian attacks are falling off, and that it seems like troops are getting transferred out of this sector to other parts of the front. Attacks are still taking place but less often and with less-numerous groups. The term he used is “significantly decreasing.” The figure he used was “about 40 percent.”
Filatov also confirmed a lot of the rumors and speculation we’ve heard about Rybne, in the Hulyaipole AO. The village was actually captured on July 30 by Ukrainian forces but it was three weeks before open sourcers confirmed its capture. According to Filatov the success was the result of a meticulous, long-term operation where the first step is cutting off supply to a targeted locality, then potential for reinforcement by infiltration, and then systematic, slow house-to-house clearing.
For those of you who like “maneuver warfare,” this is the template that the Ukrainians are using, if your country doesn’t or isn’t planning to, you are behind the curve.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Elsewhere in the sector, this is from the Ukrainian milblogger Mashovets (who in turn is sometimes often the main source of “analysis” by some big name Western think tanks I could name), Russia’s 29th Combined Arms Army has actually fallen back, having lost the village Myrne, and is trying to prevent the Ukrainians from pushing through a defense line built on the Vovcha River and the villages Komar and Perebudova. If the Ukrainians are not stopped, then Russian forces would be caught on the wrong side of the river, meaning the men might walk out but not their heavy equipment. Mashovets writes that even though elements of the much-battered 90th Tank Division have been committed to the area, it’s not clear the Russians can hold and if they can’t, then “the prospect is a collapse along the lower Mokri Yaly” River. But none of this is confirmed past a total AFU ban on ground reporting from the sector.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Pokrovsk/Dobropillya – We were graced this week by a detailed interview with the chief of staff of Azov Brigade, which is of course the hardest-fighting regular unit in 1st Army Corps, and possibly in the entire AFU, this is the core Azov. His name is Lev “Horus” Pashko and according to him, the Russians are stopped cold, the war right now is running a meatgrinder with the Russians providing the meat. According to Pashko, 1st Brigade’s AO is Dobropillya, which Azov recaptured from the Russians last summer.
According to Pashko, Russia is still trying to push into this sector using numbers and accepting losses, and the ratio of Ukrainians to Russians in some areas can be 1 to 60. Thanks to open fields of fire and drones, he said, the Russians are all killed or wounded, they do not gain ground. Most of the soldiers doing the attacking are force-mobilized, i.e., they were civilians who got in trouble with the law or had money issues and signed a Russian army contract and wound up being sent against Ukrainian positions with little training. The quality of the Russian troops is, he said, extremely low.
The main method of Russian attacks is to probe for gaps in defenses and infiltrate without regard to future supply or means of retreat. They are ordered to raise flags at locations reached, there is no instruction on fighting Ukrainians. Pashko’s evaluation: “The deeper they go, the easier it is for our scouts and special forces to destroy them… They can capture a place that has already been completely destroyed, lose 140 soldiers in two weeks – and fine, they take it. They lost half a battalion, and we didn’t.
BTW, not confirmed, but the German reporter Julian Röpcke this week reported Russian officers are sending their assault troops off with the extremely embellished – i.e. containing false information about what terrain is in Russian and what’s in Ukrainian hands – maps in hand. I hadn’t heard that before and generally reports are Russian troops find their way by being told to follow a drone or a road to an obvious location, there are no maps. But maybe that’s the case sometimes. As a result, according to Röpcke, Russian infiltration groups run headlong into solid Ukrainian positions right in the middle territory supposedly already captured by Russia.
Regarding personnel and organization, Pashko said that since Azov is National Guard, some of the reforms and new contracts are only now reaching the brigade. There is recruiting going on with men who joined for a year on the 18-24 terms, according to Pashko most intend to re-up. (Note: This should not be taken as an indicator for the entire AFU, unit morale and esprit, and also small unit commanders in Azov are exceptional). But deferrals and rotations are happening and a steady flow of replacements and reserves is building.
For those of you with experience in NATO armies, this is nothing special. In the AFU this is a very big deal, steady personnel streams and even vaguely predictable company- and battalion-level soldier rotation, never mind something resembling reasonable career progression, is something the AFU has struggled with for pretty much for as long as Ukraine has existed.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Kostyantynivka – The Ukrainian 210th Assault Regiment has been deployed to the Kostyantynivka direction, apparently supporting the defense of the city’s western flank under the 19th Army Corps. Also moving into the sector is 46th Airmobile Brigade, a veteran outfit with a good combat reputation. This is allowing the 24th Mech Brigade, who have fought as long as any formation in the entire AFU, to get a break from duty in the line; they have been in this sector for close to a year.
Parallel with Ukrainian reinforcements/fresh troops flowing to Konstyantynivka, there are reports from several units in the area that the Russian attacks into the city have fallen off to very little. Some drone crews are complaining about the absence of targets.
Lyman sector – It’s official, the AFU finally announced it, meaning 3rd Corps, had completed a slow counter-offensive over the past three months that liberated 10 villages and recaptured about 150 square kilometers of Russian territory. This had been an open secret for much of August and by early September only the AFU itself was pretending no one knew that 3rd Corps had been running successful assault operations. This review formally acknowledged the success last week. These are the first specific claims of how much territory was liberated though. It is a clear and substantial Ukrainian victory. It is all over the Ukrainian news and a bunch of Russia milbloggers are saying the same thing. So far my newspaper’s done two pieces on this:
So if you haven’t heard about it in the western mainstream, it’s not because us in Ukraine weren’t trying to get the information out. Between the two articles you will get a decent picture of what’s been happening. Graphically, I strongly recommend this excellent video by Clement Molin that shows what’s been going on.
On a connected note, the commander of 3rd Corps Andriy Biletsky got irritated at a Friday Russian propaganda TV television conference in which Putin told a bunch of officials in Bishkek the Russian army is doing great and just on Friday it captured and placed under undisputed Russian control the Ukrainian city Svyatohirsk. My newspaper did two articles on that as well.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Most Ukrainians know the place as an ancient monastery in a very wooded part of Donetsk region, tourists and newlyweds go there. These days Svyatohirsk is in 3rd Corps sector and so over the weekend Biletsky recorded himself going on a pleasant walk through leafy Svyatohirsk, and most of the the center. The monastery was peaceful, birds were singing, people were walking around, no bombs, no shooting, no Russians. Biletsky didn’t even bother wearing a helmet. His best insult was calling Putin a moron with a clown nose. And if you want even more background on Ukrainian offensive activity in Kharkiv/northern Donetsk region, here’s an article about some Colombian/Brazilian foreign fighters that, more or less where Putin said they were surrounded, took ground and destroyed enemy:
                                                                                                                                                                         
Russia bombards Ukraine
As we have seen Russia’s bombardment generals like to switch tactics from time to time. Last week the tactic was low-grade, but constant strikes against Kyiv with the probable intent of keeping the air raid warning on in the city constantly. It was a pain. Then they quit for a day so Trump’s envoys could visit Kyiv and pretend to work on the peace process.
Overnight Monday-Tuesday the Russians launched another big strike, surprising no one. It came less than a day after Kushner and Witkoff took the train to Poland. The Russians fired Onyx anti-ship “hypersonic” missiles from the Bryansk, Kursk Oblasts and from Crimea; Iskander-M/S-400/KN-23 ballistic missiles from the Bryansk and Voronezh Oblasts; and 32 Kh-101 air-launched cruise missiles from the Vologda Oblast. Also, there were about 166 strike and decoy UAVs, about half of them jet-powered, launched from the usual locations.
                                                                                                                                                                         
The Ukrainians returned to their policy of not announcing how many incoming hypersonics and ballistics there were. My personal estimate is there were at least eight explosions exactly like big missiles that night.
                                                                                                                                                                         
I witnessed one possible ballistic intercept. One. The way it seemed to me, the ballistic missiles arrived at about 3:30-3:50 a.m. and the cruise missiles maybe 40 minutes later. In the interval you could hear jet engines from time to time but whether that was Ukrainian fighters or Russian Banderole drones, I can’t say. For practical purposes, there was not air defense against the ballistic missiles. When the cruise missiles came in you could hear everything from autocannon to machine guns, not constantly, but in bursts. Sometimes tracers were visible.
The main targets, as before, were the Odesa region and the Kyiv region. According to the Ukrainian Air Force as of 9 a.m. they had shot down 2 ballistic/hypersonic missiles, 31 cruise missiles and 142 UAVs. There was one big hit during the day near the river, the southern section of the city that burned for most of the afternoon. Two people dead, about ten injured. Later the death toll rose to four.
                                                                                                                                                                         
The best-confirmed Russian hit was to a Varus grocery store in the Solomyanskyi district, which was pretty much leveled. An Epitsentr superstore in Chernhiv was hit and set on fire. In Odesa, Europe’s single most extensive site of cheap wholesale Chinese knock-off goods imported probably less than legally – the Seventh-Kilometer open air market – got some of its trading rows blasted.
On Wednesday and Thursday, the Russians hit the Manufactura shopping center/movie multitheater in Sumy with jet-powered drones. The first attack hit a car park killing two (man and woman aged 21) and injuring about 20. The second strike hit the next day, no injuries reported. However, two guided aerial bombs (KABs) hit a residential area on the outskirts of Sumy. This injured 11 people including three children (girls aged 8 and 17, and a 14-year-old boy). Later there were reports of about 20 were hospitalized. Also, a Thursday drone attack on the town Shostka, near Sumy, killed one man and injured a woman. All civilians.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Ukraine bombards Russia
We kick off this section with a Wednesday Ukrainian strike against Yamal’, up by the Arctic Circle, where the Novy Urengoy gas condensate factory fire was visited by long-range drones. Natural gas burns better than crude, so Russian social media recorded some epic fires. Early reports put the raid at 3,100 km (1,926 miles), a new record. By Thursday cooler heads had prevailed and the Ukrainian internet decided it was about 2,920 km (1,814), still a new long-range drone strike record for this war, and probably in history.
But Ukraine’s really impressive air operations this week targeted Russia’s Black Sea coast and the Kuban.
The most visible event (not counting degrading attacks against Russian air defenses, which basically never stop) was an Unmanned Systems Forces (USF) strike hitting Sochi on Sept. 9. Early reports from that based on Russian social media with summer vacationers well-represented, and some drone video from the Ukrainians, was that fuel storage sites (one had been set afire on the 3rd) and (yet more) air defense got hit. Meanwhile the Russians said everything was OK except for some small fires from falling debris.
Fast-forward 24 hours, and open source satellite imagery showed up. The damage toll almost certainly included, various targets: three military helicopters ( Mi-8, Mi-28, Ka-52 ), two oil depots, a major radar transponder on the mountain overlooking Sochi (two hits), and an S-300 position (ground systems smashed and damaged). Plus the commodities industry reported a pair of grain terminals in Anapa were shut down.
On Friday there was more news: At Anapa airport, drones had destroyed a Su-30 fighter jet and an Mi-8 military helicopter. This was on Sept. 4.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Some militaries would have beat their chests, found some media to tell the reporters how “awesome” their military is, headed back to the O-club for cocktails, and called it a day. But Russia’s opponent here is the world’s most capable and lethal drone force, the Ukrainian USF and Ukrainian special forces.
                                                                                                                                                                         
So, on Thursday, the next night, Sept. 10, the Ukrainian drones returned to Krasnodar and Russia’s Black Sea shore. This time they hit Sochi pier with sea drones, big fires, and possibly missiles. Sea drones were seen to detonate near the stern of warships tied up at the wharf, possibly in a repeat of the Ukrainian tactic of damaging Russian ships by setting off underwater explosions near the rudders and propellers.
The Ukrainians claimed that in the commotion they also put a Neptune anti-ship missile into the side of the Admiral Gessen frigate, which as many of you know sticks its bow outside Novorossiysk port from time to time to lob cruise missiles mostly at Kyiv. Thursday evening brought a credible satellite image of the damage. Other images seemed to confirm damage done to more warships, like, the small minesweeper Zheleznyakov, and the large amphibious assault ship Pyotr Morgunov, and a Buryan-M class missile boat.
Satellite images also confirmed damage to other ships but it’s not clear to me at this point which were operational and which were just there as missile sponges. In any case, anyone who remembers the humiliating Russian naval retreat from Sevastopol, it’s coming again in Novorossisisyk. Maybe the survivors will shift to Abkhazia, maybe the Russians will just try and send them up the Volga. But the Black Sea Fleet is defeated.
OK, that already would have been an excellent two days’ work for any air force on Earth.
                                                                                                                                                                         
That was not all for the USF. Same night, Dagestan, so Caspian Sea, the port Makhachkala was hit and at least one ship set on fire, type undetermined. Among the strike packages were FP-1 drones. There is wide speculation the ship was Iranian but that’s totally unconfirmed. Finally, same night, I don’t yet know the cause, a cargo ship in the Azov Sea was set afire.
That’s two major Ukrainian drone raids, 300-plus aircraft both times, strike packages hitting something like five and possibly seven or eight separate targets a night, two nights in a row. Among other targets, three warships and three cargo vessels hit. At least two USF brigades and the elite USF 1st Training Center were involved. There may have been more. These are substantial, effective and powerful Ukrainian air strikes. How can the West keep pretending this isn’t happening?
P.S. — On Friday several massive Flamingo missiles hit a military chemicals plant in Volgograd and the Russian internet seems to agree there were two good hits on the roof of the main production building, smoke and fires. Flamingos are much bigger than the standard Ukrainian drone, they are flying aerial bombs and as big as a small fighter jet, so pretty easy to shoot down. But somehow the Ukrainians got some through.

The final item in this section as always is the hit list for the week. Here’s a graphic from Istribin showing the gap between how much oil Russia could produce and export, based on OPEC estimates, and how much it is actually producing and exporting. Right now the price of oil is at a near-record high. Russia really could use the money. But Ukraine’s drone strike campaign is cutting into that, visibly and significantly.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Real and fake serious countries – true arsenals of democracy
On Monday the news came out that Britain would donate £100 million ($135 million) to Ukraine for the purchase of Patriot interceptors, other air defense systems and ammunition, artillery shells and munitions, and other stuff. The interceptors are supposed to arrive “by winter.” On Tuesday the UK Defence Secretary said that beyond that, London will supply Kyiv with 120,000 drones this year. If you are wondering where Ukraine is getting all these excellent long-range drones, there’s a suspect for you.
On Tuesday Germany announced it will transfer PAC-2 missiles for Patriot to Ukraine from Bundeswehr stocks, along with increased supplies of AIM-9 air-to-air missiles, because now the Ukrainian F-16s are running out of those as well. Ukraine meantime has ordered “several thousand” excellent German IRIS-T missiles (probably Ukraine’s best medium-range ground-to-air missile) via the European loan/frozen Russian assets facility, news reports in Berlin said.
And on Tuesday afternoon, Ukraine’s Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara announced Ukraine is signing contracts with partners, paid for by EU “frozen Russian assets loans” for the supply of about 1,000 Patriot interceptor missiles that will arrive in 2027 and 2028. Khmara went on to say now Ukraine is asking allied states to transfer Patriots from existing stocks in exchange for new missiles once the Americans produce them. For practical purposes, if the transfer takes place, it will be Greece and Spain giving up the missiles, and frankly that seems unlikely to happen. Later on in the day the EU said it would make an exception in its rules that normally mandate EU loans can’t buy non-EU weapons like Patriots. Ukrainian financial media said the next loan tranche €3.2 billion ($3.7 billion), might be transferred on Friday.
On Thursday President Volodymyr Zelensky, in Oslo, met with the Norwegian leadership to discuss joint production of the missile interceptor Freyja. This is a much more viable option, but interceptor missiles are complicated and even the usually ridiculously optimistic people at Fire Point are saying a test version without the difficult bit – the seeker – might be launched next month. Short term, none of this is likely to help Ukraine this winter. Still, responding to an air defense problem about a year and a half into the problem, is better than not responding at all.
Final foreign affairs note, this week the clown duo Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff went to Moscow, then went to Kyiv “to promote peace because Trump wants the killing to end.” They then told reporters everything is great, the talks were excellent, and the peace process is moving forward.
This is hogwash. Neither side budged, the Americans wasted everyone’s time. In fact, the only thing the American delegation did – not making this up – was serve as couriers to deliver toughened Russian terms to Ukraine, they literally did the Kremlin’s bidding. Here is an article about that utterly shameful American behavior and yet another case of ignorant US officials getting hoodwinked into pushing Russian narratives by Moscow. It should be condemned, and if you ask me this is all impeachable negligence.
The Ukrainians told the Americans they really appreciated the diplomatic engagement and Donald J. Trump’s sincere interest in peace. Translated from Ukrainian means “go away you morons and let the adults get back to work.”
When training maybe SHOULDN’T be NATO’s top priority
                                                                                                                                                                         
On Tuesday, as noted above, there was a big Russian missile+drone strike that blew stuff up and killed and injured Ukrainians, in an actual war.
The same day, two other things happened in NATO-land. First, a Russian jet-powered drone flew across half Ukraine, into Romania, flew around Romania in NATO air space for a half hour, and then returned to Moldova. The expedition covered about 500 kilometers (310 miles). It was quite the excursion, almost to the Carpathian Mountains.
NATO launched a pair of Spanish F-18s. No intercept. We don’t know why, but, last review courtesy the Polish media, we learned that the previous time NATO failed to intercept a Russian attack weapon flying in NATO air space – this happened to be a cruise missile – the Polish F-16s that should have carried out that intercept had trouble, because the spiffy high tech data link with the NATO AWACS “flying radar” watching every meter the Russian cruise missile flew, wasn’t working so ground controllers had to try to vector the pilots to the missile. It didn’t work. The malfunctioning data link system is called Link16, unsurprisingly first developed for the US Air Force. So maybe that was a problem for the Spaniards.
The other, even more humorous (some might say shocking) NATO development that day, was that Romania and NATO were simultaneously conducting two (!) major air exercises requiring air watch and so forth. It’s not like the drone flew into Romania and all of NATO’s air watch stuff was elsewhere. Based on Ukrainian sources, at minimum, the air operations training involved six NATO fighter jets, an AWACS, two fuel tankers, a recon drone, and a maritime search plane.
This produced the, I don’t know, ironic, maybe entertaining, and according to some probably negligent situation of all manner of NATO aircraft zooming and buzzing above eastern Romania and practicing defending NATO air space against any and all air threats, while, at the exact same time, about a 15-20 minute F-16 flight to the north (faster if on afterburner) an actual Russian drone with an explosive warhead was putt-putting across central Moldova and then well into central-eastern Romania, dozens of kilometers inside NATO air space, without anything stopping it. Here’s a link to a detailed article on that fiasco.
As an afternote it’s worth mentioning that all this seemingly almost intentional NATO air force energy spent not actually doing its job and defending NATO air space, over southeast Romania and the western Black Sea, took place simultaneously with the first day of the punishing Ukrainian drone raids against the Anapa, Sochi and other points in the Kuban. Some Russians might say the exercise was just a cover for nefarious NATO data-gathering on targets for the Ukrainians. I think that’s silly but the theory is out there.
Next day, so second day of those strikes, NATO flew a deep reconnaissance mission over the Black Sea that did a fairly close fly-by of Crimea and flew suspiciously close to Russia’s Black Sea coast where, as we knew, only hours before a salvo of Ukrainian Neptune anti-ship missiles had hit and to all appearances pretty solidly damaged tree to five Russian warships in the vicinity, including two missile launch platforms. The NATO recon mission, flown by an RAF Rivet Joint spy plane, had every appearance of NATO checking out the degree to which the beating the Ukrainians had laid down on the (remains of) the Russian Black Sea Fleet, would be long-lasting.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Those darn Russian “Partisans” and long Ukrainian memories
The probable SBU/HUR bloggers that are probably masquerading as a Russian partisan movement on Tuesday put out a list of claimed assassinations for the past month. Only one murder could be confirmed by other sources, but the list is worth taking a look at. This won’t affect the course of the war overly, but again, anyone thinking the war can just be ended by a neat ceasefire after which everyone goes back to playing nicely and buying cheap Russian energy, has no understanding how vicious the Russians have been in Ukraine and how dead set the Ukrainians are on hunting down responsible individuals and killing them.
- On July 27 SBU assassins in Donetsk killed Oleg Shutov, an assassin himself employed by the special services division of the DPR. The Ukrainians had been after him for the June 27, 2017 murder, in Kyiv, of Maj. Gen. Maksym Shapoval, commander of the 10th special forces detachment. Shutov also reportedly was involved in a March 31, 2017 murder, in Mariupol, of the head of the counterintelligence department of the SBU in the Donetsk region, Col. Oleksandr Kharaberyush. Some of us remember that. The SBU said it surveilled Shutov for several days before blowing up his car. The SBU announced the assassination this week.
                                                                                                                                                                         
- On July 29, in Tula, Andrei Cherezov, head of the Russian Air Transport Laboratory and a fairly high profile supporter of the invasion as well as a player in Russia’s drone manufacturing effort, was ambushed in the entryway of his apartment building and shot and wounded with a pistol. Word is he was seriously wounded and is unlikely to recover. The shooter escaped. This was reported in some media.
- On Aug. 5, in Sverdlovsk, Vladimir Tkachuk, another drone manufacturer and simultaneously host of a rah rah Russia Telegram channel called “Obsessed with War,” was blown up in his car. He survived but lost limbs and the function of major organs, reportedly he’s in a local hospital in vegetative state. The bomber wasn’t caught. Part of this was reported in some Ukrainian media.
- On Aug. 27, Aerospace Forces Lt. Col. Sergei Sechkov died in a car bombing in St. Petersburg. Reportedly the woman who planted the bomb escaped to Moldova via Turkey, and traveled onwards. The Russian police supposedly know the identity she crossed the borders with, but not much else. This was pretty thoroughly reported in Ukrainian media and even mentioned by Russia milbloggers.
- On Sept. 3, Aerospace Forces Maj. Gen. Nikolai Varpakhovich, commander of a long-range bomber division, was shot near his home as he was getting into his car in Engels. This is the home base of bombers that launch cruise missiles at Ukraine; by almost any logic he is the senior officer signing off on the strikes. A motorcyclist driving up to his car shot him twice, once in the face and once in the stomach. He survived and reportedly was airlifted to Moscow for intensive care. The motorcyclist escaped. According to Russian media the general was possibly injured in an accident.

‘Where do we go?’: How Israel’s ‘yellow line’ is closing in on Palestinians

‘Where do we go?’: How Israel’s ‘yellow line’ is closing in on Palestinians
Ola Ishtiwi sits with her children in front of the remains of her home in the Al-Tuffah neighbourhood in eastern Gaza City, a few metres away from a series of painted cement blocks Israel has placed to mark what has become known as the “yellow line”.
Initially set up following the announcement of the Israel-Hamas ceasefire agreement of October 2025, the “yellow line” splits Gaza into two sections: most of the Palestinian population is confined in the western zone, while the eastern zone is under Israeli military control.
At first, the “yellow line” left roughly 47 per cent of the Strip for the Palestinian population, but Israeli forces have gradually pushed the line inwards, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).
Palestinians currently live in less than 40 per cent of Gaza’s land area, the UN said. But, in many cases, this push by Israeli forces has led to the displacement of families living close to the line.
Displaced, again and again
For Ibtisam Malika, a resident of the Zeitoun neighbourhood near the line, the result is a recurring cycle of displacement, return and then displacement again.
“Every two to three months, we are forced to move and leave our belongings behind,” she said.
“We can’t take it anymore. We lost half of our children in the war, and only remnants of us remain.”
Nowhere else to go
Some 2.1 million people – almost the entire population of the Strip – are currently displaced and living within the limits of the “yellow line”, according to the UN.
Many live near the painted yellow blocks, with residents saying they have continued to live in these neighbourhoods – notably Al-Tuffah and Al Zaytoun neighbourhoods in eastern Gaza City – because they have nowhere else to go.
Families there are constantly on high alert, fearing that they may have to abandon their property and quickly flee if the security situation changes.
Safaa Mushtaha, an Al-Tuffah resident, said that asking where the family could move to has become part of their daily lives.
“‘Where do we go?’ This is a question we’ve been asking ourselves for three years,” she said. “We accepted living near the yellow line, but it’s become unbearable.”
Dire humanitarian needs
The United Nations said finding safer sites to establish camps for displaced people has become more difficult because much of the suitable land lies within prohibited or restricted areas east, south and north of the “yellow line” and beyond.
Some 1.98 million people, or 94 per cent of Gaza’s population, need assistance related to shelter and non-food items, according to the latest shelter assessment published by the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs.
Also, 84 per cent of families also live in extremely difficult conditions, including shelters or tents that do not provide adequate protection from the weather.
‘This is not life’
For Ms. Ishtiwi, daily life has become very difficult living near the yellow line.
“We don’t know what to do or where to go,” she told UN News. “We don’t have a tent, and we don’t have money.”
Ahmed Arhim, from the Zeitoun neighbourhood, said the sounds of gunfire and drones make it difficult to sleep, especially for children.
“We don’t sleep every night,” he said.
“The children can’t sleep. They are scared and they wet themselves. Many residents have already left. We are displaced every day, always displaced. This is not life.”
‘The bloodshed in Gaza must stop’
These testimonies come at a time when UN agencies are reporting continued Israeli military operations and strikes in Gaza despite the ceasefire declared last year.
Local authorities have reported 1,334 deaths and 4,429 injuries since the ceasefire’s announcement on 10 October 2025, according to OCHA’s latest humanitarian update.
“The bloodshed in Gaza must stop,” the UN Human Rights Office said in a recent statement, noting that over a five-day period in late August, 24 Palestinians were killed in Israeli attacks, including four children and a woman, and that 21 of them were killed in air raids.
