Romanian military disposal teams neutralized debris from multiple unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) – including fragments containing live explosive warheads – discovered across coastal regions, the Black Sea, and the border county of Tulcea on Friday, Sept. 11.
According to Romanian broadcaster Digi24, fragments were recovered from several separate sites throughout Friday. Authorities confirmed that two drone fragments were found on a beach in Tulcea County along the border with Ukraine, while two additional pieces were retrieved from Black Sea waters.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
In one instance, naval specialists discovered an unexploded warhead among the maritime debris and conducted a controlled detonation to neutralize the hazard safely. A separate fragment in coastal waters had been spotted by the crew of a commercial vessel, who alerted the Romanian Border Police. A subsequent inspection confirmed that the object contained no explosives.
Later Friday evening, at approximately 6:00 p.m. local time, military explosive ordnance disposal (EOD) teams were deployed to a coastal area north of the port city of Constanța. Specialists determined that the site contained remnants of four UAVs, including an interceptor drone with an unexploded charge. The munition was neutralized without incident.
The Ministry of National Defence did not publicly identify the specific drone models or confirm their national origin.
Drones Strike Taganrog Airfield and Tolyatti Chemical Plant
Earlier discovery near Capu Midia
The series of interventions on Friday followed an earlier incident on Thursday morning, Sept. 10, when tourists discovered drone debris on a beach in the Corbu area near the Capu Midia military training range.
Local police secured the perimeter before an EOD team from Romania’s Ministry of Internal Affairs arrived to examine the remnants. Technical experts confirmed the absence of explosive materials and removed the wreckage for forensic analysis.
Romania’s Black Sea coastline and Danube River border areas have repeatedly experienced airspace violations and falling debris amid Russian aerial campaigns targeting Ukrainian port and logistics infrastructure in the adjacent Odesa region.
Regional airspace incursions
The discoveries follow recurring border incursions involving unmanned aircraft across southeastern Europe.
On Aug. 24, an unauthorized drone transited Moldovan airspace before crossing into Romania during an overnight Russian aerial assault on Ukrainian cities. According to Moldova’s Defense Ministry, the drone crossed into Moldova near Vynohradivka in Ukraine’s Odesa region before exiting near Pașcani in Cahul District toward Romania’s Galați County.
Romania’s Defense Ministry reported that military radar systems tracked intermittent signals near Cahul before detecting an aerial contact over the Târgu Bujor area in Galați County.
In response, the Romanian Air Force scrambled two F-16 fighter jets and an IAR-330 SOCAT helicopter, while the Department for Emergency Situations issued automated RO-Alert warnings to residents in the border area. The incursion was the second such airspace breach recorded over Moldova and Romania within a three-day span in late August.

From Hacks to Bioweapons, Claude Misuse Is Now Everywhere
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

Editor’s note: After more than a decade, this is the last WIRED Security News This Week. “The roundup,” as we call it internally, started as a way to ensure that our readers knew about the latest key cybersecurity and privacy news even if we didn’t write about it ourselves. It was a simple way to highlight our own work and the wealth of other great journalism and research published in this realm every week.
Over the years, the roundup has developed a devoted following, and some editions have even become viral hits—which is honestly weird, but the cybersecurity community is great and weird, so it feels right. Rest assured that something new and exciting is coming in the roundup’s place, so stay tuned for that! For now, as always, stay safe out there.
Meta failed to catch roughly 350 AI child abuse ads, according to new research this week, including some that included images of real kids. In one case, a child depicted in an ad was a member of a European royal family. Lawmakers have said they intend to investigate, and the San Francisco City Attorney’s Office ordered the company this week to stop “allowing” AI child abuse ads.
In other Meta news, the company announced a new personal AI agent this week that can book your plane tickets or sell your car, but it emphasized heavy investment in security and privacy features, seemingly anticipating mistrust from consumers. In this vein, the company was hit with a proposed class action lawsuit this week over alleged illegal harvesting of Facebook and Instagram photos for training AI and face-recognition systems.
Clearview AI is testing a previously unreported prototype AI tool known as InquiryIQ that would help law enforcement find a target’s associates, social media accounts, and other personal information. And Apple announced a set of new “audio intelligence” features for its Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 devices this week that involve processing audio in a user’s environment. The company extensively emphasized the security and privacy protections built into the features, perhaps anticipating that they could come across as, well, creepy.
The US and Mexico have a new joint operation to detect, track, and take down drones at the border using laser tech. And there’s a new GTA V mod that lets you make (in-game) money destroying (in-game) Flock license plate recognition cameras.
But wait, there’s more! Here’s the security and privacy news we didn’t cover in depth ourselves this week. Click the headlines to read the full stories.
From State-Sponsored Hacking to Bioweapons, Claude Abuse Is Simply Everywhere
Anthropic has been perhaps more vocal than any other AI company about the ways in which its tools are prone to misuse. It published some of the first reports of its AI service Claude being used in cybercriminal hacking operations and the discovery that its AI agents had, like those of its competitor OpenAI, escaped their sandbox and autonomously breached the networks of several organizations as part of their attempts to fulfill their users’ commands.
This week, the company released a new overarching report on how Claude has been abused over the last eight months, and the results are staggering in their breadth—if, perhaps, inevitable in a world where AI is simply used as a productivity shortcut for just about everything. In case study after case study, the company documents how Claude was exploited for state-sponsored and cybercriminal hacking, disinformation campaigns and influence operations, and even attempted development of bioweapons. In all of these cases, Anthropic says that it disrupted the activity in progress.
In one case, a group of Russian state-sponsored hackers identified by Microsoft as Midnight Blizzard used Claude for reconnaissance, breaching targets that included Ukrainian and other European government networks, and stole data and maintained access. Cybercriminal group ShinyHunters used Claude in practically every stage of its hacking and extortion campaigns. Disinformation campaigns focusing on politics everywhere from Kenya to Bangladesh used the tool. And perhaps most disturbingly, in a handful of cases, Anthropic discovered what appeared to be users of its tools attempting to develop potential bioweapons like disease pathogens and toxins.
While Anthropic touts its success in the report in heading off these threats—while implicitly humblebragging at the power of its tools—the effect of the case studies is more unnerving than reassuring. After all, there’s no guarantee Anthropic has spotted every malevolent use of its AI. Factor in its competitors and less safeguarded open-source AI tools, and the report reads like less of a victory lap for AI’s guardrails than a preview of AI-enabled chaos to come.
US Feds Disrupt Xinbi Guarantee, the Internet’s Biggest Black Market
Xinbi Guarantee, over its four-year lifespan, grew into the biggest illicit marketplace on the internet. It carried out an estimated $30 billion–plus in sales, most of which took the form of money laundering for “pig butchering” crypto scam operations—largely based in Southeast Asia—but which also included sex trafficking and harassment for hire. All of it thrived on the Telegram messaging service, which shut down Xinbi a year ago only for it to rebuild and eventually grow larger than ever. This week, finally, the US government stepped in to do what Telegram did not, seizing the Xinbi’s channels on Telegram’s platform and sanctioning the market. The Justice Department simultaneously announced raids on 13 scam compounds in Madagascar—a sign that Western law enforcement is beginning to take seriously the epidemic of forced labor crypto scamming, but also evidence of how widely the operations have spread.
Conti Ransomware Gang Member Sentenced to 4 Years in Prison
The ransomware gang Conti was, until it officially disbanded in 2022, one of the most dangerous hacker crews in the world. According to US law enforcement, it hit more than a thousand victims, extorting millions and at one point disrupting government systems in Costa Rica so completely that it triggered a state of emergency. Now one member of that group is facing justice: 44-year-old Ukrainian Oleksii Oleksiyovych Lytvynenko was sentenced to four years in prison this week, in a rare example of a ransomware actor who will see the inside of a US prison.
Meta Left AI-Generated Child Abuse Videos Online After Reporters Flagged Them
Facebook is hosting a large network of accounts uploading AI-generated videos that depict violence against children, according to Futurism, which spent days cataloging the material and kept finding more than it could count. The clips show young children being beaten, burned, confined, and starved. Many attract thousands of reactions from users who appear to think the footage is real. Futurism said it found most of the accounts by opening one and then following Facebook’s recommendation feed, which supplied a continuous stream of similar videos—a sign Meta’s own systems can already identify the category of content the company says it bans.
Futurism reported eight of the accounts through the standard user channel. Meta removed two, one of them after first rejecting the report. Several decisions took more than a week. The company deleted most of the videos sent to its press office, but initially left others up, including one showing a child locked in a freezer.
In addition to blanket bans on child sexual abuse material, Meta’s written policy bars depictions of nonsexual child abuse whether real or synthetic, with exceptions for art, cartoons, movies, and games. It does not say whether AI-generated video falls under those exceptions. In a statement, Meta told the reporters that some flagged links did not break its rules and asked them not to write otherwise.

A number of Russian agents operating from Mykolaiv to Donetsk regions have been exposed in Ukraine – Prosecutor General’s Office
Kyiv • UNN
Law enforcement officers have exposed Russian agents in several regions of Ukraine. They are suspected of guiding drones, transmitting coordinates, and high treason.
Over the past month, Ukrainian law enforcement officers have exposed a number of individuals suspected of treason, working for Russian intelligence services, and collaborationist activities. Among them is an artilleryman who carried out an assignment from a Russian handler for $30, the Office of the Prosecutor General reports, according to UNN.
Details
According to the OPG, from August 14 to September 10, 2026, law enforcement officers documented the activities of Russian agents in several regions of Ukraine.
In Mykolaiv region, authorities exposed a local resident who, according to the investigation, carried out assignments from a Russian handler. Law enforcement officers also exposed an artilleryman who agreed to carry out an assignment from a representative of Russia for $30. Two other residents of the region have already been convicted, including for passing information about the Defense Forces to the Russians.
They directed drones and passed on the coordinates of military personnel
In Dnipropetrovsk region, the case of a man accused of directing Russian drones toward Ukrainian military personnel and HIMARS in a frontline area was submitted to court. Another person was exposed while passing the coordinates of Ukrainian military personnel in the Zaporizhzhia sector to a representative of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces.
In Donetsk region, law enforcement officers exposed agents who, according to the investigation, passed the Russians data on the location of personnel, military equipment, air defense systems, and fortifications of the Defense Forces. In addition, nine men were detained, and the guilt of nine more residents of Donetsk region and Sevastopol was established; they had voluntarily joined the Russian army and taken part in combat operations against Ukraine.
In Sumy region, a father and son were sentenced in absentia to 14 years in prison with confiscation of property. According to the prosecutor's office, in 2022 they switched to Russia's side and fought as snipers. Another employee of the Nova Kakhovka City Military Administration was sentenced to 15 years for cooperating with an FSB representative and passing information about Ukrainian military personnel.
Separately, 10 former servicemen of the Armed Forces of Ukraine were notified of suspicion; after the occupation of Crimea, they switched to Russia's side. In Odesa region, a serviceman suspected of passing the enemy the coordinates of personnel and equipment was remanded in custody without the right to bail.
In addition, in Poltava region, law enforcement officers said they had prevented a terrorist attack, the preparation of which a university student is accused of. His case has already been submitted to court.
The investigation has also been completed into the owner of zoos in Crimea, who is accused of looting the Askania-Nova nature reserve. According to the investigation's assessment, the damage caused exceeds UAH 67.3 million.

Good morning. Angela Skujins penning this Friday newsletter from the bitter Baltics, where I’ve just spent the last few days immersed in beetroot soup, battlefield tactics and the scintillating spirit of the rīdzinieki, aka Rigan people.
I’m in Latvia for the two-day Rīga Conference, which started yesterday with security and defence very much at the top of the agenda. (And the timing is curious, with today serving as the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks on the Twin Towers).
The big takeaway so far? There is perhaps no place or populace that understands the reality of Russian aggression quite like this pine-covered country. Latvia is a small but mighty nation that has endured centuries of foreign domination, from the swords of German crusaders to the boot of the Soviet Union.
In lockstep: From chats with officials to ordinary people on the street, the reality of Russian aggression bleeding out across Ukraine’s borders — a place where a full-scale invasion has raged on for more than four years — is clear. Often, I see the carmine red and white Latvian flag flapping on flagpoles next to Ukraine's yellow and blue.
But I have a Latvian grandfather who was forced to flee to Australia after World War Two due to resisting Russian fighters. I wanted to know, decades on, how Latvia and the other Baltic nations now really perceive Russian aggression, particularly off the back of increased hybrid warfare attacks.
This was what I asked none other than Kyrylo Budanov, who heads up the Office of the President of Ukraine. I managed to speak to him in the margins of the conference, and quizzed him about whether Europe is taking Kyiv’s warnings seriously when it comes to cable-cuts, arson, drones rigged with explosives, weaponised migration and more. You can read his responses here.
My editor, Maria Tadeo, was also in attendance at the conference and spoke to some heavy hitters in the margins of the talks. This includes the European Commissioner for the Economy, Valdis Dombrovskis — a former Latvian Prime Minister. (In Riga, locals told me they remember him as a stable and reliable leader during his five-year tenure).
Economic forecast: Ukraine has asked its allies to plug a €23 billion funding shortfall. According to the EU’s top money-cruncher, Brussels needs to "pin down" the precise scope of Ukraine's growing budget needs before deciding how to fill the gap.
"We obviously need to do a proper, detailed assessment, but we understand that the war continues to rage at high intensity. If anything, Russia is intensifying its attacks," Dombrovskis said. "There are still open questions."
Walking on eggshells: A conflict of another kind occupied the focus of another chat Maria had — this time with Espen Barth Eide, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Norway. She asked him about the widening gulf between Israel and its allies, exacerbated by the rise in settler violence in the occupied West Bank and sanctions by several European nations and Canada.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar has previously said support for Gaza and Palestine is a prize for Hamas and a reward for terrorism. “It is absolutely not true that this in any way is a reward for terrorism,” Oslo’s top diplomat said when asked by Maria for a response to those comments, while referring to recently announced measures.
“This is a strong signal of support for all those Palestinians who want to have a decent Palestinian state… These are the people who reject violence. The Palestinian authority has nothing to do with Hamas, who is actually their enemy, and this is support to the moderate Palestinians.”
While I have been in Riga, my colleagues have been holding down the fort in Brussels. But the big conversations seemingly haven't strayed too far from the frontline. My colleague Vincenzo Genovese reports that more than 100 Members of the European Parliament have called on EU leaders to reopen talks on using Russia’s frozen assets to support Ukraine in response to that aforementioned shortfall.
Break the bank: Meanwhile, work continues under the already approved €90 billion loan to prop up Ukraine’s defences and budgetary needs, according to Jorge.
The European Commission is expected to announce today the allocation of an additional €6 billion in military aid for Ukraine, including €3.2 billion for the purchase of US-made Patriots interceptors, which the country badly needs to repel Russia’s ballistic missiles.
Lunch for 28: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will today have lunch with the bloc’s true powerbrokers: the 27 ambassadors who represent the member states in Brussels.
The meeting, scheduled to begin at noon, will allow envoys to sense the Commission president’s top priorities for the working year, expected to be laid bare next week at the State of the European Union speech.
Yesterday, she confirmed that social media restrictions for children will feature prominently in her address. But ambassadors shouldn’t hold their breath, Jorge reports. Von der Leyen is known for keeping her cards close to her chest and enforcing the no-spoilers rule with an iron fist.
NATO allies successfully thwart Russian undersea cable sabotage operation
Allies from the 31 North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) have caught Russian submarines training to carry out undersea cable sabotage using a secret weapon that leaves no trace.
According to reporting by Reuters, citing two Western officials, the undercover Russian operation was carried out by the country's highly secret undersea warfare directorate in Arctic waters near Norway's Svalbard archipelago.

U.S. Army tests robotic machine gun against drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
10:27:27 UTC
19:27:27 KST

- Allen Control Systems demonstrated its autonomous Bullfrog machine gun system against drone targets at Yuma Proving Ground, Arizona, on September 9, 2026.
- The Austin-based company has raised $200 million in Series B funding at a $2.2 billion valuation, and Bullfrog is already used by the Army and Navy.
An autonomous machine gun system engaged drone targets in the Arizona desert, according to official photos from a U.S. military exercise.
The system, called Bullfrog and built by Texas startup Allen Control Systems, pairs a standard M240 machine gun with a robotic turret, in this case bolted into the bed of a pickup truck.
The demonstration took place at Cibola Range, part of the Joint Experimental Range Complex at Yuma Proving Ground, Arizona, during an exercise called Falcon Peak 26.2. North American Aerospace Defense Command and U.S. Northern Command run the recurring exercise, which they describe as a counter-small drone experiment meant to test new technologies, expand what the military calls “Low Collateral Defeat” methods of bringing down drones, and give developers fast feedback to speed up work on capabilities the Department of War could use across multiple branches.
Bullfrog is built to solve a specific problem: standard machine guns can shoot down drones, but aiming one accurately at a small, fast-moving target usually requires a skilled human gunner. Allen Control Systems’ robotic mount adds computer vision and targeting software that can find, track and fire at a drone. The company’s pitch to the military is straightforward: bullets for a machine gun cost far less than the missiles most air defense systems use, so a gun that can reliably hit small drones offers a much cheaper way to counter them.
Allen Control Systems was founded in 2023 and is based in Austin, Texas, with additional offices in Alexandria, Virginia, and an innovation lab in Huntsville, Alabama. The company has grown quickly on the strength of that pitch, raising $12 million in seed funding in 2024, a $30 million Series A round in March 2025, and, most recently, a $200 million Series B round at a $2.2 billion valuation. Bullfrog is already fielded with the U.S. Army and U.S. Navy, and the company says it posted a 100 percent success rate at a Department of War test called Technology Readiness Experiment 2026 earlier this year, following earlier demonstrations at Camp Atterbury, Indiana, in 2024.
“Bullfrog provides governments with a scalable and affordable solution,” said early Mike Wior, co-founder and chief executive of Allen Control Systems, describing the system as an alternative to costly missiles and interceptors.
Allen Control Systems has said it has also received contracts through Joint Interagency Task Force 401, the Army-led organization that runs the broader Falcon Peak series of counter-drone experiments alongside NORTHCOM.

Syrian private airport plans spark outcry over mass graves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
10:25:10 UTC
19:25:10 KST

Breadcrumb
Syrian private airport plans spark outcry over mass graves, land rights
Syrian government plans to turn a former military airport in Damascus into a hub for private jets are raising alarm among rights groups and residents who say redevelopment could disturb suspected mass graves and override private land claims.
Syria's civil aviation authority said last week it was preparing to reclassify Mezzeh military airport for limited civilian use, focused on private and executive aviation, to complement Damascus International Airport, according to a report on Syria's state news agency, SANA. Rubble removal and infrastructure upgrades had already begun, the report said.
The project is emerging as a test of how Syria's new authorities balance a drive to attract investment and redevelop state assets with two unresolved legacies of Assad’s family rule: the fate of tens of thousands of missing Syrians and property rights clouded by decades of expropriation.
New documents show airport's role as execution site
Under ousted ruler Bashar al-Assad and his father Hafez, Mezzeh housed key branches of the powerful Air Force Intelligence Directorate, as well as numerous detention facilities where suspected government opponents were tortured, executed and subjected to enforced disappearance. Parts of the air base were used for presidential and other official flights.
Air Force Intelligence (AFI) documents recently obtained by the Syria Justice and Accountability Centre (SJAC), a US-based Syrian-led human rights group, and shared exclusively with Reuters, show that senior Syrian military officials approved Mezzeh in 2012 as a site for carrying out executions of detainees sentenced to death by military field courts.
One document proposed moving executions from Sednaya - the country's most notorious prison at the time - to Mezzeh because it was a "closed security compound" close to Damascus. Subsequent correspondence discussed a firing range and later a hangar beside the runway as execution sites.
The documents, which underscore the central role of Mezzeh in the Assad-era security system, show officials ordered construction of a platform at the hangar, requested nylon rope and directed that the work be carried out under AFI supervision "in utmost secrecy."
A 2025 investigation by SJAC identified two suspected grave sites linked to people who died in detention at Mezzeh, where it said more than 1,150 detainees died, some by execution and others from torture or maltreatment.
In a July 2025 letter seen by Reuters, SJAC provided Syria's National Commission for Missing Persons with the coordinates of the two suspected graves inside the airport, urging authorities to prevent construction or excavation until the sites were investigated.
The commission told SJAC at the time that there were no construction or refurbishment plans for Mezzeh, SJAC told Reuters.
SJAC wrote to the commission again on 8 September after the redevelopment plans emerged, warning that excavation, rubble removal or other works could damage human remains and evidence crucial to identifying victims, according to a second letter seen by Reuters.
SJAC told Reuters it had not yet received a response to its second letter.
Amer Matar, founder of the Syria Prisons Museum, a Germany-based NGO documenting detention facilities including those at Mezzeh, said the planned works showed a lack of respect for Syrian families who still have no answers on the fate of loved ones detained under Assad.
"To construct a business airport on a site that may contain mass graves, without a thorough prior investigation, without site protection, without searching for the missing and their remains, and without preserving evidence, is an act of extreme recklessness and disregard," Matar told Reuters.
The Syrian civil aviation authority, Syria's National Commission for Missing Persons and Syria's defence ministry, which has been operating the airport, did not respond to questions from Reuters about suspected graves and land claims.
SANA cited the civil aviation authority's spokesperson as saying that Mezzeh's refurbishment would take into account the surrounding urban area and relevant legal and social issues, but did not specifically mention the graves or land rights. It is unclear who will develop the airport.
Residents protest over land claims
The dispute over the land on which airport facilities were built is decades old.
Under the Assads, private land was regularly expropriated for government projects, often without compensation.
Mezzeh airport was built on land belonging to hundreds of private citizens across 2.76 sq km (1.1 square miles), according to land records from the Moadamiya municipality shared with Reuters.
A former municipal official, who asked not to be named, told Reuters that expropriation decrees retroactively justified the government's use of those lands when the airport was built in 1956, and that compensation had not been paid.
Residents demonstrated in Moadamiya a day after the redevelopment plans were announced. "We welcome investment, but we should be sitting at the table and discussing our share with investors, not the state," said one protest organiser, who gave his name as Abu Khaled. "We have a documented right to this land."
The dispute comes as Syria faces calls to address Assad-era property seizures.
On 2 September, United Nations land rights experts appealed to Syria's government to suspend and repeal laws they said had enabled systematic property dispossession under Assad, and to either establish mechanisms to return properties to their legitimate owners, or provide adequate compensation.

‘Aegyo’: how adults make their voices sound more childlike
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
10:25:00 UTC
19:25:00 KST

‘Aegyo’: how adults make their voices sound more childlike
Anyone who wants to appear especially cute apparently also makes their voice sound smaller. A new study involving the University of Zurich shows how adults alter their voices when using aegyo, a speaking style that is widespread in South Korea.
Aegyo refers to a deliberately childlike, playful way of speaking that adults use, particularly in romantic situations, to come across as cuter and more endearing. K-pop stars, too, frequently adopt this style of speech at the request of their fans.
But what actually makes a voice “cute”? Phonetician Volker Dellwo from the University of Zurich and Ji-eun Kim from Duksung Women’s University in South Korea have investigated this question. “I’m fundamentally interested in how people adapt their voices to different social situations, conveying not only linguistic content but also something about themselves and their relationship with the person they’re speaking to,” Dellwo told the Swiss News Agency Keystone-SDA.
For the study, 12 Korean men and women aged 25-31 read the same text once with and once without aegyo. The researchers found a striking change, as they report in the journal JASA Express Letters: when using aegyo, the voice changes acoustically in such a way that it resembles a shorter vowel tract – a characteristic that contributes to more childlike voices. Adults may thus be able to acoustically mimic a smaller vocal tract.
More
Stars of Korean boy band BTS film series in Switzerland
‘Cute voices’ in Switzerland too
Although aegyo is particularly deeply rooted in Korean culture, the phenomenon is not limited to Korea. “People across cultures alter their voices when addressing their partners romantically,” says Dellwo.
According to the researcher, there is probably no direct Swiss equivalent of aegyo. However, functional similarities can be found in terms of terms of endearment or childlike speech between partners.
“In Swiss German, one might informally refer to a ‘Jöö voice’: the voice becomes softer, more melodic or higher-pitched, and diminutive forms ending in ‘-li’ are often added,” Dellwo explains. Unlike aegyo, however, this is not a clearly defined style of speech that is so strongly codified in social and situational terms.

None of Saturday's teams were in finals contention, but pride was still on the line, and both games were genuine contests.
The matches were played under the experimental rule that allows the side conceding a try to choose whether to kick off or receive, and both games saw teams use the latter option and score shortly after.
In the day's first game, the Eels scored five second-half tries and overcame a 16-point deficit to win a thriller at Western Sydney Stadium.
After losing their opening six matches of the season, the Eels ended 2026 with four wins from their last five starts.
The Cowboys' Charlize Lloyd-Phillips got the scoring under way after just four minutes, but suffered a suspected ACL injury in the process.
Parramatta took less than three minutes to reply, strike centre Rory Owen crossing for her sixth try in four games, before former Wallaroos star Ash Marsters posted the only other try of the half to see the Cowboys up 10-6 at the break.

However, with veteran Kennedy Cherrington sin-binned, the 12-player Eels scored tries to Zali Fay and Jasmin Morrissey to get within six points.
Keilee Joseph then made it three tries in eight minutes to tie things up.
Cowboys interchange hooker Nadia Windleborn put her side back on top, before Joseph again tied the scores.
Experienced half Rachael Pearson stepped up to nail a one-pointer for Parramatta with four minutes remaining, before Owen sealed victory with a stunning 90m effort moments later.

It marked Cronulla's first back-to-back wins in 2026 following their upset of the Warriors in Auckland last week.
It took 20 minutes for the first points to be registered, Dragons front-rower Ruby-Jean Kennard-Ellis powering over from 12 metres out for the only score of an opening half littered with 15 errors.

Ellie Johnston made it three tries within 13 minutes for the Sharks, and when Dragons centre Tyra Ekepati was sin-binned for a high shot it looked like Cronulla may run away with it, but the Dragons held strong in those 10 minutes.
Shenae Ciesiolka scored a consolation try for the Dragons in her 50th NRLW appearance, but it was too little, too late.

PM Modi proposes seafarers' safety network on the opening day of Brics summit
The safety of Indian seafarers has emerged as a recurring focus of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Brics engagements. On Saturday, he proposed a seafarers emergency support network among BRICS members to provide distress alerts, medical aid, family communication and evacuation support.The proposal came on the opening day of the 18th Brics Summit in New Delhi, where the safety and wellbeing of seafarers emerged as a recurring theme in PM Modi’s remarks amid heightened tensions in West Asia and disruptions to key shipping routes.
“Seafarers make a significant contribution to global trade, but they often find themselves without adequate support during difficult times. My proposal is: Can we create a Seafarers Emergency Support Network?”, PM Modi said during his opening remarks while addressing the summit.“Through this, the Maritime Authorities and Missions of the concerned countries can be connected. It can provide support for distress alerts, medical assistance, informing families and evacuation,” he added.
Modi’s proposal follows his remarks at the Brics Business Forum on Friday, when he highlighted the importance of safe sea lanes and the protection of seafarers, particularly amid the conflict in West Asia.
“Global trade can move forward only when sea lanes are secure, supply routes remain open, and seafarers are safe. That is why India is a staunch advocate of freedom of navigation and the safety of seafarers,” PM Modi said at the forum.The issue also featured in PM Modi’s meeting with Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian on Friday. According to the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA), PM underscored the need to ensure “freedom of navigation and commerce, and the safety and well-being of seafarers” during discussions on the conflict in West Asia.The concern has a direct bearing on India, which has a large seafaring workforce and has faced casualties amid the wider regional conflict. In July, the government had said in Parliament that 16 Indian nationals, including 10 seafarers, have lost their lives in the region since the outbreak of the of the conflict, while 75 have been injured.The summit is taking place against the backdrop of continuing geopolitical and economic uncertainty, including the West Asia crisis, disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz, the Russia-Ukraine war and US trade and tariff policies. India has repeatedly stressed the importance of keeping shipping and commercial routes open.On Saturday, PM Modi also linked the maritime proposal to a wider call for Brics to translate its consensus into practical outcomes as the grouping marked two decades since its formation.“I am delighted to welcome you all to India. India’s chairship is based on a people-centric and humanity-first approach. Resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability have been our priority,” PM Modi said.
He said India had organised more than 350 meetings across nearly 30 cities during its chairship and thanked member countries for their participation.“This year's Brics summit marks a historic milestone. We are celebrating the 20th anniversary of Brics. In human life, the age of twenty heralds the beginning of a new phase of maturity and responsibility,” PM said.
“This is the stage where responsibility aligns with aspirations, and potential finds a new direction. Today, Brics, too, is at a moment of coming of age,” he added.“Now is the time for us to translate the unity and consensus within Brics into tangible outcomes on the global stage.”The summit was attended by Chinese president Xi Jinping, Russian president Vladimir Putin, Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince, South African president Cyril Ramaphosa, Egyptian president Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, Ethiopian prime minister Abiy Ahmed Ali, Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian, Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan and Indonesian president Prabowo Subianto, among other leaders and representatives.

In St. Petersburg, amid a fuel shortage, drivers are standing in queues at gas stations for hours, with some lines stretching for 2 km. Details

According to him, cars occupy an entire traffic lane, and the queue at one of the Gazprom gas stations began approximately 2 km from the station itself. Due to the large number of cars, public transportation is experiencing problems on some sections.
Gas stations are introducing limits
At the gas station mentioned by the St. Petersburg resident, there was a limit of no more than 60 liters of gasoline per vehicle. A liter of fuel cost about 73 rubles. At the same time, only 2 of the 6 pumps were operating; the reasons for this are unknown.
According to ASTRA's source, transport services are also recording violations by drivers who stop under prohibition signs because of the queues, after which they may be fined.

Revealed: the university courses students regret – and those they don’t
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
10:20:02 UTC
19:20:02 KST

Gloomy headlines might claim that a degree is less worthwhile than it once was, but one sliver of good news is that the most recent graduates don’t regret their time on campus.
When those who graduated in the summer of 2024 were surveyed 15 months later, more than eight out of 10 said they would still go to university ahead of any other option, despite a media drumbeat of pessimism about graduate jobs and increasing levels of student debt.
Matt Hiely-Rayner, an analyst who compiles the Guardian’s University Guide, says the new data supplied by the Higher Education Statistics Agency, was positive news. “Very few students say they would do something different than go to university – only about 20% of graduates say they would do something completely different.
“And the proportion who are happy with the provider they selected has stayed strong and has actually gone up slightly this year, suggesting that people were more satisfied with their choice.”
But fewer of the recent graduates appeared to be happy with their choice of subject, with just 70% saying they would stick with their original subject.
“Even that is relatively good, there hasn’t been a collapse, which is interesting because we’ve seen positive outcomes around graduate jobs continue to come down faster than in previous years,” says Hiely-Rayner. “So with hindsight, 15 months after graduation, students are more likely to regret their subject choice than they are going to university at all or which institution they went to.”
According to the latest data, the University of Bath’s graduates were happiest with their choice of institution, leaping above its rivals at Oxbridge and the Russell Group of research universities. The top five universities clustered around 90% of their graduates saying they remain happy with their choice, with just 0.8 of a percentage point separating Bath at the top from Oxford in fifth place.
But that happiness doesn’t extend to subject choices – with dissatisfaction visible even among most highly selective professional courses that offer well-paid graduate careers.
Fifteen months after graduation, fewer dentists, vets and paramedics than in the previous year said they would choose the same course, while architecture and computer science have fallen out of the top 10 in terms of course satisfaction.
The fall in computer science may be linked to the way AI has replaced entry-level jobs, as well as early career employment opportunities not being as abundant as they once were. Four years ago, 66% of computer science students went on to graduate-level employment but the latest figures show just 56% did so.
AI may also be harming the career prospects of graduates who studied animation and game design, who are now among the least enthusiastic about their career choices. Fewer than two out of three animation and game design graduates would choose the same course again, putting it in the same league as journalism, marketing and PR graduates for highest levels of regret.
The latest data also highlighted a surprising fall in satisfaction in economics, which regularly tops league tables for graduate pay and has seen a surge in interest among A-level students and university applicants.
This may reflect the fact that not all economics courses are created equal, says Hiely-Rayner. “Economics has always been quite a secure one [in terms of graduate jobs]. It seems like a safe bet, but the proportion who are getting a job varies by institution.”

Diesel in Portugal hits record high, Spain introduces new discount
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
10:19:13 UTC
19:19:13 KST

Many Portuguese already cross the border to fill up; the trend is now even clearer, as Spain's government adds a 20-cent-per-litre discount, making Spanish diesel the second cheapest in the EU.
The price of diesel is expected to rise slightly in Portugal at the start of next week, according to forecasts from the National Association of Fuel Retailers (ANAREC), while the price of petrol is set to fall. However, the increase is being offset by changes to the discount on the Petroleum Products Tax (ISP) announced by the Portuguese government on Friday evening.
The new rates unveiled on Friday effectively raise the tax on petrol by about one cent per litre, meaning the price of a litre of 95 unleaded petrol should fall by around five cents on Monday, instead of the six cents previously forecast.
The price of diesel, meanwhile, is set to continue breaking historic records. The increase in the tax discount announced by the government is very small, at only around 0.10 cents, leaving virtually unchanged the forecast rise of four cents per litre. As a result, the indicative price of a litre of diesel is expected to reach about €2.15 from this Monday, a new all-time high.
ANAREC president João Durão accuses the government of "lying" to Portuguese people when it says it is not profiting from rising fuel prices.
Spanish government introduces €0.20 discount
Speaking to journalists at a petrol station in Caminha, in Alto Minho near the Spanish border, the head of the main industry association said the government would have to take action against what he described as "fuel smuggling from Spain", where fuel is 30 to 40 cents per litre cheaper, and warned of the loss of competitiveness this is creating. He insisted that, contrary to the government's claims, the state is profiting from the rise in fuel prices, since "out of one euro spent on diesel, 60 cents are taxes" and "in Spain that is not the case", in his words.
In fact, more and more Portuguese drivers are filling up on the other side of the border. Unlike in Portugal, fuel prices in Spain are among the lowest in Europe.
That gap has widened further with the introduction of a discount of 20 cents per litre, brought in last week by Pedro Sánchez's government to counter the impact of the price rises.
Previously, seven countries had cheaper diesel and petrol than Spain, but now only Malta manages to offer even lower prices. Spain now has the second-cheapest diesel in the European Union, at €1.795 per litre. Malta has the lowest prices, followed by Spain, Bulgaria and Hungary. In the case of the Mediterranean island nation, prices have been frozen by the government since 2020 at €1.34 per litre of petrol and €1.21 per litre of diesel.
At the other end of the scale, it is in Finland that motorists pay the most for a litre of diesel (€2.477), followed by the Netherlands (€2.442), Denmark (€2.434) and Germany (€2.328).
The Middle East crisis triggered by the war launched by Israel and the US against Iran in February, and the resulting blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, has been pushing oil and fuel prices to record highs. The price of crude oil has recently risen above 100 dollars per barrel.

‘New &amp; ambitious agenda’: PM Modi proposes Brics continuity mechanism with Troika system, digital repository
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
10:16:37 UTC
19:16:37 KST

PM Modi speaks during the 18th Brics Summit, at the Bharat Mandapam, in New Delhi
NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday proposed a new implementation and continuity mechanism for Brics, anchored by a “Troika” system and a secure digital repository to track decisions, nodal points and timelines as the grouping’s annual presidencies rotate.Addressing the 18th Brics Summit in New Delhi under India’s 2026 chairship, PM Modi said a seamless follow-up mechanism was essential to maintain institutional momentum as Brics entered its third decade and began shaping an ambitious agenda for the next 20 years.
“We need to work on a new and ambitious agenda for the next 20 years. We must begin this process with our own internal working systems. While the Brics presidency rotates annually, this should not disrupt our institutional momentum. I propose the establishment of a Brics continuity and implementation mechanism,” PM Modi said.He said the proposed mechanism would allow initiatives and outcomes to be followed up through the Troika arrangement.“This would enable the follow-up of all initiatives and outcomes through the 'Troika' arrangement. We could also create a secure digital repository to record the nodal point, timeframe, and implementation status associated with every decision,” PM Modi said.
The Troika mechanism provides for coordination among the previous, current and incoming Brics chairs to ensure continuity as the presidency changes annually.The proposed system draws a parallel with the G20 Troika, under which the previous, current and incoming presidencies work together to maintain continuity in the grouping’s agenda and priorities. PM Modi’s proposal seeks to apply a similar continuity framework to Brics, alongside a digital repository to track the implementation of decisions.
PM Modi calls for time-bound global governance reforms
Alongside reforms to Brics' internal working system, PM Modi called for time-bound changes to global multilateral institutions, saying reform of the United Nations Security Council could no longer be delayed.He proposed a three-pillar framework of Representation, Responsiveness and Rule-making to guide the future roadmap for global governance and the Global South.“In formulating this roadmap, we must focus on three key aspects: Representation, Responsiveness, and Rule-making. Regarding representation, I would like to state that reform of the UN Security Council can no longer be postponed. Negotiations on this matter must be linked to a definite timeframe and clear outcomes,” PM Modi said.He also called for voting power, leadership positions and policy priorities within international financial institutions to reflect current economic realities.“Countries that drive global economic growth should also play an appropriate role in shaping global economic governance,” he said.PM Modi said developing countries continued to face an imbalance in global decision-making and proposed that Brics members jointly formulate 10 proposals for global governance reform, with the aim of finalising them as a Brics reform roadmap by the next summit.“Today, the Global South stands in the front row of global crises but in the back row of decision-making. We must transform this 'pyramid of privilege' into a 'platform of partnership'—one where every nation has a voice, every member has a stake, and the development of humanity lies at the heart of every endeavour,” he said.The Prime Minister said the existing global governance structure resembled a pyramid, with power and decision-making concentrated at the top while countries affected by those decisions remained unable to shape them.“While strengthening Brics, we must also chart a course for global reform. The current structure of global governance resembles a pyramid: power and decision-making are concentrated at the top, while the lower tiers consist of nations that are affected by these decisions yet unable to shape them,” PM Modi said.The Prime Minister said the Global South must become a “rule shaper” to deal with the challenges facing the world. He also proposed a seafarers’ network among Brics countries to ensure their safety.
Brics marks 20 years as India hosts summit
PM Modi thanked participating countries for their contribution and support during India’s Brics chairship, describing the grouping’s 20th anniversary as a historic milestone.“I express my heartfelt gratitude to all of you for your active contribution and support in making India’s Brics chairmanship a success. This year’s Brics summit marks a historic milestone. We are celebrating the 20th anniversary of Brics. In human life, the age of 20 marks the beginning of a new phase of maturity and responsibility,” he said.India is hosting the 18th Brics Summit under its 2026 chairship, with the grouping entering its third decade.The summit is expected to deliberate on protecting developing economies from the global impact of wars in Ukraine and West Asia.PM Modi also said Brics had established a distinct identity on the global stage and was “not against anyone”.The summit is being attended by leaders including Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim and Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto.Other leaders attending include Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed Ali, Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi and Vietnamese Prime Minister Le Minh Hung.
Joint statement after intensive negotiations
A joint statement is also set to be issued by Brics nations during the summit after intensive negotiations.The negotiations continued until 4 am on Saturday, with differences reported on several contentious issues. India led consultations to bridge competing positions and build consensus among members.
The statement comes against the backdrop of differing positions among Brics members, including Iran, Saudi Arabia and the UAE, on regional and geopolitical issues.India assumed the Brics chairship for 2026 under the theme “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability.”The theme focuses on strengthening existing achievements and institutional effectiveness while placing development, sustainability and innovation at the centre of the grouping’s agenda.PM Modi welcomed Brics delegates, including Xi and Putin, to Bharat Mandapam, the venue for the summit in New Delhi.Brics has emerged as a platform for cooperation among major emerging economies, with its agenda covering development, finance, technology, trade and people-to-people exchanges.

Our system is Ukrainian, European, pan-European. We call it Freyja. This is a major experiment, but a real one. Saudi Arabia shuts oil pipeline after drone attacks from Iraq
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
13:14:07 EEST
19:14:07 KST

Saudi Arabia has shut a major oil pipeline after drone attacks originating in Iraq as Houthi forces seized Yemen’s Red Sea coast, putting two routes used for Gulf energy exports under pressure. The fighting has displaced about 46,000 people in Yemen and pushed oil above $100 a barrel.
The Saudi Energy Ministry said the East-West pipeline was stopped as a precaution after several drones struck sites in the Riyadh and Medina regions. Saudi authorities reported injuries and damage.
The 1,200km pipeline carries crude from Abqaiq in eastern Saudi Arabia to Yanbu on the Red Sea. Riyadh has relied more heavily on the route during the six-month US-Iran war as tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has fallen.
Ship-tracking companies and analysts estimate that the pipeline has carried between four million and five million barrels a day in recent months, Reuters reported. That represents about 4 to 5 per cent of global oil supply.
Satellite images showed smoke near the pipeline route south of Medina following the attack.
Both Saudi Arabia and Iraq said the drones came from Iraqi territory. Baghdad condemned the strikes and dismissed the military commander responsible for operations in Maysan province, which borders Iran.
Reuters, citing two Iraqi security sources, reported that authorities also closed the Shalamcheh border crossing with Iran as a precaution and launched an operation to find those responsible.
Saudi Arabia has stopped short of military retaliation. Riyadh said it had agreed to an Iraqi request to allow Baghdad time to prevent further attacks, while reserving the right to protect Saudi territory and infrastructure.
The disruption comes as Iran-aligned Houthi forces make gains across western Yemen.
The Houthis captured Mocha and advanced along the Red Sea coast before taking Perim, also known as Mayun, an island in the Bab al-Mandab strait. Four Yemeni government sources confirmed the seizure of the island to Reuters.
The Bab al-Mandab connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and forms part of the shipping route between Asia and Europe. The Houthis said commercial navigation remained open except for Saudi vessels, which the group placed under a maritime blockade in July.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government has responded with air strikes. Government news agency Saba said forces struck Houthi vehicles, weapons and personnel near Mocha and along the Mocha-Dhubab road.
The latest Houthi offensive has killed more than 500 people, according to sources from both sides.
The UN’s International Organization for Migration said about 46,000 people had fled their homes in Taiz and Hodeidah. Some families have now been displaced for a second or third time.
About 500 Yemenis have also reached Djibouti, including women and children rescued from boats stranded without fuel, according to Djibouti’s government.
The offensive adds to a humanitarian emergency that predates the latest fighting. About 5.2 million people were already internally displaced, according to UN figures, while more than 22 million require humanitarian assistance.
UN special envoy Hans Grundberg told an emergency Security Council meeting that Yemen had entered “a new and more dangerous phase of war”.
“This renewed war should alarm us all,” Grundberg said. He said the fighting marked the end of more than four years of relative calm following the UN-brokered 2022 truce.

Ahmad Adil
12 September 2026•Update: 12 September 2026
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday called for equal participation in global rule-making as well as reform of the UN Security Council.
Delivering an opening statement at the BRICS Leaders' Summit in New Delhi, Modi said the bloc was at its "coming-of-age" moment.
“Today, the Global South is at the forefront of global crises. But it is in the back row of decision-making. We have to turn this pyramid of privilege into a platform of partnership,” he said, while addressing the two-day BRICS Leaders’ Summit in the Indian capital.
Proposing global governance reform, Modi said BRICS has to "focus on three main aspects of this roadmap (which include) representation, responsiveness, and rule-making."
"First, I would like to say that the UN Security Council reform cannot be delayed any longer," he stressed.
It is “important to ensure equal participation in deciding the global rules of the future," said the Indian prime minister.
Noting that the BRICS bloc members “respect each other's views and move forward with consensus,” Modi said, “We do not oppose anyone, but try to move forward with the thought of taking everyone along. Now is the time to turn our unity and co-operation on the global stage into strong results.”
Turning to economics, Modi said voting power, leadership positions, and policy priorities in financial institutions should be "based on today's economic realities."
"Countries that accelerate global economic growth should also play a role in guiding global economic governance," he added.
The weekend summit in New Delhi is attended by the Chinese, Russian and Iranian presidents, among others, and comes at a time when the US-Iran war has dragged on for seven months, while the Russia-Ukraine war has continued for more than four years.

Zelensky says he is ready to meet Putin at G20 summit in Miami
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
10:06:55 UTC
19:06:55 KST

Editor's Note: Read Russia's response to Zelensky's statement here.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said he is prepared to travel to the G20 summit and meet Vladimir Putin there if the Russian leader attends, he told Deutsche Welle in an interview published on Sept. 12.
The G20 leaders' summit is scheduled to take place in Miami in December.
"Yes, of course. We have to come. We have to meet, to speak and make decisions," Zelensky told DW.
"It's not about words. What I will tell him or what he wants to tell me, it doesn't matter," Zelensky added. "Results matter. That's it."
Zelensky and Putin have not met in person since before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov said Moscow had not yet discussed whether Putin would attend the G20 summit, he told the pro-Kremlin outlet Izvestia on Sept. 12.
"As for the possibility of Putin's trip, this issue has not even been discussed yet," Ushakov said, adding that preparations for the summit were continuing at the expert level.
Putin has not personally attended a G20 leaders' summit since 2019, according to DW.
Later on Sept. 12, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told reporters that Zelensky should come to Moscow if he wishes to meet directly with Putin.
Zelensky's comments come amid renewed U.S.-led efforts to bring Kyiv and Moscow back to negotiations. U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Kyiv earlier in September after talks in Moscow.
Zelensky told DW that Ukraine was now in a "good position for negotiations," arguing that Russia continues to suffer heavy battlefield losses for relatively limited territorial gains.
He also said Kyiv had discussed a possible energy and grain ceasefire with the U.S. envoys as a potential first step toward broader negotiations.
"What can bring us to any kind of negotiations? So energy and grain. This is step number one. What we can achieve," Zelensky said.
The latest U.S. diplomatic push has so far failed to produce a breakthrough. People familiar with the negotiations told the Kyiv Independent that Moscow remained unwilling to make meaningful concessions, despite revised U.S. proposals aimed at reviving talks. Zelensky said after the Kyiv meeting that he expected the war to continue into the winter.
The Kremlin has said it does not rule out renewed trilateral talks involving Ukraine, Russia, and the U.S., though no date or venue has been agreed.

US House Prepares Vote on Russia Sanctions Bill Giving Trump 100% Tariff Powers
The US House of Representatives plans to hold a vote next week on a sweeping Russia sanctions bill that recently passed the Senate with strong bipartisan support, according to Bloomberg on September 11.
The legislation would grant US President Donald Trump the authority to impose 100% tariffs on the five largest foreign buyers of Russian crude oil and natural gas, as well as the five top nations helping bypass energy restrictions.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Countries like China, India, and Turkey currently lead as the largest importers of Russian energy products.
Floor action will proceed under a standard voting procedure requiring a simple majority for passage. The measure has generated pushback among some House lawmakers who express concern over broadening executive tariff powers and triggering higher oil prices.
Despite those concerns, House leadership resolved to move forward with the bill—which maintains support from both parties and the White House—following their return from a Republican retreat.
At the same time, retail associations and the US Chamber of Commerce have voiced worry that the bill provides the White House with fresh legal grounds for expansive tariffs. In response, business coalitions drafted a letter urging congressional leaders to alter the text.
“We urge Congress to remove the tariff authority from the bill and instead focus on targeted sanctions, stepped-up enforcement against sanctions evasion, and coordinated diplomacy with nations purchasing Russian energy,” the groups stated.
The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act passed the Senate with an overwhelming 86-11 majority after more than two years of development.
However, the bill was omitted from the House’s immediate voting schedule as lawmakers returned from their summer recess, which placed the high-profile legislation at serious risk of languishing indefinitely ahead of the congressional elections.
House Republican leadership showed little momentum toward bringing the measure to the floor, while Speaker Mike Johnson remained noncommittal on whether the bill would receive a vote.

Russia Expands Ready-to-Launch Nuclear Arsenal to Highest Level in Nine Years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
10:05:51 UTC
19:05:51 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Expands Ready-to-Launch Nuclear Arsenal to Highest Level in Nine Years
Russia has expanded the number of nuclear warheads ready for deployment to 1,796, reaching its highest level in nine years, according to The Moscow Times on September 11.
Data from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) shows that Moscow has increased the quantity of nuclear warheads mounted on delivery systems for four consecutive years.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
In 2026, Russia’s total nuclear arsenal stood at 5,420 warheads.
This total includes 2,604 warheads stored in reserve, 1,020 categorized as retired and awaiting dismantlement, and 1,796 active charges mounted directly on operational missiles and heavy bombers. Moscow expanded its deployed warhead stockpile by 78 units over the past year.
In contrast, the United States maintained an unchanged inventory of 1,770 deployed warheads out of a comparable overall nuclear capacity. Other major nuclear powers kept their deployed counts stationary, with France holding 280 and the United Kingdom maintaining 170.
China increased its deployed warheads to 34, up from 24 in 2025, out of a total stockpile of 620. India placed 12 warheads into deployed status for the first time, out of an estimated total arsenal of 190.The volume of operational Russian nuclear warheads has risen every year during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Records show 1,588 deployed charges in 2022, 1,674 in 2023, 1,710 in 2024, and 1,718 in 2025. Compared to 2020 figures, the Kremlin has expanded its active delivery-ready nuclear strength by 14 percent, adding 226 warheads to achieve its highest deployment count since 2017, when the total reached 1,950.
Russian land-based nuclear forces, consisting of silo launchers and mobile missile systems, have the physical capacity to hold 1,092 warheads. Current operational deployments occupy 892 of these slots, with the remaining allocation kept in storage facilities.
Across the naval branch, 13 strategic submarines operating in the Northern and Pacific Fleets are built to carry 208 missiles and 928 warheads. However, because two submarines are currently undergoing full overhauls, the total number of naval warheads available for immediate deployment drops to 704.
An additional 586 warheads are assigned to strategic bombers. This figure remains below the maximum potential load of 650 warheads that Russian heavy aviation can carry.
Analysts noted that only a portion of the bomber fleet is in fully operational condition, pointing out that Russian Aerospace Forces sustained operational aircraft losses following military strikes during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) dismantled Russia’s RM-48U ballistic missile and revealed that the weapon was assembled from repurposed S-300 and S-400 missile components.
Intelligence analysts discovered that the missile relied heavily on foreign electronics, including dozens of parts manufactured by companies based in the United States.
Following their technical assessment, HUR published a detailed breakdown of the missile on its War&Sanctions portal, showcasing its internal systems, electronic components, and an interactive 3D model.
