====================================================================================================

Kfar Aza’s slow return after October 7: ‘We’re rebuilding trust’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
10:05:47 UTC
19:05:47 KST

Nearly three years after the October 7 massacre, residents of Kfar Aza are beginning to return home. The key word in that sentence is "beginning."
This is not a single moment, not a day when the gates open and the entire community returns together, but a slow, cautious and sometimes painful process in which one family after another packs up its life again and tries to imagine rebuilding it in a place where everything has changed.
Many are still debating whether to return and many will not. On Sept. 1, the sound of children could once again be heard in the kibbutz. Kindergartens opened, the clinic is on the way, the resilience center is being rebuilt, a pre-military academy is already operating there and amid the returning signs of life, tractors are everywhere.
After a prolonged evacuation, spent mainly at Kibbutz Shefayim and Kibbutz Ruhama, the official return began last month. About 50 families out of roughly 300 households that lived in Kfar Aza before the war have already returned, with another one or two families arriving each week. The community hopes the pace will accelerate after the holidays.
But there is still a long way to go. About 30% to 40% of families remain undecided about whether to return at all, while 10% to 15% have said they will not return and are looking for alternatives.
The shadow of October 7 alongside every sign of life
The kibbutz estimates that about 70% of residents will return by the end of 2027. "That's a realistic target that depends on the security situation," said Sigal Moran, chairwoman of the kibbutz.
"The return process is complex. It is shaped by fears, trauma and a lack of trust. We are rebuilding the kibbutz and rebuilding trust."
Tzion Regev, the community manager, said: "We're celebrating and not celebrating. It's moving to see the kindergartens open on Sept. 1. You start seeing people walking around, there are students from the new pre-military academy, new residents are arriving, new families. Life is starting to return."
But he, too, knows there is no room yet for a full celebration. "Everything is incredibly sensitive. We're cautious about our celebrations. Many people still aren't coming back. There's uncertainty. People are still deciding."
That may be the most striking thing about Kfar Aza these days: Alongside every sign of life, the shadow of October 7 remains.
According to an IDF investigation, about 250 terrorists invaded the kibbutz that morning. For the first two hours, 14 members of the local security team fought them alone. Half were killed.
The terrorists breached the fence, and among the first to enter the kibbutz were attackers who arrived on paragliders.
ynet photographer and kibbutz member Roy Idan, who documented the invasion in those first minutes, was murdered along with his wife, Smadar, and their daughter Abigail was kidnapped.
Now, nearly three years later, people are returning to the place where it all happened. The most powerful symbol in the kibbutz of that catastrophic failure is the devastated "Young Generation" neighborhood, where 11 residents were murdered and seven were abducted, including captivity survivors Gali and Ziv Berman and Emily Damari, who strongly opposed demolishing the homes.
In a vote among kibbutz members, residents decided to clear the neighborhood and move several buildings to a memorial site outside the kibbutz.
Several bereaved families who oppose the evacuation petitioned the Supreme Court sitting as the High Court of Justice. Until the court rules, the kibbutz decided to reroute the entrance to the neighborhood outside the community and erect a fence that will separate and conceal it from the rest of the kibbutz.
'We wanted to stop feeling like our lives were temporary'
Viki and Nadav Nasi Tzantzifer arrived in Kfar Aza only in September 2022. They wanted to leave Ashkelon and move somewhere more rural, and with the help of Nadav's cousin, a kibbutz member, they found an apartment.
Within a year, they already felt at home and described it as nothing short of a dream year.
On October 7, Viki was six months pregnant with Guy, who is now almost 3.
On the morning of the massacre, they were at home. The sirens caught them, like everyone else. They entered the safe room and remained there for hours.
Gunfire, shouting and exchanges of fire could be heard outside. The safe room's exterior wall carried the sounds of shooting directly to them, and at one point Nadav saw a cell of terrorists outside the house.
They sat on the floor in darkness and silence, without food or water, and a laundry basket became a makeshift toilet.
Then came the moment that frightened Viki most: She stopped feeling the baby move.
"It was very frightening," she said. "Every so often I felt short of breath and had some anxiety. It came and went. At one point I stopped feeling the baby's movements, and then I started to panic."
Nadav also remembers the fear. "There was a very real fear that she would give birth right then. It's an extreme situation. You don't know how you'll react or how the body will react. The terrorists reached the entrance to the house."
They were evacuated from the kibbutz close to midnight.
Then began a journey that seemed endless: a month in Shefayim, nearly a year in Tel Aviv, a month at Viki's parents' home in Ashkelon, then Ruhama.
Including their move back to Kfar Aza three weeks ago, they lived in five different places in less than three years.
"The dream was to walk with the stroller along the kibbutz paths, not through the streets of Tel Aviv or Yarkon Park."
They even expanded their family while living in Ruhama. Viki became pregnant with their second child, but their desire to return to Kfar Aza only grew stronger.
"It was clear to us that we wanted to return," she said. "There were important things we needed in place to make that possible, like an education system. The rest mattered less."
For Nadav, returning was also an attempt to escape the sense of limbo that had been imposed on them.
"It was a complicated period. It's a new place, we're carrying everything that happened in the kibbutz and trying to understand what is happening to us, and suddenly a new member joins the family.
"Today we understand how important it is to have a community surrounding you. We had a very strong desire to return to the kibbutz and get out of that feeling of 'temporariness' in Ruhama. They were wonderful hosts, but we wanted to go home."
Their original house, however, was no longer an option. After several attempts to enter it, they realized they would never be able to live there again.
"We went into the safe room and I told Nadav there was no chance, that I couldn't do it," Viki said.
They found another apartment to rent and decided to start over somewhere else within the same place.
On Aug. 21, they returned to Kfar Aza. The kibbutz they found was completely different from the one they had left.
"The kibbutz looks like a construction site today. Everything is torn up, and some of that keeps that day present," Nadav said.
Still, amid the ruins and construction work, he feels he has come home. "With all the difficulty — and there is difficulty — it's good for us here. We want to raise our children here."
The war beyond the fence can still be heard. Sometimes it brings the memories back with it. But now there is also a community around them.
"We see friends who have also returned walking along the kibbutz paths, because now there's one area where people can move around. It's complicated, but we're dealing with it. I'm glad to be among the first to return to the kibbutz, and it gives me a sense of pride," Nadav said.
Viki feels the return is also a kind of repair. "There's an element here of deciding for yourself what you do with yourself and your family. There's also a feeling of rebuilding and of being able to help shape the place."
For Guy, meanwhile, the rehabilitation effort is mainly one enormous show of tractors and excavators. "He's thrilled," she said.
Both know the Kfar Aza they will live in will be different from the one they knew. But for them, that is not necessarily bad news.
"It will be good here, and we hope it will be even better," they said. "It will be different, that's for sure, but different in a good way."
The couple are expecting another child in October.
'People are moved to tears seeing the kindergarten operating'
And then there are the children. If there is one sign that Kfar Aza is truly beginning to come back to life, it can be found along the kibbutz paths leading to kindergarten.
Einat Hemias Bons, 54, a kibbutz member, has been a special education teacher for 20 years.
When she realized the kindergartens were about to reopen in Kfar Aza, she took unpaid leave from the Education Ministry and decided not only to return home, but also to run the kindergarten.
"I felt this was what I needed to do right now," she said. "I told myself, I'm doing it. Mainly to give those returning a sense of security, so there would be someone from the kibbutz with experience and they could at least feel calm about that."
She moved from Ruhama, where the community had been evacuated, back to Kfar Aza at the end of August.
Alongside boxes in her new home, she also prepared the kindergarten.
On Sept. 1, 10 children entered it, with several more expected to join after the holidays. One of them is Guy, Viki and Nadav's son.
On October 7, Einat was at home in the kibbutz with her eldest son, Ofek. "Luckily, he had been playing on the computer until late and decided to sleep here instead of going back to his apartment in the 'Young Generation' neighborhood," she said. "His neighbors were murdered."
Her former partner, Yaron, tried to reach Kfar Aza. On the way, he evacuated wounded people and the bodies of partygoers who had fled the Nova festival. He later entered the kibbutz and fought terrorists in the "Young Generation" neighborhood. He was shot twice in the chest and critically wounded.
During those hours, Einat and her son were in the safe room. Terrorists took positions on the roof of her home and a gunbattle later erupted. The terrorists were killed, but Einat and her son were not evacuated until nighttime.
"I remember walking toward the entrance to the kibbutz. We called it the 'death march.' We walked on foot and crouched down because we were afraid of gunfire. There were bodies of terrorists along the way. From there, they took us to the gas station at the entrance."
In Shefayim, the family gradually began to understand the scale of the disaster — who had been killed, who had been abducted and who had survived.
Einat stayed there for a year, then moved to Ruhama. But for her, the question of whether she would return to Kfar Aza was never really open. The only question was when.
When she decided to take over the kindergarten, she realized she could not do it from Ruhama. "I told myself I wasn't going to live in Ruhama and run the kindergarten here. I need to live here and set an example."
But returning has not been easy. Her neighbors have not returned, and many of them lost loved ones. "I still don't walk around the kibbutz. I drive from home to the kindergarten and back. It's still hard for me to walk around," she said.
"When a few more people return, it will be easier. For now, the children and the work fill me up. It's simply happiness. I'm tired from the work, but they fill me up. That's what occupies me and helps me, because I'm busy with good, positive things."
When she sees children heading to kindergarten and walking along the kibbutz paths, she sees something larger than the start of another school year.
"People are moved to tears seeing the kindergarten operating, seeing children on the paths after three years. To me, the children coming to kindergarten are the revival. They are the foundation of the kibbutz."
Moran, the kibbutz chairwoman, said of the reopening of the kindergarten and daycare center: "It's not a rational step because most of the community is still in Ruhama, but it creates movement in the kibbutz and it's symbolic."
'The dream is on hold — but home is home'
Sharona Kessler, 60, and her husband Alon arrived in Kfar Aza in 2020. During the massacre, they were in Haifa, but their daughter and two grandchildren were in the kibbutz, in the heart of an area where heavy fighting took place.
From afar, she tried to understand what was happening and help her family while Alon, an IDF colonel, was called up for reserve duty.
"It was an insane feeling of helplessness." The family moved from place to place. First they evacuated themselves to Shoham, then to Shefayim, Tzukey Arsuf and Rishpon.
Four different apartments, with a family of 10 trying each time to turn a temporary place into a home. "We moved around as a tribe. Good people opened their hearts to us," she said.
But at some point even the best hospitality could not replace the feeling of home. "We were tired of another temporary house. We wanted to take responsibility for our lives and decided we were going back to Kfar Aza."
In October 2024, while most of the community moved to Ruhama, Sharona and Alon returned to Kfar Aza. They knew they would be almost alone, that they were pioneers. They knew the place was still far from ready.
Even so, they chose to return. "We fully accepted that we'd be pretty much alone here. We understood that this was what the moment required," Kessler said. "We told our daughters, 'We're part of the community' — active, involved grandparents."
Sharona, an interior designer by profession, did not only return to live in Kfar Aza. She is also working on its rehabilitation.
The kibbutz workshop she operated during the evacuation moved with her from Shefayim to Ruhama. Later, she began helping with renovation and planning projects, and today she works on the rehabilitation and infrastructure team.
Among other things, she is involved in renovating the building for veteran members, known as "the Vatican," and developing a building that will become a welfare and treatment center for the community.
"For me, it meant getting under the stretcher and working for the community. Nothing feels normal, but because both Alon and I are part of the rehabilitation and the team working here to bring the kibbutz back to what it was and make it even better, it's actually very rewarding to live here too.
"Every little patch of grass that's planted, every path that's poured — I see it and I'm part of it. We're walking through powdery dirt and dust, but we can see the progress."
She knows some people prefer to return only when everything is ready. To her, that is also a legitimate choice. "It's important to me that people take a deep breath and feel: Here I am, I'm home."
Her and Alon's dream was to live in Kfar Aza as an extended family, with their children and grandchildren around them. For now, that dream remains distant.
One daughter will return, but another, whose children experienced October 7 in the kibbutz, still cannot bring herself to come back.
"Right now that dream is on hold, or maybe it won't happen at all. We'll continue to be involved grandparents even if they don't live nearby."
'We just need quiet in Gaza — everything depends on that'
As noted, the return to Kfar Aza is unfolding alongside a debate over what the kibbutz should look like after the disaster. For now, the kibbutz has decided not to take any irreversible steps regarding the "Young Generation" neighborhood.
"Until the High Court ruling, we're not touching anything and we're not doing anything irreversible. We didn't receive an injunction or anything like that, but we decided to respect the process. We're planning, but for now we're waiting patiently for final decisions," community manager Regev said.
Outside the kibbutz, construction of a visitors center is moving ahead, while tours for the general public inside the kibbutz have already been canceled. The sense of security is still far from taken for granted.
Kites that recently crossed in from the Gaza Strip and were found in the border communities caused anxiety among residents.
The community is working with an expert to rebuild its emergency system and operational procedures for the local emergency response team.
Soldiers stationed in the area give some residents a sense of security, but the larger question remains unresolved: Will it be possible to live here again without the constant fear that history could repeat itself?
"We have no control over the security situation," Moran said. "A return to the border conditions that existed before October 7, Hamas rebuilding its strength — these are things that influence people's decisions about whether to return."
Regev, the community manager, is optimistic. "I see the future kibbutz as a large community. We were 950 people, but obviously we're not starting again from the same point. There are people who were murdered, there are people who won't return, but the young people's neighborhood will be full and the kindergartens will be full. "We just need quiet in Gaza. Everything depends on that."
Moran wants to highlight the community's demand that the state provide solutions for those who are unable to return to the kibbutz. "We are working to ensure that the state fulfills its duty to those who still don't know how to return, and we need to help those who have to rebuild their lives."
With elections approaching, Kfar Aza residents say they hope for change. Nadav said he "hopes things will be better." Viki said change is essential.
Sharona wants leadership that will see the residents of the Gaza border communities and restore their trust.
Einat, who prefers not to discuss politics, put it simply: "Anyone who was here on October 7 needs to hand over the keys and go home. That's how we'll regain our trust."
Kfar Aza is still far from what it once was. There are homes that will no longer stand, families that will not return, memories that will not disappear and questions with no answers.
But after nearly three years in which home existed mainly as a memory, the sounds of life are beginning to be heard there again.

Taiwan flags Russian film screening for being part of China’s ‘new militarism’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – Kinmen's Animal and Plant Disease Control Center said Friday that spray drones are reducing fire ants in the region.
Fire ants are said to have migrated to Taiwan in freight containers. They have been sighted feeding on crops in regions like Taoyuan and Chiayi, causing huge economic losses for decades.
The center sprays bait over fire ant mounds two to four times a year. It has accelerated the effort by flying more drones this year.
The center conducted drone sprays at Lieyu Township in May and has since expanded to Jinning in June and Jinsha in September. Spraying is typically scheduled after dawn, at temperatures between 21 and 38 C on sunny days, as ants dislike wet bait.
The center said spraying does have its limits. It said that patrolling populated areas is what's leading to fewer fire ants. It said that the county still needs to coordinate district offices for frequent patrols at busy venues like Otter Park.
Director Fan Te-cheng (樊德正) said the initiative began in 2024, when the Ministry of Agriculture's Animal and Plant Health Agency and National Fire Ant Prevention Center met with Kinmen officials to discuss drone deployment.
Fan said that with agency support, trial runs saw immediate effect, as drones can reach areas inaccessible to field agents, with precise and controlled spraying at predetermined locations. He said the entire county has adopted the tactical measure ever since.
Fan said Kinmen also encourages residents to actively participate. He noted the center has invited experts such as Prevention Center Chief Lai Hung-kuan (賴鴻寬) for seminars and hands-on training.
Regarding wildlife conservation, Kinmen’s two artificial wetlands were invaded by fire ants, which drove away the sea otters there. The county said outdoor cameras spotted otters returning after six months of spraying in cooperation with conservation groups.
Fan said the plan was proven effective as the otters gradually returned in droves. He said the measure extended to the county itself, prioritizing more populous settlements.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan Coast Guard vessels will fire Hsiung Feng-series anti-ship missiles during a joint precision munitions exercise next week to test their ability to rapidly convert from peacetime law enforcement ships into wartime combat platforms.
The exercise will test a capability already demonstrated during the Han Kuang military exercises in August, when an Anping-class patrol ship underwent the conversion after arriving at a naval port, per Liberty Times. The process, from installing missile launchers to having a Navy weapons team board and deploy from port, can be completed within several hours, according to military sources.
Vessels from this class can be configured to carry up to 16 subsonic Hsiung Feng II or supersonic Hsiung Feng III anti-ship missiles, giving Taiwan an additional mobile coastal strike capability. The capability is intended to strengthen the military's deterrence and flexibility in littoral operations.
The vessels were built with space reserved on the aft deck for missile launchers, Liberty Times reported. Removable protective panels cover the area during peacetime, allowing the vessels to operate without missiles.
When a wartime conversion order is issued, a Coast Guard vessel can sail to a designated naval port, where personnel remove the protective panels and use heavy-duty cranes to install preassembled missile launcher modules. The launchers are secured to reserved mounts, and their signal cables are connected to interfaces built into the vessel.
Instead of replacing crews, the conversion lets the Coast Guard keep operating the ship while the Navy handles the missiles, according to Liberty Times. The Navy sends a weapons team of about four to six personnel, including a fire-control officer, operators, and communications specialists, to operate the missile-control system and receive target coordinates from military command networks.

The EU listed him in 2022 as a pro-Kremlin oligarch close to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
France picks up a demand Bratislava has carried for years
Paris has called for the delisting of Usmanov, an Uzbek-born multi-billionaire under EU sanctions since the full-scale invasion in 2022, four EU diplomats told Euronews. His money came out of metals and mining and later out of telecoms and tech holdings. Usmanov denies being close to the Kremlin. Forbes ranks him 10th among Russia's wealthiest people this year, at $14.5 billion.
One diplomat, speaking anonymously because of the sensitivity of the discussions, said the request raised questions about the motive and that it "seems mostly economic reasons at play here." All four diplomats described huge frustration among other member states, against the background of Russia's widening hybrid attacks in Europe, among them the explosive-laden drone found beside a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig airport. A French official said Paris supports renewing the sanctions but would not discuss the negotiations.
Slovakia holds out for two names
Bratislava has pushed for years to remove both Usmanov and a second Russian oligarch, Mikhail Fridman, and it repeated the demand when the sanctions were last extended in March. Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico's government has threatened to block EU decisions on Ukraine before, and it halted all military aid to Kyiv in January. It has opposed the rollover across several ambassadors' meetings and wants the six-month review cycle kept.
Paris pitched the move as a political trade-off, wagering that Bratislava would stand by both of its delisting demands this time instead of dropping them as it did at the last renewal, Euronews reported.
EU lawmakers renew push to seize frozen Russian assets as Ukraine faces its toughest winter yet with a €23 billion defense funding gap
What runs out on 15 September
The deadline falls on 15 September. The listings at stake cover around 2,600 people and companies by the Council's own count, while Euronews puts the whole regime at more than 3,000, from arms-industry firms to individuals the bloc blames for sustaining the war against Ukraine. Individual listings have run in six-month blocks, and a 12-month cycle is now under discussion. The bloc's economic measures switched to annual renewals over the summer, and a July package added 218 names. Renewal requires unanimity, so one capital can let everything lapse. Ambassadors return to it on Monday.
How the last delisting in Usmanov's family was arranged
Recordings of a 2024 call, published this spring, showed Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov asking Hungary's then-foreign minister, Péter Szijjártó, to help remove Usmanov's sister, Gulbahor Ismailova, from the list. The Hungarian minister replied that his country and Slovakia were submitting a delisting proposal together. Ismailova came off the list in March 2025.

====================================================================================================

3D-printed food: from niche technology to a potential future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
10:02:21 UTC
19:02:21 KST

3D printers can now transform more than two dozen types of food into edible shapes. While the technology remains costly and impractical for everyday use, experts see significant potential in clinics, care homes and personalised nutrition.
3D printers have long since moved beyond producing plastic parts. Increasingly, they are also being used to print food: instead of plastic filament, the machines extrude soft ingredients such as chocolate, cheese or plant-based meat alternatives through a nozzle, building them up layer by layer. The desired shape must first be designed on a computer.
Several manufacturers are already established in the market, including the Ukrainian-Bulgarian company Chocola3D, the Spanish provider Natural Machines and the German firm Print2Taste. So far, the technology has mainly been used in niche applications, from patisseries to hospitals, while a breakthrough into everyday life has yet to materialise.
Printer can process more than 26 materials
According to the manufacturer, Chocola3D has been in development since 2014, with the company itself founded a few years later. The company says customers are now using the device in Ukraine, Bulgaria, Germany and Estonia. Users fill refillable syringes with pastes such as chocolate, cheese, meat, vegetables or pea protein. In total, the system is said to work with more than 26 different materials.
Unlike devices that use closed capsule systems, the Chocola3D does not tie users to specific refills. However, users have to determine the appropriate printing settings themselves. Depending on the manufacturer, food printers can cost anywhere from a few hundred to several thousand euros.
The shape of the food is designed digitally
Food technologist Mario Jekle from the University of Hohenheim is researching the technology independently of individual manufacturers. The individual steps are familiar from any kitchen, he explains in an interview with Euronews: “We first produce a fine paste, for example. This paste is then shaped, which is exactly what you do at home with a piping bag when making fine pastries. Then everything is heated, just as it would be at home in an oven or a pan.”
What is new above all, he says, is the digital preparation: “Bringing everything together, and above all the digital design.” The shape of the final product must first be created digitally.
Confectioners are already using the technology to make marzipan figures for wedding cakes. According to Jekle, its potential lies above all in customised products or small production runs of up to around 200 items. The bigger challenge comes after printing: the material has to be deposited in liquid form but must then become firm enough to be eaten with a knife and fork. This can be achieved by heating it in an oven or in a heated printing chamber.
Printing a plant-based steak at home could take just 15 minutes
Jekle also describes what using a food printer in everyday life could look like. Someone wanting to print a plant-based steak alternative would simply send the design to the printer, with the process taking between five and 15 minutes. The digital templates could come “either from databases, from an app, or from the specifications of the cartridge.”
For Jekle, the key advantage lies in the precise control of ingredients through a kind of modular building-block system. A printed meat alternative could, for example, have a significantly higher fibre content “than conventional meat, which contains no dietary fibre in the first place”.
He estimates that widespread household use is still at least five to ten years away, and there is currently no supply chain for refill packs. Jekle also believes it is important to use raw materials that require as little processing as possible. His team works, for example, with by-products from the food and agricultural industries – residual streams that are generated as part of conventional production – and uses 3D printing to turn them into new foods.
The less a raw material needs to be processed beforehand, the less energy is required – a benefit, Jekle says, for both the environment and consumers’ budgets.
Applications in medicine and care
The technology is most advanced in areas where small quantities need to be dosed precisely. As reported by the German newspaper Tagesspiegel, a team at the University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf is testing raspberry-flavoured chewable tablets in the shape of hearts and stars, designed to make it easier for children with cancer to take their medication during chemotherapy. Many children struggle with the taste or size of conventional tablets, says senior physician Beate Winkler. The hospital is also conducting trials of individually dosed medication for patients with Parkinson’s disease.
3D-printed food could also help older people who have difficulty chewing or swallowing. Nutrition scientist Dorothee Volkert from Friedrich-Alexander University Erlangen-Nuremberg investigated whether 3D printing could restore familiar shapes to puréed food – for example, creating a sausage-shaped dish that retains the appearance of the original despite its puréed consistency. The response was positive, and participants also consumed more energy and protein than before, as additional protein and fat can be incorporated into the food.
Meat from the 3D printer: many consumers remain sceptical
A representative Bitkom survey (source in German) of 1,004 people aged 16 and over, conducted in 2025, shows how open people in Germany are to the idea of printed food.
At present, 24 percent of people in Germany can imagine eating cultivated meat produced using a 3D printer, up from 13 percent six years ago. Cultivated meat is grown from animal cells in a bioreactor and given a meat-like structure using the printer.
Openness is greatest among younger people: around one third of those aged 16 to 49 would consider eating it, compared with 18 percent of 50- to 64-year-olds and 14 percent of those aged 65 and over.
Margareta Maier from Bitkom explains: “The process makes it possible to give products an appearance and texture similar to conventional meat, while having a significantly smaller ecological footprint.”
Price remains an obstacle: only 7 percent would be willing to pay more for 3D-printed meat than for conventional meat, and 17 percent regard it generally as a luxury product. Maier attributes this to the high purchase costs and the specialised ingredients: “That is why these products are not yet suitable for the mass market and are currently used mainly in catering and the food industry.”
How advanced is the technology?
Researcher Mario Jekle stresses that 3D-printed food is not intended to replace conventional food production: “We have no vision of replacing half of food production with this in the future. That is a utopia – and a misguided one at that.”
He sees the technology as particularly useful for people who do not have time to cook and for groups with specific nutritional needs, such as patients in hospitals or residents of care homes: “In effect, it gives us a way of producing food specifically for these smaller, clearly defined groups, containing exactly what they need.”
Another advantage, according to Jekle, is the potential to reduce food waste, as portions could be tailored more precisely to individual needs. A plant-based salmon alternative made using a 3D printer is already available in a major supermarket chain.
However, it will still be some time before food printers become common household appliances. As with 3D-printed houses, the technology is already viable for specific applications, but there is still a long way to go before it becomes part of everyday life.

Having multiple partners does not compromise sexual health, large study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
10:00:42 UTC
19:00:42 KST

A recent study published in Journal of Social and Personal Relationships provides evidence that engaging in multiple romantic or sexual relationships does not compromise sexual health. Across two large datasets, researchers found that people in non-monogamous relationships, whether through mutual consent or secrecy, tended to report sexual functioning, satisfaction, and health outcomes that were comparable to, and in some cases slightly better than, those of people in strictly monogamous relationships.
Consensual non-monogamy involves partners mutually agreeing to allow outside romantic or sexual relationships, such as in polyamory or swinging. Infidelity, by contrast, involves engaging in outside relationships secretly and without a partner’s consent.
It is a common assumption that monogamy is inherently safer and more satisfying, but prior work paints a different picture. A study covered by PsyPost in 2016 found that more than one in five single American adults have engaged in consensual non-monogamy at some point. Following this demographic realization, research has sought to understand how these relationship structures operate. For instance, a 2015 study found that people in mutually agreed-upon open relationships were just as likely to practice safe sex and had similar rates of sexually transmitted infections compared to monogamous couples.
Expanding on that, a 2012 study indicated that people who cheat on their partners tend to be less likely to practice safer sex than those in openly non-monogamous relationships. In terms of sexual satisfaction, a 2019 study suggested that polyamorous individuals often experience higher levels of passion and eroticism with secondary partners than with their primary partners.
The current study builds on this progression by testing whether sexual functioning, desire, and the risk of sexually transmitted infections actually differ across relationship types. By strictly distinguishing between consensual non-monogamy and secret infidelity, the researchers used both targeted and large representative population datasets to answer this question.
The research was led by Michelle Larva-Ruhala, a doctoral researcher at the University of Turku’s INVEST Research Flagship Centre in Finland, who aimed to capture a comprehensive picture of how managing multiple partners influences sexual wellbeing.
“We addressed two gaps in research on [consensual non-monogamy],” Larva-Ruhala told PsyPost. “Firstly, we know from previous research that [consensually non-monogamous] relationships are similar to monogamous relationships in relationship quality and sexual satisfaction, but sexual functioning among people with multiple partners has not been studied outside the context of infidelity.”
“Second, the presumption has been that the transparent, negotiated, ‘ethical’ nature of (consensual) non-monogamy is what leads to these better outcomes and sets it apart from infidelity, which we associate with lower quality, conflict, etc.,” she continued. “So, in a nutshell, we wanted to know if having other partners had any ‘spillover effects’ into the bedroom, and whether the consensual vs. non-consensual nature of the non-monogamy had anything to do with it.”
The researchers utilized a two-study approach. In the first study, the team analyzed data from 888 adults recruited through an online survey across multiple countries, including the United States, Portugal, Italy, and Finland. Participants reported their relationship identity as either monogamous or consensually non-monogamous, which included categories like polyamory and open relationships. They also answered questions about how often their interactions with others felt like infidelity or involved keeping sexual and emotional secrets from their primary partner.
To measure sexual functioning, the survey used validated questionnaires assessing domains like desire, arousal, lubrication, and satisfaction for women, and erection, ejaculation, and satisfaction for men. Participants with multiple partners completed these measures for up to two partners. The survey also asked about participants’ history of testing for and being diagnosed with sexually transmitted infections.
The results of the first study showed that sexual functioning was largely similar between monogamous and non-monogamous individuals. However, partner-specific differences emerged. Women with multiple partners reported greater sexual desire, arousal, and satisfaction with their non-primary partners compared to their primary partners, and their scores with non-primary partners were also higher than the scores reported by single-partnered women.
These findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2019, which found that polyamorous individuals report greater eroticism with secondary partners, suggesting they may diversify how their sexual needs are fulfilled across different relationships. Among men, sexual functioning did not differ by relationship type or between partners.
When looking at sexual health practices, polyamorous individuals were 3.6 times more likely to have ever been tested for a sexually transmitted infection compared to monogamous individuals. Despite this higher rate of testing and having more partners, the prevalence of sexually transmitted infection diagnoses did not differ between the two groups.
For the most part, infidelity was not linked to worse sexual functioning. There was one exception: men who reported keeping emotional attachments and sexual encounters secret from their primary partner tended to report lower sexual satisfaction in that primary relationship.
“We were surprised by the finding that infidelity was not associated with worse outcomes,” Larva-Ruhala noted. “Both studies suggest that, on average, having multiple concurrent partners isn’t necessarily tied to poorer sexual health, whether through consensual or non-consensual non-monogamy.”
The second study expanded the investigation to a population level, utilizing a pooled dataset of 10,503 participants from Finland. This dataset combined responses from genetic and behavioral research projects. Participants self-reported their relationship structure and completed broad measures of sexual wellbeing.
For women, this included overall sexual desire and functioning. For men, the researchers assessed premature ejaculatory symptoms, meaning how well they could control ejaculation. The study also measured general dyadic desire, which is the level of sexual interest a person feels toward an attractive partner.
To ensure fair comparisons between the small fraction of non-monogamous individuals and the large monogamous majority, the researchers statistically matched participants on factors like age, gender, and sociosexual orientation, a measure of how willing a person is to engage in uncommitted sex. They also controlled for whether the couples lived together and the gender of their partners.
This approach provided a unique advantage over previous work. “The method used in Study 2 is important for the current research on [consensual non-monogamy],” Larva-Ruhala explained. “Most studies… use data collected from online surveys that people in [consensually non-monogamous] relationships opt into, which is partly necessary in order to obtain a big enough pool of participants to conduct the analyses we want to do, but it also means heavy selection-bias.”
“People who are generally happy in their relationships and interested in representing their relationship configuration may be more quick to participate in these surveys,” she added. “However, study 2 used data from population-representative samples in studies not focused on [consensual non-monogamy], so we can assume people all across the board completed the survey, lowering some of that bias. It improves the generalizability of the results.”
In this population-based sample, non-monogamous men reported fewer early ejaculatory symptoms than monogamous men. Non-monogamous women reported higher global sexual desire than monogamous women. Both men and women in non-monogamous relationships reported slightly greater dyadic desire.
Again, when the researchers specifically isolated the effects of infidelity, defined here as cheating or having partners who were unaware and non-consenting, they found no effect on these sexual health outcomes. This broader lack of negative effects aligns with a major review covered by PsyPost earlier this year, which found that consensually non-monogamous individuals report levels of relationship and sexual satisfaction that are statistically indistinguishable from those of monogamous couples.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The studies relied entirely on self-reported measures of sexual functioning and health, which can sometimes differ from objective physiological indicators or medical records. People might misremember their history of sexually transmitted infections or bias their answers to appear in a more favorable light.
Additionally, the first study grouped some participants under the broad umbrella of non-monogamy without distinguishing the specific agreements they had with their partners, such as whether they cohabitate or adhere to strict relationship hierarchies. The measure of infidelity in the second study also combined current and past cheating, meaning some participants may have reconciled with their partners long ago, potentially diluting the measurable impact of the infidelity on current sexual health. Future research could benefit from tracking couples over time to see how relationship structures and sexual health influence each other as relationship agreements evolve.
“Just because we didn’t find many differences in sexual health between those who cheat and those who practice ‘ethical’ forms of non-monogamy, doesn’t mean that doing one or the other is of no consequence,” Larva-Ruhala emphasized. “The results certainly don’t condone infidelity. They simply show that people can maintain sexual health under both versions of non-monogamy.”
To build on these findings, the research team hopes to see this work expanded. “We need replication research to validate or contradict these findings with further evidence, preferably in population-based samples from other countries,” she said.
The study, “Sexual Health in Monogamous and Non-Monogamous Relationships: Evidence From Convenience and Population-Based Samples,” was authored by Michelle A. Larva, David L. Rodrigues, Annika Gunst, Patrick Jern, Sabina Nickull, Marie-Pier Larose, Markus J. Rantala, and Justin K. Mogilski.

London Underground workers exposed to asbestos without protective masks, documents reveal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
10:00:32 UTC
19:00:32 KST

Hundreds of London Underground workers could have been exposed to asbestos for almost 20 years without protection required under safety regulations, according to documents seen by the Guardian.
Under 2002 rules on controlling asbestos and other hazardous materials, employers are required to take a series of precautions, including ensuring exposed workers are given individually fitted face masks to prevent inhalation of toxic dust.
Emails and minutes of meetings reveal that London Underground managers admitted that face-fitted masks were not issued to staff until as late as 2020.
The documents suggest Transport for London (TfL), the public body responsible for London Underground, is at risk of more expensive legal claims after already paying out more than £7m in asbestos-related compensation and legal fees.
The documents were disclosed as part of an employment tribunal hearing brought by a former London Underground cleaner, Micky Steeds, who successfully claimed he was unfairly dismissed after raising concerns about exposure to asbestos and other toxic dust.
In one set of minutes, a manager said he had no recollection or record of face-fitted masks being issued in 2018 to the team responsible for cleaning dust from vents, which included asbestos-sheathed cables. He said such masks were not introduced to London Underground’s civils teams, responsible for all the tube buildings, until late 2020.
In December 2020, another manager who was head of lifts and escalators said: “A lot of people aren’t face-fitted,” adding: “Staff shouldn’t have worked without face fit, but it has happened.”
He blamed the failure on a lack of training.
In 2019, an email from a third manager said allowing Steeds to carry on working without a face-fitted mask was oversight that would be rectified in future. In a 2023 email, a fourth manager admitted that asbestos dust fibre sampling, which is also required under the law, was not conducted.
TfL has recorded more than 20,000 asbestos-containing materials across its network, according to data released under freedom of information to Confront Power – an investigative newsletter on industrial harms.
TfL insists it has controls in place to manage the risk of asbestos exposure to its staff and the public. In an email in December 2022, a senior engineer responsible for hazardous materials said test results showed levels were “below the relevant workplace exposure limits for both respirable and inhalable dust”. But he said dust being cleaned contained “traces of asbestos fibre occasionally”.
But Steeds and one of his former colleagues point out that tests were not conducted while the asbestos was being cleaned and disturbed.
And minutes of meetings between staff and a manager also revealed issues with damaged asbestos, which is more dangerous. One experienced cleaner said he encountered asbestos on cables 90% of the time and sometimes: “Broken chunks of asbestos or cable shearing.”
Asked what he did when he found asbestos, he said: “We would just carry on and use common sense … don’t bash cables and do what you can.”
Catriona Ratcliffe, a solicitor from the personal injury team at LeighDay, said: “Where the asbestos materials are damaged or in poor condition, the risk of exposure is higher because there is more opportunity for the fibres to be released into the atmosphere.”
Earlier this year Ratcliffe secured a six-figure settlement from TfL for a former inspector who was diagnosed with sarcomatoid mesothelioma 27 years after supervising the removal of asbestos from the Northern Line.
She said the documents in Steeds’ case could result in more injury claims. She added: “If someone is exposed to asbestos over many years, even at low levels, that is going to put that person at risk. And if the employer had knowledge of the risk of exposure, that could result in a legal claim if they have not taken the precautions required under regulations.
“Under the control of asbestos regulations [if exposure to asbestos is unavoidable] employers should be giving workers full protection including face-fitted respiratory masks to reduce that risk as far as possible.”
Steeds, who was not fitted with a proper mask for 15 months, said: “Over the years, TfL must have put the health of hundreds of workers at risk by failing in their legal duty to provide fitted masks. It makes me so angry that even when I told them about it, they ignored my concerns and tried to cover it up. The incompetent managers who allowed this to happen now have serious questions to answer.”
Rob Donnan, a former LU cleaner who is appealing against an employment tribunal’s rejection of his claim for unfair dismissal, said he worked without a fitted mask for three years. He estimated that up to 80 cleaners in the vents department alone were not fitted with masks between 2002 and 2020 and that a further 300 staff in the escalator department were similarly unprotected.
A TfL spokesperson said: “We have strict controls in place, in line with the government’s control of asbestos regulations, which ensure customers and staff are not at risk from exposure to asbestos when travelling or working on the tube network. Our specialist teams monitor and manage locations where asbestos has been found to ensure the safety of everyone travelling or working on the network.”
They added that, as TfL was appealing against Steeds’ successful tribunal ruling, it was unable to comment further.

Tensions simmer on US-Canada border for two towns relying on each other
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
10:00:31 UTC
19:00:31 KST

Like many Canadians, Tom Reid isn’t crossing the US-Canada border as often these days. But he needed a haircut.
The woman who cuts his hair lives in International Falls, Minnesota – her “sister is married to my wife’s cousin”, he explained – and so Reid, whose duty free shop in Fort Frances, Ontario, has to travel to her.
That’s how it goes for the residents of the two towns, divided by the Rainy River and an international border. They’re longtime friends and, in many cases, family. People cross the border frequently to shop, dine, go bowling, take their kids to sports and visit each other.
But Trump’s trade war against the US’s northern neighbor, and his derogatory comments about their country, has Canadians – known for their politeness – angry. Furious, actually. They’re shopping less at US businesses, and, in an unusual show of patriotism, encouraging consumers to “buy Canadian instead”.
Reid is buying Canadian more and more, he said at the register in his shop, with the Canadian flag on the wall behind him. “I don’t have that much choice, eh?” he said.
American business owners have seen declines in Canadian sales, while grappling with the uncertainty and costs associated with tariffs on their products. With tourist season winding down, and the leaves starting to change into yellows and oranges, the two towns are quieter.
Canada’s retaliatory tariffs went into force this week, though no one who lived in the towns had seen that directly reflected in prices yet. It was the latest heated battle between the two countries in the last nearly two years.
The mayors of the two towns call each other friends, and signed a joint declaration in 2025 affirming that friendship after Trump retook the White House. The flags of Minnesota, Ontario, both towns, and both countries fly outside the town offices in Fort Frances. But there’s only so much – and really, nothing – that a local official can do to blunt the economic effects of slipshod tariffs put in place by one man, more than a thousand miles away in Washington.
Hoping for the best
Most Canadians recognize this, according to Andrew Hallikas, the mayor of Fort Frances. They like Americans, and Fort Frances residents can relate to Minnesotans a lot: they share similar interests, in the outdoors and in community, he said. But they’re “irate” at Trump – for bullying their country, for going against an ally – and for suggesting Canada should become the 51st US state.
“You cannot imagine how angry that makes us,” Hallikas said. “Please quote me on this. I cannot make this clear enough: we will never become the 51st state. We consider ourselves to probably be the best country in the world in which to live, and we’re quite content to remain that way, thank you very much.”
For two towns that rely on each other, the tension of the trade war simmers underneath the surface. They all want it to end. They don’t know how, or when, it will.
As the Guardian interviewed the mayor of International Falls at a coffee shop on the town’s main drag, a Fort Frances resident interjected angrily to tell the mayor that Canadians are “so pissed off” at Trump for how he’s attacked their country and that International Falls needed Canadians to survive. Their town was suffering, and their businesses losing longtime customers from Canada, because of it, he said.
“I’m originally from the Falls, but I’m an American living in Canada,” the man said. “I’m scared to put that American flag on my shirt, what he’s done.”
Residents, and the leaders of the towns, are worried about how they will rebuild the relationship between their two countries if this continues for much longer. Businesses will find other suppliers. Shoppers will replace their favorites with homegrown options. The sense of nationalism hardens.
“We just hope for the best at this point,” said the International Falls mayor, Drake Dill.
Grant Hauschild, a Democratic Minnesota state senator who represents 65% of the state’s border with Canada, said he’s heard from businesses that have lost up to 30% of their revenue from Canadians. With people already struggling with inflation and high costs, he said a hit like that goes from “a concern to devastation”.
“My hope is, of course, that the relationship goes back to normal once we pass these chaotic times,” Hauschild said. “I think that’s what really scares me most … Even if people want to go back to the way things were, they might have unfortunately kind of moved on – and moved beyond – the relationship.”
Two towns, one community
To cross the Rainy River into either side, people use a toll bridge, with the cost for an average car now $10. They present documents to customs agents on whichever side they’re entering, and answer questions about their purpose in town. People who cross regularly recognize the agents and ask after their families.
The main parts of each respective town sit on either side of the crossing, with both towns initially growing around paper mills. Fort Frances’ mill has since closed; International Falls’ is still running. Fort Frances is larger than International Falls, and because Canada is more sparse, Fort Frances serves as a regional hub. Its hospital will soon be getting an MRI machine – a huge boon for its aging population.
The shops on either side carry gifts from both countries, catering to tourists who fly in to fish, mostly for walleye, and largely on the Canadian side. In a Fort Frances store, kids books called “Little Minnesota” and “Little Canada” sat right beside each other on a shelf. In International Falls, shelves of souvenir cups carried designs for International Falls and Canada.
While Canadian flags line the shop windows and fly throughout downtown Fort Frances, Hallikas said this is not a reflection of increased patriotism, but just a border town welcoming visitors to their country. The two towns are “neighbors by geography, but we are friends by choice”, he said.
“The bridge is over 100 years old, and we’ve been going back and forth it for over 100 years,” Hallikas said. “Before that, there was a ferry. But our friendship is still going to exist when Trump is long gone.”
Dill, the International Falls mayor, owned a business and lived in Canada for 11 years. Many of his friends are Canadian. This fall, he will go up to an island in Canada to meet up with friends.
“There’s no politics in that. There’s no thought of exchange rate, or trade war, or tariffs. It’s just – we’re friends,” he said. “But then you come home and you talk and you watch the news. … I would be really disappointed if it gets to a point where we can’t work through it, and there’s a fundamental change that will hurt International Falls significantly.”
Residents on both sides have favorite products they grab whenever they cross. For Heather Johnson, executive director of the Fort Frances chamber of commerce, it’s Top the Tater, an iconic Minnesota chive and onion dip. She also checks prices on cheeses, and peruses the wider variety of pastas for sale in US stores. Johnson bowls weekly in a league in International Falls, made up of both Americans and Canadians.
Leanne Guba, a Canadian who owns Hometown Hobby and Crafts in International Falls, crosses back into her home country once or twice a month, usually walking across the bridge, to buy ketchup chips, chocolate bars and Dad’s brand oatmeal chocolate chip cookies.
American liquor is no longer on the shelves at government-run Ontario liquor stores, by order of Premier Doug Ford. The push to buy Canadian is “pretty well elbows-up”, Johnson said. “I’m drinking Canadian red wine now.”
‘Mr T took care of that’
Reid, the duty-free shop owner, said the tourist season was about average for him, with no noticeable decline in sales. He has seen some change in his customers.
A couple of years ago, they’d come in with the signature red Maga (Make America Great Again) hats. Last year, not as many. This year, he didn’t see any red hats, and customers would tell him they didn’t vote for Trump. They’ll ask about the missing American bourbon from his shelves, and he’ll tell them, “Mr T took care of that”.
He used to cross the border to go to a show, or the grocery store, or Menard’s, a hardware store, but not anymore. His daughter and her husband used to cross weekly for a date night and shopping, but no longer. People over here are “really upset” with Trump, he said. It has renewed his sense of Canadian pride, but “I’ve always had good pride”.
Johnson, whose kids are now grown, said: “I’m glad that my kids grew up knowing both countries, and they know that there really isn’t a difference in people.”
Across the border in International Falls, craft store owner Guba said she was seeing fewer Canadians, for several reasons. They’re dealing with rising costs, too, and the exchange rate is unfavorable. Some of it is politics, she said. Canadian regulars are coming less frequently.
“They’re definitely being a little more picky about when they come over or being more careful about what they buy,” she said.
The decline, while dealing with unpredictable tariffs on goods she brings in from overseas, has had an impact on her business. She’s adapted by seeking out new suppliers, bringing in new merchandise lines, and trying to reduce costs. She has a few companies she orders from in Canada – including a toy brand and a puzzle company – and expects the new tariffs will likely increase costs on those products.
People are upset about the political dynamics, but they don’t tend to vent their political frustrations openly, she said. There may be the odd joke here and there, but not usually full-blown political debate. “We tend to try to stay friendly,” she said.
The latest tourist season was “decent”, she said. “Overall, we’re still surviving … You can’t really control it.”
‘We remain neutral’
It’s tough to gauge the full impact of declining Canadian spending in the border town, though anecdotally, people are noticing it. The International Halls chamber of ommerce wouldn’t comment on the impact of the tariffs, or deteriorating relationship between the two countries, on the town.
“We remain neutral on political matters so that we can best serve our diverse membership, which includes individuals and organizations with a wide range of views. Because of that, the Chamber does not have an official comment on the political issues surrounding the US-Canada relationship,” the chamber said in an email.
Isaac Johnson, who owns the Coffee Landing café in International Falls and lives above it with his wife, said he still sees a lot of Canadians who come over to grab espresso and breakfast. He loves his Canadian customers, including the couple he watched meet up at the coffee shop from across the border. They later married.
The locals are caught in the middle of political games, said Johnson, who tries to just focus on himself, his family, and his faith. But people do get emotional about it at times, and “if you definitely bring up politics, for sure,” he said – just as the man who confronted Dill, the mayor, did.
The man, who didn’t share his name or want to have a longer conversation with a reporter, said he’s noticed far fewer Canadians around town, nothing like it used to be. He described Canadians as “very pissed off” and said snowbirds were selling their houses in the US. International Falls voters went for Trump in 2024.
These broader issues, like the trade war, “pit us against each other”, Johnson said, noting that the man got mad at the mayor “over a guy that’s making billions off us all”.
“I love the Canadians, I love Americans, and I love them coming over here and enjoying what we have here, and we can go and enjoy what they have,” Johnson said.
Dill, the town’s mayor, said Canadians are “definitely” not coming to International Falls as much as they were, though he thinks it has more to do with the exchange rate. Still, he said later, “we need all the Canadian commerce we can get, and I would like to think they feel the same way”.
Local officials are in a tough position. They have no control over the tariffs, though with their communities at the center of the impact, they are expected to answer questions and concerns over levies. They have no direct line to the Trump administration, if that would even make a difference. And their communities are suffering.
Hope springs eternal
Hauschild, the Minnesota state senator, said he meets regularly with the Canadian consulate in St Paul, and reiterates his belief in a strong relationship with Canada. But as a state lawmaker, he has little to no control over any of it, beyond using his bully pulpit.
Hallikas, the Fort Frances mayor, said most Canadians have “no rancor for individual Americans” and treat them kindly when they visit, largely avoiding talking about Trump or American politics. Americans will have to work to undo the damage Trump has done to the relationship between the two countries, and that will take time, even after the trade war simmers down or ends, he said.
“But we’ll still be friends with the folks in Minnesota and International Falls,” Hallikas said.
Dill said he doesn’t often run into the frustrations directed at him by the man in the coffee shop, though it happens. He doesn’t have any way he can directly fix the issue.
“The US elected our current president and he has his own agenda and I don’t see that I can stop it,” he said. “I don’t want it to affect us locally. We’ll see. Hope springs eternal. I mean, I thought that everything was going along fine, but apparently it wasn’t.”
The uncertainty of it all is “frustrating”, and he’s most curious about where it all lands, when a truce could be signed so that businesses can have a sense of comfort in planning for their futures. The two countries are engaged in a heated dispute – or a “donnybrook,” as they would say in Canada, noted Dill.
He likened the current situation to two longtime best friends, who hunted and fished and vacationed together for years – until one of them said, you’ve been taking advantage of me for years.
“That’s like driving a nail in a fence,” he said, “and then you pull it out, and even if the fence still stands, there’s a hole where the nail was.”

‘We can see into the other room’: insurers face surge in subsidence claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
10:00:30 UTC
19:00:30 KST

“We’ve got one wall with an absolutely huge diagonal crack, through which we can see through to the other room; you could easily put your fingers in it and chunks of plaster are falling off,” says Henry Biggs, 49, from Stroud in Gloucestershire.
He and his partner started noticing cracks in their family home in June 2025, a few months after buying it, and filed an insurance claim for subsidence that was accepted by their insurer, Admiral, in the spring. Monitoring devices were only recently fitted, about a year after they first submitted the claim, and they have no idea when the damage might start to be repaired.
They are among a growing number of UK homeowners who face subsidence after two record-hot summers. August was the joint-hottest month ever recorded around the world. Signs of subsidence include widening and lengthening diagonal cracks, typically around window and door frames, as well as sloping floors, and sticking doors and windows.
Millions of homes are at risk of subsidence because of the worsening climate crisis, the British Geological Survey has warned. Under its worst-case scenario, 11% of UK homes could be at risk of subsidence by 2070, more than 4.2 million houses.
As hotter, drier summers and warmer, wetter winters become more frequent, the ground under houses can shrink and drag down a property’s foundations. Older properties with shallow foundations are more at risk, and those built on clay-rich soils. The most vulnerable areas include London, Essex, Kent and a tranche of land from Oxford up to the Wash on England’s east coast, according to scientists.
Insurers have experienced a rise in claims for subsidence in recent months. Hastings says it had record subsidence claims in August, up 140% on last August. So far in 2026, its claims are up by 30% year on year. Axa, one of the biggest home insurers, has talked of a “surge year” for subsidence, and Aviva is reviewing its reserves and pricing models.
During this year’s heatwaves the damage at Biggs’s house, which was built in 1970, worsened progressively. “There are cracks now throughout the house, diagonal cracks around almost every window, windows are getting harder to open and close, and the door lintels have dropped, so we have doors now that won’t close,” he says. “In the main part of the house, the kitchen, dining room, the hallway, the floor is dropping and cracking because it’s just falling away in the middle.”
He adds: “It’s quite upsetting when you’ve just bought your first home, and we can’t even decorate at the moment.” The couple have hired their own loss assessor as subsidence claims tend to be complex and lengthy, often lasting several years.
The average subsidence claim in the UK hit a record £20,000 between April and June, more than £2,000 higher than a year earlier, according to the Association of British Insurers (ABI). Insurers paid out £72m for domestic subsidence claims, compared with £60m in the same period last year.
Timothy Farewell, a geospatial environmental data scientist, whose company MapleSky advises 20 insurers, as well as water companies, on ground movement, says: “We have seen widespread drying of soils across the UK in 2018, 2022, 2025 and 2026 leading to an uptick in the number of cracking houses, bursting water mains and failing roads.”
It is all about “differential movement”, he says. “You can imagine if your house, road or pipe is built across two different soil types, with one soil more shrinkable than the other, then this differential movement is when you get significant problems, with one part moving more than the other. And differential movement could also happen when you have a tree on one side of the house that is drying out (and shrinking) the soil more on one side of the house than the other.”
As old water pipes are more vulnerable than houses to ground movement, summer failures on the water network can indicate that the subsidence risk is increasing in that region. While fewer houses are built on peat-rich soils, movement in these soils has a considerable impact on rural roads and pipe networks, Farewell adds.
Shaune Worrall, the deputy head of insurance of the British Insurance Brokers’ Association, has warned of a “double surge” of claims, as many subsidence claims from last year are still being processed.
As well as environmental conditions, modern housing layouts can affect the risk, he says. Open-plan extensions, larger kitchens and interconnected living areas can mean that extensive structural repairs are needed.
Subsidence excess is usually much higher than for other perils, and a figure of more than £1,000 has become common. This sum could rise to £10,000 for a property that has had subsidence in the past, despite underpinning works.
Melissa, who works in the arts and has two children, says she and her husband “reluctantly” lodged an insurance claim for subsidence last month. While the cause of the extensive cracks in their 1901 home in Walthamstow, north London, is still to be determined, the couple felt they had no choice.
“When we came back from holiday towards the end of August, our cracks had got a lot worse, in a short period of time. In some parts, wider than 1cm that you can fit a pencil in. Our front door was also sticking such that we could barely open or close it.”
Structural engineers have still not been round to look at the damage, with long delays due to the general surge in insurance claims. Repair schedules will also be affected, with insurers stating months before remediation. Melissa says she has been warned that even if it turns out not to be subsidence, once a subsidence claim is lodged, “that will potentially affect your ability to get future insurance with other providers and will likely drive up your premiums”.
Several homeowners told the Guardian that they might not make an insurance claim for subsidence because they worry about rising premiums, or not being able to get insurance cover in future.
Rachel Hogarth Smith, 58, a recently retired headteacher, says she has been “quite stressed” about subsidence at her late Victorian/Edwardian house. She has held off from making an insurance claim after her insurer warned her about the potential repercussions. She has been advised by a structural engineer to wait until the spring before doing any repair work, while an olive tree near the house should be removed because it sucks moisture from the ground, exacerbating the situation.
“I’m now not opening any of the windows in the bay window because they’re sticking a bit and I don’t want to be in a position where I can’t get them closed again,” she says. “There’s a small gap between the skirting board and the floorboards underneath the bay so you can see daylight in between them.” If the subsidence remedial works end up costing a lot more than hoped, she may file an insurance claim after all.
Modern homes are considered less vulnerable, but Richard Smith, the head of standards, innovation and research at the National House Building Council, says it is reviewing whether changes should be made to its standards.
Subsidence claims can be costly and complex, but underpinning or other remedial work should resolve the issues.
Sarah Dodd, founder of the law firm Tree Law, says: “In around 25 years working with tree-related subsidence cases [that led to legal disputes], I can recall fewer than 10 cases where significant subsidence has recurred following underpinning.”

A symbol of harmony: Chinese scientists discover earliest dragon-phoenix pairing in ancient tomb
Unknown

A symbol of harmony: Chinese scientists discover earliest dragon-phoenix pairing in ancient tomb
The two mythological creatures represent the peaceful balance created when opposing forces come into union
It sometimes guards kingdoms and empires; other times, it hoards treasures within a hidden cave. The dragon frequently symbolises power, strength, and good fortune. In contrast, its counterpart, the phoenix, meets its end in a pile of ashes only to be reborn at the pinnacle of its beauty, symbolising grace, beauty, and rebirth.
Individually, the dragon and phoenix are iconic figures in Chinese mythology. Together, these contrasting creatures embody a yin-and-yang that serves as an important emblem of harmony in Chinese history.
At its height, the dragon-and-phoenix image functioned as the state emblem of the Republic of China from 1913 to 1928, appearing on coins minted during that period. It was ultimately replaced when the Kuomintang came to power under Chiang Kai-shek.
However, the dual imagery of the dragon and phoenix reaches much further back in Chinese history, nearly to the dawn of China itself.
In mid-August, a group of scientists unveiled the discovery of the oldest known pairing of the dragon and phoenix, dating back about 4,300 years.
According to the Global Times, the symbols were positioned as clay statues about the size of a human body, placed beside the deceased in a grave located in Inner Mongolia, northern China.
