EXPLAINER – What is Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline, and what its ‘precautionary' shutdown means?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
08:20:12 UTC
17:20:12 KST

Saudi Arabia’s shutdown of its vital East-West oil pipeline following drone strikes has brought renewed attention to its role in carrying crude from the kingdom’s eastern oil-producing region to the Red Sea while bypassing the Strait of Hormuz.
The Saudi Energy Ministry said Friday that the pipeline had been targeted Thursday morning by several drones in the Riyadh and Medina regions, prompting authorities to halt its operation as a precaution.
An official ministry source, cited by the Saudi Press Agency (SPA), said emergency and technical teams had begun securing the pipeline and checking its safety, adding that any further developments would be announced as they became available.
The Saudi Foreign Ministry said the attack was carried out using several drones launched from Iraq and resulted in injuries and material damage.
The ministry did not specify the number of casualties, the extent of damage to the pipeline or its pumping stations, or how long the shutdown was expected to last.
However, the East-West pipeline’s central role in Saudi Arabia’s oil export system, particularly as shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has declined amid the current US-Iran conflict, means its suspension carries implications beyond damage to a domestic energy facility.
The East-West pipeline, also known as Petroline, is one of Saudi Arabia’s most important crude oil transportation systems.
Operated by the state energy company Aramco, it stretches approximately 1,200 kilometers (745 miles) from Abqaiq in the kingdom’s Eastern Province to Yanbu on the Red Sea coast.
The pipeline lies entirely within Saudi territory and does not cross another country’s borders.
Its strategic function, however, extends beyond domestic transportation. It carries crude from the kingdom’s main production and processing areas in the east to refineries, storage facilities and export terminals on its western coast.
This allows Saudi Arabia to move large quantities of crude to the Red Sea without shipping it through the Strait of Hormuz amid the current military conflict between the US and Iran.
The Saudi Energy Ministry said on April 12 that the East-West pipeline’s full pumping capacity stood at approximately 7 million barrels per day.
The announcement followed an earlier attack on one of its pumping stations, which Saudi authorities attributed to Iran. That strike reduced the pipeline’s capacity by around 700,000 barrels per day before the ministry announced days later that its full capacity had been restored.
In its first-quarter results for 2026, Aramco said the pipeline had been ramped up to its maximum capacity of 7 million barrels per day to support supplies and exports through Saudi Arabia’s western coast.
According to a company presentation, around 2 million barrels per day of the pipeline’s capacity is directed toward refineries on the western coast.
This means that, arithmetically, as much as 5 million barrels per day of capacity could be available for other destinations, including exports. It does not mean, however, that Saudi Arabia was necessarily exporting 5 million barrels per day through Yanbu before the shutdown.
Tanker-tracking data indicate that volumes of crude oil and condensate loaded at Yanbu remained below the pipeline’s theoretical maximum capacity.
According to Vortexa, a British company specializing in global energy-market analytics and maritime cargo tracking, Yanbu loadings rose to approximately 3.7 million barrels per day in early September, from 3.2 million barrels per day in August.
Kpler, which tracks vessels and analyzes global commodity, energy and trade flows, estimated September loadings at around 2.9 million barrels per day, up from approximately 1.5 million in August.
The difference reflects the companies’ varying tracking and calculation methodologies.
Both estimates, however, show that actual flows through the western coast remained below the East-West pipeline’s maximum capacity.
Yanbu also has several storage and loading facilities. The pipeline’s transportation capacity should therefore not be confused with the capacity of the maritime export terminals or with the volume of crude actually loaded onto tankers.
The pipeline’s strategic importance increased significantly this year as shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, previously the principal outlet for Saudi crude exports, declined sharply because of the US-Iran war.
Saudi Arabia consequently became more dependent on transporting crude overland to Yanbu before loading it onto tankers in the Red Sea.
The US Energy Information Administration has identified the East-West pipeline as one of the principal routes capable of bypassing the Strait of Hormuz during a supply disruption.
The shift toward the pipeline helped increase oil flows through the Red Sea route during the second quarter of the year as volumes of crude and other petroleum liquids moving through Hormuz fell sharply compared with the end of 2025.
The pipeline has therefore become one of Saudi Arabia’s most important tools for limiting the consequences of disruption in Hormuz and keeping part of its crude exports moving to international markets.
However, this route also faces growing risks amid escalating tensions in the Red Sea and around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The Saudi Energy Ministry’s description of the shutdown as “precautionary” means that pumping was stopped to allow the targeted sites to be secured and the pipeline, pumping stations and operating systems to undergo safety inspections.
The term does not, by itself, mean that the pipeline suffered extensive destruction or will remain out of service for a prolonged period.
The duration of the suspension will depend on the nature and location of the damage and whether the strikes affected the pipeline itself, pumping stations, power supplies, control systems or safety equipment.
For as long as the shutdown continues, however, crude cannot be transported normally through this route from eastern Saudi Arabia to the western coast.
Its impact on exports cannot be assessed simply by assuming a loss of 7 million barrels per day, since that figure represents maximum capacity rather than the amount being transported or exported when operations stopped.
The direct effect on fuel supplies in Saudi cities, including Riyadh, is also less closely connected to the pipeline.
The East-West system is not a distribution network carrying gasoline or diesel to consumers. It is a high-capacity pipeline designed primarily to transport crude oil.
Its most significant potential effect therefore concerns Saudi Arabia’s ability to deliver crude to western-coast refineries and Red Sea export terminals, as well as its capacity to use Yanbu as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.
The full consequences remained impossible to quantify as of Friday evening because the Energy Ministry had not disclosed the scale of the damage, the volume of affected pumping capacity or when operations could resume.
Following a previous attack in April, the ministry explicitly placed the temporary capacity loss at around 700,000 barrels per day before announcing the restoration of full operations.
It has so far provided no comparable estimate for the Sept. 10 attack.

Boeing KC-46A export deal ceiling jumps to $19.1 billion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
08:17:46 UTC
17:17:46 KST

- The U.S. Air Force raised the ceiling on a Boeing KC-46A Foreign Military Sales contract to $19.1 billion from $5.7 billion, without ordering new aircraft.
- The contract already covers tanker sales to Japan and Israel, with capacity added for unnamed future foreign buyers.
The U.S. Air Force just gave itself a lot more room to sell Boeing’s aerial refueling tanker overseas. In a contract modification worth $13.4 billion, the Air Force raised the ceiling on an existing Foreign Military Sales agreement for the KC-46A Pegasus tanker from $5.7 billion to $19.1 billion, more than tripling how much business can flow through that single contract.
It’s worth being clear about what this modification is not: it doesn’t order any new planes, and no money is actually changing hands with this award. What the Air Force did was simply widen the lane ahead of time, similar to a company raising the credit limit on an account before the big purchases start coming in rather than making those purchases itself. Work connected to the contract will continue through April 28, 2035, which gives some sense of how long the Air Force expects this sales pipeline to stay active.
The contract already covers KC-46A sales to two close U.S. allies, Japan and Israel, and the Air Force left the door open for what it called future country partners without naming who those might be. Raising the ceiling now means that if another country signs on later, or if Japan or Israel wants more aircraft, the Air Force can process that business under the same contract instead of starting from scratch each time.
To understand why any of this matters, it helps to know what the KC-46A actually does. Modern combat aircraft can’t fly forever on a single tank of gas, and refueling tankers exist to solve that problem, meeting fighters and bombers mid-flight and pumping fuel into them so missions can stretch on for hours longer than they otherwise could. The KC-46A is built on the frame of Boeing’s 767 commercial airliner, adapted with a boom, hoses and fuel systems, and it’s meant to eventually replace the Air Force’s KC-135 Stratotankers, some of which have been flying since the Eisenhower administration.
The KC-46A’s road into service hasn’t been smooth. Since deliveries began in 2019, the program has been dogged by a persistent problem with its Remote Vision System, essentially a set of cameras and screens that let a boom operator, sitting inside the tanker rather than lying in a rear compartment as on older tankers, watch the refueling boom connect with the aircraft behind it. When the imagery came out distorted, it made the job harder than it should have been, and there have been real incidents where the boom scraped against the aircraft it was trying to refuel. Boeing has spent years working on a fix, an upgraded system called RVS 2.0, paired with a redesigned operator’s station.
That history is directly relevant to the foreign sales covered by this contract. Japan’s Air Self-Defense Force has already bought at least four KC-46As, and a separate order placed in October covered delivery of its third and fourth aircraft for $342.1 million. Israel’s path to the tanker has been bigger still: the U.S. State Department cleared a sale of eight KC-46As to Israel valued at roughly $2.4 billion, and earlier this year a contract under this same vehicle covered four of those aircraft along with the specific engineering work needed to fit them with the upgraded RVS 2.0 camera system and its companion operator station. In other words, some of the foreign buyers are effectively helping fund the fix for a problem that has troubled the Air Force’s own fleet.
There’s also a business logic to why the Air Force wants a bigger ceiling on this particular contract rather than negotiating fresh paperwork for every future sale. Foreign military sales don’t just bring in money for Boeing; they help spread out the fixed costs of running a production line, and they tend to keep a program’s supply chain healthier over a longer stretch of years. A tanker sold to Tokyo or Tel Aviv still depends on the same parts suppliers and technicians that build tankers for the U.S. Air Force, so more foreign orders can mean a steadier drumbeat of work at Boeing’s Seattle-area facilities.
What isn’t clear yet is which countries might take advantage of the newly expanded ceiling, or how many additional tankers the extra $13.4 billion in capacity is actually meant to cover. The Air Force didn’t say, and neither figure will likely become public until a specific country’s order shows up in a future contract announcement.

Germany Moves to Block Far-Right AfD From Accessing Classified War Plans
German defense officials are considering steps to block a regional government from viewing confidential military defense plans if the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party comes to power in upcoming state elections.
In recent regional voting in Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD secured 44% of the vote, taking 39 of 83 seats in the state parliament and coming just three seats short of an outright majority, according to Bloomberg on September 10.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Defense Minister Boris Pistorius aims to ensure that a state government in Saxony-Anhalt led by the pro-Russian AfD would not be able to share sensitive operational details with Russia.
The document in question, known as OPLAN, is a 1,000-page operational blueprint created by German authorities and NATO to coordinate defense responses between federal and regional governments during a military crisis.
An insider revealed that Pistorius outlined these intentions during a closed meeting with defense policy experts from governing coalition parliamentary groups. German defense leadership operates under the assumption that OPLAN could be triggered in the event of an escalation involving Russia.
The strategy heavily relies on Germany's central geographic location, serving as a primary transit hub for NATO troops moving toward eastern positions if an alliance defense situation arises. While the full version of OPLAN is provided to the heads of all 16 German federal states, lower regional bodies are granted access only to the parts pertinent to their specific areas.
German officials have been debating options to protect sensitive military data should the far-right party take command of regional security authorities.
Proposals under discussion over recent months include removing or reclassifying specific information to limit access. Germany's domestic intelligence agency partially classifies the AfD as a threat to the nation's constitutional order.
Previously, German law enforcement agencies identified two suspects involved in an attempted FPV drone sabotage operation at Leipzig Airport. The planned attack targeted Ukrainian cargo planes on August 5, when explosive-laden drones were discovered near four An-124 transport aircraft.
Investigators determined that the operation was carried out by a native of Russia with a Latvian passport and a Belarusian citizen holding Russian citizenship. Authorities tracked the movements and phone numbers of at least four individuals using cell tower location data.
German Federal Minister of the Interior Alexander Dobrindt stated that Russia directly organized the attack, with the perpetrators acting on instructions from Russian intelligence services.

Nuclear rhetoric and threats against Lithuania

Swiss canton wants to slow spread of raccoons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
08:15:42 UTC
17:15:42 KST

Swiss canton wants to slow spread of raccoons
The canton of Aargau in northern Switzerland wants to slow down the further spread of raccoons. However, it is virtually impossible to halt the growth of the population, according to the authorities. Last year, 60 raccoons were shot or recovered as roadkill in Aargau.
Aargau, together with neighbouring canton Basel Country, lies on the “southern expansion front of the raccoon”, the cantonal government wrote on Friday in its response to an interpellation tabled by members of the Social Democrats, Swiss People’s Party, Centre Party and Greens.
To tackle the issue, the cantonal government is relying primarily on raising public awareness and on the support of the hunting community. The Neobiota specialist unit has produced an information leaflet setting out specific protective measures for residential buildings.
According to the leaflet, people should not leave food scraps or animal feed out in the open. Compost should also be covered, and access to houses via cat flaps should be prevented. Anyone who spots a raccoon should report it to the hunting authorities.
More
Cute but invasive: raccoons spotted in northwestern Switzerland
For the targeted capture of raccoons, the cantonal hunting and fisheries department provides hunting societies with 11 specially developed box traps for permanent use, as stated in the response.
A carpenter from Aargau manufactures these traps, complete with a catch basket, for around CHF800 ($980) each. The box trap design was developed by the hunting and fisheries department. As setting such traps is considered a hunting activity, their use is restricted to hunters.
Population continues to rise
According to the canton’s figures, the first raccoon was recorded in the hunting statistics ten years ago. There had previously been reports of raccoons being shot or killed in accidents in 1999 and 2001.
Since 2019, hunters have bagged raccoons every year. Last year, 60 raccoons were shot or recovered as roadkill. The response states that this trend is expected to continue.
The raccoon, which originates from North America, was brought to Germany in the 1930s for fur production and was later released into the wild. In the wild, their population has grown significantly over the past 20 years. According to experts, this adaptable, predatory omnivore poses a threat to native wildlife.

That’s all from us on the US politics blog, thanks for following along. Here is a recap of the day’s developments:
While in Ireland for a two-day visit that combined political meetings with a stop at his Doonbeg golf resort, Donald Trump said he backed Irish reunification. Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald called on Trump to apply the lessons of the Northern Ireland peace process to Palestine, urging the US to end arms sales to Israel and “stop facilitating the genocide of Palestinian people”.
The US president also weighed in on the Falkland Islands row, questioning whether Britain would be willing to defend the islands and saying he could potentially help settle the dispute between the UK and Argentina.
Trump said the war with Iran would end “very soon”, possibly after the US midterm elections in November, adding that he expected oil prices to “come tumbling down” afterwards.
When asked about the crisis engulfing the strait of Hormuz, he said: “Everything will work out fine.”
Trump ended his Dublin engagements before heading to Doonbeg, where he arrived at his golf resort for an afternoon of golf and an overnight stay, with the Irish Open taking place on the course.

On Trump’s comments on Irish unification, McDonald said they should prompt the Irish government to start preparing for a united Ireland.
Sinn Féin has long campaigned for Irish unification and supports holding a referendum on the issue when the conditions set out in the Good Friday Agreement are met. NEW DELHI: Brics countries on Saturday reached an agreement on a joint declaration that is "unlikely to name any country but will condemn unilateral war by any nation," Reuters reported on Saturday, citing four sources.The agreement came after intensive negotiations aimed at bridging differences among the grouping’s members, particularly Iran and the United Arab Emirates, which have taken opposing positions in the Gulf conflict.
The leaders of the 11-member bloc are expected to approve the declaration later on Saturday, the sources said.The development assumes significance as the Brics summit is being held amid escalating tensions in West Asia and renewed tit-for-tat strikes between the United States and Iran. The conflict followed a pause in fighting through much of August, while Iran-aligned Houthi rebels strengthened their position in the Red Sea region.Foreign policy experts had identified the wording on the Middle East crisis as a key test for the summit. A joint statement would need to accommodate the positions of both Abu Dhabi and Tehran.Although the declaration is unlikely to immediately alter the geopolitical situation, experts said it could demonstrate unity among emerging economies and opposition to economically damaging measures such as Western sanctions.
Brics foreign ministers meeting in New Delhi in May had failed to issue a joint statement because of differences between Iran and the UAE.The grouping is seeking a stronger role in shaping international rules and has called for reforms in institutions such as the World Bank, International Monetary Fund and World Trade Organization, which some members believe are dominated by Western powers.Leaders attending the summit include Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa and Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan.India, which maintains relations with the United States, Russia, Israel, Iran and the Gulf Arab states, is also seeking to deepen trade cooperation, reduce barriers and expand business opportunities among BRICS members.The Brics grouping comprises Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the United Arab Emirates. Its partner countries include Belarus, Bolivia, Cuba, Kazakhstan, Malaysia, Nigeria, Thailand, Uganda, Uzbekistan and Vietnam.
The bloc was established in 2009 and represents more than 40% of the world’s population and nearly a quarter of the global economy.India is hosting the 18th Brics Summit in New Delhi under the theme “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability.”India began its fourth Brics chairship on January 1, having previously chaired the grouping in 2012, 2016 and 2021. The year 2026 also marks 20 years since Brics was established.

U.S. Army’s top ammo supplier lands another big contract
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
08:05:06 UTC
17:05:06 KST

- The U.S. Army awarded Olin Winchester a five-year contract worth up to roughly $788.4 million for 5.56mm, 7.62mm and .50-caliber ammunition.
- Olin Winchester already operates the Army's Lake City Army Ammunition Plant, the country's main source of small-caliber military ammunition.
The U.S. Army has awarded Olin Winchester a contract worth up to roughly $788.4 million for 5.56mm, 7.62mm and .50-caliber ammunition. The five-year, indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contract combines firm-fixed-price and price-adjustment terms, runs through September 10, 2031, and was awarded without competition after only one bid was submitted.
Army Contracting Command at Rock Island Arsenal, Illinois, is managing the deal. Specific work locations and funding will be set order by order rather than fixed at signing, a common structure for ammunition contracts of this size.
In an era when so much Army procurement news involves drones, loitering munitions and counter-UAS systems, this contract is a reminder that the service still needs a basic supply of bullets. Rifles, machine guns and sniper systems in Army and Marine Corps units all depend on 5.56mm, 7.62mm and .50-caliber rounds, and none of that demand disappears as unmanned systems take on a larger share of the fight.
The award builds on Olin Winchester’s existing role as the backbone of the Army’s small-caliber ammunition supply. The company has operated and managed the Army’s Lake City Army Ammunition Plant in Independence, Missouri, since October 2020, a facility with the capacity to produce up to 1.4 billion rounds a year across the calibers this contract covers. Olin Winchester also runs its own production line in Oxford, Mississippi, which has handled past Army orders for the same three calibers.
That production capacity came under real strain earlier in the decade. Washington’s military aid to Ukraine included more than 200 million rounds of small arms ammunition drawn from U.S. stockpiles between 2021 and 2023, most of it 5.56mm and 7.62mm, pushing the Army to keep Lake City running at a high tempo to replace what had been sent overseas. Contracts like this one are part of how the Army keeps that pipeline funded years in advance rather than reordering caliber by caliber.
The ammunition covered by this contract is separate from the Army’s newer 6.8x51mm Common Cartridge, developed for the Next Generation Squad Weapons program and currently sole-sourced through Sig Sauer. That round is meant to eventually replace 5.56mm in close-combat units, but the transition is gradual, and the vast majority of the Army and Marine Corps still fire the legacy calibers this contract will keep flowing.
The Winchester name traces back to 1866, when Oliver Winchester founded the Winchester Repeating Arms Company in New Haven, Connecticut. Its Model 1873 rifle became known as “the gun that won the West,” selling more than 700,000 units. Winchester began supplying the U.S. military during World War I, and during World War II the company built more than half a million M1 Garand rifles and over 800,000 of the six million M1 carbines produced for Allied forces. Olin Corporation took over the Winchester brand in the 1930s, and the combined Olin Winchester ammunition business has supplied the U.S. military for decades since. When it took over Lake City’s operations in 2020, the company described itself as the world’s largest small-caliber ammunition manufacturer, a claim that has only grown harder to dispute given its current footprint across Army contracts.

====================================================================================================

‘Immature playground boasting’: Mathematicians uneasy at OpenAI’s latest scalp
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
08:00:28 UTC
17:00:28 KST

It was a week that left mathematicians reeling. Hot on the heels of a flurry of cases of artificial intelligence furthering the field, OpenAI declared a major scalp: its latest AI model had cracked a Millennium Prize Problem, a puzzle with a $1m reward that had defied human brains for decades.
The achievement bore little resemblance to how mathematical problems normally fall. A near-trillion dollar private company had unleashed 10,000 agents – AI systems that carry out tasks autonomously – on the problem. The bill was estimated at $15m.
The trajectory towards AI capable of superhuman maths has long been clear, but to nail such a substantial problem so swiftly sent shock waves through the field. Mathematicians are asking what will be left for them if works in progress are hoovered up and claimed by others, and how they should train the next generation when even fiendish assignments can be solved at the press of a button.
“I feel slightly shell-shocked,” said Prof Colva Roney-Dougal, the head of pure mathematics at the University of St Andrews. At a recent public lecture, she said she believed that AI was unlikely to do anything remarkable soon. “Three months later, I’m totally wrong,” she says. “We’re all just waiting to see what happens. It’s coming so fast.”
Prof David Silvester, a mathematician at the University of Manchester, said the field felt “very unstable” given the pace of change. “All the open maths problems could fall with enough resources,” he said. “This is irreversible. This is not going to change.”
Prof James Robinson, a mathematician at the University of Warwick, said hard problems were the fuel of mathematics, driving creative approaches across successive generations. “It’s frustrating to see these big tech companies burning this fuel up just so that they can show off about how great their latest model is,” he said. “It seems like immature playground boasting writ large, underpinned by billions of dollars and the potential for significant environmental damage in an age when climate change is probably the biggest challenge we face.”
One reason Silvester went into maths was the rush that comes from cracking a problem. For many mathematicians it is the weeks, months and years spent circling a problem, breaking it down, trying one approach after another, and never quitting that appeals. “Without that, the subject seems completely different to me,” Silvester said.
Mathematicians already devote considerable time to verifying each other’s proofs. It was this kind of review that found a gap in Andrew Wiles’s work on Fermat’s Last Theorem in 1993, prompting a year of further effort to fix the flaw. Silvester suspects mathematicians might find themselves poring over ever more proofs dashed out by AI. “It’s more like becoming an accountant, you’re auditing, you’re checking,” he said.
There are knock-on effects throughout the field. Mathematicians are recruited on the strength of their published papers, but problems they have been working on for months might now be solved by AI in days. “There’s a real sense of ‘I could spend the next month thinking about something and somebody else does it by pushing a button’,” says Roney-Dougal. “That’s horrible, and I think it’s going to be horrible for a few years.”
It’s also a headache for teaching undergraduates. Universities routinely set students problems and quizzes to work through at home. That kind of coursework is now dead. “There’s no point in doing it because we can’t vouch for its authenticity,” says Silvester. Lecturers are now having to tell students not to use AI for some problems, while ensuring they can use it for others: after all, AI-assisted maths is the future.
For all the upheaval, Prof Alexander Paseau, who studies the philosophy of mathematics at the University of Oxford, believes maths will not lose much of its appeal. “The challenge still remains, even if AI is eventually better than humans at research,” he said. “You’ll still want to be able to understand the mathematics yourself. And we’ll still enjoy it and appreciate its beauty: the sheer enjoyment and the beauty of a mathematical proof will always be there. AI is not going to take any of that away.”
A lot of AI maths does not solve problems from scratch, but builds on work by humans, he added. The OpenAI breakthrough, for example, relied heavily on work by the Madrid-based mathematicians Diego Córdoba and Luis Martinez-Zoroa.
OpenAI’s work described a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem which involves equations that predict how fluids, and even the weather, behave. It is one of seven Millennium Prize Problems published by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000. The company’s announcement on Tuesday has led to further concerns in the community. OpenAI set its latest model to work after hearing rumours that two Millennium Problems had been solved by mathematicians. Prof Tristan Buckmaster at New York University and Levent Alpöge at Anthropic were doing related work on Navier-Stokes and had used OpenAI’s products in the process. They suspected OpenAI’s model had learned from their work-in-progress. After an investigation, OpenAI denied this was the case.
Some mathematicians are still wary, however. “The big story now in mathematics is that nobody wants to share anything,” Buckmaster told the Guardian. “Mathematics is different today than it was only a few days ago. We have to decide what to do about that.”

A young Malagasy woman was stopped at Madagascar’s Ivato International Airport last month as she prepared to travel to China for a proposed marriage, according to local media reports citing police. She had reportedly been promised 10 million ariary (US$2,300) once she arrived and married a Chinese man.
The case led police to investigate a suspected network involved in arranging similar marriages. Four people were detained, and police reportedly recovered false stamps, documents and 10 Malagasy passports.
Investigators said several women might have already travelled to China through the network.
These arrangements are often marketed as a solution for Chinese men struggling to find a partner at home. Men are told they can travel abroad, pay a matchmaking fee and bride price, then return home with a wife.
But recent cases reported in Malawi and Madagascar show that Chinese men can face fraud, extortion and criminal investigation, while women recruited as brides can face deception, coercion and human trafficking.
Such cases have prompted warnings from Chinese embassies and raised questions about whether they are isolated incidents or part of a broader, emerging pattern.

Swiss arms industry and EU funds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

Swiss arms industry and EU funds
The Swiss government is seeking a security partnership with the European Union. But is this interest mutual?
Despite its neutrality, there has never been any doubt about Switzerland’s alignment with the West. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, it has drawn ever closer to its Western partners, including militarily – for instance, by joining the European Sky Shield Initiative and strengtheningExternal link cooperation with NATO.
Last year, the Swiss government announcedExternal link its intention to hold talks with the European Union (EU) on a security agreement. In summer 2026, the Swiss parliament gave the government a mandate to conduct exploratory talks. If these go well, parliament will then decide on a specific negotiating mandate.
What the Swiss government has in mind is a security and defence partnership. This is above all a political agreement and declaration of intent, explains Gesine Weber, an expert on security and defence at the Centre for Security Studies (CSS) at the federal technology institute ETH Zurich. “Under such partnerships, the parties agree to deepen their dialogue and cooperate more closely at a strategic level. The agreements typically also specify the various policy areas in which they wish to cooperate.”
As Weber notes in a CSS AnalysisExternal link, the EU has significantly stepped up its cooperation with non-member states in the realm of security and defence since 2022, following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. And, as the analysis shows, it is doing so relatively quickly and flexibly. Since late 2024, the EU has signed 12 such partnerships with countries as diverse as the United Kingdom, India and Ghana.
The EU has concluded defence agreements with non-EU European states such as Norway and the UK, but also with partners further afield, such as Canada and India. These are countries that the EU already cooperates with on security matters. “With such agreements, the EU aims to provide a more robust political framework for existing cooperation. A further aim is often to strengthen cooperation in the defence industry,” says Weber.
This is no minor matter. The member states are set to invest €800 billionExternal link (CHF750 billion) in EU defence by 2030.
And Switzerland wants to be in on this, too.
A chance for the Swiss defence industry
As a neutral, armed country, Switzerland has always set great store by having its own defence industry. This has also been partly financed by sales to European partners. Since the start of the Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, however, Switzerland has been in a bind, as it bans the resale of Swiss-made weaponry to countries at war. This has not only triggered a crisis of confidence among its partner states in the EU, but also led to tangible export losses, as Swiss arms have been shunned ever since.
More
Switzerland eases arms export rules as its industry is shunned by Europe
This situation has also prompted movement in Swiss politics. The country has revised its regulations governing war materiel exports, and the potential security agreement with the EU should be viewed in the same context. As Swiss Defence Minister Martin Pfister, declared in parliament this summer, such an agreement could help Switzerland participate more effectively in European defence procurement, “If we can carry out procurement in Europe together with other countries, it will make it cheaper due to economies of scale. This will also open up opportunities for our own industry, which will be able to play a role.” Pfister stated during the parliamentary debateExternal link on the issue.
Overlapping interests
But how receptive is the EU to an agreement of this kind with Switzerland? Last spring, EU spokeswoman Anita Hipper External linkannouncedExternal link that Switzerland was a potential candidate for a partnership. The European Commission is interested in partnerships that “serve the EU’s political and strategic interests and support the universal values upheld by the EU”, she said.
On the Swiss side, the focus so far has mainly been on the business aspect. This seems to sit well with the “Given Switzerland’s huge research strength, cooperation on defence industry policy would be of particular interest from the EU’s perspective. I think this is the area that Brussels is potentially looking at,” says Weber.
Switzerland is especially well-positioned in the drone sector. The defence ministry recently announcedExternal link that it would be placing a strategic focus on drones, drone defence and robotics. Universities and industry are also to play their part here.
In late September, the Swiss will vote on neutrality initiative, , which aims to insert an article into the constitution requiring a stricter practice of neutrality. Formally, this has nothing to do with defence deals. However, the text seeks to abolish sanctions, which are central for the EU above all in their dealings with Russia. The Swiss government opposes the popular initiative, which, if accepted, would likely raise the same questions in Brussels as a rejection of the Bilateral Agreements III.
Likewise, on paper, the Bilateral Agreements III – the updated set of treaties between Switzerland and the EU – have nothing to do with a potential defence agreement. But what if the Swiss electorate rejects the bilateral package? “I can hardly imagine a scenario in which, should significant tensions arise over the Bilateral Agreements, Brussels would suddenly be interested in cooperating more closely with Switzerland in other fields,” says Weber.
The referendum on the Bilateral Agreements III is expected to take place in 2027. It is likely to be even longer before any defence agreement with the EU is reached.
Edited by Benjamin von Wyl. Adapted from German by Julia Bassam/ds

A U.S. state has sued L&apos;Oréal over the alleged cancer risk from hair-straightening products

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
10:58:24 EEST
16:58:24 KST

A U.S. state has sued L'Oréal over the alleged cancer risk from hair-straightening products
Kyiv • UNN
Arizona accuses L'Oréal of concealing a possible link between hair-straightening products and ovarian and uterine cancer. The state is seeking fines and warnings.
Arizona authorities have filed a lawsuit against L'Oreal, accusing the cosmetics giant of concealing information about a possible link between hair-straightening products and the development of cancer in women. Reuters reports, UNN writes.
Details
The lawsuit was filed by Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes. The state became the first in the United States to take legal action over the alleged cancer risks of such L'Oreal products.
The company is accused of violating consumer protection laws. According to the attorney general's office, L'Oreal marketed products predominantly used by African American women without warning of the possible risk of developing ovarian and uterine cancer.
Arizona demands restrictions on product sales
The state is seeking fines and damages, as well as a court order prohibiting L'Oreal from selling the products in question without warning consumers about the possible risk of cancer.
The lawsuit also alleges that the company promoted such products among women and children for decades, using established beauty standards and social pressure on people of African descent while placing profits above consumer safety.
L'Oreal is already facing more than 12,000 similar lawsuits from women and their families. These cases have been consolidated in federal court in Chicago as part of multidistrict litigation.

U.S. Air Force funds research into orbital combat tools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
07:57:42 UTC
16:57:42 KST

- The Air Force Research Laboratory awarded BlueHalo a five-year contract worth up to nearly $100 million for a program called Leveraged Orbital Battlespace Optimization.
- Only about $1.7 million has been obligated so far, covering two initial task orders worth a combined roughly $20.2 million.
The U.S. Air Force Research Laboratory has awarded BlueHalo a contract worth up to nearly $100 million for research and development work under a program called Leveraged Orbital Battlespace Optimization. The five-year, indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contract runs through August 29, 2031, and came out of a competitive process in which BlueHalo was the only company to submit a bid.
Only a small fraction of that ceiling is funded so far. The Air Force obligated roughly $1.7 million in fiscal 2026 research and development funds at the time of the award, covering two initial task orders with a combined value of up to roughly $20.2 million. Work will be split between BlueHalo’s site in Huntsville, Alabama, and Kirtland Air Force Base in New Mexico, home to AFRL’s Space Vehicles Directorate, which is managing the contract.
The contract notice describes the work only in broad terms, as research meant to advance scientific knowledge and state-of-the-art technology for space systems. AFRL has not published a detailed public description of what the Leveraged Orbital Battlespace Optimization program is meant to produce, and neither the lab nor BlueHalo has said what the first two task orders will cover.
BlueHalo, based in Huntsville, Alabama, and Arlington, Virginia, builds systems across space superiority, directed energy, counter-drone technology, autonomy and signals intelligence. The company has a running relationship with the Air Force Research Laboratory beyond this new contract. On September 2, 2026, the Air Force added $11.2 million to a separate BlueHalo research contract called Aiman Improved Readiness, bringing that deal’s total value to $41.2 million, with work performed in Beavercreek, Ohio, near AFRL’s headquarters at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base. The Air Force has not disclosed what the Aiman Improved Readiness program is meant to develop.
BlueHalo has also built up a track record in space communications specifically. In March 2025, the company said it had successfully demonstrated a long-haul, two-terminal laser communication system built to simulate conditions across low-Earth, medium-Earth and geosynchronous orbit, advancing the technology to Technology Readiness Level 6, a designation indicating a system has been proven in a relevant environment and is ready for accelerated development. Mary Clum, president of BlueHalo’s Product & Space Systems Portfolio, said at the time that the terminals were meant to support rapid production for satellites “across all echelons of space.” When U.S. Space Force Chief of Space Operations Gen. Chance Saltzman toured BlueHalo’s Albuquerque facility in June 2024, the Air Force described the company’s focus there as improving orbital warfare, space domain awareness, resilient communications and command-and-control processes, the same general areas the new contract’s title points toward.
What remains unclear is how the new program differs from BlueHalo’s existing space work at Kirtland, and how large the eventual body of task-order work might grow within the contract’s nearly $100 million ceiling.

Commissioner of Police Joe Chow Yat-ming warned on Saturday that national security risks persisted despite the sentencing.
“The public may think that society appears peaceful after a major national security case has concluded. But as always, undercurrents are everywhere. We cannot state that there are no other risks. There are undercurrents and soft resistance,” Chow said after attending a police passing-out parade.

Feature: A guardian of the Yellow River follows it to the sea
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
15:53:58 CST
16:53:58 KST

Gechu poses for a photo in Yushu Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, northwest China's Qinghai Province, Jan. 31, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhang Long)
by Xinhua writers Wang Jinjin, Yuan Min and Ma Yunfei
XINING, Sept. 12 (Xinhua) -- Standing at the bow of a boat, Gechu spent a considerable amount of time gazing at the spot where the Yellow River meets the sea in east China.
For most of his 39 years, the herder had known the Yellow River only at its source in the highlands of Qinghai Province, northwest China. The grasslands there were his home, where he patrolled the pasture, watched over the headwaters and measured the grass with a tape measure.
Until this summer, he had never seen where the river flowed.
"My father used to say, 'The Yellow River doesn't enter the sea, and the sea doesn't enter the Yellow River,'" Gechu said.
It was an old saying among herders at the river's source, referring to the distinct boundary that can sometimes be seen where the sediment-laden Yellow River meets the clearer, saltier seawater. Differences in sediment concentration and water density can make the two bodies of water appear to remain separate before gradually mixing.
"I didn't understand," Gechu said. "They are both water. Why wouldn't they mix? Now I've seen it."
Gechu lives in the Yoigilangleb basin, deep in the Sanjiangyuan area known as China's "water tower," where the Yellow River begins its long journey across the country.
Gechu grew up there. In his late teens, he started to notice changes in the surrounding landscape. The grass grew shorter and the water shallower. A river that once had to be crossed on horseback could later be crossed on foot, he recalled.
As an adult, he took on the work of patrolling the grasslands, traveling on horseback and by motorcycle, picking up rubbish, helping injured wildlife, and keeping track of changes in the pasture.
A tape measure has long been one of his essential tools. He worried when the grass grew thin. But in recent years, as it became thicker, he found that these positive changes left him with a refreshing sense of satisfaction.
Monitoring data show the change on a wider scale. Vegetation cover in the Yellow River source section of Sanjiangyuan National Park has reached 68.7 percent, while coverage in restored areas of severely degraded grassland has risen from below 20 percent to more than 80 percent.
This year marks five years since Sanjiangyuan National Park was formally established and 10 years since its pilot program began. After the park was established, Gechu formally became an ecological ranger.
His respect for the headwaters was rooted in rules passed down by his father's generation. People were not supposed to shout near the source at night. Animals were not to be slaughtered there. Even after butchering cattle elsewhere, people were not supposed to wash their hands in the headwaters.
His father passed away in 2009. Before his death, he told Gechu to protect the source of the Yellow River, not to lease out the pasture, and not to leave. In his 20s at the time, Gechu became the head of the household and has lived in and patrolled the area ever since.
Someone once asked him what rubbish at the source of the Yellow River had to do with them. Gechu had no grand answer. The headwaters, he said, supplied water to countless people downstream. If the source became dirty or damaged, "that would be bad for the country."
This year marks the 80th anniversary of China's efforts to protect and harness the Yellow River. In 2025, the river's main stream maintained a Class II water quality rating along its entire course for a fourth consecutive year, a level that meets the hygienic standard for drinking water after conventional water purification treatment, according to the Ministry of Ecology and Environment.
Gechu's part in that story remains small and intensely local. He had rarely traveled far from the headwaters. He cannot read and speaks little Mandarin, and before this summer, the farthest he and his family had been was Lhasa, capital of Xizang Autonomous Region which is adjacent to Qinghai. He had long wanted to see more, he said, but had never managed to make it very far.
The idea for this journey began with a question from his nephew, Sonam Doje: What does the Yellow River look like where it meets the sea? Gechu did not know. He wanted to find out.
This summer, accompanied by his nephew, Gechu left the headwaters for his first trip off the plateau. On his first flight, he sat quietly by the window, watching unfamiliar landscapes pass below and thinking about his father.
When the plane crossed the lower reaches of the Yellow River, he leaned toward the window. "This is the first time I've seen that the Yellow River can be so wide," he said.
By plane, car and boat, the journey eventually brought him to the Yellow River estuary in east China's Shandong Province.
At the Yellow River Delta National Nature Reserve, Gechu learned about the wetlands around the estuary, saw rare birds including Oriental storks and Saunders's gulls. In 2025, the reserve recorded 536 oriental stork chicks, the highest annual number on record, while the breeding population of Saunders's gulls remained above 10,000. He also met people working to protect the river at its other end.
"The Yellow River is like a mother," he said. Its water nourishes the land and allows grass and other plants to grow.
When the journey was over, Gechu and Sonam Doje returned to the headwaters. The pasture was still there, and the river continued to run downstream. Gechu went back to patrolling, watching the water and measuring the grass.
"Don't worry," he told his nephew. "The grass will grow back." ■
Oriental white storks forage at a wetland at the Yellow River's estuary in Dongying, east China's Shandong Province, Sept. 6, 2026. (Photo by Yang Tingkui/Xinhua)
An aerial drone photo taken on March 10, 2026 shows a view of the Gyaring Lake at the Yellow River's source in Maduo County, northwest China's Qinghai Province. (Xinhua/Li Zhanyi)
An aerial drone photo taken on Sept. 5, 2026 shows a view of the Yellow River's estuary in Dongying, east China's Shandong Province. (Photo by Yang Tingkui/Xinhua)

KABUL, Sept. 12 (Xinhua) -- Afghan security forces have uncovered a cache of firearms and ammunition concealed in a truck transporting returnees at the Torkham border crossing in eastern Nangarhar province, a local police official said Friday evening.

Luke Evans spoke about Tim Curry’s serious condition before his death
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
10:52:00 EEST
16:52:00 KST

Luke Evans spoke about Tim Curry’s serious condition before his death
Kyiv • UNN
Tim Curry was seriously ill and could barely speak before his death at the age of 80. Luke Evans spoke about their connection through an iconic role.
Luke Evans revealed that Tim Curry was seriously ill and could barely speak shortly before his death at the age of 80. E! News reports this, citing the actor's interview with Entertainment Weekly, UNN writes.
Details
Evans, who played Dr. Frank-N-Furter in the Broadway production of "The Rocky Horror Show," said that Curry sent him a letter before his death. According to him, the actor managed to receive it and was very grateful.
I think he was very ill when he received the letter. It was very difficult for him
He later learned from Curry's representative that the actor was already having difficulty speaking. Tim Curry died on August 25 at the age of 80. Ischemic heart disease was named as the cause of death.
Evans felt a special connection with Curry
According to Evans, he had never met Curry personally, but felt a special connection with him through the role of Frank-N-Furter, which Curry had made iconic in his time.
Evans noted that after the actor's death, numerous retrospectives of his career repeatedly named this character as one of his best-known roles.
Curry's death coincided with the end of Evans's period working in New York on "The Rocky Horror Show." The actor called it a "strange, beautiful and tragic" conclusion to his Broadway experience.

Trump lands in Ireland for golf tournament, PM talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
07:51:20 UTC
16:51:20 KST

Trump says unified Ireland ‘would be fantastic' during Dublin trip
US President Donald Trump on Saturday said a unified Ireland would be “fantastic" during a weekend visit to a major tournament at his Irish golf course. The two-day trip to Ireland is the latest example of how the US leader blends his official duties with his personal interests.
US President Donald Trump said Saturday that a unified Ireland would be “fantastic,” wading into a complex and politically charged subject during a weekend visit to a major tournament at his Irish golf course
At a meeting with Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin in Dublin, Trump said he would love to see the reunification of the Republic of Ireland with the UK’s Northern Ireland.
“I don’t want to cause any problems but I’d love to see it unified," Trump said. "It’s going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now.
“I think it would be a fantastic thing," he said, adding that "the UK will have something to say about it, obviously.”
The US president touched down at Dublin airport in his Qatari-gifted plane shortly before 8:25am (07:25 GMT), AFP reporters saw.
At least 4,000 police and other personnel, including snipers, have been mobilised for the visit, in what has been dubbed one of the biggest security operations ever mounted in Ireland.
Thousands of anti-Trump protesters are planning to rally in Dublin, where the US leader is holding separate meetings with Ireland's leaders.
Trump is then due to fly to his luxury resort in Doonbeg, on Ireland's west coast, where some of the world's top golfers are competing in the Irish Open tournament.
The golf-mad president – whose relaxed relationship with the game's rules was documented by sports journalist Rick Reilly in the 2019 book "Commander in Cheat" – may even award the trophy on Sunday.
"He's really just visiting the golf resort he owns and dropping into Dublin for a courtesy visit," Daniel Geary, a US history professor at Trinity College Dublin, told AFP.
"He sees little difference between his private interests and his role as president."
'Business'
The 80-year-old billionaire has promoted his family's golf business unabashedly since returning to the White House for his second stint as president in January 2025.
Last summer, he welcomed then-UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer and European Union chief Ursula von der Leyen to his plush resort at Turnberry on the west coast of Scotland.
Trump then inaugurated another golf course bearing his name in the town of Balmedie, near Aberdeen on the northeast Scottish coast.
"He certainly sends a message that he is passionately interested in his own family's business," University of Minnesota law professor Richard Painter said ahead of the Ireland trip.
"It's not going to help the Republican party in the midterms to have the president... promoting his golf courses for the super-wealthy, when other people are having trouble making ends meet," the expert on government ethics added.
Read moreTrump's sale of access to Truth Social raises eyebrows
The security operation for Trump's visit is reportedly costing Ireland 20 million euros ($23 million) and comes as the country already grapples with a massive policing operation for its six-month presidency of the EU.
Trump's attendance at Doonbeg – a remote, coastal site in County Clare that the Trump Organization purchased in 2014 – adds an extra layer of complexity to the security effort.
Some 40,000 fans are expected at the tournament over the weekend, with six-time major winner and current world number two Rory McIlroy the main draw.
McIlroy, who has played golf with Trump, told the BBC this week that the tournament will feel "different" with the US president on site, but that the players will just "keep our heads down and play".
'Short and courteous'
Trump's first meeting is with Connolly, who occupies the largely ceremonial role of president. She is a left-winger and Trump critic, who is under pressure to raise Gaza during their discussions.
Trump will then see Irish leader Martin, whom he has hosted twice in the Oval Office and appears to get on well with.
The Middle East, including America's and Israel's war on Iran, and US tariffs on EU pharmaceuticals and immigration are likely to be on the agenda.
Ireland and the United States have long been close allies, partly because of their common ancestral ties.
But the Irish government's politics diverge sharply with that of the Trump administration on many issues – particularly support for the Palestinians.
Ireland is among several countries, including Spain, the UK and France, that have announced a trade ban targeting Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
"Martin is experienced enough that it should be fine at the political level. The big uncertainty is President Connolly," Eoin O'Malley, a political scientist at Dublin City University, told AFP.
"She protested against his last visit (in 2019), and her supporters will expect her to make some show for them. But she's also aware that she cannot do or say anything that might inflict damage on the relationship.
"I expect it will be short and courteous."
(FRANCE 24 with AFP and AP)

Poroshenko calls on EU to boost financial aid to cover Ukraine's budget deficit

Russia Is Hunting Civilians in Kramatorsk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
07:49:00 UTC
16:49:00 KST

Kramatorsk is not falling in a single assault. It is being strangled. Russian forces are using first person view (FPV) drones to hunt people in streets and courtyards, dropping guided glide bombs on apartment blocks, and striking vehicles that carry the markings of humanitarian work.
This is not collateral damage. It is a method.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
You do not “accidentally” fly a first-person drone into a vehicle painted with humanitarian markings. You do not accidentally hit a civilian standing in a courtyard when the pilot is purposefully watching and maneuvering a drone towards an innocent victim.
Kramatorsk, like Kherson, is being hunted by drone safaris. Brave humanitarians will still go in and evacuate the elderly, deliver heat and pull the injured out of the rubble, all the while being hunted by soulless drone operators. These are a war crime in plain sight. Document it. Name it. Stop pretending this is just the fog of war.
Drones that see the victim before they kill
FPV drones, including fiber-optic models largely immune to jamming, now operate inside Kramatorsk itself, well behind the line that used to define the “front.” Operators fly them in real time; they see an elderly woman; they choose to kill.
Publicly reported incidents this year include:
• June 6, 2026 – a civilian man killed in a residential area. Ukrainian authorities stated the operator could see the target before impact.
• Sept. 4, 2026 – two civilian cars struck by FPV drones in the city; fires started beside homes.
EU Clears €3.2B Patriot Purchase for Ukraine Under €90B Loan
• Repeated strikes on parked cars, public transport and anyone moving in the open. “Waiter Drones” are left on rooftops overnight and used at first light to attack the unsuspecting.
Ukraine has documented more than 11,000 Russian FPV attacks on civilians nationwide, including double-tap strikes that hit the same site after medics and firefighters arrive.
The UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine has already classified the systematic FPV targeting of civilians in Kherson Oblast – known predatorily as “Drone Safaris” – as crimes against humanity. The same pattern is now being recorded across the Donetsk region, including Kramatorsk.
Aftermath of evacuation vehicle destroyed by a drone near Kramatorsk. (Video courtesy Kiwi K.A.R.E)
Glide bombs on homes
Guided aerial bombs – FAB-250s fitted with UMPK kits – are cheap, hard to stop, and used against housing as well as military positions.
• Sept. 9, 2026 – five glide bombs were dropped on Kramatorsk, wounding four civilians (women aged 59, 70 and 74; a man aged 72), damaging 27 private homes and a car.
• Late August – some nine glide bombs hit apartment blocks in Kramatorsk with dozens wounded, including an infant.
• Bridges and crossings have been struck as a warning that the way out can be impeded and ultimately closed.
These strikes sit inside a wider campaign of Shahed-type drones and missiles against Ukraine. Kramatorsk’s daily reality, however, is closer and more personal: an FPV drone patrolling a courtyard; a glide bomb hitting a block of flats; roads that are no longer safe to drive.
Targeting people who come to help
The most damning evidence is the targeting of marked civilian and humanitarian vehicles whose purpose is visible from the air.
To date, the “Road-of-Life” program, which falls under the umbrella of Kiwi K.A.R.E (Kiwi Aid & Refugee Evacuation) charitable trust, has come under enemy fire 11 times with five vehicles completely destroyed: two ambulances, one armored ambulance, and two passenger vehicles. Fortunately, there have been no fatalities however several volunteers have been injured with one person remaining in hospital.
• June 1, 2026 – FPV strike on a clearly marked Civil Protection Department vehicle of the Kramatorsk City Council injuring one official. The city’s military administration called it deliberate as the markings were clearly visible; civilian cars stood nearby.
• Sept. 5, 2026 – a volunteer “Road-of-Life” vehicle was destroyed by a drone attack in Kramatorsk while being loaded for evacuation and aid work.
• Sept. 7-8 – three more “Road-of-Life” vehicles were attacked and destroyed, including an armored ambulance, seriously injuring an evacuation team member who was hospitalized.
• Numerous other missions in the Donetsk-Kharkiv belt has logged well over 100 attacks on staff, vehicles, offices and warehouses.
It is for this reason that humanitarian operations in and around Kramatorsk have become extraordinarily hard: driving under drone nets, detectors are a must in vehicles, teams aborting pickups when a drone threat represents clear and present danger.
Evacuations do still happen albeit with reduced frequency, at a slower pace, and with the recognition of significantly heightened danger. Every kilometer is a calculation.
International humanitarian law requires parties to distinguish civilians from combatants and to spare those who bring aid and conduct evacuations. Russia is doing the opposite – they use attacks on humanitarians as a method of warfare.
A city being emptied on purpose
Kramatorsk still stands. Ukrainian forces still hold it and will for the foreseeable future. But life is leaving. Cafés that were full a year ago are quiet. Supermarket shelves are empty. People stay indoors except for essential movement.
Police and local authorities have said it is time for remaining civilians to leave. Tens of thousands have already been displaced from the Kramatorsk district this year. The method is familiar: isolate the city with drones and bombs, punish movement, hit the rescuers, and wait for the population to drain away.
                                                                                                                                                                         
This is a war crime pattern – not an accident
Kiwi K.A.R.E calls these acts what they are:
• Willful killing and targeting of civilians.
• Attacks on civilian objects and housing.
• Attacks on humanitarian and civil-protection personnel and vehicles displaying distinctive signs.
• Terror against a civilian population to force displacement.
These are prohibited under the Geneva Conventions and customary international humanitarian law. They are being documented, daily, by Ukrainian prosecutors, city authorities, emergency services and independent journalists. The operators who fly a drone into a marked aid vehicle, and those who order the method, must be named and held to account.
What we ask
• Governments and media: treat FPV hunting of civilians and strikes on marked humanitarian vehicles as the war crimes they are – not as “battlefield friction.”
• Donors and partners: frontline aid in Sumy, Donetsk and Kherson is still possible, but only with the equipment, protection and funding levels that match the threat. Well-marked humanitarian vehicles are being destroyed. Replacing them is now a matter of life and death.
• New Zealand and allied governments: sustain political, military and humanitarian support for Ukraine. Isolation of cities like Kramatorsk is a strategy. Silence assists it.

Yemeni government forces launch drone strikes on Houthi positions in Al-Dhale
Unknown

Mohammed Sameai and Rania Abushamala
12 September 2026•Update: 12 September 2026
Yemeni government forces said Saturday that they had carried out “precision” drone strikes on positions belonging to the Houthi group in the southwestern Al-Dhale province amid a rising escalation in the Arab country.
In a statement, the Nation’s Shield Forces said that they had conducted “precision strikes” using drones on Houthi positions in Al-Dhale, without specifying the exact location of the attacks.
They released video footage of the strikes, showing an aerial attack targeting a gathering of dozens of Houthi members.
There was no immediate comment from the Houthis on the statement.
Yemen’s map of territorial control has changed in recent days amid escalating confrontations between government forces and the Houthis since early July, following years of relative calm.
The Houthis now control the entire western Al-Hudaydah province, according to the group, after advancing in western Taiz province and capturing the coastal city of Mokha and its Red Sea port.
Their advance has also brought them close to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the world’s most important maritime passageways.
Government forces, meanwhile, have made gains in the northern Al-Jawf province along the Saudi border and approached its provincial capital, Al-Hazm.
Clashes are also continuing on fronts in Marib, Al-Bayda and Al-Dhale provinces.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis captured the capital Sanaa and several provinces in September 2014.
A Saudi-led Arab coalition intervened in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government.

Drones from Iraq attack and set pipeline on fire in Saudi Arabia

16:47:02 KST

The East–West pipeline is crucial for shipping Saudi oil to the Red Sea, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz. This latest incident risks driving oil and fuel prices even higher.
An oil pipeline in Saudi Arabia, deemed "essential" for bypassing the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, has been shut down after a fire that, according to the authorities, followed a drone attack launched from Iraq.
The East-West pipeline links Abqaiq, near the Persian Gulf, to the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea, and is used as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz for transporting Saudi oil to the Red Sea. A statement from the Saudi foreign ministry referred to a fire near Medina, said to have caused "human and material damage".
A government official in Riyadh had already told the media that people had been injured in the drone attack and the subsequent blaze. The same official said the pipeline had been shut down as a precaution.
The Iraqi government acknowledged that the attack was launched from its territory and announced that it had dismissed the commander of Maysan province in the south of the country as a consequence.
Saudi Arabia frequently accuses Iran-linked armed groups based in neighbouring Iraq of targeting its oil facilities with drones.
The Gulf Cooperation Council, which brings together six countries in the region, issued a statement expressing concern and describing the incident as "a dangerous escalation and an unacceptable threat to the security of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia".
The government in Riyadh said it would not respond to the attack for the time being, stating that it intended "not to react at this stage and to support the efforts of the Iraqi government to prevent attacks launched from its territory against the Saudi kingdom and neighbouring countries".
This incident comes just a day after the Houthi rebels in Yemen, backed by Iran, took control of an island of strategic importance in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a location of crucial importance for global oil trade. It marks an escalation in the Houthis' attempts to block Saudi Arabia's trade; Riyadh backs Yemen's government. According to the rebels, navigation in the strait was "safe for everyone except the Saudis".
This latest attack adds another layer to the series of incidents in the war launched by the United States and Israel against Iran in February, which has pushed oil and fuel prices to new record highs. The price of a barrel of oil climbed above 100 dollars on Friday, with fuel prices hitting fresh records.

why does living underground feel so strange?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
07:45:05 UTC
16:45:05 KST

Across China’s Loess Plateau, an entire house can disappear beneath a field. The dikengyuan begins with a courtyard excavated several meters into the earth, then expands sideways as vaulted rooms are carved from its walls. Seen from above, the agricultural landscape continues nearly uninterrupted. Only the rectangular opening gives the house away, a patch of sky surrounded by ground where we expect to find a roof.
Living here reverses some of the most familiar cues of domestic space. The earth moves from beneath your feet to around your body. Entering means descending, and exterior walls become geological mass.
Even though humans have lived this way for centuries, underground space still brings an unusual psychological charge. A buried room can suggest protection and intimacy, but that same depth can cause unease. Between these contrasting reactions is the basic architectural question of, ‘what makes being underground feel like shelter?’
Shanzhou Silo-cave, Loess Plateau, Sanmenxia City, China | image via Trip
the house has always had an underground mind
Gaston Bachelard gives the cellar an unusually powerful role in The Poetics of Space. His imagined house stretches vertically between attic and cellar, with each end belonging to a different mental world. The roof can be understood through construction and weather. The cellar reaches into what he calls the ‘irrationality of the depths,’ a space connected with darkness and whatever lies beneath the familiar parts of the home.
Rosalind Williams follows that cultural pull further in Notes on the Underground, in which she traces subterranean space through literature and infrastructure as both refuge and source of fear. Tunnels and sewers opened hidden worlds beneath nineteenth-century cities at the same moment writers were filling the underground with imagined civilizations and technological futures.
These associations are culturally specific, of course. Someone raised in an underground courtyard house may understand descent very differently from someone whose strongest references are basements and bunkers. Architects must reckon with those associations and negotiate with them.
image courtesy Penguin Classics
earth can do much of the work of a house
The practical case for going underground is surprisingly direct. Soil changes temperature far more slowly than air, allowing thick earth to buffer interiors against large swings outside. Across the Loess Plateau, this thermal mass helps dikengyuan rooms stay more stable through hot summers and cold winters. Similar logic appears in Matmata’s excavated dwellings in Tunisia and the cave houses of southern Spain, where the ground becomes wall and roof at once.
A University of Hong Kong team recently revisited the dikengyuan with its Underground House of the Future in Henan. Existing earthen chambers were reinforced with brick vaults, and skylights and rear openings brought daylight deeper inside.
The central courtyard became a stepped communal space beneath a translucent canopy. While digital fabrication enters through 3D-printed earthen elements, the spatial idea remains centuries old. The space is excavated and built sideways, with the sky left open in the center.
Underground House of the Future, University of Hong Kong, 2026 | image courtesy Olivier Ottevaere
a piece of sky underground
That vital opening to the sky appears again and again throughout subterranean architecture. A 1979 earth-sheltered house in Scottsdale arranges its rooms around an open-air court below the Arizona desert, where full-height glazing pulls sunlight into spaces buried on every side. From ground level, much of the architecture disappears. Descend the stairs and the interior opens outdoors again.
Environmental psychology helps explain why this gesture carries so much weight. Studies of underground environments repeatedly connect discomfort with reduced daylight, weak orientation and diminished control over one’s surroundings. Recent research has also found emotional state and performance decline as daylight decreases underground.
Seen through that lens, the courtyard does much more than just ventilate the house. It brings part of the surface down with you, so that eventually the sky becomes a way to orient yourself.
underground house in Scottsdale, Arizona, 1979 | image courtesy Zillow
the comfort of the burrow
Javier Senosiain, the architect best known for Quetzalcóatl Park outside Mexico City, approached the buried house through the idea of refuge. His Organic House, completed in Mexico in 1985, draws from the logic of animal shelters and early human dwellings by placing curved ferrocement rooms beneath grassy mounds. Walking across the garden means crossing the roof. Inside, windows pierce the enclosing shell and pull greenery close to the curved walls.
There is another side to enclosure here. Humans often seek spaces that wrap closely around the body, from sleeping alcoves to deeply recessed rooms. The psychological difference seems tied to agency. Research into subterranean environments repeatedly returns to perceived control, and studies of earth-sheltered homes suggest that expectations can differ dramatically from lived experience.
One post-occupancy study of homes around Minneapolis and St. Paul found high resident satisfaction, with attitudes toward earth-sheltered living improving after people moved in. The underground house may feel stranger in imagination than it does in use.
La Casa Orgánica (Organic House), Javier Senosiain, Naucalpan de Juárez, Mexico, 1985 | image courtesy Javier Senosiain
geology enters the room
At Casa Tierra in Córdoba, UMMO Estudio occupies an existing limestone formation, placing domestic space directly against rough calcarenite surfaces. Polished floors and inserted partitions sit beneath stone shaped long before the house arrived. Part of the room belongs to geology, and the architecture works around it instead of fully controlling its form.
Olgooco’s Inside Home in Ammameh, Iran, takes another approach, arranging cave-like spaces around an interior void while planted surfaces continue overhead. Across these projects, a pattern begins to emerge. Architects bury rooms, then cut openings back toward daylight. They cover roofs with earth, then remove sections to make courtyards. The ground provides enclosure, while architecture decides how intensely the body should feel it.
On the Greek island of Serifos, MOLD Architects makes that negotiation especially clear with its nCAVED. The dwelling is embedded into a steep rocky slope, with rooms arranged between long stone walls that direct the eye toward the Aegean. Most of the building disappears into the hillside, yet the main spaces open broadly toward the sea. Toward the rear, buried gardens bring daylight and air into the deeper portions of the house.
Standing inside nCAVED expands the idea of what an underground room can feel like. Several feet of landscape might be above your head, but your vision can still extend across open water. In this case, the idea that the body is buried while the eye travels far beyond the house may help explain the difference between a cave and a room that happens to sit beneath the ground. The horizon gives the occupant somewhere to go visually.
Looking back at the dikengyuan from above, almost every familiar sign of a house has disappeared. Its facade faces inward, its roof has become terrain, and its rooms occupy the thickness of the earth. The element that remains visible is the courtyard, the opening through which daylight and weather enter. The same impulse keeps resurfacing across houses separated by centuries and geography: bury the architecture while preserving a readable connection to the world above.
Going underground seems to make that connection unusually intense. A rectangle of sky becomes something you continually notice. Sunlight through a deep opening gives time a physical presence. At nCAVED, the sea can make the mass overhead recede from awareness; inside a dikengyuan, the courtyard tells you exactly where the surface is.
Of course, underground architecture begins with disappearance. But occupying it reveals the extent of a home’s dependence on sensing what lies beyond the room. How much of the outside world do we need to feel at home inside?
pit courtyard, Luoyang, Henan, China, 2009 | image via Kevin Poh, Wikipedia
This article is part of designboom’s MODES OF HABITATION chapter, exploring how the spaces we inhabit can reshape the ways we live together. Discover more stories rethinking domesticity, shared living, and the many forms a home can take here.

Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis have seized key positions near the entrance to the Red Sea, raising concerns over shipping as Saudi Arabia shut a major oil pipeline following a drone attack.
The group captured the port city of Mokha from Saudi-backed government forces on Sept. 10.
Yemeni government sources told Reuters that Mayun Island, also known as Perim, fell to the Houthis the following day. Zuqar Island in the Red Sea was also reported to have been captured.
Mayun lies in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and forms part of the shipping route between Asia and Europe through the Suez Canal.
Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on its Red Sea ports for oil exports amid disruption to tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.
The Saudi Energy Ministry said the East-West pipeline had been shut as a precaution following drone attacks.
Saudi Arabia and Iraq said the attacks originated in Iraq, but responsibility remained unclear. The pipeline carries crude from eastern Saudi Arabia to the Red Sea coast.
Rashad al-Alimi, head of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, said defending Bab al-Mandeb meant protecting a major route for trade, energy and food supplies, as well as Yemen’s sovereignty.
Axios reported that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called U.S. President Donald Trump twice on Sept. 10 to request strikes against the Houthis, but Trump declined.
U.S. officials had told Riyadh that American forces would remain focused on Iran and the Strait of Hormuz, the report said.
CNN separately reported that more than 100 U.S. military advisers were providing intelligence and targeting support to Saudi Arabia.
U.S. Central Command chief Adm. Brad Cooper also traveled to the kingdom for coordination talks.
Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan discussed the attacks on Saudi Arabia and regional developments with his Saudi counterpart, Prince Faisal bin Farhan, in a phone call on Sept. 11, Turkish Foreign Ministry sources said.
