BRICS leaders gather in India as wars reshape global economy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
05:19:17 UTC
14:19:17 KST

BRICS leaders and senior officials gathered in New Delhi on Saturday for the group’s 18th summit, with the prolonged US-Iran and Russia-Ukraine wars casting a shadow over discussions on global trade, energy security and economic stability.
The summit comes as the US-Iran conflict has fueled an energy crisis and heightened concerns over inflation, trade disruptions and energy supplies worldwide.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said he hoped the meeting would produce “positive” and “meaningful” discussions, while China said it looked forward to working with fellow BRICS members to promote dialogue and negotiations and safeguard regional and global peace and stability.
Expanded BRICS puts multilateralism at center
The 11-member grouping brings together Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa, the countries that gave BRICS its name, alongside Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.
Chinese President Xi Jinping, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Russian President Vladimir Putin and South African President Cyril Ramaphosa are among the leaders attending, alongside officials representing other member states.
The first day features a closed-door session focused on “Inclusive Global Governance and Strengthening Multilateralism.” Leaders will also visit the Bharat Innovates Exhibition, participate in a tree-planting ceremony and attend a dinner hosted by Modi.
Brazil is represented by Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira, while Saudi Arabia is represented by Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud.
BRICS seeks greater role in global economy
The bloc has also expanded its outreach through a partner-country framework that includes Belarus, Bolivia, Kazakhstan, Cuba, Malaysia, Nigeria, Thailand, Uganda, Uzbekistan and Vietnam.
Day two will focus on “Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability: Shaping the Future for Inclusive Global Growth,” with leaders expected to issue a joint statement.
According to figures cited by BRICS, the expanded grouping now represents about 49.5 percent of the world’s population, 40 percent of global GDP and 26 percent of global trade, underscoring its growing weight in the international economy.
The previous BRICS leaders’ summit was held in Rio de Janeiro in 2025.

Anyone wearing smart glasses can take photos, film videos, listen to music, make phone calls, translate text or interact with an AI assistant, with sales now hitting the millions.

A 2013 push by Google failed to take off but Meta's smart spectacles, developed in partnership with Ray-Ban maker EssilorLuxottica, have fared much better.

But with exponential growth came the backlash.
Worries reached a peak in the summer in Europe, especially in Britain which saw intense media coverage of so-called "pervert glasses" alongisde reports that Meta is developing a facial recognition feature to be integrated into the devices.
In one case, a 17-year-old girl told British broadcaster Channel 4 News in August how she had been approached by a man who covertly recorded her and their interaction.
Contacted by AFP, Meta said it has taken multiple steps to prevent tampering with the blinking LED light intended to show other people the device is recording – a key concern of critics.

"These investments are already having a deterrent effect," it said, saying companies offering to disable the LED lights had shut down as a result.
EU 'must act'

There are similar calls for the European Union to take up the issue, while France's CNIL data protection watchdog has urged "vigilance".
A Swedish designer, Mateusz Pozar, launched a "Ban Ray" site earlier this year, providing signs to ban smart glasses from venues and selling stickers.

Economic Watch: China's "golden outer ring" highways fuel new economic corridors
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
13:12:14 CST
14:12:14 KST

SHENYANG, Sept. 12 (Xinhua) -- A scenic coastal highway in China has left a deep impression on Lee Jae-jae, a cycling enthusiast from the Republic of Korea (ROK).
Lee was among a group of 49 cyclists that visited Dandong, a border city in northeast China's Liaoning Province, aboard a passenger-and-cargo ferry from Incheon, ROK.
"Dandong has a very comfortable climate and beautiful roadside scenery. The cycling paths, rest areas and other facilities are well-equipped, making for a smooth and pleasant riding experience," he said.
The Dandong section of the G228 national highway offers just a glimpse of the many attractions along the emerging "golden outer ring." China plans to fully link three national highways -- the G219, G331 and G228 -- creating an ultra-long ring route that traces China's borders and coastal areas during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030).
Stretching over 26,000 kilometers if connected, nearly two-thirds of the equatorial circumference, the route traverses a diverse tapestry of landscapes and tourist attractions, from coastlines and snow-capped mountains to glaciers, grasslands, deserts, lakes and border crossings. It is poised to become a major corridor driving tourism and broader industrial development.
Dandong, where the G331 and G228 begin, is already reaping considerable benefits from its location. "Two national highways pass through our village, attracting a constant flow of self-driving travelers and border-tourism lovers throughout the year," said Wang Chunhai, Party chief of Hushan Village of Dandong.
Leveraging this advantage, the village transformed its idle land into recreational vehicle (RV) campsites and homestays, drawing praise from visitors while generating additional collective income for the village, according to Wang.
"Many visitors have told me that the drive from Dandong along the Yalu River offers beautiful scenery the whole way," said Zheng Jinhua, a resident of Guoyuan Village in adjacent Jilin Province, adding that a growing number of villagers have opened homestays or started to sell local farm produce to visitors.
Statistics show that the G331, which traces the country's northern border, welcomed more than 2 million tourists in the first half of this year. For residents of border villages along the route, tourism has become a source of livelihood at their doorstep, with many investing in homestays, running specialty restaurants or selling local agricultural products.
Serving as a principal artery along China's western and southern frontier, G219 is home to a remarkable diversity of ecological and geographical landscapes, winding through the Taklamakan Desert, China's largest, and the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, widely known as the "roof of the world."
In June, the China Tourist Attractions Association, joined by state-owned cultural and tourism groups from Xinjiang, Xizang, Yunnan and other provincial-level regions, initiated preparations for a coordinated development mechanism for the G219 cultural and tourism industry, with the goal of better aligning cultural and tourism resources along the route.
"As China's longest border road, G219 boasts abundant cultural and tourism resources along the way, such as snow-capped mountains, glaciers and grasslands, which can directly fuel tourism, rural revitalization and border stability and prosperity," said Liu Rangqun, general manager of Xinjiang Culture & Tourism Investment Group Co., Ltd.
Meanwhile, the G228, which stretches along China's eastern coastline, links coastal ports and forms a transportation and logistics channel connecting land borders to coastal ports, noted Li Hongchang, a professor at Beijing Jiaotong University.
"By organically integrating transportation hubs, it helps drive the all-round economic and social development of the areas it passes through," Li said.
Along the route in Dandong, for example, cross-border e-commerce transaction volume posted a double-digit increase over the past year.
A well-developed road network can transform what was once a transportation periphery into a frontier for openness, said Ma Jiangbo, deputy director of the China economic research center under the China Institute for Innovation & Development Strategy.
An integrated network, rather than three separate channels, can further reduce cross-border logistics costs and make China's industrial layout more balanced, Ma added.
During the 15th Five-Year Plan period, the country has planned to work faster to boost its strength in transportation and improve the modern integrated transportation system, raising the completion rate of the main framework of the national integrated multidimensional transportation network to 95 percent. ■

Earth has hottest August on record: world meteorological agency
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
13:12:12 CST
14:12:12 KST

GENEVA, Sept. 12 (Xinhua) -- Earth had the hottest August on record, according to newly released weather data, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said Friday, noting that the effects were felt around the planet.
The Northern Hemisphere had its warmest summer, while the Southern Hemisphere had a near-record warm winter. Meanwhile, the Arctic and Antarctic each had below-average sea ice coverage in August.
Western Europe saw heatwaves in August, continuing an exceptional run of extreme heat that began in May, and severe drought conditions were reported in France, Hungary, Romania, Serbia and Britain.
Large parts of central and eastern Europe also saw widespread dryness in August, in some cases persisting since May. Water flow levels were exceptionally low in major European rivers, including the Rhine, Danube, Southern Bug and Dnieper.
El Nino was one of the drivers of August's record climate conditions, WMO said, adding that the climate pattern influenced global tropical cyclone activity as well as heavy rainfall and floods in some countries.
Data indicates that all 10 of the warmest Augusts on record have occurred since 2016, the agency said. ■

Syrian private airport plans spark outcry over mass graves, land rights
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
05:11:14 UTC
14:11:14 KST

Syrian private airport plans spark outcry over mass graves, land rights
- Syrian plans to convert Mezzeh military airport into a private jet hub raise concerns over disturbing suspected mass graves and ignoring private land rights.
- Documents reveal Mezzeh was used for executions and detentions under Assad, with over 1,150 detainees believed to have died there, prompting calls for investigation before redevelopment.
- Residents protest land expropriation without compensation, demanding involvement and rights amid UN calls for Syria to address Assad-era property seizures.
AI generated
DAMASCUS – Syrian government plans to turn a former military airport in Damascus into a hub for private jets are raising alarm among rights groups and residents who say redevelopment could disturb suspected mass graves and override private land claims.
Syria’s civil aviation authority said last week it was preparing to reclassify Mezzeh military airport for limited civilian use, focused on private and executive aviation, to complement Damascus International Airport, according to a report on Syria’s state news agency, SANA. Rubble removal and infrastructure upgrades had already begun, the report said.
The project is emerging as a test of how Syria’s new authorities balance a drive to attract investment and redevelop state assets with two unresolved legacies of Assad’s family rule: the fate of tens of thousands of missing Syrians and property rights clouded by decades of expropriation.
New documents show airport’s role as execution site
Under ousted ruler Bashar al-Assad and his father Hafez, Mezzeh housed key branches of the powerful Air Force Intelligence Directorate, as well as numerous detention facilities where suspected government opponents were tortured, executed and subjected to enforced disappearance. Parts of the air base were used for presidential and other official flights.
Air Force Intelligence (AFI) documents recently obtained by the Syria Justice and Accountability Centre (SJAC), a US-based Syrian-led human rights group, and shared exclusively with Reuters, show that senior Syrian military officials approved Mezzeh in 2012 as a site for carrying out executions of detainees sentenced to death by military field courts.
One document proposed moving executions from Sednaya – the country’s most notorious prison at the time – to Mezzeh because it was a “closed security compound” close to Damascus. Subsequent correspondence discussed a firing range and later a hangar beside the runway as execution sites.
The documents, which underscore the central role of Mezzeh in the Assad-era security system, show officials ordered construction of a platform at the hangar, requested nylon rope and directed that the work be carried out under AFI supervision “in utmost secrecy”.
A 2025 investigation by SJAC identified two suspected grave sites linked to people who died in detention at Mezzeh, where it said more than 1,150 detainees died, some by execution and others from torture or maltreatment.
In a July 2025 letter seen by Reuters, SJAC provided Syria’s National Commission for Missing Persons with the coordinates of the two suspected graves inside the airport, urging the authorities to prevent construction or excavation until the sites were investigated.
The commission told SJAC at the time that there were no construction or refurbishment plans for Mezzeh, SJAC told Reuters.
SJAC wrote to the commission again on Sept 8 after the redevelopment plans emerged, warning that excavation, rubble removal or other works could damage human remains and evidence crucial to identifying victims, according to a second letter seen by Reuters.
SJAC told Reuters it had not yet received a response to its second letter.
Amer Matar, founder of the Syria Prisons Museum, a Germany-based non-governmental organisation documenting detention facilities including those at Mezzeh, said the planned works showed a lack of respect for Syrian families who still have no answers on the fate of loved ones detained under Assad.
“To construct a business airport on a site that may contain mass graves, without a thorough prior investigation, without site protection, without searching for the missing and their remains, and without preserving evidence, is an act of extreme recklessness and disregard,” said Matar.
Syria’s Syrian civil aviation authority, National Commission for Missing Persons and defence ministry, which has been operating the airport, did not respond to questions from Reuters about suspected graves and land claims.
SANA cited the civil aviation authority’s spokesperson as saying that Mezzeh’s refurbishment would take into account the surrounding urban area and relevant legal and social issues, but did not specifically mention the graves or land rights. It is unclear who will develop the airport.
Residents protest over land claims
The dispute over the land on which airport facilities were built is decades old.
Under the Assads, private land was regularly expropriated for government projects, often without compensation.
Mezzeh airport was built on land belonging to hundreds of private citizens across 2.76 sq km, according to land records from the Moadamiya municipality shared with Reuters.
A former municipal official, who asked not to be named, told Reuters that expropriation decrees retroactively justified the government’s use of those lands when the airport was built in 1956, and that compensation had not been paid.
Residents demonstrated in Moadamiya a day after the redevelopment plans were announced.
“We welcome investment, but we should be sitting at the table and discussing our share with investors, not the state,” said one protest organiser, who gave his name as Abu Khaled. “We have a documented right to this land.”
The dispute comes as Syria faces calls to address Assad-era property seizures.
On Sept 2, United Nations land rights experts appealed to Syria’s government to suspend and repeal laws they said had enabled systematic property dispossession under Assad, and to either establish mechanisms to return properties to their legitimate owners, or provide adequate compensation. REUTERS

Trump says he would 'love' to see a united Ireland
DUBLIN, Sept 12 - U.S. President Donald Trump said on Saturday he would "love" to see British-run Northern Ireland unify with Ireland, remarks made during a visit to Dublin that drew a sharp response from pro-British unionists in Northern Ireland.
Trump's comments come weeks after new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said a referendum on Northern Ireland leaving the United Kingdom was "off the table", a position Downing Street on Saturday said remained unchanged.
"Well, I don't want to cause any problems, but I will tell you, I'd love to see it unified," Trump told reporters sitting next to Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin after the pair met in Dublin. "It's going to happen eventually ... I think it would be a fantastic thing."
"Now the UK will have something to say about it ... but I think it would be a great thing," he added.
COMMENTS BREAK WITH NEUTRAL STANCE OF PREVIOUS PRESIDENTS
Trump later said that there "was no good answer" to the question on Irish unity but repeated that he thought it would be "a very cool thing".
Under the terms of the 1998 Good Friday Agreement, a referendum can be held only at the discretion of the British government. The accord ended three decades of violence between Irish nationalists seeking a united Ireland and unionists who wanted Northern Ireland to remain part of the UK.
While polls show a comfortable majority in Northern Ireland favour remaining in the UK, the gap has narrowed slightly since Britain's departure from the European Union pushed unity higher up the political agenda.
The leader of the Democratic Unionist Party, Northern Ireland's largest party advocating continued union with Britain, rejected Trump's prediction, saying unification with Ireland would lead to "the destruction of our country."
"Northern Ireland's constitutional future will be decided by the people of Northern Ireland, not by commentary in London, Dublin or Washington," Gavin Robinson, who has publicly supported Trump in the past, wrote on X.
In Belfast, supporters of Irish unity gave a guarded response.
"I think it's just headline grabbing ... I don't think he gives a toss whether there is a United Ireland or not," said Eamon Hanna, a supporter of the nationalist SDLP party, which has been a strong critic of Trump's policies.
Previous U.S. presidents, including those with strong Irish heritage like Joe Biden, have been careful to remain neutral on Irish unification. The U.S. government played a key role in brokering the 1998 peace deal.
'YOU FLEECED US'
Trump also met Irish President Catherine Connolly, who had joined a protest against his 2019 visit to Ireland, before she was elected to the mostly ceremonial role last year.
Connolly, formerly a long-time left-wing lawmaker, said in a statement that she conveyed to Trump "the strong view of the Irish people that the normalisation of war and genocide can never be accepted."
Her statement did not reference any conflict, but she has been previously critical of the U.S. war with Iran and Israel's assault on Gaza, which Ireland, in common with a U.N. inquiry and several human rights groups, has described as a genocide.
Israel rejects that characterisation, saying that it is fighting the militants who attacked it from the Palestinian enclave in 2023.
Thousands of protesters, some holding posters calling Trump a warmonger and chanting "Free free Palestine", marched through central Dublin shortly after Trump left to watch a golf tournament at one of his resorts in the west of Ireland.
It was one of the country's largest anti-war protests in recent years.
The centrist premier Martin had earlier focused his remarks on the countries' close economic ties. U.S.-owned companies, mainly in the technology and pharmaceutical sectors, employ about 10% of workers in Ireland after successive governments prioritized the companies' jobs and tax revenues over decades.
"You took all our medical companies, we've got to get a couple of them back," Trump said.
"You fleeced us but that's okay ... There's a lot of room to go around and our relationship with you is fantastic." REUTERS

‘Recovery becomes self-propelling’: Five positive tipping points that can save the world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
05:05:36 UTC
14:05:36 KST

“For too long a sense has prevailed that solutions to the climate and nature are out of reach. This new research explodes that myth once and for all.”
The world risks irreversible damage as our reliance on planet-heating fossil fuels pushes ecosystems towards catastrophic climate tipping points.
A recent report from the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) warned that global temperature rise will exceed 1.5°C, likely within the next few years, overshooting the limit set out in the legally binding Paris climate agreement.
This would accelerate much of the environmental degradation the natural world is already experiencing, from shrinking ice sheets to rising sea levels and “unprecedented dieback” of coral reefs and rainforests.
The UNEP says that there are “no good outcomes if we remain above 1.5°C” and that governments must focus on making the overshoot as small and short as possible.
However, landmark new research from The Earthshot Prize and the University of Exeter has revealed 51 solutions that can trigger “rapid and transformative change” to repair the planet over the next five years. Out of these 51 solutions, five priority clusters – or ‘Earthshots’ – were identified.
Following the hottest August on record – tied with July 2023 – and a strong El Niño developing across the Pacific, researchers say that the study provides a “new, unifying agenda for positive action”.
“To reverse damage to our ecosystems before it’s too late, we need to unlock positive tipping points where progress builds on itself, costs fall with scale and recovery becomes self-propelling,” says Professor Tim Lenton, chair in climate change and earth system science at the University of Exeter.
Clean energy as a ‘master cascade’
Renewable energy such as solar and wind has already crossed positive tipping points in many markets – and is essential to end reliance on fossil fuels.
Last year, solar and wind accounted for a record 30 per cent of EU electricity, overtaking fossil power for the first time on record. During this time, EU solar generation hit a record 369TWh, up 20 per cent from 2025.
By 2030, solar power alone is projected to reduce EU emissions by 154 million tonnes of CO2-equivalent per year. This is the equivalent of the total greenhouse gas emissions of the Netherlands in 2023.
“Because clean power unlocks electric mobility, heat pumps, clean industry and clean air simultaneously, this is the highest-leverage transition across all five Earthshots,” the report says.
“The binding constraints are now grid expansion, permitting reform and the clean energy investment gap in the Global South.”
Despite hosting 60 per cent of the world’s best solar resources, Africa receives less than two per cent of global clean energy investment.
Some of the continent’s largest economies, such as South Africa, Morocco and Nigeria, are already accelerating plans to build more domestic solar manufacturing capacity to reduce dependence on Chinese imports that currently dominate the global market.
Morocco has doubled production to around one gigawatt a year. South Africa maintains a similar capacity, while Egypt has gigawatt-scale projects coming online.
“A few years ago, local solar manufacturing was barely on the agenda anywhere in Africa,” Benjamin Clarke, policy director at the Africa Solar Industry Association, tells news agency AP.
“It is now becoming a recognised pillar of industrial policy and green economic development.”
Clean cooking and clean household energy
Despite the clean energy boom, around 2.1 billion people still rely on solid fuels for cooking.
This is the largest source of indoor air pollution and a major source of ‘black carbon’, commonly known as soot.
“Clean cooking is close to a tipping point in several markets as pay-as-you-go solar and clean cooking businesses scale across East and Southern Africa,” the report states.
“In Latin America and parts of Asia, the liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) transition is substantially complete, bringing health benefits to millions.”
How marine protected areas are becoming ‘self-reinforcing’
Researchers highlight that well-designed and well-enforced ocean conservation has produced “visible recovery” of fish stocks and biodiversity within recent years.
“As communities have reaped the benefits of marine conservation, protection areas have expanded and progress accelerated,” the report states.
“In turn, food security for coastal populations and climate resilience has strengthened with examples including the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park in Australia.”
Earlier this year, the highly anticipated High Seas Treaty came into force, marking a “historic milestone” for global ocean conservation.
The High Seas is often used to describe all areas beyond national jurisdiction, including the seafloor and water column (the vertical section of water from the surface to the bottom). This equates to international waters that cover more than two-thirds of our ocean – almost 50 per cent of the planet’s surface area.
Once considered barren and desolate, the High Seas are now regarded by scientists as one of the largest reservoirs of biodiversity on Earth. They play an important role in regulating the climate, supporting “crucial” carbon and water cycles.
However, human activity poses a growing problem for the High Seas. The High Seas Alliance (HSA) warns that destructive fishing practices such as bottom trawling and illegal fishing are harming High Seas marine life, along with issues such as plastic and chemical pollution, seabed mining and ocean acidification from global warming.
The Treaty now means that nations will be empowered to establish a connected network of High Seas marine protected areas (MPAs) – which can be adopted by a vote when consensus cannot be reached. This helps prevent a single nation from blocking MPAs being established.
It also supports developing countries through capacity building and the transfer of marine technology so that they are better empowered to develop, implement, monitor and manage future High Seas MPAs.
The ‘gatekeepers’ for tropical deforestation
Multiple studies have identified that rising global demand for meat, particularly beef, as a key force behind the destruction of the Amazon rainforest.
Research from the University of Manchester earlier this year, for example, found that up to 80 per cent of cleared forest land is converted into cattle pasture, while gaps in supply chain oversight allow deforestation to continue.
The ‘Positive Tipping Points’ report warns that concentrated global supply chains for beef, soy (which is often used to feed cattle), palm oil, timber, cocoa and coffee make a small number of buyers and financiers the “gatekeepers for tropical deforestation”.
However, legislation like the EU Deforestation Regulation, which “guarantees that the products EU citizens consume do not contribute to deforestation or forest degradation worldwide”, could make a significant difference – especially if it triggers a market-wide shift across other major importers such as China, the UK and the US.
How can positive tipping points be achieved?
Researchers stress that creating the right conditions for a solution area to tip is critical, outlining three prerequisites that are needed across all potential Earthshots. These are affordability, accessibility and attractiveness.
The report also states that the five Earthshots are “deeply interconnected” and often share the same conditions, infrastructure and risks within a single system.
For example, the boom in clean electricity could accelerate positive tipping points across all five Earthshots, while barriers such as a lack of investment in the Global South could stall progress in the regions that need it most.
“For too long a sense has prevailed that solutions to the climate and nature [crises] are out of reach. This new research explodes that myth once and for all,” says Jason Knauf, CEO of The Earthshot Prize.
“This pivotal research gives us reasons for optimism. This is a blueprint for turning ambition into action to place our planet on a path of rapid repair.”

— reporting by AAP
Parramatta have scored a thrilling 33-28 come-from-behind victory over the Cowboys, and the Sharks have handed the Dragons the wooden spoon with a 16-8 win in the final round of NRLW action.
None of Saturday's teams were in finals contention, but pride was still on the line, and both games were genuine contests.
The matches were played under the experimental rule that allows the side conceding a try to choose whether to kick off or receive, and both games saw teams use the latter option and score shortly after.
In the day's first game, the Eels scored five second-half tries and overcame a 16-point deficit to win a thriller at CommBank Stadium.
After losing their opening six matches of the season, the Eels ended 2026 with four wins from their last five starts.
The Cowboys' Charlize Lloyd-Phillips got the scoring under way after just four minutes, but suffered a suspected ACL injury in the process.

Sharks sink Cowboys to stay alive in NRL finals
— reporting by AAP
Braydon Trindall has produced 80 of the gutsiest minutes in a Cronulla jersey, defying shoulder pain to boot the Sharks to a 26-16 knockout win over North Queensland.
After entering the finals with four losses from their past five games, Trindall's return helped the Sharks hit back in Saturday's elimination final at the Sydney Football Stadium.
Sione Katoa scored a double to help end the season of the Cowboys side he will join next year, while Siosifa Talakai busted seven tackles and also scored Cronulla's opening try.
But the hero of the night was Trindall, who dislocated his shoulder against Canberra just four weeks ago.
The five-eighth spent most of the night awkwardly carrying his right arm, but was barely beaten in defence as the Cowboys failed to pick him out.
And while Trindall played with virtually one arm, he at least had his kicking boot.
Twice he forced an error out of Scott Drinkwater with his mid-field bombs, with one of those leading to a Katoa first-half try from the ensuing scrum.
With his arm looking slightly more comfortable in the second half, Trindall then put Will Kennedy over for the decisive try with a long ball for his fullback to make it 26-12.
That was Trindall's 31st assist of the year, with no player having laid on more tries in 2026.
Trindall delayed surgery to be fit to play the finals, and while the No.6 didn't look comfortable the good news for Cronulla is he got through the game.
The Sharks will no doubt need him next week if they are to cause an upset against the winner of Penrith or Sydney Roosters.
For a side who had the worst defensive record of any finalist of the NRL-era, the Cowboys did well to hang on in Saturday night's game for as long as they did.
In the first 20 minutes alone, Cronulla had 79 per cent of the ball and 22 tackles on the Cowboys' line.
But unlike when they let in 82 points against the Roosters in round 22 and conceded 50 against Canberra last week, North Queensland kept turning up.
Tom Dearden twice denied Jesse Colquhoun close to the line, while Drinkwater and Braidon Burns pulled off a tremendous try-saver on KL Iro.
North Queensland even got back to 12-6 down at halftime through Burns, and 16-12 with 22 minutes to go when Dearden put on a long cut-out ball for Zac Laybutt.
But ultimately the pressure told, and while a late Jaxon Purdue try offered a faint hope the Sharks were never really endangered.
The only down side for Cronulla will be the crowd of 17,429, which marked the lowest for a final at the Sydney Football Stadium since 2012.
Officials will no doubt point out that only an extra few thousand fans turned up than would have fit in at Shark Park, had they been able to play there.

Meera Sodha’s vegetarian recipe for mushroom claypot rice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
05:00:31 UTC
14:00:31 KST

In the nine years that I’ve been writing this column, I’ve had two babies, a breakdown and very little time away from writing a weekly recipe. I love this column, and creating recipes for you makes me feel like the luckiest duck alive, but I don’t believe that anyone can be endlessly creative without occasionally filling up their own cup. So, I’m taking six months out to travel, replenish and see what treasures I can find for us out there in the big wide world. Treasures such as this gentle claypot rice, which is based on the magical one at Dongnae in Bristol. Until then, so long.
Mushroom claypot rice
You’ll need a casserole pot with a tight-fitting lid. Weighing the stock will ensure just the right amount of liquid to rice, so use digital scales, if possible.
Prep 10 min
Soak 30 min
 Cook 1 hr
Serves 4
400g white short-grain rice, or sushi rice
60g (4 tbsp) light soy sauce
  60g (4 tbsp) Shaoxing wine
  30g (2 tbsp) mirin
  15g white-wine vinegar
Fine sea salt
  400g mixed enoki, shiitake, king oyster and oyster mushrooms
  4 tbsp neutral oil – I use rapeseed
  2 tbsp toasted sesame oil
10 spring onions (100g), whites and greens trimmed, finely sliced and washed
1½cm x 1½cm piece fresh ginger, peeled and finely minced
2 large garlic cloves, peeled and minced
4 eggs (medium or large ones)
Put the rice in a large bowl, cover with cold water, then swish with your hands until the water turns cloudy. Pour away the water, then repeat five more times, until the water is clear-ish. Leave the rice to soak in cold water for 30 minutes, then drain.
Meanwhile, weigh out the soy sauce, Shaoxing wine, mirin and vinegar into a jug, add 380ml water and half a teaspoon of salt, and mix well.
Tear the oyster mushrooms into 2cm-thick strips and chop the shiitake into ½cm-thick slices. Put three tablespoons of neutral oil in your widest frying pan on a medium to high heat. When bubbles form around a wooden spoon, add half the mixed mushrooms, or as many as will fit without (really) overlapping, and leave for three to four minutes without touching them. Turn over the mushrooms and cook for another three to four minutes, or until beautifully bronzed all over. Transfer the mushrooms to a plate, season with a big pinch of salt, then repeat with the remaining mushrooms; add a drizzle of more oil, if need be.
Put the last tablespoon of neutral oil and the sesame oil in a casserole pot on a medium heat. When it’s hot, add the spring onions, ginger and garlic, and fry for two minutes, until the onions are Kermit-green and the garlic smells good. Add half the fried mushrooms, mix, then add the drained rice and mix again.
Add the stock and bring to a boil. Scatter the remaining mushrooms evenly over the top and pop on the lid. Turn down to a simmer and leave the rice to cook for 15 minutes. Take off the heat and, with the lid on, leave to rest for 10 minutes.
In the meantime, soft-boil the eggs (for a soft, slightly jammy egg, I cook medium eggs for six and a half minutes), then peel them.
Divide the mushroom rice between four bowls, use the back of a spoon to make a dent in the middle of each portion and serve with two soft-boiled egg halves (or a raw egg yolk, to be stirred in before eating).

From black-clad agitators to an appeal for ‘Tommo’s Mum’: an unsettling week with the Patriot Platform
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
05:00:30 UTC
14:00:30 KST

Shortly after 7am last Saturday in the English coastal town of Dover, livestreamed footage distributed by Britain’s newest anti-migrant movement showed dozens of men in paramilitary outfits jumping out from the backs of vehicles, their faces covered beneath balaclavas, their hands in black gloves.
Within an hour, hundreds more masked agitators, dressed head to toe in black, some wearing silver crosses around their necks, were marching through the town’s streets, clapping and chanting “Stop the boats” and “Christ is king”, blockading the busy port for hours.
Anti-immigration protests have become a familiar sight in Britain over the past five years, with demonstrators expressing anger at successive governments’ inability to stop people arriving in small dinghies from France, across the Channel. But last weekend’s launch of the new Patriot Platform movement appeared to mark a significant shift both in rhetoric and tactics, disrupting once again the shifting ecosystem of the British far right.
A disciplined, well-organised and militaristic operation was unleashed. The new movement also displayed features of online influencer culture, with manosphere undertones, led by people who seem skilled at swiftly pulling together flashmobs of protesters and highly adept at exploiting social media’s algorithms to attract attention to their cause and fundraise. Most unnerving was the masked appearance of protesters, and the intertwining of Christian chanting with anti-migrant sentiment.
Footage of the weekend’s disruption posted on the YouTube page of the movement’s leader, Daniel Thomas, who calls himself Danny Tommo, has had, in total, more than a million views, with visitors to the site invited to pay a £4.99 monthly fee to subscribe to his channel and join the community of so-called patriots.
“We’re doing this under Christianity. We’re doing this with Christian British and English men. We’re not doing this with thugs,” Thomas, 37, tells his viewers.
But most politicians, even on the hard right, expressed instant scepticism. Reform UK’s leader, Nigel Farage, said the display was “disgusting”. “Nobody, at any political protest, whether they’re on the left or right, should be wearing balaclavas. It is wrong, it’s horrible,” he said.
Concerned that police forces had revealed themselves to be unprepared, the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said on Thursday that the government expected police officers in future to make “full use” of new powers allowing them to ban face coverings at protests.
Academics and analysts of the far right have spent the week trying to assess whether the new grouping has staying power and whether Thomas is himself sufficiently disciplined to unite a splintered anti-immigrant right.
“Is Danny Tommo a threat or a clown?” the anti-racist organisation Searchlight asked this week, before concluding: “A bit of both.”
Joe Mulhall, the director of research at Hope Not Hate, the anti-fascist organisation, who has been charting the movement’s growth over the summer, described last weekend’s protests as “an alarming development”, which could prove dangerous if protesters continued to target boats carrying asylum seekers. He said the rhetoric, the optics and the movement’s recruitment strategy all represented a shift. “It’s much more vigilante in style, and organised in a more clandestine way,” he said.
In the decades since Oswald Mosley launched the British Union of Fascists, with its blackshirted followers, Britain has seen an evolution of different far-right movements, their fortunes rising and falling. The National Front in the 1970s was followed by the British National party in the 1980s and 90s. The English Defence League, Britain First and Patriotic Alternative have had time in the headlines before receding in prominence. The secretive, militant neo-Nazi movement National Action, whose followers also appeared in masks and balaclavas, emerged in 2013, before it was banned as a terrorist organisation in 2016.
To many, Thomas is just the latest iteration of that tendency, but an effective one at a febrile moment. Thomas, who previously ran a roofing firm and enjoys cage fighting and boxing in his spare time, has worked as a bodyguard to the UK’s leading far-right activist, Tommy Robinson (real name Stephen Yaxley-Lennon). The father of five has spent two years in prison for attempted kidnapping. After being released, Thomas said: “I repented; I gave my life to Jesus.” On social media he describes himself as “dedicated to defending my family and homeland, trusting in Jesus Christ, Our Saviour”.
The week began triumphantly for his agitators, with blanket media coverage both of Saturday’s visually startling protest and a second demonstration on Sunday in Portsmouth, another major port on the south coast. Late that evening and in the early hours of Monday morning, Thomas was knee-deep in the chilly seawater, attempting to prevent the landing of a boat thought to be carrying about 120 asylum seekers. He quickly rallied more masked protesters to try to stop coaches from taking the arrivals to an immigration processing centre.
As a supporter brought phone chargers and other supplies by canoe to protesters in the water, he shouted at police and volunteers with the Royal National Lifeboat Institution: “I need these migrants to go home.” Uneasily watchable as it was, the four-hour livestreamed recording of events that night has had more than 700,000 views.
The police initially described the Dover demonstration as “spontaneous”. But in fact, throughout the heatwaves of the summer, Thomas had been travelling across Britain, pulling together volunteers from small localised anti-migrant protest groups into his new umbrella movement. In clips posted to Instagram, Facebook, YouTube and X, he charted his progress towards building a network of men, who would, he claimed, become a “mass resistance group”, and would spark a “shockwave around the country” and send “shivers down the spines of those that have put this upon us”. He filmed new recruits, wearing black, lined up outside a village church and on village greens, describing them as “working-class men, bricklayers, roofers and carpenters”.
The protesters’ media coup will have made awkward viewing for Reform politicians, coinciding with their party’s annual conference, which proved fractious amid lingering questions around overseas funding.
The movement has no manifesto; its website offers vague outlines of intent, claiming that its followers are patriots who refuse “to stand by while Britain is dismantled”. Thomas has set out some of his views in short clips recorded on his phone, sitting in the driving seat of a stationary car. “For too long we’ve been walking down roads and waving flags and thinking this is somehow going to save us,” he says in one. “Migrants are having a detrimental effect on the safety of our women and children.”
By Wednesday, Thomas’s self-declared claims to be making the country safer for all Britain’s daughters, sisters and mothers had veered unexpectedly into a more idiosyncratic campaign: one to protect his own mother, and secure new housing for her, amid a row over whether an article in the Daily Mail had made it possible to identify where she lived. That afternoon, Thomas brought dozens of masked men in black shorts and hoodies to the newspaper’s central London headquarters, livestreaming himself threatening that unless the newspaper organised his mother a new home within 48 hours, he would be back again with a larger contingent of men.
Later he made an online appeal for donations to help his mother move house, because she was living in “a state of absolute fear”. “It would be right for the country to rally together and help her in this time of need,” he wrote on an online fundraiser, headed: “Help Danny Tommo’s Mum Relocate: a fresh start after unfair media harassment.” By Friday afternoon more than £62,000 had been raised.
Some online commentators said they were sympathetic to his broader aims, but were irritated by this personal fundraising drive, condemning it as grifting. Even among supporters, Thomas’s leadership style is not to everyone’s taste.
Over the past two years, Tommy Robinson has attempted to make his anti-immigration movement mainstream, explicitly calling on supporters not to attend rallies wearing face coverings, in an attempt to secure wider support. Details of his events are circulated on open Facebook groups, and often publicised weeks in advance, with police notified. Women are free to protest alongside men.
Thomas appears to be trying something new. Mulhall said: “This is less about attracting mass numbers, and more about them saying: ‘We’re going to take things into our own hands.’ They want small committed numbers of people willing to take direct action.” Success was not guaranteed, he added, noting that an attempt to launch similar action on the beaches of northern France earlier this year, branded Operation Overlord (a reference to the second world war allied D-day landings), had failed, resulting in Thomas being banned from returning to France by the French authorities, who said: “Violent and hate-inciting tactics have no place in our territory.”
Thomas has said that he wants to bring discipline to the protest movement, aims to avoid arrests and talks of having lawyers at the end of the phone. “We have clear rules, no shouting, no alcohol, no flag waving, no drugs,” he says (although the Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary reported damage to their vehicles and some injuries on Sunday night).
Several researchers have noted the movement’s success at spreading its message through social media. Thomas’s claims that the British way of life is under threat as a result of immigration offered “a strong sense of purpose, belonging and orientation to those anxious about their future”, said Beatriz Lopes Buarque, a fellow in AI trust and security at the University of Manchester. “Racist conspiracy theories are profitable to tech companies and, consequently, there is little incentive on their part to reduce their amplification,” she added, noting that politicians needed to “raise awareness of the nexus between harmful conspiracy theories and algorithmic amplification”.
Darja Wischerath, a research assistant at the University of Bath, who specialises in studying online and offline mobilisation of the far right, said Thomas displayed a celebrity influencer’s skill at uploading bits of content on to numerous social media sites throughout the day to keep followers engaged, building a community of like-minded people. There were manosphere undertones to some of the content, with the “misogynistic suggestion that women are helpless people need[ing] to be protected”, she said.
Footage distributed by Thomas suggests activists have been drilled over the summer to respond in unison to his questions, like troops responding to a sergeant major. “Are we here to hurt the police?” Thomas asks lines of black-clad men in a clip of the Daily Mail protest. “No,” the lines of men shout back. “Are we here to stand up for our country?” The men respond: “Yes!” “Are we here to stand up for our women?” he asks. The men reply: “Yes!” Thomas concludes by bellowing “Amen!” at his volunteers, who shout back: “Amen!”
Thomas was a tank driver with the King’s Royal Hussars, but was discharged on medical grounds before seeing active service.
The movement’s regular references to Christ have triggered dismay within the Church of England. Thomas has posted videos of himself attending church, holding a prayer book. It is not clear where he attends church, but he tells followers: “When we go to church every Sunday, we go to church as a unit.” People donating to his fundraising pages can opt instead to press a button notifying organisers that they will pray for the cause rather than giving money.
Over the past few years, Christian anti-migrant protesters have begun to position themselves against the inclusive, pro-refugee position of the established Church of England. Madeleine Pennington, the head of research with the thinktank Theos, where analysts are currently finalising a project on the rise of Christian nationalism in the UK, said research in 2013 had found little trace of the phenomenon in Britain, but said there had been a “step-change” in the past few years.
“There are many Christians who are very concerned about a framing of Christianity that they don’t recognise as their own,” she said, adding that the bulk of the marchers’ rhetoric appeared focused on anti-immigration issues rather than religion.
The bishop of Kirkstall, Arun Arora, who is the co-lead for racial justice in the Church of England, said the display of the cross on protest marches was not the cross of Christ “but rather a fashion accessory utilised by opportunists”.
This week, Thomas was branded “an idiot” by the man he and two co-conspirators tried to kidnap at knifepoint in 2016. The trio had wrongly accused their victim of stealing £10,000 of drugs from them. Thomas pleaded guilty to attempted kidnapping and was jailed for two years; a judge condemned all three men for their “stupidity”. Thomas is due in court again in October, accused of going into a restricted zone in Dover earlier this year, and of threatening behaviour.
There is some uncertainty about whether he can maintain momentum and continue to rally units of protesters. But Thomas has described the Dover protest as a “dummy run” and local politicians remain uneasy.
Tony Vaughan, Labour MP in the neighbouring Folkestone and Hythe constituency, said he was concerned by the group’s “significant online coordination” that had allowed it to bring people into Kent “at very short notice and under the radar”. Police needed to “be alert to this tactic and have the intelligence and resources to respond effectively”, he said, to prevent further “intimidation and disruption”.

Call it the Miliband doctrine. Let’s hope the new Israeli settlement boycott is just the start | Steve Bloomfield
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
05:00:30 UTC
14:00:30 KST

Almost 30 years ago, the Labour titan Robin Cook announced his arrival at the Foreign Office by laying out what would become described as an “ethical foreign policy”. The UK, he said, “must support the demands of other peoples for the democratic rights on which we insist for ourselves”. Human rights would be “at the heart of our foreign policy”.
In the 25 years since Cook was demoted, Britain has had a further 14 foreign secretaries – including seven in the past six years – few of whom can claim to have placed progressive ideals at the heart of their actions. Ed Miliband’s speech on Tuesday outlining the UK’s decision to impose economic sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank – and unveiling the international coalition he has built to support it – suggests that Cook may finally have a successor.
Describing what is happening in the West Bank as “ethnic cleansing” carried out by “settler terrorists”, Miliband used language that Palestinians have longed to hear from a British foreign secretary. Vital, too, was his official recognition that the occupation of the West Bank is “unlawful”.
Britain was not acting alone. Miliband and diplomats at the Foreign Office have carefully formed a 12-nation coalition, including France and Canada, that spoke with one voice. A cautious European Union, partly blocked by a handful of Benjamin Netanyahu allies, could not have taken such action; while US membership of the G7 – regardless of Donald Trump – would have always made that avenue impossible too.
The consequences of the sanctions for Israel could be profound, although much will depend on the implementation. The most far-reaching proposal announced by Miliband was the targeting of those who “finance … illegal settlements”. That could mean every single Israeli bank. For those banks it will pose a crucial question: do you want to do business with the settlements or the UK? It could pose a question for Israeli citizens too: do you want your credit card to work in the settlements or when you’re on holiday in London?
Ahead of elections at the end of next month there is growing awareness in Israel of the lack of western allies the country can now rely upon. Support is ebbing away in the US too. More Americans now sympathise with the Palestinians than the Israelis, while more than half now back a Palestinian state.
Even centrist Democrats are beginning to suggest the US position could change. In the wake of Miliband’s announcement, Hillary Clinton, the former secretary of state, on Thursday called for a “crackdown on settler violence” and said the US should “take a very tough position” if Netanyahu is re-elected.
Beyond Israel, the past few days have shown that Britain now has a government that understands that the world has changed since Trump’s re-election. Since the second world war, the US has been Britain’s most important diplomatic partner. For many of those in Whitehall, adjusting to the realisation that Washington is no longer the first phone call when trying to come up with a diplomatic solution has not been straightforward.
It is enormously promising that the Foreign Office could not only pull together a strong coalition but also lead it. This time the phone calls to Washington came at the end, once the policy had been agreed – Andy Burnham briefing Trump, and Miliband talking through the details with his secretary of state, Marco Rubio.
Alongside the E3 of Britain, France and Germany, which has taken the lead on forming a rival western policy on Ukraine, it is clear we’re moving into a new era of ad hoc diplomatic groups that may be just as effective as their more formal predecessors.
Traditional alliances, from the G7 to Nato, are falling apart – destroyed from the inside by a US president who is opposed to multilateralism, liberal democracy and the rule of law. For the first year of Trump’s second term in office, the “rest of the west” was inert: some leaders simply refused to believe that the US was no longer an ally, while others fully understood the challenge but hadn’t worked out how to meet it.
But since the start of 2026, the debate has been over, thanks to the publication of Trump’s incendiary national security strategy and his relentless desire to annex Greenland, threatening a Nato ally with invasion. As Mark Carney laid out in Davos, there has been a “rupture” in the international rules-based order and it is vital that the middle powers come together.
The big question for Burnham and Miliband is whether they can build on this start and turn Britain into a progressive international force. How they deal with three key issues will be indicative. The easiest – but most expensive – will be aid. Both have expressed a desire to reverse Keir Starmer’s 40% cut to the international aid and development budget, a decision that managed to be both immoral and self-defeating. If this can be done, the UK may regain some of the soft power it so carelessly threw away.
They will face a bigger challenge in Ukraine, where the E3-led “coalition of the willing” has so far had little impact on the only two men who count, Trump and the Russian president, Vladimir Putin. While the US president so far appears unwilling to waste any political capital in saving Netanyahu, he seems more disposed to come to the aid of his counterpart in Moscow.
Finally, there is another war that Miliband should be striving to end: the long-running conflict in Sudan. Just as with Israel, it will involve standing up to a close ally in the Middle East, in this case the United Arab Emirates (UAE). For the past few years, the UAE has been funding and arming the Rapid Support Forces, a militia group that now controls large swathes of the country and has been accused by a UN report of committing atrocities that bear the “hallmarks of genocide”.
The bravery that the government has displayed on Israel has been, so far, sadly missing on Sudan. The UK has consistently failed to criticise the UAE, merely urging nameless “external actors” to stop “supplying, funding and fuelling the war”. Another coalition of the willing exists here, too, the E4+, which includes France, Germany and Norway. But they need to move beyond statements expressing “deep concern” if anything is going to change.
These ad hoc alliances may not last. By next spring, Emmanuel Macron will no longer be in the Élysée palace, possibly replaced by a far-right president. Friedrich Merz is fighting for his political survival in Germany too, where again the biggest threat is a far-right party aligned with Trump. It is vital that Miliband makes use of these alliances while he can.
Placing values at the heart of foreign policy is fraught with political risk. Within days of Cook’s speech in May 1997, it emerged that the UK was planning to sell more Hawk jets to an Indonesian regime that was attacking its own civilians in East Timor. “Ethical foreign policy” became a joke, rather than a doctrine.
But it’s worth noting that Cook didn’t actually use the phrase he was credited with. Instead he said the UK’s foreign policy “must have an ethical dimension”, a caveat that showed an understanding that human rights cannot always trump realpolitik.
During his four years in office, that ethical dimension could be seen in the banning of landmines, an annual human rights report and the Nato-led military action to stop ethnic cleansing in Kosovo.
Miliband, too, is no wide-eyed idealist. There were those who would have wanted him to go further – for instance, by declaring that there has been a genocide in Gaza. He has also come to the conclusion that however dangerous Trump is, the UK must be careful about how – and when – it stands up to him.
But the past few days have shown that foreign policy with an ethical dimension is not only possible but can make a difference. There will be many people around the world, from Gaza to Darfur, who hope it continues.
- 
  Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the Observer and a previous winner of the Orwell prize

Sweden’s extremely close election could see far right enter government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
05:00:30 UTC
14:00:30 KST

Sweden goes to the polls on Sunday in an extremely close election that could see the far right enter government for the first time if the country’s rightwing parties can form a majority.
Opinion polls show the centre-left opposition alliance ahead, with Magdalena Andersson of the Social Democrats the favourite to become prime minister again after four years in opposition, but her bloc’s lead has narrowed considerably in the final days of the campaign.
In 2022, the current prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, the leader of the centre-right Moderates, broke a longstanding taboo to make a deal with the far-right Sweden Democrats (SD), so that his minority coalition could form a government.
That agreement gave the SD outsized influence over government policy, especially on crime and immigration, and Kristersson has now gone further, promising ministerial posts for the SD if he is returned to power.
The election comes days after Germany’s nativist Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) seized first place in a state election, and as Marine Le Pen leads the polls for next year’s presidential vote in France.
Legal and civil rights experts have warned that such a result could further undermine Sweden’s long-held reputation as a global champion of human rights, which has significantly deteriorated under the current government.
“What we have seen in the past four years is huge changes when it comes to policies on crime and immigration,” said John Stauffer, legalthe director at Civil Rights Defenders.
“That is also the concern moving forward into the next mandate period: that this government will continue with a clear aim to further decrease the number of people coming to Sweden, the number of people who can get protection, and also that as many people as possible with migrant backgrounds leave Sweden – either by force or voluntarily.”
SD’s manifesto includes pledges to introduce “anti-Swedish sentiment in legislation on incitement against ethnic groups”, revoke permanent resident permits and further cut immigration.
One of its slogans is a promise to “make Sweden Sweden again”.
Despite recent changes – including the deportation of teenagers, lowering the age of criminal responsibility and sending 14-year-olds to adult prisons – many voters and politicians continued to see Sweden as a “champion of human rights and a champion of the rules-based world order where human rights is an important part”, Stauffer said.
“But it is quite clear that the Sweden Democrats do not have that ambition. They don’t see Sweden as an important player on these issues on human rights. So there will be less focus on this and Sweden contributing to developing the judicial framework around human rights.”
He added: “It’s a fair guess that the negative trend will continue with SD in government, the view from abroad of Sweden will continue to deteriorate, less and less will [Sweden] be seen as a champion of human rights, but as any other country maybe. For some time Sweden has been seen as the exception.”
In an attempt to win back voters, Andersson’s Social Democrats have also moved to the right on crime, immigration and integration, meaning that a win for the left is unlikely to mean a reform of current hardline policies, said Stauffer.
“With a Social Democrats-led government, many of the things we see as problematic are not going to be rolled back. But maybe negative development will not continue in the same way,” he said.
With polls so tight and record early voting expected, the performance of smaller parties could prove critical.
The Liberals, who are tiny but part of the governing coalition and whose leader, Simona Mohamsson, has controversially cosied up to the SD’s leader, Jimmie Åkesson, in recent months, could be crucial for the right’s ability to form a coalition. And, on the left, turnout for the Centre party could also prove significant.
Meanwhile, the Left party (Vänsterpartiet) has made some headway in the polls, which it hopes could be a sign of a surge. In Stockholm municipality, in particular, it is gaining ground on the Moderates and hopes to become the second biggest party.
The SD had already won the immigration argument among mainstream Swedish political parties, said Bo Petersson, a political science professor at Malmö University, who argued that the election could become a test of whether the far-right party had any further appeal to Swedish voters. “The mainstream parties have taken the restrictive immigration politics and then there isn’t so much for SD to say ‘we are unique and stand for this’,” he said. “They have been a very clear part of the establishment.”
Fredrik Furtenbach, a senior political correspondent for Sveriges Radio, Sweden’s public broadcaster, said that if the rightwing parties won, the SD was likely to get several ministerial posts which would be a “big breakthrough for them”.
If the rightwing coalition lost, he expected there to be a post-election debate within the centre-right parties about “whether they allowed the Sweden Democrats to get too close”.
The biggest issues among voters are healthcare, law and order, immigration and the economy.
After heated television debates between leaders, the last of which was held on Friday night, election results are expected on Sunday night, but it could take weeks or even months of talks to form a government.
The latest polls show an extremely tight race, with a Dagens Nyheter/Ipsos poll showing on Friday just 0.3 percentage points between the left and right blocs, which would leave Andersson’s left-leaning side with 175 seats and 174 for Kristersson’s right-leaning side.

From roughing it to Arctic luxury: Two sisters and three countries in two weeks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
05:00:22 UTC
14:00:22 KST

Greenland, Iceland and Norway offer some of the most cinematic landscapes on Earth. But travelling through them reveals three very different relationships with tourism – one thrust into the geopolitical spotlight, to tourism-savvy Iceland and the breathtaking beauty of Norway.
There are probably more glamourous ways to begin a luxurious Nordic adventure than boarding a crammed Ryanair flight at London Stansted, but that’s exactly how this adventure started – a once in a lifetime tour for two weeks.
My sister Nyeema and I were fairly certain they had squeezed a few more seats onto the aircraft since either of us last flew with them. But there we were, two British sisters embarking on a girls-only holiday that would take us through Greenland, Iceland and Norway – from the decidedly and deliberately non-luxurious to the seriously expensive, with an extraordinary amount packed in between.
By the end, we decided we could describe each destination in just three words.
For Nyeema, Nuuk was “remote, dystopian and mesmerising”. Mine were “sci-fi, raw and out-of-this-world”.
Reykjavík? She chose “charming, colourful and vibrant”. I went for “fresh-fishy, stunning and commercial”.
And Norway?
“Picturesque, historic and rainy,” according to my sister.
For me: “Luxurious, fairytale and quality.”
Those words turned out to say rather more about our journey than we realised.
Greenland: Raw, beautiful and suddenly everyone is talking about it
After a quick stopover in Copenhagen, we headed for Nuuk, Greenland’s capital, arriving to a spectacular bright daytime sky after midnight and a landscape that immediately felt unlike anywhere else.
There is undoubtedly something almost otherworldly about Greenland.
The scale, silence, water and mountains, punctuated by tiny splashes of colourful buildings, can make you feel as though you have landed on a film set... or the moon.
Filmmakers have already discovered it. Borgen: Power & Glory, starring Sidse Babett Knudsen put Greenland at the heart of a story about resources, Denmark and competing global interests in the Arctic.
Watching the real Greenland, those themes suddenly don’t seem particularly fictional.
Because one man seemed to be everywhere we went.
Donald Trump.
We had travelled to Greenland expecting to talk about landscapes, ice, culture and Arctic tourism. Instead, the US President’s name followed us around Nuuk.
Restaurants. Shops. Museums. Conversations with people we met and everybody seemed to have an opinion.
Some people we spoke to believed Trump’s repeated interest in taking control of Greenland had inadvertently done the country a favour. Whatever they thought of his politics, they liked the attention he had brought – and some thought it could ultimately benefit tourism.
A few were surprisingly relaxed, even telling us they didn’t particularly care if America took over. Most of the people we encountered, however, hated the idea.
What fascinated me was that a US president thousands of kilometres away had somehow become part of the everyday experience or travelling through Greenland.
We met Alice Burton, a former Head of Press Section at the US Embassy in Vienna, in our shared accommodation, who would become our partial travel companion, who had been hearing similar things from the locals.
“Nuuk is the most quiet capital I’ve ever visited,” she told me.
There are for sure few cars, little honking, hardly any sirens and remarkably few people on the streets.
“A world in itself,” Alice reflected.
Yet politically, Greenland now feels anything but isolated.
Official tourism research estimated that just over 149,000 international tourists visited Greenland in 2024, with almost two-thirds arriving by cruise ship. Nuuk’s international airport is meanwhile transforming access to the capital.
For a destination with a population of fewer than 60,000 people, those numbers really matter.
What tourists don’t necessarily see in Greenland
It was how strongly I sensed a “them and us” relationship between Greenlanders and the Danes.
Along with Donald Trump, the divide surfaced in conversations with people we met unprompted, and in the way some Greenlanders spoke about Denmark, language, history and identity.
These individuals are not a measure of wider public opinion, but the sense of separation was striking – especially in the museums we visited.
Rather than presenting visitors with a sanitised Arctic idyll, Nuuk’s cultural institutions openly explore Greenland’s complicated relationship with Denmark.
Alice, Nyeema and I were all particularly struck by Nuna, an exhibition at Nuuk Art Museum examining land, identity and Greenland’s relationship with outside powers. At its entrance was a message requiring little explanation.
'Greenland is not for sale'
Talk to people and another Greenland begins to emerge – a society having its own conversation about identity, autonomy and Denmark while simultaneously confronting extraordinary new interest from the outside world.
Climate change, military security, natural resources, Indigenous identity, tourism and the interests of global powers increasingly collide here.
And yet everyday life carries on around the geopolitical noise.
On the water, however, there are bright blue mini-icebergs, mountains rising directly from the waves, rocks, sky and sea stretching into the distance and an undeniable silence, exactly the Greenland one imagines.
Perhaps “out of this world” wasn’t such an exaggeration after all.
Iceland: When tourism becomes a well-oiled machine
Arriving in Reykjavík after Greenland felt like jumping several stages forward in the evolution of a tourism industry.
If Greenland feels like a destination being on the cusp of something, Iceland has had years to work out what international visitors want.
And it shows.
The statistics underline just how important tourism has become. Statistics Iceland recorded an estimated 10.16 million overnight stays in registered accommodation in 2025, up 9.1% in a year.
Tourism directly accounted for 8.8% of Iceland’s GDP in 2025, while tourism consumption by domestic and international visitors reached almost ISK 914 billion, which equates to over 6.5 billion euros.
Those are substantial numbers for a small island nation and as a traveller, you can see the sophisticated industry that has grown around them.
Reykjavik is charming and colourful but also extremely tourism-savvy.
Excursions are offered everywhere and so are restaurants, shops selling Icelandic designs, outdoor clothing galore, Viking paraphernalia and row upon row of traditional woollen jumpers.
The latter look as they are going to itch and after my sister and I tried on a very wide variety of designs, we realised that they didn’t.
They do, however, shed hair like a loveable dog.
And then there was the food.
Fish was a highlight: extraordinarily fresh cod, tasting unlike any cod that you will be served in the UK, despite it being renowned for fish and chips.
There’s also smoked salmon, shrimp and warming soup served inside a bread bowl.
For the more adventurous, menus can venture into horse, whale steak and slithers of smoked puffin.
Iceland has become extremely good at turning what makes it distinctive into an experience visitors can easily access, but there is, however, one unavoidable issue.
It is very expensive.
But again, as in Greenland, there is no ignoring the disappearing glaciers, pollution of the oceans and land and the doom of climate change and for a country so dependent on both tourism and fishing, these aspects are difficult to ignore.
And perhaps at that is the contradiction at the heart of Iceland’s success. It has become supremely good at selling the experience of Iceland. But the thing that everybody has fundamentally travelled there for is something nobody has created.
Nature.
Our own excursion beyond Reykjavik may have had us packed together liked sardines, but once the city disappeared behind us it became increasingly difficult for us to complain.
Iceland straddles the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates. Fissures cut through the landscape, geothermal activity bubbles beneath it and volcanoes, waterfalls and vast expanses of open land make it feel as though the planet is showing.
Hollywood clearly agrees.
Game of Thrones turned Icelandic landscapes into territory north of “the Wall”, while Christopher Nolan transformed parts of the country into another planet for Interstellar starring Matthew McConaughey and Anne Hathaway. The Star Wars universe has also found a home within Iceland’s otherworldly scenery.
Norway: When expensive starts to feel worth it
Bergen greeted us with torrential rain, which cleared the following morning.
We wanted to travel from Bergen through Myrdal to Flam, but there was one problem, and that was the direct trains we wanted were all sold out, but we found an alternative router from Bergen towards Myrdal via Voss, before joining the famous Flam Railway.
Mountains stretched beyond what the eye – or an iPhone camera – could properly absorb.
Water cascading from waterfalls and wild rivers, tiny settlements beneath enormous peaks.
The Flam Railway runs for around 20 kilometres through spectacularly dramatic mountain scenery towards the fjord below and has become one of Norway’s best-known rail experiences.
Hollywood has also exploited this country with good reason. Tom Cruise has repeatedly returned with the Mission Impossible franchise. Mission Impossible: Fallout features the spectacular clifftop finale at Preikestolen with Cruise and Henry Caville and in Dead Reckoning, Cruise launched a motorcycle from Helsetkopen. Daniel Craig’s final James Bond film, No Time to Die, also used Norwegian locations, as did the hit series Succession, featuring Brian Cox and Jeremy Strong.
The price of luxury
Norway is also expensive, but tourist don't appear to be staying away.
Norwegian commercial accommodation recorded 40.6 million guest nights in 2025 up 5.2% in a year.
International visitors accounted for a record 14.2 million guest nights – an increase of 14% – and around three quarters of foreign guest nights came from European markets.
Germany was the largest overseas market, followed by Sweden, the Netherlands, the UK and Denmark.
Bergen itself is flourishing, with the wider region recording around three million commercial guest nights in 2024, 13.5% higher than in 2019.
Eirik Gjøvåg Berge, Chief Communications Officer at Visit Bergen, told Euronews that it is important to distinguish between Norway’s reputation for high prices and what visitors are actually doing.
He points out that the evidence, does not suggest high costs are driving international travellers away.
“In fact, favourable exchange rates for many international visitors, combined with Norway's strong appeal as a nature and experience destination, have helped drive continued growth,” he says.
Does quality justify the price?
Hilde Berentsen, General Manager of Home Hotel Havnekontoret, seems to think so. “If you pay for a service then you can have a higher quality,” she told me. “If you always go for the cheapest thing, then you don’t have quality around you.”
Berentsen has watched Bergen’s tourism industry develop since the hotel opened in 2006.
One of its first celebrity guests was football legend Diego Maradona, who stayed with his team and the hotel has subsequently attracted considerable publicity for its luxury suite, which became known as Bergen’s most expensive hotel room. More famous guests have since followed suit.
“Everything cannot be for everybody,” she said, pointing to camping, caravans and cheaper accommodation as alternative ways of experiencing the country.
According to Visit Bergen, tourism supports around 13000 jobs and generates approximately more than 617 million euros (NOK 6.7 billion) in annual value creation.
Three countries, three very different versions of northern tourism.
By the time my sister and I had reached the end of our journey, that decidedly non-luxurious flight out of Stansted seemed a very long way away.
We had travelled through three countries united by extraordinary natural beauty but offering remarkably different experiences.
There were no Mediterranean beaches, no sun loungers and frankly, not a great deal of sun on this holiday.
Instead, there were fjords, mountains, volcanoes, waterfalls, tectonic plates, Viking jumpers, fresh fish, packed trains, unexpected friendships and Donald Trump.
Two sisters beginning this journey with no expectations, but the end allowing three words to describe each location, but probably, they were nearly not enough.
