Masked men, lorries and road blocks: How anti-migrant activists are changing tactics
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
00:06:39 BST
08:06:39 KST

Hardened activists are changing tactics and mobilising the anti-migrant vote
- Published
At around seven o'clock last Saturday morning, dozens of men dressed in black climbed into the backs of lorries in a quiet Kent village called Preston-next-Wingham.
The men had arrived under cover of darkness the night before, leaving their cars everywhere: in the village hall car park and on the recreation ground.
In an operation with a degree of military precision, the small fleet of lorries departed for Dover just after sunrise, where the men staged an intimidating show of strength near the port.
In disciplined, serried ranks, they wore paramilitary-style balaclavas as they blocked roads around the port. There were at least three waves of arrivals, including the men who had spent the night in Preston-next-Wingham. Glaring ominously at motorists and police officers, they stood their ground.
Hardened anti-immigration campaigners were using their newly developed tactics for the first time.
It bore little resemblance to the running battles seen in cities in the Midlands in the days of Tommy Robinson's original vehicle, the anti-Muslim English Defence League (EDL).
"I seriously thought we'd been invaded by Russians," a Dover resident, Robin Burkhardt, told the BBC.
The main organiser Danny Thomas, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, said on Instagram afterwards: "This is our warning."
The style of protest is a new development in the crowded world of British hard-right and far-right politics. It was visually striking, and the men - who were part of a new group called Patriot Platform - chanted "Christ is King" as well as "Stop the Boats".
On Sunday, using a social media live stream, Thomas was able to organise a second, more impromptu protest of a few hundred people in his home city of Portsmouth.
His activists tried to block coaches that had come to collect migrants, who had arrived illegally, brought ashore after making the long journey from Normandy in France.
On Thursday, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood met senior police officers and urged them to make full use of their powers to stop activists wearing face coverings.
"These scenes have caused disruption for people and, given that people are dressed in black wearing balaclavas, there is a fear factor and obvious malign intent being communicated to our residents," she said.
"This makes it different from other protests, so we need to make sure we are learning lessons."
Some of Patriot Platform's disruptive, eye-catching tactics seem to have been borrowed from environmental groups like Just Stop Oil. But its leaders are also getting ideas and funding from the growing "Christian nationalism" seen in the United States.
Its organisers say they are building a working-class "voting bloc" to persuade political parties on the right to adopt their agenda.
'Smarter' tactics
The website for Patriot Platform was registered on 18 May this year, two days after a big anti-immigration "Unite the Kingdom" march in London.
Thomas, its most visible founder, first posted about the group on YouTube on 8 June.
"We need to be a bit smarter," he said, referencing arrests or offences including the assaults on police officers and violent disorder during recent Unite the Kingdom marches, that had been organised by Robinson. "Good men and women are now away from the fight stuck in jail cells."
Thomas told his supporters he had a few ideas that would be "more powerful than committing acts of violence and criminal damage".
There needs to be a "different MO", he said. "We are looking for the strong, the able, the ones that are willing to do things a bit different."
What sets Patriot Platform apart is the scale and co-ordination of their action, says William Allchorn of Anglia Ruskin University, an expert on far-right movements.
"There hasn't [previously] been co-ordinated mass activism with hundreds of people descending and trying to take matters, as it were, into their own hands," he says.
Thomas spent the summer posting further videos about the group and staging meetings in the North West, Essex, Leicester and Kent. He said he was trying to organise a "mass resistance" movement.
What happened in Dover demonstrated some of his new ways of working. The protesters were almost exclusively male. They arrived in well-organised waves in the backs of lorries. They did not engage with the media, and said little to members of the public whose journeys and weekends they were disrupting.
Then, after a few hours, before the police could get organised, the men all marched off to Dover Priory Station and left. Estimates vary as to how many were there but it looks like between 200 and 500.
The anti-racism group Hope Not Hate said Patriot Platform should be seen "for what it is: a far-right network of men happy to intimidate and inconvenience an entire town for what was effectively a publicity stunt".
Nick Lowles, the group's CEO, said Thomas had "been upfront about his intention to create a 'patriotic army that is able to take control of the United Kingdom'".
At a protest outside the Daily Mail offices in London on Wednesday, Thomas could be seen giving clear instructions to his supporters about his preferred tactics.
"Don't intimidate anyone," he ordered. "No one talk. Keep a distance. Five metres away from police".
Patriot Platform is coming into a crowded space of activists campaigning against immigration. Robinson's is the most high-profile brand. A former close associate of Danny Thomas, Robinson (whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon) has given Patriot Platform public support since Saturday.
But there is also Paul Golding's Britain First, Turning Point UK and the neo-Nazi Patriotic Alternative.
Thomas was once close to Ryan Bridge, the founder of a group called Raise the Colours, who have put up flags in towns across England over the last year.
But the pair have since publicly fallen out, with Thomas telling Bridge in an online rant: "Do I need to stab you in the eye?"
Thomas was jailed for two years in 2016 after he and two others tried to kidnap a man at knifepoint in Portsmouth in a dispute over money linked to drugs.
What seems to be different about Patriot Platform's approach now is that Thomas is explicitly talking about creating a "voting bloc" of supporters to back a yet-to-be decided party, which offers policies closest to what he wants, at the next general election.
"I do not support any political party at this moment in time," he said, adding that once the bloc was established, it would be made "extremely clear" which way the group's vote would go.
It's not clear whether Reform UK would get his backing. In a public confrontation with Reform UK home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf in Portsmouth on Monday, Thomas complained that Nigel Farage had branded his Dover protest "disgusting".
"The working class do not vote," Thomas said. "We are going to make it a fashionable thing to take all your family members to the voting booth.
"But if your leader keeps slandering people, it's going to push them to other parties."
Waiting in the wings is the new party Restore Britain, launched by Rupert Lowe after he was suspended from Reform UK. On X, the party said it "stands with the patriots peacefully protesting against the invasion".
It is not clear how much support Thomas has. Parties like Reform and Restore will be very aware of the potential power that activists like Thomas and Robinson can now wield with their large social media followings. On X, Robinson has two million followers to Farage's 2.3 million, while Thomas has almost 163,000.
The role of the Christian right
At Wednesday's protest, Thomas offered to pay supporters for any work they had missed to be there - in cash.
This kind of generosity might help explain why his activism - and that of his some-time mentor Robinson - have such a strong Christian message now. The Christian right in America can be a good source of funds.
Christianity is now a big part of Danny Thomas's brand. His calls for action are peppered with the occasional "Amen", pronounced in the American way, with the first syllable said "ay" rather than "ah".
He was pictured at St Lawrence church in south London in February and March.
The local diocese told BBC News that while it welcomed "people of various political and ideological perspectives", it remained "committed to the inclusion of all people" and the focus of worship would "always be the person of Christ, who is for everyone".
Thomas has spoken publicly about his new-found faith: "I have repented my sins and, under Jesus Christ, I am a new man."
Thomas is trying to raise money for Patriot Platform through a popular American Christian crowdfunding platform. Just below the "Give" and "Share" buttons, there is a "Pray" button.
On the page, Thomas says he is trying to raise £5,000 a month to pay for the likes of transport, boats and a studio. This month alone he has raised around £9,000.
This attempt to build Christianity into the brand is potentially also a way of painting the UK as a Christian country, and Muslim immigrants as outsiders.
As for what comes next for the Patriot Platform after its initial surge in supporters, far-right expert Allchorn thinks it's an unclear picture.
"A lot of these groups don't really have an end goal in mind," he says. "This often comes kind of later on when they are kind of forced to to come up with more concrete proposals and goals."

Military aircraft reportedly blamed for UK air traffic control outage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
23:04:27 UTC
08:04:27 KST

The air traffic control outage that caused thousands of flights to be grounded across the UK earlier in the week was caused by a military aircraft entering “spurious” flight data into the system, according to a report.
Hundreds of thousands of passengers were affected after more than 2,000 flights were cancelled on Tuesday when the system used by the National Air Traffic Services (Nats) shut down for four hours.
According to the Financial Times, four people briefed on the incident claimed that the shutdown was caused by a flight plan submitted by a UK military aircraft, which caused a meltdown in air traffic control systems used by Nats which remained unfixed for several hours.
The paper also reported that Nats operations officer Kathryn Leahy called the operations managers of numerous airports and airlines, and “tensions boiled over” after Leahy informed them their flight processing system did not have a dedicated backup due to Nats being in the midst of a “complete overhaul of its systems” and because the amount of data it keeps meant duplicating it would cost “vast amounts”.
The crisis has put pressure on Martin Rolfe, the chief executive of Nats, who was summoned to a meeting by transport secretary Heidi Alexander on Wednesday.
Alexander, who said she did “not believe the issue was unavoidable”, was understood to have given Rolfe a week to report on the causes of the shutdown, while also commissioning an independent review by the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) into the incident.
The outage is the most serious to affect British commercial airspace since August 2023, when a technical problem led to almost 1,600 flights being delayed. Nats came under fire after that episode, with the CAA setting out 34 recommendations to improve its systems to avoid similar incidents, all of which were said to have been fully implemented.
Rolfe ruled out a cyber-attack, which was initially suspected, saying he “believes we’ve never seen an incident happen more than once, so this will be something different that we’ve never seen in 50 years of operation”.
Numerous airlines have already called for Rolfe to resign or be fired over the outage. Ryanair’s chief executive, Michael O’Leary, accused Rolfe of “telling lies to save his own skin” and said his position was “untenable”.
O’Leary added: “We don’t need more investigations, we don’t need more reports and we don’t need another parliamentary committee hearing where Martin Rolfe will promise change, will promise resilience and will promise an effective backup system.”
The delays led to someaircraft full of passengers being stuck waiting for information for more than four hours, while flights due to arrive in the UK were diverted to different airports, with some forced to land in Germany.
Despite the far-reaching effect of the outage, it was understood that passengers affected were unlikely to be able to claim compensation, as delays were due to “extraordinary circumstances”.
The Ministry of Defence said it did not believe there was any indication of an error on the part of the military, but that it would be inappropriate to comment further until the Nats investigation had concluded.

Newly released CIA files show Clinton and Bush received repeated alerts before 9/11 attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
23:00:07 UTC
08:00:07 KST

The CIA has published 71 declassified items from daily intelligence briefings given to US presidents Bill Clinton and George W. Bush related to the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks, calling this the largest release of such material to date.
The documents, posted on the agency's website on Friday to mark marking the attacks’ 25th anniversary, span February 13, 1998 to September 12, 2001 and trace the intelligence community's tracking of Osama bin Laden and al-Qaeda — the terror group he led, which carried out the attacks — in the runup to 9/11 attacks.
Nearly 3,000 people were killed when al Qaeda hijackers crashed planes into the World Trade Center in New York, the Pentagon and a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, in 2001.
The earliest brief, "Terrorists Seeking WMD Capability," is dated February 13, 1998.
Subsequent releases include "Reports That Bin Ladin is Planning Attacks Inside the US" (July 3, 1998), "Bin Ladin's Location and Intentions" (September 10, 1998), and "Bin Ladin Preparing To Hijack US Aircraft and Other Attacks" (December 4, 1998).
A September 10, 1998, memo, "Bin Ladin's Location and Intentions," said bin Laden had told associates that his preferred option was to strike the US "on its own soil in Washington," adding that the same network responsible for the 1998 East Africa Embassy bombings "may fly an explosive-packed airplane into a US city."
A brief from February 13, 1998, titled "Terrorists seeking WMD capability," said bin Laden had "agreed to procure unspecified chemical, biological and nuclear substances from open markets," adding that his followers had previously sought material allegedly to target US military installations in Saudi Arabia.
A December 4, 1998, memo, "Bin Laden Preparing To Hijack US Aircraft and Other Attacks," said reporting suggested bin Laden and his allies were preparing US attacks, including a hijacking to secure the release of high-profile al-Qaeda members.
It also cited a source indicating that a hijacker cell had evaded security checks during a "recent trial run" at an unnamed New York airport.
'Single largest release of CIA analysis'
A December 23, 1999 brief, "Terrorism: Diverse Groups Planning Anti-US Attacks," said the CIA was monitoring threats worldwide, with bin Laden's al-Qaeda network and allied groups posing the greatest concern.
Intelligence reports to the White House showed the Taliban would not expel Bin Laden.
The "Taliban is not likely to give up bin Laden for less than full diplomatic recognition and significant reconstruction aid," said an intelligence memo from March 26, 2001.
On May 2, 2011, US special forces killed bin Laden in Abbottabad, Pakistan, nearly 10 years after the 2001 attacks.
US President George W. Bush took office in January 2001, several months before the attacks that September, succeeding Bill Clinton, who had served two terms in the Oval Office.
CIA Director John Ratcliffe called the files "the single largest release of CIA analysis related to 9/11 ever."
"Americans can now see for themselves the intelligence leading up to this tragic day for our Nation," Ratcliffe wrote on X.
After the attacks, the US established a 9/11 Commission that revealed systemic failures in communication, imagination, and management across the US government allowed the September 11 attacks to happen.
The September 11 attacks served as a catalyst for the US' so-called "War on Terror", which included the invasions of Iraq and Afghanistan and led to the deaths of an estimated 4.5 to 4.7 million people, according to Brown University's Costs of War project.

NATO troops in Ukraine would mean war with Russia – Putin
The deployment of troops from European NATO countries to Ukraine would mean a direct war with Russia, President Vladimir Putin warned, arguing that political shifts across the EU reflect growing public discontent with the policies of the Western “globalist elites.”

“They are now talking about how they are considering sending troops into Ukrainian territory. This means war with Russia.”
Moscow has warned that it will not accept troops from NATO countries being stationed in Ukraine under the guise of security guarantees or a peacekeeping mission. Flavio Bolsonaro faces corruption probe weeks before Brazil election

Unknown Publisher

Flavio Bolsonaro faces corruption probe weeks before Brazil election
The investigation came to light as Brazil’s Supreme Court unseals files related to the Banco Master corruption scandal.
Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, a leading right-wing candidate in Brazil’s presidential election, is under investigation for his ties to a disgraced banker involved in a wide-reaching corruption scandal.
Brazil’s top court unsealed court documents on Friday showing that Supreme Court Justice Andre Mendonca opened an probe into the senator in July, at the request of federal police.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Brazilian Supreme Court roiled by dispute between justices
- list 2 of 3Brazil Supreme Court rift deepens as justice suspends federal police chief
- list 3 of 3Brazil’s Supreme Court shuts down early as political chaos mounts
According to the documents, investigators are looking into whether the senator engaged in corruption, money laundering and tax evasion in connection to Daniel Vorcaro, the former head of failed lender Banco Master.
Vorcaro was arrested in March and stands accused of engineering one of the largest fraud scandals in Brazilian history, with an estimated 800,000 bank clients among its victims. The fraud, according to federal police, was valued at roughly $2.3bn.
Police said data extracted from Vorcaro’s cellphone showed that he transferred about $12m to a US-based fund linked to Flavio Bolsonaro’s brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, in 2025.
The money was allegedly for the 2026 film Dark Horse, which portrays Eduardo and Flavio’s father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, in a flattering light.
Investigators are seeking to establish the origin of the funds, the companies that made the transfers and the ultimate beneficiaries, according to court documents.
A screenshot included in the documents also suggests that Eduardo, a former Brazilian legislator, advised Vorcaro on managing the US-based funds.
“They want to frame this as bribe money, which it isn’t,” Eduardo told Reuters on Friday. “That’s a lie.”
He said that the transfers were intended to shield the funds from interference by Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, a frequent target of right-wing criticism.
De Moraes oversaw the 2025 criminal case against Jair Bolsonaro, who was sentenced to 27 years in prison for plotting an attempted coup. Later, the justice also participated in a separate case that resulted in Eduardo Bolsonaro’s own conviction for soliciting foreign interference in Brazil’s politics.
Scandal threatens to affect election
Allegations of ties between Flavio Bolsonaro and Vorcaro emerged in May, when the publication Intercept Brasil published leaked messages between the two.
Flavio Bolsonaro has denied wrongdoing, saying he was simply seeking private investment for his father’s film. He is challenging incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva for the presidency on October 4 in the general election.
The race is currently expected to head to a run-off, with neither candidate receiving an outright majority in pre-election polls.
Both Flavio Bolsonaro and Lula have issued statements calling for full transparency in the mushrooming scandal, which has involved political figures across Brazil’s government.
“Investigate everything and everyone with transparency,” Flavio Bolsonaro said during a campaign event on Friday. “Show it to the press, show it to the people. Let’s see who is right.”
In a television interview on Thursday, Lula likewise called for a full probe into the matter.
“Investigate everything, disclose everything, regardless of who it hurts,” Lula said.
The investigation into Flavio Bolsonaro came to light after the Supreme Court’s Chief Justice Edson Fachin ordered the full Banco Master case to be unsealed this week, releasing thousands of pages of court records.
The court itself has been grappling this week with its own members’s involvement in the Banco Master scandal.
Justice Mendonca, one of Jair Bolsonaro’s judicial appointees, unsealed on September 1 a series of documents purporting to show Vorcaro seeking advice from de Moraes, his colleague on the court.
De Moraes shot back that Mendonca had abused his position in the government by unsealing those documents and seeking a private audience with Vorcaro, without prosecutors or police present.
The court is set to decide whether to launch an investigation into de Moraes next week.
The broader implications of the newly unsealed documents remain unclear, with parts of the case, including the probe into Senator Bolsonaro, still sealed as police investigate.

Saudi Arabia ends 'potential danger' alert for southern, southwestern areas
Unknown

2026-09-11

Ekrem Biceroglu, Merve Aydogan, Mohammed Al Ragawi and Rania Abushamala
12 September 2026•Update: 12 September 2026
Saudi Arabia announced early Saturday that a "potential danger" alert issued for Sharurah, Taif and Khamis Mushait in the south and southwest of the kingdom has ended.
 
Saudi Arabia's Civil Defense said on US social media company X that residents should continue to follow instructions for their safety, urging them to strictly avoid gathering in crowds or filming incident sites, even though the alert has ended.
 
The alerts had urged residents of the three areas to follow official instructions, move to a safe location, stay away from windows, and remain indoors until the danger passed.
 
The warnings came after Saudi Arabia announced Friday that several attacks on its East-West oil pipeline in the Riyadh and Medina regions had caused injuries and prompted a precautionary shutdown.
 
The Saudi Press Agency cited an official Energy Ministry source as saying the pipeline was targeted several times on Thursday morning.
 
The Saudi Foreign Ministry said separately that the pipeline was attacked by several drones launched from Iraq, causing injuries and material damage.
 
The National Early Warning Platform on Thursday had issued "potential danger" alerts for the southern cities of Abha and Khamis Mushait
 
The latest alerts followed amid rapidly escalating fighting in neighboring Yemen, where the Houthis have announced taking control of strategic areas near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, including the districts of Hays and Al-Khawkhah in the western Al-Hudaydah province.
 
Fighting between Yemeni government forces and the Houthis has also intensified on several fronts, particularly in the Taiz, Al-Jawf, and Al-Bayda provinces, amid airstrikes targeting Houthi positions.
 
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and several provinces in 2014. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015 in support of Yemen’s internationally recognized government.

Russia uses AI in cyberattacks against Ukraine, Europe, targeting WhatsApp accounts, government ministries, Anthropic says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Russia uses AI in cyberattacks against Ukraine, Europe, targeting WhatsApp accounts, government ministries, Anthropic says
Russia has been using Claude AI in cyberattacks against Ukraine and Europe in recent months, targeting various government ministries and the WhatsApp accounts of high-level officials, Anthropic said in a Sept. 10 report.
"The most commonly recurring targets were members of the Ukrainian government, military and diplomatic staff. The actor scanned email services and remote access systems across more than two dozen Ukrainian government organizations," the report read.
Russia has been able to use AI to circumvent defenses against cyberattacks that would be more costly for hackers to do so without the tool.
Russian state-sponsored hacking group Midnight Blizzard "increased their speed by automating their operations using AI" for an actor labelled as GTG-20006 by Anthropic.
"Our attribution is consistent with public reporting linking the actor to Midnight Blizzard. One of the operators is a Russian speaker using the handle 'JackPoterz' whose tradecraft and targeting are consistent with Russian state-nexus espionage," the report read.
Military intelligence targets in Ukraine and Europe, diplomatic and defense organizations, as well as individuals connected to U.S. foreign policy were attacked.
"The actor also took over victims' WhatsApp accounts, using a platform of headless browsers to link victim accounts as companion devices... the actor's configuration suppressed read receipts so victims would not notice while it bulk-exported Russian and Ukrainian language conversations. At least two former high-level Ukrainian officials were targeted in this way."
GTG-20006 used AI to track if known security defenses were evaded and would autonomously modify malware to circumvent existing detections, Anthropic said.
"Our investigation identified more than 20 distinct organizations targeted in the actor's operational planning, reconnaissance, and live operations. They included government ministries, defense and intelligence bodies, embassies and diplomatic missions, think tanks, and defense-industrial companies, concentrated in Ukraine and Europe but extending to the Middle East and maritime-related government agencies in Asia," the report read.
"A common theme of the targeting was Ukraine and military drone technology providers and supply chains."

Israeli Arms Maker Elbit's Planned German Plant Faces Far-right AfD Scrutiny
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
22:40:48 UTC
07:40:48 KST

The far-right politician likely to become the next premier of Germany's Saxony-Anhalt signaled on Thursday that he could support an arms-production facility reportedly being considered by Israel's Elbit Systems, saying such production could provide resources for his party's planned deportation campaigns.
The Alternative for Germany party (AfD), which wants to restore ties with Russia and brands itself a "party of peace", opposes Germany's record defence spending under Chancellor Friedrich Merz and military support for Ukraine, raising questions about the future of the planned defense industry investment in the city of Sangerhausen.
Speaking at a press conference on Thursday, the AfD's Ulrich Siegmund indicated the AfD was not opposed to arms production for domestic purposes when asked about the site.
"We do not condemn the production of military equipment across the board, because we will naturally need the appropriate resources for future repatriation and deportation campaigns," he said.
"This is also in the interest of internal security, our own stability, and national defence," he added.
Local public broadcaster MDR has reported that Israel's Elbit Systems is in talks to build a plant there to manufacture components for other German companies. City officials say no complete weapons systems, drones or artillery shells would be produced at the site, which could create up to 400 jobs.
Elbit Systems Deutschland told Reuters on Friday that it continuously evaluates opportunities for further expansion in Germany, but no locations have yet been selected for future expansion.
"As a long-standing partner, the company operates across several locations in Germany, employs hundreds of German employees and continues to strengthen its local industrial presence," it said.
DEPORTATIONS 'FROM THE FIRST MINUTE'
The anti-immigration AfD, which is seeking to form a state government after winning a historic election victory just short of an outright majority, has pledged deportations "from the first minute", citizen patrols and separate classrooms for refugee children.
Siegmund said the party was monitoring developments in Sangerhausen.
"We want to take a close look at exactly what is being produced and under what conditions, and whether this runs the risk of involving us in foreign conflicts," he said.
Any backing for the project could complicate talks with the left-wing populist BSW, the only party not to rule out cooperation with the AfD.
The BSW, which, like the AfD, opposes German military support for Ukraine, has campaigned against the Sangerhausen project, rejecting economic arguments for attracting foreign defence manufacturers.

Gal Gadot and Jimmy Kimmel blow the shofar to celebrate Rosh Hashanah

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
22:33:04 UTC
07:33:04 KST

Shortly before Jews around the world celebrated Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year, on Friday night, Gal Gadot appeared on Jimmy Kimmel Live, bringing not one, but two shofars, the ram’s horn that is blown in synagogues in a holiday ritual.
Gadot went on the show to promote her latest movie, The Runner, on Amazon’s Prime Video, a thriller where she runs all over London at the behest of a sinister criminal who has kidnapped her son and who is blackmailing her. The movie, released on September 2, quickly shot to first place on Amazon’s rating charts.
While she spent much of the interview chatting with the host about the challenges of parenting, toward the end he wished her a happy holiday and asked about gefilte fish, which is eaten on Rosh Hashanah. Kimmel wondered whether it was like baccalà, a traditional Italian dish eaten on Christmas Eve, which he said no one in his family really liked, but which they ate anyway.
Gadot said, “I love gefilte fish, for the horseradish,” with which it is traditionally served. “I eat it just for the horseradish, but I like it.” She added that she and her family also eat apples and honey or honey cake.
Next, they spoke about the shofar, and Gadot had brought one for each of them, which she said she had gotten from her rabbi. Hers was relatively straight, and she managed to get some sound out of it, but the one she gave Kimmel was twisted, and she said it would be harder to play. But she said she thought he could handle it because, “You used to play the clarinet or the trumpet or something,” and he said he had played the clarinet. He tried and managed to elicit a passable sound from the instrument.
Gadot explains Jewish shofar tradition to Kimmel
Before they played, Gadot explained the tradition to Kimmel. “The idea is really nice because it’s for everybody and the mitzvah, the good deed, is to hear the shofar and it’s basically supposed to awaken the soul for a good year for everybody to come.”
“Oh, good. We could use a good year,” said Kimmel as he picked up the shofar. After he played, they sat and improvised together until they burst out laughing, and Kimmel joked, “We should start a band,” before wishing Gadot a happy new year.

J Street goes on the offensive against AIPAC-backed candidates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
22:32:55 UTC
07:32:55 KST

J Street, the liberal Jewish Middle East advocacy group, announced that it will spend $3 million to defeat a handful of Republican candidates backed by AIPAC, joining the plethora of progressive groups targeting the American Israel Public Affairs Committee this election year.
Such an attack campaign is an unusual initiative for J Street, which typically endorses candidates but does not target opponents on the basis of an AIPAC endorsement. Until now, according to J Street President Jeremy Ben-Ami, the likelier scenario for his organization was finding its endorsed candidates on the defensive against AIPAC’s spending.
“It’s a new era for us,” Ben-Ami said in an interview. In 2022, J Street targeted an AIPAC-backed candidate - but only after AIPAC barraged the J Street-endorsed candidate with negative spending.
In a statement, J Street said that this will be the group’s largest super PAC investment in its history, referring to political action committees that can raise unlimited funds but are forbidden from coordinating with campaigns.
The $3 million will be spent on ads targeting Republican Rep. Mike Collins, who is running for U.S. Senate in Georgia against Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff, who is Jewish, and a handful of incumbents: Ohio Rep. Max Miller, who is running for reelection amid allegations of domestic abuse, which he denies; Wisconsin Rep. Derrick Van Orden; Pennsylvania Rep. Ryan Mackenzie; and Iowa Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks.
Ben-Ami said J Street targeted those particular candidates in part because they each face competitive races as the Democrats look to take control of the House and Senate, and they have ideological distance from J Street. Many of them were also connected to the movement to deny and overturn the 2020 election results, Ben-Ami said.
J Street’s campaign comes as AIPAC’s brand has become increasingly toxic among voters, and as a growing number of Democratic politicians cross its red line of supporting conditions on U.S. military aid to Israel. J Street’s position, meanwhile, has recently drifted toward supporting a phasing out of military aid to Israel in 2028.
AIPAC responds to, criticizes J Street campaign
AIPAC blasted the campaign in a post on X/Twitter. “Is this from J Street or Justice Democrats?” AIPAC wrote, referring to the progressive organization that has increasingly aligned with pro-Palestinian advocacy.
“A dark money super PAC spending millions to defeat pro-Israel candidates and lie about AIPAC,” the group wrote. “Not a word about helping elect pro-Israel candidates further exposes the difference between J Street and actual pro-Israel organizations.”
AIPAC has spent heavily since launching its super PAC, United Democracy Project, ahead of the 2022 midterms, and is the top outside spender in this election cycle, according to OpenSecrets. A number of anti-AIPAC, pro-Palestinian groups have emerged over the past year to counter the pro-Israel lobbying group’s spending.
Unlike those groups, J Street and AIPAC overlap in the candidates they back: Both groups endorsed moderate, pro-Israel Democrats such as Reps. Hakeem Jeffries and Dan Goldman. J Street’s super PAC has also previously targeted individual candidates for their AIPAC endorsement, such as Rep. Haley Stevens in 2022, citing AIPAC’s donations from right-wing megadonors.
AIPAC: J Street campaign 'disappointing' but 'not surprising'
An AIPAC spokesperson wrote that it is “disappointing, but not surprising, that J Street continues to amplify lies about our community.”
“AIPAC members are focused on helping elect Democrats and Republicans who will strengthen the U.S.-Israel partnership, while J Street is focused on turning support for the Jewish state into a partisan political football,” said AIPAC’s spokesperson.
Ben-Ami said this year’s campaign is not about “the relationship between us and AIPAC,” but is rather about emboldening candidates who may otherwise worry that they will be up against AIPAC’s war chest.
“We are very conscious that there are many candidates who are afraid of what AIPAC might be able to do politically, and therefore adopt positions and say things about policy because they are afraid, and their fear and intimidation is holding them back,” Ben-Ami said.
Now, he said, J Street is putting “the shoe on the other foot.”
“If you are going to oppose American democracy and provide carte blanche to this Israeli government, then you need to be afraid,” he said.

Russia spent 18 months building the road to Sloviansk. Ukraine spent three taking it back
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
22:29:54 UTC
07:29:54 KST

- Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps has retaken 150–240 sq km north of Lyman since May
- It erased 18 months of Russian groundwork for a northern march on Sloviansk
- Almost nobody reported it for three months—not even Russian war correspondents
- The fighting continues north of Lyman, but on Ukraine's terms
On 22 May, a mechanized battalion of Ukraine's 3rd Assault Brigade—backed by at least two more brigades, the 60th Mechanized and the 66th, attached to the 3rd Army Corps for the operation—attacked Russian positions around the village of Nove, 15 km north of the town of Lyman in eastern Ukraine's Donetsk Oblast. Russian drones were heavily jammed that day. Roughly five Ukrainian vehicles were hit, most by fiber-optic drones—the only kind still able to fly.
Nobody outside the Ukrainian army reported it for three months. The first fragmentary accounts surfaced in late August; the full picture only this week. By then the 3rd Army Corps had taken back somewhere between 150 and 240 sq km and wrecked Russian plans for a northern siege of Sloviansk, one of the last two big free cities in Donetsk. Observer Thorkill, writing in Polish, called it a success on an operational scale.
The presence of that Ukrainian armor around Nove, which at the time anchored the right flank of a 100 sq km salient held by regiments of the Russian 20th Combined Arms Army, was an ominous sign for the Russians. After months of careful preparation by the 3rd Army Corps, the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) were strong north of Lyman. Russian forces were weak.
"The moment AFU could start moving vehicles through the area, the battle was basically over," mapper Vitaly wrote three months later. "Vehicles didn't win it, they showed up because the conditions that had made vehicle movement impossible were already gone." Ukrainian drones were everywhere. And Russian drones, effectively jammed by electronic warfare, could barely fly.
Not everyone reads those months the same way. Thorkill, who tracked the sector throughout, puts the breakthrough at 17 to 18 August, and writes that for most of July and early August the 3rd Corps' attacks were repelled by the Russian 144th Motor Rifle Division. On that account the slow months were not a steady advance. What turned them, he says, is not clear: someone on the Ukrainian side made the difference north of Kolodiazi. He is candid about the limits of what can be seen. Some sources say the Russians withdrew, others deny it, others say they were partly cut off. What he can confirm from satellite imagery is that Ukrainian forces retook Serednie and Zelena Dolyna.
Overextended and pummeled by drones, the Russians barely clung to their salient north of Lyman, which sat between the Nitrius and Zherebets rivers. They were especially exposed at its western edge, where they had pushed across the Nitrius. The Russians had hoped the salient would be a "base for an offensive on Lyman, which could have allowed further offensives to Izium and Sloviansk [and] threatened the northern supply road to Donbas," according to mapper Clément Molin.
Instead, the salient became a trap as the Ukrainian 3rd Army Corps relentlessly—but quietly—exploited the fragility of the Russian 20th Combined Arms Army. The Russians have now been pushed back toward the Zherebets, leaving behind their uncounted dead ... and their ambitions for a quick northern march on Lyman and then Sloviansk and neighboring Kramatorsk.
It had taken Russian forces 18 months to set the conditions for a push toward Sloviansk from the north. In the three months beginning with that mechanized assault around Nove, the Russians "apparently lost 1.5 years of progress in the area," Vitaly concluded. Estimates of the ground retaken vary: Molin puts it at more than 200 sq km, the AKM Mapping account at 151, and Konrad Muzyka of Rochan Consulting at around 240.
The appearance of Ukrainian armor around Nove in late May was a strong indication that the 3rd Army Corps had the momentum. But that doesn't mean the Corps' eventual victory in the battle for the Lyman salient was a foregone conclusion. On paper, the Russians have a manpower and firepower advantage in Donetsk.
A bridgehead too far
The 20th Combined Arms Army advanced too far, too fast. And the terrain favored the Ukrainian defenders, who could pluck at the Russians' supply lines from entrenched positions until the time was right for a counterattack.
"Russia putting itself inside a deep, narrow pocket only made the final phase easier," Vitaly explained. "Once AFU had enough control over the surrounding movement, every new Russian mission sent into the area walked into a reinforced perception trap—troops committed to hold positions that existed far more convincingly in reports than as a functioning front."
The silence
What kept the trap working was that nobody talked about it. The Ukrainian general staff said nothing. Pro-Ukrainian analysts, who normally map every advance within hours, held their tongues until late August. So did the Russians.
Observer Andrew Perpetua, who has followed Ukraine's other quiet operations around Kupiansk and in southern Donetsk, called this one tighter still. The Lyman operation "seemed even more protected since even the most in the know and honest Russian reporters seem to be missing it. Or at least silent about it," he wrote. "It was honestly shocking to watch how out of the loop the Russians really were, which I think is in large part due to the collective action of OSINT to avoid speaking about the situation."
Perpetua's reading is that the lying is heaviest exactly where Russian forces are being pushed back. Nearby Sviatohirsk is the case in point. Vladimir Putin recently announced its capture. On 7 September, the commander of the 3rd Army Corps, Brig. Gen. Andrii Biletskyi, walked around the town on camera.
The 3rd Army Corps cut across the salient around three weeks ago, reaching the northern edge of Kolodiazi and trapping an unknown number of Russian stragglers between the Ukrainian vanguard and the old Russian bridgehead. Most of the encircled Russians appear to have escaped. "There is a large area where there may still be Russian soldiers," Molin warned. "Most of the villages westwards have been cleared, but not the treelines."
On 24 August the Ukrainians mounted a second mechanized attack, so the operation has not stopped. But the 3rd Army Corps is likely shifting from attacking to consolidating and defending—and clearing out the Russian stragglers that, left alone, could sow chaos in the new gray zone that was once a Russian salient.
Russian channels have started to admit the problem. Rybar wrote of "problems near Lyman," conceding that Ukrainian units have been attacking southward from Ridkodub for months and that Russian forces "do not even control the airspace immediately near the front line." The fighting continues, but on Ukraine's terms, for now.
How much it changes is the one thing the analysts do not agree on. "This is one of the most important victory for Ukraine in 2026," Molin wrote, a victory that "will delay the offensive on northern Donbas." Thorkill, in the same post that called it an operational-scale success and rated it larger than the 7th Rapid Reaction Corps' gains near Velyka Novosilka in July, ends on the opposite note: it will not, he writes, affect in any way the situation of Ukrainian forces on the direction that matters most at present, the Kramatorsk agglomeration.

How Russian companies are fending off drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
22:28:25 UTC
07:28:25 KST

How Russian companies are fending off drones
Hello! Welcome to your weekly guide to the Russian economy, written by Maria Kolomychenko and brought to you by The Bell. This week we look at how Russian companies — forced to pay for their own defenses — are trying to protect against the threat of Ukrainian drones.
‘Cover everything with metal nets’
Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian industrial and infrastructure targets have spiraled in recent months. Wildberries and Ozon have seen their warehouses set ablaze, dozens of oil refineries and sea ports are under fire, while chemical and microelectronics businesses are also suffering. With no military solution at hand, Vladimir Putin is trying to force businesses to organize their own defenses under the threat of seizing their assets if they can’t protect them. The Bell talked to Russian business figures about how companies that have nothing to do with the war effort are protecting themselves against drones and how much this indirect tax is costing them.

While You Were Sleeping: 5 stories you might have missed, Sept 12, 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
22:28:05 UTC
07:28:05 KST

While You Were Sleeping: 5 stories you might have missed, Sept 12, 2026
Yemen’s Houthis cement hold on shipping corridor
The Iran-backed Houthis seized control of Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast and captured three strategic islands on Sept 11, in a lightning offensive that cemented their hold on a vital shipping corridor linking Europe and Asia.
The developments are likely to deepen the Middle East war’s impact on international commerce, as Saudi Arabia shut down an oil pipeline following attacks, and after months of Iran’s blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.
Following a week-long offensive that has left hundreds dead, government officials said the Houthis seized the Yemeni side of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the southern gateway to the Red Sea and the Suez Canal.
A local official with Yemen’s Saudi-backed government said on Sept 11 that the Houthis had “completed their takeover of the Bab al-Mandab area and Mayyun Island”.
Oil pipeline hit by drones launched from Iraq, says Saudi
Saudi Arabia on Sept 11 said drones launched from Iraq hit the East–West pipeline and led to its closure.
The foreign ministry condemned “the targeting of the East–West pipeline in the Riyadh and Medina regions by several drones coming from Iraq, which caused human injuries and damage”.
“The pipeline was stopped as a precaution, and the attacks resulted in some injuries,” an energy ministry official told the SPA news agency earlier.
North Korea fires projectile towards sea, says South Korea
North Korea fired an unidentified projectile towards the Sea of Japan on Sept 12, South Korea‘s defence ministry said.
The South’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said it detected the launch towards the body of water that Koreans call the East Sea, but it gave no details.
The North fired a barrage of missiles into the sea on Aug 20 even after an overture from US President Donald Trump, who said he planned to meet this year with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
UK lawmakers throw out Bill to legalise assisted dying
British MPs on Sept 11 rejected a Bill to legalise assisted dying in a knife-edge vote and blow to campaigners in favour of the controversial procedure that is legal in a host of countries including Canada and Switzerland.
Plans to legalise assisted dying have had a long, emotional and ultimately stalled passage through Parliament, with protesters on both sides of the debate regularly demonstrating in Westminster.
Lawmakers in the House of Commons had taken the historic step to back a separate but identical Bill legalising the practice for some terminally ill adults in 2025, before that was scuppered in the unelected upper House of Lords.
Doctors held after music star dies during plasma treatment
Two doctors have been placed under arrest in Greece after a prominent music star died during a blood cleaning treatment, raising questions about private clinic licences in the country.
Giorgos Mazonakis, 54, died of cardiac arrest on Sept 9 during a plasma exchange appointment, a treatment used to remove harmful elements from the bloodstream.
Originally employed to treat disorders such as multiple sclerosis, plasma exchange has increasingly been used as an anti-ageing and longevity treatment.

CIA releases dozens of presidential daily briefs on Bin Laden and al-Qaida from before 9/11
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
22:27:21 UTC
07:27:21 KST

Several dozen presidential briefing documents declassified on Friday, the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks, detail intelligence that government officials had gathered about Osama bin Laden and al-Qaida leading up to the hijackings that killed nearly 3,000 people and upended American national security.
The documents illustrate security analysts’ tracking of Bin Laden’s movements and support system, as well as concerns about possible threats to US targets. They also detail officials’ understanding of his network in the United States and other countries, including how his operations were financed.
Proclaiming it “an act of exceptional transparency”, the CIA director, John Ratcliffe, said the documents were the agency’s single largest release of declassified presidential daily briefs – the highly classified briefings prepared by the nation’s intelligence community for the government’s most senior leaders.
The documents range from a February 1998 file – prepared for then president Bill Clinton – titled “Terrorists seeking WMD capability” and mentioning Bin Laden and other Islamic extremists – to a 12 September 2001 report in which a source indicated the attacks had been planned for two years and had also targeted the US Capitol.
An April 1998 document described the Taliban’s unwillingness to hand over Bin Laden, at the time seen as their “guest” in Afghanistan, noting their “gratitude for his assistance during the Soviet occupation” was making them “reluctant to alienate him by monitoring or controlling his activities”.
Briefers in July 1998 called it “plausible that Bin Ladin places a high priority on conducting attacks in the United States” and noted his “interest in conducting attacks with chemical and biological agents”.
Two months later, a briefer wrote that Bin Laden’s “preferred option is to strike the US on its own soil in Washington”, and that al-Qaida “may fly an explosive-packed airplane into a US city”.
Potential hijackings were also discussed in December 1998, when a briefer described how conspirators “had evaded security checks during a recent trial run at an unidentified New York airport”, and “some members of the Bin Ladin network have received hijack training”.
Other documents detail Bin Laden’s pursuit of materials for making “dirty bombs”, conventional weapons infused with radioactive material. By June 1999, according to intelligence officials, his operatives had conducted such experiments with explosives to “increase their energy output”.
About two years before the attacks, intelligence officials were aware that Bin Laden appeared to be misleading the Taliban about his reluctance to launch an unprovoked attack on the US. Briefs prepared for George W Bush in early 2001 focused in part on Bin Laden’s “experimentation by crude means to make and deploy biological agents”.
A report a month before the attacks indicated Bin Laden’s commitment “to conduct terrorist attacks in the US”, noting that the 1998 al-Qaida attacks on US embassies “demonstrate that he prepares operations years in advance and is not deterred by setbacks”.
At that time – August 2001 – officials wrote of “suspicious activity in this country consistent with preparations for hijackings or other types of attacks, including recent surveillance of federal buildings in New York”, adding that the FBI was “conducting approximately 70 full field investigations throughout the US that it considers Bin Ladin-related”.
Many of the documents were redacted to conceal sources’ names and other identifying information. They didn’t appear to break any new ground on the planning of the attacks or on US officials’ understanding of how they had unfolded.
In the years immediately after the attacks, a bipartisan commission highlighted a lack of information-sharing among agencies such as the CIA and FBI, and issued recommendations that yielded new positions, including a centralized director of national intelligence, as well as the National Counterterrorism Center, which analyzes domestic and foreign terrorism information across different government branches.
Asked for comment on the release, the White House noted the release of another batch of documents by the National Archives, also on Friday. That batch, including interviews with national security officials in the Clinton and Bush administrations, was a product of the commission that investigated the attacks from 2002 to 2004.

Unknown

Lula maintains lead over Flavio Bolsonaro ahead of Brazil election, Datafolha poll shows
SAO PAULO, Sept 11 - Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva maintained the numerical lead over Senator Flavio Bolsonaro in a potential runoff of the October election, a Datafolha poll showed on Friday.
• Lula is seen with 46% of the vote in a potential runoff, against 44% for the senator, a son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, according to Datafolha.
• The figures did not change from the previous poll last week.
• In a first-round scenario, Lula would lead with 39% of the vote, followed by Bolsonaro (35%), Augusto Cury (6%), and Ronaldo Caiado (4%).
• In the previous poll, Lula had 38%, and Flavio Bolsonaro, 33%, in the first round.
• If no candidate wins more than 50% of valid votes in the first round, the two frontrunners advance to a runoff, which has happened in every presidential election since 2002.
• Datafolha surveyed 2,002 people between September 8-10, and has a margin of error of two percentage points. REUTERS

Iraqi authorities seize 47 drones, 46 projectiles in Anbar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
22:17:45 UTC
07:17:45 KST

Emre Demiral and Serdar Dincel
12 September 2026•Update: 12 September 2026
Iraqi authorities announced Friday that they had seized 47 drones and 46 projectiles in the western province of Anbar.
On US social media company Facebook, the Interior Ministry said units from Anbar's provincial police command, acting on intelligence, discovered an abandoned site.
It said the site had previously been used as a vehicle tire repair shop and contained drones, projectiles, and equipment related to the operation.
A search of the site resulted in the seizure of 47 drones and 46 projectiles prepared to be attached to and used with the drones, as well as control devices, batteries, equipment, and related materials, according to the statement.
The site has been secured and all items there seized and stored safely, the ministry added.
The statement said authorities have begun procedures to determine the source of the materials and parties linked to them, and to take the necessary legal measures.
The announcement comes as Iraq works to ensure that weapons are held exclusively by the state.
On June 3, Iraqi army spokesman Sabah al-Numan announced the formation of a committee to place weapons under exclusive state control, saying that the committee has begun its work.
That followed a June 1 announcement by the Coordination Framework, which brings together Shiite political forces, expressing support for placing weapons exclusively under state control and strengthening the authority of official institutions.
Weapons outside state control remain one of Iraq’s main security and political challenges, amid the presence of armed factions, some of which are part of the Popular Mobilization Forces, while others operate independently.
Political forces and sectors of the public have urged strengthening the authority of official security institutions as Iraq continues to face intermittent security tensions, attacks, and clashes that affect internal stability.

Five Great Reads: Gloria Steinem, men’s therapy, and slime moulds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
22:17:13 UTC
07:17:13 KST

Good morning, and welcome to your weekly roundup of the best stories from across the Guardian. Are you interested in living for ever? Maybe you just want to be a bit happier, or spend your time making the lives of others better? You could dedicate your life to saving the planet or contemplating the meaning of intelligence.
Either way, you can find some of the answers to life’s big questions in the reads below.
Enjoy.
1. What Gloria Steinem meant to feminist writers
Tributes have been flooding in for Gloria Steinem, the groundbreaking US feminist campaigner who died last week. The journalist, writer and activist fought tirelessly against domestic violence, female genital mutilation and the pornography industry and for women’s reproductive rights. Her death has already raised questions over what the feminist movement will be without her. But here leading contemporary writers reflect on her legacy.
How she made women’s lives better: As Rebecca Solnit writes: “Some of the hot takes I’m seeing now on Steinem, and the women’s movement she was at the heart of, act as reminders that a lot of people have no idea of what women’s lives were like before second-wave feminism.”
Notable quote: “Steinem, the silence-breaker. The truth-teller who had inspired millions of women around the world to find our voices and use them.”
How long will it take to read: Six minutes.
Further reading: Gloria Steinem is remembered by readers, celebrated by authors, actors and musicians and her life is beautifully detailed in this podcast.
2. The science and mysticism of a limitless life
Hoping for a longer or potentially limitless life? For the small cost of A$200,000, you can now be suspended upside down in liquid nitrogen at -196C in the hope of being reanimated in the future. Catie McLeod trekked out to a small town in regional Australia to be the first journalist inside the facility selling the dream of immortality.
They’re basically big Thermos bottles: To prevent damage to the body and its cellular structure, people who opt to be cryogenically frozen undergo an eight-hour process as soon as they die. Their corpse is pumped with “antifreeze-like embalming chemicals”.
Not everyone is a believer: Scientists are not convinced it is possible to revive someone’s consciousness, even if the freezing process preserves and protects the body. Associate Prof Saffron Bryant, a cryopreservation expert, considers this question to fall into the realm of mysticism, rather than science.
How long will it take to read: About four minutes.
Further reading: Take it on faith, or find another way to lay yourself to rest.
3. Outrunning extinction
Can an entire ecosystem evolve fast enough to adapt to the climate crisis? While scientists have long thought that adaptation is a “survival of the fittest” race to outrun extinction, a first-of-its-kind project in the streams of the Arctic posits that a more communal approach could be the ecological answer to climate resilience.
‘Things won’t completely fall apart’: The climate emergency and global heating is upending the order of life, according to Linda Deegan, a senior scientist at Woodwell climate research center in Massachusetts. But Deegan also believes if species can evolutionarily band together, those connections will help them not only survive, but prosper.
How long will it take to read: Charles Darwin reportedly spent five weeks exploring the Galápagos Islands developing his theory of evolution. But you can read this article in just over four minutes.
Further reading: Why not take a look at the place that never freezes – and, separately, having lived through the ice age, can the mighty musk ox survive the heat?
4. Slime moulds and the debate about intelligence
In 2010 a group of scientists embarked on a somewhat unusual – but now famous – experiment in which they proved that a brainless organism, called a slime mould, could reproduce the route map of greater Tokyo railway system. It even gave hints on how to improve the design. Understandably, scientists have since been battling over whether simple life forms such as these should be considered intelligent.
Dunce or deliberate? A slime mould can appear to be just a small cell, capable only of feeding and reproducing. But it’s impossible to watch a slime mould – apparently – without sensing some deliberation at play. In another famous experiment, the organism found the shortest route through a maze in search of food.
A mystery: Toshiyuki Nakagaki, a scientist, betrays a sense of wonder while discussing the slime mould’s “intelligence”, a word that biologists invoke carefully. Others have since justified the use of the word, as well as other fraught ones such as “learning” and “memory”, in describing it. Which poses a mystery: how is this cell without even a semblance of a brain, capable of it all – the decision-making, the memory, the processing of information?
How long will it take to read: A slimy 12 and three-quarter minutes.
Further reading: ‘I have an understanding housemate’: the student who makes videos of fungus on faeces.
5. Turning towards grief
Most men go to therapy looking for answers. Maybe they want to work on their anger, or break out of a prison of isolation? But the psychotherapist Matthew Willner writes that most of his clients leave with nothing to show for their hours in the chair but grief. So why, if they are looking for happiness, do they leave feeling so empty?
Being told to ‘talk to someone; or that ‘it’s OK to cry’ can feel ridiculous: Finding the root cause of your own unhappiness can be a tricky nut to crack when you don’t know what caused your declining mental health. And if you can’t name the event that brought you to therapy in the first place, it can go unresolved.
The war with your own feelings: Rather than trying to fight what brought them in the door, Willner encourages the men he works with to “get curious” about their own feelings. Men often find themselves lonely and unhappy, he writes, but turning inwards toward their own sadness may allow them to feel less controlled by it.
How long will it take to read: Two and a half minutes.
Further reading: Eight reasons why men don’t go to therapy, and why men find it hard to make friends.

UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- The UN Security Council on Friday adopted a resolution on the technical rollover of sanctions against Sudan in relation to the Darfur region.
Resolution 2828, adopted unanimously by the 15-member council, extends the sanctions regime, including an arms embargo and targeted measures of travel ban and asset freeze, until Oct. 9, 2026.
The resolution also extends the mandate of the Panel of Experts assisting the Sudan Sanctions Committee until Nov. 9, 2026.
The technical rollover, a straightforward short-term extension of the measures, was approved to allow additional time for negotiations.
The United States, the penholder for the Sudan sanctions file, drafted Friday's resolution. In an explanation of vote after the adoption, the U.S. representative reiterated Washington's demand that the arms embargo be expanded to cover the entire territory of Sudan.
The Sudanese representative expressed opposition to the proposal, while Russia and China also opposed the U.S. position. ■

====================================================================================================

Interview: China's AI advances, inclusive governance approach gain global significance, says Polish scholar
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
06:14:12 CST
07:14:12 KST

KARPACZ, Poland, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- China has made substantial progress in artificial intelligence (AI), and its development-oriented and inclusive approach to AI governance is also gaining global significance, a Polish AI scholar has said.
"China has done something quite unusual in AI in less than a decade," Lukasz Gacek, head of the Department of China at the Institute of the Middle and Far East at Jagiellonian University, told Xinhua in a recent interview on the sidelines of the 35th Economic Forum in Karpacz, southwestern Poland.
Gacek has been an expert on contemporary China, global governance, energy transition and AI in international politics.
Gacek closely followed the rollout of China's New Generation Artificial Intelligence Development Plan in 2017, when he was working in Shanghai. The strategy set out a three-stage roadmap: keeping pace with leading countries in AI technology and applications by 2020, achieving major theoretical breakthroughs by 2025, and becoming a major global center for AI innovation by 2030.
"What caught my attention was how quickly the plan moved beyond government institutions and entered universities, companies and other fields," Gacek said.
One example, Gacek said, is the rapid expansion of AI education since 2017. Around that time, Chinese universities were beginning to establish dedicated AI degree programs. Less than a decade later, his research shows that more than 300 Chinese universities offer dedicated AI degree programs, while hundreds of others have introduced AI-related courses or integrated AI into their broader curricula.
In his view, the significance of China's experience extends beyond its technological progress. China has brought greater attention to capacity-building and the participation of developing countries in global discussions on AI governance.
Much of the international discussion on AI has focused on safety, regulation and competition among leading technological powers. China, Gacek said, has raised an important question: How can countries without advanced chips, large AI models or sufficient computing infrastructure participate meaningfully in the AI transformation?
In July 2024, the UN General Assembly adopted a China-led resolution on strengthening international cooperation on AI capacity-building. Later that year, China put forward an action plan for inclusive AI development, with proposals covering infrastructure, open-source cooperation, training and exchanges on AI governance.
Gacek added that similar priorities can be seen in China's cooperation with African countries, ASEAN members and BRICS countries.
This has particular appeal for developing countries, as it promises to help them build their own technological capacity and gain a stronger voice in shaping the rules governing emerging technologies, Gacek said. ■

Belgium reports first probable locally acquired human West Nile virus cases

Unknown Publisher

06:13:52 CST
07:13:52 KST

BRUSSELS, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- Belgian media said Friday, citing the Flemish Department of Care, that five probable locally acquired cases of West Nile virus (WNV) infection had been detected in Belgium's northern region of Flanders.
All five cases, the first probable human WNV cases ever recorded in Belgium, were considered probable and required further testing for final confirmation, according to the media reports.
Four of the patients developed neurological symptoms, and one person was hospitalized. The cases were identified in the provinces of Antwerp and Flemish Brabant, where the virus had previously been detected in horses and birds.
Anneleen De Sadeleer, spokesperson for the Flemish Department of Care, said the reports of human infections did not mean people in Flanders should be alarmed. "For most people, the risk of severe illness remains very low," she said.
The department said more cases could still emerge before the mosquito season ends in October, although the risk is likely to decline as temperatures fall.
WNV is mainly transmitted to humans through the bites of infected mosquitoes and does not spread from person to person through ordinary contact.
Across Europe, 1,086 locally acquired human cases had been reported in 15 countries as of Sept. 3, including 61 deaths. The figure exceeded the average of 736 cases reported during the same period over the previous decade. ■

====================================================================================================

Houthis seize key Yemeni island in Bab el-Mandeb, taking control of the strait
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
22:08:14 UTC
07:08:14 KST

Houthi fighters reached Perim Island which divides the Bab el-Mandeb into two shipping lanes after government forces withdrew, completing the group's takeover of the strait. Together with Iran's Hormuz blockade, this puts roughly a third of the world's seaborne trade under hostile control.
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis took control of the Bab el-Mandeb strait on Friday, after capturing an island located in the middle of the crucial Red Sea waterway, a local government official and eyewitnesses said.
"Boats carrying armed Houthi fighters reached Mayyun Island after government forces withdrew from it yesterday," the official said, referring to a rocky volcanic island also known as Perim that divides the narrowest part of the strait into two shipping lanes.
"The Houthis have completed their takeover of the Bab el-Mandeb area and Mayyun Island, which is located in the middle of the strait," he added, speaking on condition of anonymity.
An eyewitness said gunmen were "deploying along the Bab el-Mandeb shore and are driving around in military vehicles."
Further reports emerged on Friday that the group also seized the town of Dhubab and the coastal village of Murad, meaning that all of Yemen's Red Sea coast was now under Houthi control in an 18-hour blitz.
Government military sources said that the Houthis have besieged government troops on the Hanish islands, following earlier reports that the Zuqar island — the largest of the three major islands in the Red Sea archipelago further north from Bab el-Mandeb — was already captured.
They said they were unsure about the status of their soldiers, who number more than 2,000, but believe the Houthis have ordered them to surrender.
A senior military official said that the besieged forces have appealed to authorities for "rescue, food and water, and the lifting of the siege, which would require air support".
On Thursday, Houthis captured the strategic port city of Mokha from government forces in a blitz offensive that also saw them taking control of Zuqar Island in the southern Red Sea "after rocket attacks and a ground assault carried out using boats transporting fighters," according to military sources.
By Thursday evening, multiple videos appeared online of Houthi fighters' apparent celebrations in Mokha and their seizure of considerable weapons and equipment left behind by government forces. Euronews could not verify the authenticity of the footage.
Another crisis on the horizon
The Houthis, who controlled about one-third of Yemen's territory prior to the offensive, have previously targeted shipping in the narrow waterway which links Asia to Europe via the Red Sea and Suez Canal.
Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb account for more than one quarter of seaborne crude oil and petroleum trade. Nearly one-third of the world's container traffic passes through the Red Sea alone.
The Houthis have also reportedly consulted with Tehran on imposing a safe passage toll through the strait over the summer, in an apparent plot to further strain global economies.
Yemen's internationally recognised government has repeatedly warned of Houthi plans for taking control of the waterway, whose name in Arabic means "Gate of Tears".
Yet a member of the Houthis' politburo on Friday sought to allay global fears for international shipping, stating the group posed "no danger" to Red Sea cargo routes.
"Freedom of navigation and international trade in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab are safe and orderly," Hazem al-Assad told the Al-Araby al-Jadeed news outlet. "There is no cause for international concern, as they face no danger from the Yemeni side."
The Houthis corrected this statement to say Saudi Arabia remains an exception.
"Maritime navigation is safe for all companies except Saudi ships, which have already been banned," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on Friday evening.
According to Senior Director at the Soufan Center Caroline Rose, the Houthi takeover of Perim Island and Yemen's coastline creates in a chokehold which fill force shipping operators to reconsider costlier alternatives, while also impacting the key infrastructure the region relies on, such as the Suez Canal.
"Instead of going through the Red Sea, Suez, then Europe, they now have to explore a much more onerous path through Asia, the Cape of Good Hope, the Atlantic, then to Europe," Rose told Euronews.
"This adds weeks, greater insurance requirements given the proliferation of drones and overall risk, cost, and personnel needs to the journey, something that will undoubtedly increase prices."
Houthis marching on
Formally known as Ansar Allah, the Houthis came to power in late 2014 after storming Sana'a and seizing the presidential palace and key military sites, forcing Yemen's government into exile.
The group is part of Tehran's so-called Axis of Resistance — a loose network of militant groups in several countries in the region including Hezbollah in Lebanon, Hamas in Gaza and militias in Iraq, all backed, trained and equipped by the IRGC to varying degrees.
The group triggered a return to hostilities in Yemen's civil war in July, when they let an Iranian plane land in defiance of Saudi control of Yemeni airspace.
Riyadh retaliated by striking the airport, triggering the Houthis to declare a blockade on the kingdom targeting its oil trade in July.
The Houthis engaged in a large-scale offensive last week against government forces backed by Saudi Arabia, while also launching attacks on Saudi territory that left dozens wounded, leading Riyadh to respond with daily strikes on Houthi-held parts of Yemen.
Saudi Arabia, which earlier this week said it had always offered “opportunities for negotiation,” also said it has the right to defend itself.
Houthi attacks on oil infrastructure and Saudi tankers have further contributed to a spike in oil prices, which surpassed $100 a barrel on Thursday.
A friend in need
Last month, Saudi Arabia signed a NATO-style mutual defence agreement with Turkey and nuclear-armed Pakistan in Mecca, but it seems unlikely either of the two would get involved.
On Tuesday, Pakistani Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said Pakistan would "honour" the pact "in case there is a need".
Just one day later, the Pakistan foreign ministry said that the Mecca pact was a "defensive alliance focused on deterrence".
"There is no such thing under discussion right now. When the time comes, we will act under the agreement," spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan told the press at the weekly media briefing.
In July, US President Donald Trump said Washington would respond against the Houthis if they attempted to block maritime traffic in the Red Sea, after weeks of US strikes from March 2025 — early in Trump's second term — hit a range of military and industrial targets.
However, Washington is reportedly reluctant to enter the fray at this time as it remains bogged down in its own war with Iran since February.
According to US outlets, Trump rejected a request from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman for strikes on Houthi positions as they approached Mokha on Thursday. Riyadh and the White House are yet to comment on these reports.
Meanwhile in Brussels, the EU's External Action Service strongly condemned Houthi attacks earlier this week, calling for the group to "end all attacks inside and outside Yemen, including attacks against commercial shipping in the Red Sea" and respect UN resolutions.
Brussels had not publicly commented on the Houthis' seizure of Perim Island and the Bab al-Mandeb shoreline at the time of publication.
Operation Aspides, the 27-member bloc's defensive naval mission stationed in Djibouti has been tasked with protecting freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, but its current mandate does not cover offensive action against Houthi positions on land or on islands.
It is not clear at this time whether the group's lightning takeover of Bab el-Mandeb will expedite talks about expanding its mandate which EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas told Euronews in mid-July were already under way.
"What is tricky about the Houthis is that they have proven resilient with on-and-off-again maritime campaigns and coalitions directed at degrading their offensive capabilities," Rose said.
"Neither the US nor the EU have revived former efforts to consolidate a concerted campaign around the Houthis’ recent expansion, though it’s possible in the next few months as the US seeks leverage with Iran," she added.
Tehran salutes 'resounding victory'
Tehran chimed in on Friday, calling for an end to Saudi Arabia's blockade of Yemen and the immediate resumption of talks, in its first public statement since the Houthi Red Sea offensive.
In a statement carried by the state-run IRNA news agency, Iran's foreign ministry said Yemen’s sovereignty must be respected, and its problems cannot be resolved through a blockade or military alliances.
Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Iranian Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, congratulated the Houthis on their "resounding victory" on Friday.
Meanwhile, reports have claimed that Iran's elite paramilitary IRGC has deployed dozens of advisors to aid the Houthis in their operations. Euronews could not independently verify the claims at this time.
A potential disruption to Bab el-Mandeb would work in Tehran's favour, as its blockade of Hormuz has put significant pressure on the world's energy markets, sparking a crisis that could worsen even further as the northern hemisphere approaches winter.
"The Houthi offensive to capture territory near the Bab al Mandeb advances Iranian objectives under the current regional campaign that Iran is waging against the United States and its allies," Washington-based think tank Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said in its latest analysis on Friday.
"Iran has recently pursued the following lines of effort under this regional campaign: targeting US naval forces, attacking US forces across the region, (and) disrupting traffic through the Strait of Hormuz," it added.
"The Houthis and Iran may currently share a common objective in Houthi control over the Red Sea coastline, but the nature of their relationship means that the Houthis will independently determine their level of involvement in supporting other Iranian objectives."
The leader of Yemen's internationally recognised governing council on Thursday urged Arab and other nations to help it defend the country's coasts.
"The protection of Yemen's coasts and the restoration of state control over its territory, ports and waters is a joint Yemeni, Egyptian, Arab and international interest," Rashad al-Alimi, who heads Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, said during a meeting with Egypt's ambassador.
The Houthi offensive has cost more than 500 lives and has displaced about 46,000 people, the UN migration agency said on Friday.

Ukraine’s Yaroslava Mahuchikh made athletics history on Friday, Sept. 11, becoming the first-ever women’s high jump champion at the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest.
The Olympic champion and world record-holder cleared 1.99 meters to secure the title, defeating reigning world champion Nicola Olyslagers of Australia, who finished second with 1.95 meters. Australia’s Eleanor Patterson and Serbia’s Angelina Topić shared third place after clearing 1.91 meters.

Mahuchikh opened at 1.91 meters and cleared both that height and 1.95 meters on her first attempts. She needed two tries at 1.99 meters, but the height proved enough for victory after Olyslagers failed to clear the bar.

Its $10 million prize fund is the largest ever offered at a single track and field competition.
